paper_title: Ultra-Dense Cell-Free Massive MIMO for 6G: Technical Overview and Open Questions
context_brief: Choice of centralized, local, or hybrid processing
original_question: What user-centric signal-processing design should an ultra-dense cell-free massive multiple-input multiple-output (CF-MMIMO) system use for uplink combining and downlink precoding when the alternatives include centralized processing at central processing units (CPUs), local processing at each access point (AP), and cluster-level combinations that trade spectral efficiency, fronthaul traffic, CPU computational load, robustness to AP additions or failures, and support for multiple-antenna APs?
self_contained_problem:
Consider an ultra-dense cell-free massive multiple-input multiple-output (CF-MMIMO) wireless network consisting of a large number of geographically distributed access points (APs), each possibly equipped with multiple antennas, connected via a fronthaul network to one or more central processing units (CPUs), and jointly serving a set of single-antenna user equipments (UEs) on the same time-frequency resource. Each UE k is served by a user-centric cluster M_k of nearby APs. For the uplink, the signal received at AP l from UE k passes through a channel h_{kl} estimated locally; the system must form a combined estimate of the transmitted symbol. For the downlink, the system must compute precoding vectors w_{kl} for each AP l in M_k. The following three architectures are available:

(i) Fully centralized processing: APs forward all received pilot and data samples to a CPU, which performs channel estimation, uplink combining (e.g., MMSE) and downlink precoding jointly across all APs.

(ii) Fully local (distributed) processing: each AP estimates channels locally and computes its own combining/precoding vectors (e.g., local MMSE or maximum-ratio), forwarding only soft symbol estimates or precoded signals over the fronthaul.

(iii) Hybrid cluster-level processing: APs are grouped into clusters; processing is centralized within each cluster and decentralized between clusters.

For each architecture one can quantify: per-UE spectral efficiency (uplink and downlink), aggregate fronthaul traffic (bits/s on each fronthaul link), CPU computational load (floating point operations per coherence block), robustness to dynamic addition or failure of individual APs, and ability to exploit multi-antenna APs.

Problem: Determine the user-centric uplink combining rule and downlink precoding rule, together with the choice among centralized, local, or hybrid cluster-level processing, that should be adopted in an ultra-dense CF-MMIMO system so as to achieve the most favorable joint trade-off among spectral efficiency, fronthaul traffic, CPU computational complexity, resilience to AP additions/failures, and support for multiple-antenna APs. In particular, characterize whether a single architecture dominates the others in this multi-objective sense and, if not, identify the operational regimes (in terms of AP density, cluster size, fronthaul capacity, and number of AP antennas) in which each architecture is preferred.
status_search_result: The choice between centralized, local, and cluster-level processing in ultra-dense cell-free massive MIMO remains an active open research problem. Recent surveys and research papers from 2024–2026 continue to investigate the trade-offs and propose new distributed and hybrid schemes, with no consensus that a single architecture dominates across all metrics.

paper_title: Ultra-Dense Cell-Free Massive MIMO for 6G: Technical Overview and Open Questions
original_question: Under what propagation, density, antenna, processing, and traffic conditions is the channel-hardening or use-and-then-forget bounding technique a reliable achievable-rate tool for cell-free massive multiple-input multiple-output (CF-MMIMO), and when should researchers instead use full-side-information bounds with downlink training, blind channel estimation, non-coherent bounds, enhanced normalized precoding, or scheduling changes?
self_contained_problem:
Consider a cell-free massive multiple-input multiple-output (CF-MMIMO) wireless system consisting of a large number of geographically distributed access points (APs), each equipped with one or more antennas, jointly serving a set of single-antenna user equipments (UEs) over a shared time-frequency resource. The channel from UE k to AP m is modeled as a random vector h_{mk} whose distribution depends on a large-scale fading coefficient β_{mk} (capturing path loss and shadowing) and a small-scale fading component (e.g., Rayleigh, Rician, or correlated complex Gaussian). Each UE is served by a (possibly user-specific) subset M_k of APs. Channel state information is obtained at the APs by uplink pilot transmission and (potentially) further refined by downlink pilots, blind estimation, or non-coherent schemes. Linear precoders/combiners (such as maximum-ratio, zero-forcing, or MMSE) are applied at the APs, and per-user achievable downlink and uplink rates are evaluated.

A classical analytical tool, called the "use-and-then-forget" (UatF) or hardening bound, lower-bounds the ergodic achievable rate of UE k by treating the effective channel mean as a deterministic known coefficient and lumping all deviations from it into a Gaussian-noise interference term. This bound is tight when the effective channel exhibits channel hardening, i.e., when |h_eff,k|^2 concentrates sharply around its mean E[|h_eff,k|^2].

Problem. Characterize, rigorously and quantitatively, the regimes—specified in terms of (i) propagation conditions (line-of-sight vs. NLOS, spatial correlation, channel-vector independence across APs), (ii) AP/UE density and geometry, (iii) per-AP antenna numbers and array configuration, (iv) signal-processing choices (precoder family, normalization, pilot allocation, power control), and (v) traffic and scheduling assumptions—under which the UatF/hardening lower bound is a reliable (asymptotically tight) achievable-rate tool for CF-MMIMO. Conversely, determine for which of these regimes the UatF bound becomes loose, and identify which alternative achievable-rate techniques—full-CSI / genie-aided bounds, bounds incorporating downlink pilot training, blind channel estimation–based bounds, non-coherent capacity bounds, enhanced normalized precoding schemes, or modified user scheduling—yield provably tighter achievable rates. Provide quantitative thresholds (e.g., on the variance-to-mean-squared ratio of the effective channel gain) separating these regimes.

original_question: How can distributed access points (APs) in cell-free massive multiple-input multiple-output (CF-MMIMO) be synchronized and reciprocity-calibrated in time, frequency, and phase with acceptable cost, signaling overhead, and disruption to time-division-duplex (TDD) operation, particularly when inexpensive oscillators may drift quickly and over-the-air calibration can require bidirectional AP measurements?
self_contained_problem:
Consider a cell-free massive multiple-input multiple-output (CF-MMIMO) wireless system in which a large number of geographically distributed access points (APs), each equipped with one or more antennas and a local radio-frequency front-end driven by its own local oscillator, jointly serve a set of user equipments (UEs) over the same time-frequency resources using time-division-duplex (TDD) operation. Coherent joint transmission and reception across APs requires three forms of network-wide alignment:

1. Time synchronization: the sampling clocks of all APs must be aligned to within a small fraction of the symbol duration.
2. Frequency synchronization: the carrier frequencies generated by the APs' local oscillators must be aligned so that residual carrier-frequency offsets do not destroy beamforming gains over a coherence block.
3. Phase synchronization and reciprocity calibration: the unknown complex gains of each AP's transmit and receive RF chains must be jointly calibrated so that channel-state information acquired on the uplink can be used to precode coherently on the downlink (TDD reciprocity), and so that the relative phases of signals transmitted from different APs are predictable.

Assume that:
- APs may be equipped with inexpensive free-running local oscillators whose phase and frequency drift on time scales that may be short compared to the channel coherence time.
- Wired distribution of a common reference clock to every AP is costly and may not be feasible at scale.
- Over-the-air calibration is possible but requires bidirectional measurements between pairs (or groups) of APs and consumes channel resources that would otherwise be used for serving UEs, thereby disrupting the TDD frame structure.

The problem is to design a scheme (specifying the signaling protocol, the set of pairwise or broadcast calibration transmissions among APs, the estimation algorithm for the per-AP transmit/receive calibration coefficients and clock parameters, and the schedule at which recalibration is performed) that achieves simultaneous time, frequency, and phase synchronization together with joint reciprocity calibration across all APs, such that:
(a) the residual time, frequency, and phase errors are small enough to preserve coherent joint processing gains for a target spectral efficiency;
(b) the total signaling overhead and the fraction of TDD resources consumed by calibration are minimized;
(c) the scheme remains feasible when AP oscillators drift rapidly and when the number of APs is large;
(d) the hardware cost (e.g., no requirement for high-stability oscillators or dedicated synchronization cabling) is kept low.

Quantify the achievable trade-offs among synchronization accuracy, calibration overhead, oscillator quality, and TDD throughput, and determine whether such a scheme exists that simultaneously satisfies (a)–(d) for practically relevant CF-MMIMO deployments.
status_search_result: Synchronization and over-the-air reciprocity calibration for distributed CF-MMIMO access points remains an active open research area as of 2026. While numerous partial solutions exist (e.g., over-the-air calibration protocols, beam-based phase synchronization, PLL-aided schemes), no single approach is generally accepted as solving the joint time/frequency/phase synchronization and reciprocity calibration problem at scale with low overhead under cheap free-running oscillators.

original_question: How can cell-free massive multiple-input multiple-output (CF-MMIMO) systems exchange or acquire the channel state information (CSI) needed for distributed cooperative precoding under tight time constraints while keeping the CSI-sharing overhead low-dimensional, avoiding fronthaul dominance, and preserving performance when access points (APs) may have transmitter-specific or delayed estimates of the global channel state?
self_contained_problem:
Consider a cell-free massive multiple-input multiple-output (CF-MMIMO) wireless system consisting of L geographically distributed access points (APs), each equipped with N antennas, jointly serving K single-antenna user equipments (UEs) over a flat-fading channel with coherence block of tau_c symbols. Let H in C^{LN x K} denote the global channel matrix, partitioned into per-AP blocks H_l in C^{N x K}. Each AP l acquires a local estimate hat{H}_l of H, possibly noisy, delayed, or transmitter-specific (so that hat{H}_l need not equal hat{H}_{l'} for l != l'). The APs cooperate to design a distributed precoder W in C^{LN x K}, with W_l computable at AP l from hat{H}_l and from a limited amount of side information exchanged through a finite-capacity fronthaul or via over-the-air signaling.

Design a CSI-sharing protocol and an associated distributed cooperative precoding rule satisfying all of the following:
1. The total CSI-related information that any AP must receive from other APs or from a central unit, per coherence block, is bounded by a quantity that grows at most as o(LNK) bits (i.e., strictly sub-dimensional compared to full global CSI exchange), so that CSI sharing does not dominate the fronthaul.
2. The protocol respects the tight latency constraint imposed by tau_c, i.e., all exchanges must complete within one coherence block.
3. The resulting per-user spectral efficiency, under realistic estimation errors and exchange delays, matches—up to a vanishing gap as L,N,K grow—the spectral efficiency achievable by an idealized centralized precoder that has access to perfect global CSI.
4. The protocol remains robust when different APs hold inconsistent or asynchronously updated estimates of the global channel state.

Provide such a protocol together with a proof that the four properties above hold, or prove that no protocol can simultaneously satisfy them and identify the fundamental tradeoff.
status_search_result: Low-overhead, low-latency CSI exchange for distributed cooperative precoding in cell-free massive MIMO remains an active and open research problem. Recent works propose partial solutions (over-the-air CSI signaling, local precoding under partial CSI, scalable DCC clustering, and bi-directional training), each with tradeoffs in uplink overhead, robustness to mismatched/delayed CSI, or performance gap to centralized precoding, but no protocol is known that simultaneously achieves sub-dimensional sharing, low latency, robustness to inconsistent estimates, and near-centralized performance.

original_question: At what level of access-point densification does cell-free massive multiple-input multiple-output (CF-MMIMO) become truly beneficial for a wireless network, and under what deployment, propagation, interference, cost, or coverage conditions is CF-MMIMO not actually needed despite increasing network density?
self_contained_problem:
Consider a wireless network deployed over a planar region of area A in which access points (APs) are placed according to a stationary point process of intensity λ_AP (APs per unit area), and single-antenna user equipments (UEs) are placed independently with intensity λ_UE. Each AP is equipped with N antennas and is connected via fronthaul to a central processing unit, enabling coherent joint transmission and reception (the cell-free massive MIMO, CF-MMIMO, paradigm), in which every UE may in principle be served by any subset of APs without cell boundaries. Channels between an AP at location x and a UE at location y are modeled as h(x,y) = sqrt(β(x,y)) g, where g ~ CN(0, I_N) is small-scale fading and β(x,y) = C · ‖x − y‖^{-α} · χ(x,y) is large-scale fading with path-loss exponent α > 2, shadowing χ, and constant C. Pilot contamination, fronthaul capacity limits, and AP/UE hardware and energy costs are modeled by parameters τ_p (pilot sequence length), R_fh (fronthaul rate per AP), and per-AP cost c_AP.

For comparison, consider an ultra-dense network (UDN) operating under the same intensities λ_AP, λ_UE and propagation parameters but with each UE associated to a single serving AP (no joint processing). Let R_CF(λ_AP) and R_UDN(λ_AP) denote the corresponding ergodic sum spectral efficiencies per unit area under optimal precoding/combining and pilot assignment, and let SE_min(λ_AP) denote the 95%-likely per-user spectral efficiency.

(a) Determine the threshold density λ*_AP, as a function of (α, λ_UE, N, τ_p, R_fh, c_AP, χ), at which CF-MMIMO becomes strictly beneficial in the sense that R_CF(λ_AP) > (1+δ) R_UDN(λ_AP) and SE_min^{CF}(λ_AP) > (1+δ) SE_min^{UDN}(λ_AP) for all λ_AP > λ*_AP and some prescribed δ > 0.

(b) Characterize the regimes of (α, λ_UE, N, τ_p, R_fh, c_AP, shadowing statistics, coverage requirements) under which CF-MMIMO offers no asymptotic gain over UDN; in particular, identify conditions guaranteeing that lim sup_{λ_AP → ∞} [R_CF(λ_AP) − R_UDN(λ_AP)] ≤ 0 (no densification gain) or that the UDN itself suffers a "densification collapse" lim_{λ_AP → ∞} R_UDN(λ_AP) = 0 while CF-MMIMO does not.

Provide explicit, quantitatively justified thresholds and regime boundaries.

original_question: How can cell-free massive multiple-input multiple-output (CF-MMIMO) support communication with backscattering or energy-neutral devices, including integration with simultaneous transmission and reception from different distributed panels, without breaking the time-division-duplex flow or compromising coherent cell-free operation?
self_contained_problem:
Consider a cell-free massive multiple-input multiple-output (CF-MMIMO) wireless system consisting of a large number L of geographically distributed access points (APs), each equipped with multiple antenna panels, jointly serving K single-antenna user equipments (UEs) over the same time-frequency resources. The APs are connected via a fronthaul to one or more central processing units that perform coherent joint signal processing (joint precoding on the downlink and joint combining on the uplink). The system operates in time-division-duplex (TDD) mode: each coherence block of length τ_c channel uses is partitioned into an uplink pilot phase of length τ_p, an uplink data phase of length τ_u, and a downlink data phase of length τ_d, with τ_p + τ_u + τ_d = τ_c. Channel state information is acquired at the APs via uplink pilots and used coherently in both transmission directions by exploiting channel reciprocity.

Suppose that, in addition to the K active UEs, the system must also serve a set of M energy-neutral backscatter devices. Each backscatter device m has no active radio-frequency source: it modulates information by reflecting an incident carrier signal with a complex reflection coefficient Γ_m(t) ∈ ℂ, |Γ_m(t)| ≤ 1, drawn from a finite signaling constellation. Communication with such a device is therefore inherently bistatic: at any given instant, a subset of the APs (or panels) must transmit an illuminating carrier waveform toward the device while a (possibly disjoint) subset must simultaneously receive and decode the backscattered signal. This simultaneous transmit/receive operation across distributed panels does not fit the standard TDD partitioning above.

Formulate and analyze a system-level framework that achieves all of the following simultaneously:

(a) A precise definition of frame structure, pilot allocation, and scheduling rules that allow a subset of APs/panels to transmit illumination signals to backscatter devices while another subset coherently receives the backscattered signal, without destroying the coherent uplink/downlink TDD operation for the K active UEs.

(b) Channel estimation procedures for the composite forward (AP→device) and backward (device→AP) backscatter channels, including handling of the direct AP-to-AP self-interference and clutter induced by simultaneous transmission and reception.

(c) Joint precoding for illumination and joint combining for backscatter reception, designed coherently across distributed APs, together with downlink precoding and uplink combining for the active UEs, such that interference between the two services is controlled.

(d) An achievable-rate or detection-performance characterization for the backscatter devices and an achievable spectral-efficiency characterization for the active UEs under the proposed framework, identifying the fundamental trade-offs between the resources (time, frequency, spatial degrees of freedom, fronthaul) allocated to backscatter service versus conventional CF-MMIMO service.

Determine whether such a framework exists and, if so, exhibit one and quantify the resulting trade-offs.

status_search_result: The question is posed as a future-research direction in the area of cell-free massive MIMO. Existing literature has begun to study CF-MMIMO with backscatter/ambient backscatter and bistatic sensing, but a complete framework that handles joint TDD scheduling, coherent operation, and energy-neutral device integration without disrupting the cell-free pilot/data structure has not been established as of 2026. The problem is treated as an open research direction.

original_question: How should cell-free massive multiple-input multiple-output (CF-MMIMO) be combined with other advanced 6G technologies, including reconfigurable intelligent surfaces, near-field transmissions, and artificial-intelligence methods, while preserving scalable channel estimation, scheduling, synchronization, signal processing, and resource allocation in ultra-dense deployments?
self_contained_problem:
Consider an ultra-dense wireless deployment modeled as cell-free massive multiple-input multiple-output (CF-MMIMO): a large set of geographically distributed access points (APs), each equipped with multiple antennas and connected via fronthaul links to one or more central processing units, jointly and coherently serve a much smaller number of single- or multi-antenna user equipments (UEs) on the same time-frequency resources, without forming traditional cells. Let the wireless channel between AP m and UE k be a vector h_{mk} ∈ C^{N_m} that must be estimated from uplink pilots of finite length τ_p, and let scheduling, synchronization across APs, signal processing, and radio-resource allocation be carried out by algorithms whose per-UE computational and fronthaul complexity must remain bounded as the number of APs M and UEs K grow (the scalability requirement).

Augment this baseline with three additional components:
(i) Reconfigurable intelligent surfaces (RISs): passive planar arrays of N_R reflecting elements whose per-element phase shifts θ_n ∈ [0, 2π) can be programmed to reshape the propagation channel, so that h_{mk} = h_{mk}^{(d)} + G_m Φ f_k where Φ = diag(e^{jθ_1},…,e^{jθ_{N_R}}) and G_m, f_k are AP-RIS and RIS-UE channels.
(ii) Near-field transmissions: when UEs or scatterers lie within the Fraunhofer distance of the collective aperture formed by all APs, the planar-wave model fails and channels must be described by spherical-wave models depending on both angle and distance, so beamforming and channel estimation operate in a higher-dimensional angle-distance domain.
(iii) Artificial-intelligence methods: data-driven models (e.g., deep neural networks, reinforcement-learning agents) used in place of or alongside model-based algorithms for one or more of channel estimation, precoder/combiner design, user-AP association, pilot assignment, and power control.

Problem. Design joint protocols and algorithms for such a CF-MMIMO system that simultaneously incorporate RISs, near-field propagation, and AI-based processing, such that the following scalability and performance criteria all hold as M, K, N_R → ∞ with K/M and N_R/M bounded:
(a) the per-UE pilot overhead, channel-estimation computational cost, and fronthaul signaling per coherence block remain O(1);
(b) the scheduling, synchronization, and resource-allocation procedures admit distributed implementations with bounded per-AP complexity and bounded information exchange between APs;
(c) the achieved per-user spectral efficiency is no worse, up to a vanishing additive term, than that of a fully centralized, fully informed benchmark that jointly optimizes RIS phases, near-field beamforming, and power allocation under perfect channel state information.

Provide such a construction, or prove that no scheme satisfying (a)–(c) exists, and characterize the fundamental trade-offs among densification level, mobility, channel-state-information quality, RIS configuration overhead, near-field aperture size, and AI model complexity that govern when these joint designs are beneficial.

paper_title: Norming Markushevich bases: recent results and open problems
original_question: If X is an Asplund Banach space and X admits a norming Markushevich basis, must X be weakly compactly generated?
self_contained_problem:
Let X be a Banach space. Recall the following definitions:

- X is called an Asplund space if every separable subspace of X has a separable dual.
- A biorthogonal system {(x_i, x_i^*) : i ∈ I} ⊂ X × X^* is called a Markushevich basis (M-basis) of X if the linear span of {x_i : i ∈ I} is norm-dense in X, the family {x_i^* : i ∈ I} separates points of X, and x_j^*(x_i) = δ_{ij}.
- An M-basis is called norming if the closed linear span of {x_i^* : i ∈ I} in X^* is a norming subspace of X^*; that is, there exists a constant c > 0 such that for every x ∈ X,
  ‖x‖ ≥ sup{|x^*(x)| : x^* ∈ span{x_i^*}, ‖x^*‖ ≤ 1} ≥ c‖x‖.
- X is called weakly compactly generated (WCG) if there exists a weakly compact subset K ⊂ X whose linear span is norm-dense in X.

Question: If X is an Asplund Banach space and X admits a norming Markushevich basis, must X be weakly compactly generated?

A construction of an Asplund Banach space admitting a norming Markushevich basis that fails to be weakly compactly generated has been given by Hájek, Russo, Somaglia, and Todorčević (arXiv:2007.14201), resolving Godefroy's question from the early 1990s.

original_question: Let K be a scattered Valdivia compact space that contains a copy of the ordinal interval [0,ω₁]. Is there a bounded linear extension operator from C([0,ω₁]) to C(K)? More generally, does C([0,ω₁]) embed into C(K)?
self_contained_problem:
Background and definitions. For a compact Hausdorff space L, write C(L) for the Banach space of real-valued continuous functions on L with the supremum norm. The ordinal interval [0,ω₁] is the set of ordinals up to and including the first uncountable ordinal ω₁, equipped with the order topology (a compact Hausdorff space).

A Σ-product in a product space [0,1]^Γ is the subset
  Σ([0,1]^Γ) = { x ∈ [0,1]^Γ : { γ ∈ Γ : x(γ) ≠ 0 } is countable }.
A compact Hausdorff space K is called Valdivia if, for some index set Γ, K can be embedded homeomorphically into [0,1]^Γ in such a way that K ∩ Σ([0,1]^Γ) is dense in K.

A topological space is scattered if every nonempty closed subset has an isolated point.

If L is a closed subspace of a compact Hausdorff space K, a bounded linear extension operator from C(L) to C(K) is a bounded linear map T : C(L) → C(K) such that (Tf)|_L = f for every f ∈ C(L).

paper_title: Norming Markushevich bases: recent results and open problems
original_question: If a Banach space X has a norming Markushevich basis and Z is a subspace of X, must Z also admit a norming Markushevich basis?
self_contained_problem:
Let $X$ be a real or complex Banach space with topological dual $X^*$. A biorthogonal system $\{(x_\alpha, x_\alpha^*) : \alpha \in \Gamma\} \subset X \times X^*$ is called a Markushevich basis (M-basis) of $X$ if $\overline{\operatorname{span}}\{x_\alpha : \alpha \in \Gamma\} = X$ and the functionals $\{x_\alpha^* : \alpha \in \Gamma\}$ separate the points of $X$. The M-basis is said to be norming if the closed linear subspace $F := \overline{\operatorname{span}}\{x_\alpha^* : \alpha \in \Gamma\} \subseteq X^*$ is a norming subspace of $X^*$, meaning there exists a constant $c > 0$ such that
$$\|x\| \le \tfrac{1}{c}\sup\{|f(x)| : f \in F,\ \|f\| \le 1\} \quad \text{for all } x \in X.$$
Question: If a Banach space $X$ admits a norming M-basis and $Z$ is a (closed) subspace of $X$, must $Z$ also admit a norming M-basis?

Partial positive results exist (e.g., WLD subspaces of spaces with a λ-norming M-basis inherit a λ-norming M-basis), but the general question remains open.

paper_title: Norming Markushevich bases: recent results and open problems
original_question: If Z is a subspace of a Plichko Banach space X, must Z also be Plichko?
self_contained_problem:
Let X be a (real or complex) Banach space with topological dual X*. A subset D ⊆ X* is called a Σ-subspace of X* if D is a linear subspace such that:
(i) D is 1-norming for X, i.e. ‖x‖ = sup{|f(x)| : f ∈ D, ‖f‖ ≤ 1} for every x ∈ X; and
(ii) D is countably σ(X*,X)-closed, i.e. whenever (f_n)_{n∈ℕ} is a sequence in D whose weak* limit f ∈ X* exists, one has f ∈ D.

A Banach space X is called Plichko if X* contains a Σ-subspace.

paper_title: Norming Markushevich bases: recent results and open problems
original_question: Let Z be a complemented subspace of a Plichko Banach space X. Must Z be Plichko?
self_contained_problem:
Background and definitions. Let $X$ be a (real or complex) Banach space with dual $X^*$. A biorthogonal system $\{(x_\alpha, x_\alpha^*) : \alpha \in \Lambda\} \subset X \times X^*$ is called a Markushevich basis (M-basis) of $X$ if the linear span of $\{x_\alpha\}$ is dense in $X$ and the functionals $\{x_\alpha^*\}$ separate the points of $X$. For a subset $\Gamma \subseteq \Lambda$, let
$$X^*_\Gamma := \{x^* \in X^* : \{\alpha \in \Lambda : x^*(x_\alpha) \neq 0\} \subseteq \Gamma \text{ is countable}\}.$$
An M-basis $\{(x_\alpha, x_\alpha^*)\}$ is said to be norming if there exists a constant $\lambda \in (0,1]$ such that the subspace 
$$N := \{x^* \in X^* : \{\alpha \in \Lambda : x^*(x_\alpha) \neq 0\} \text{ is countable}\}$$
is a $\lambda$-norming subspace of $X^*$, meaning $\|x\| \le \lambda^{-1} \sup\{|x^*(x)| : x^* \in N,\ \|x^*\| \le 1\}$ for all $x \in X$. A Banach space $X$ is called Plichko if it admits a norming M-basis.

A closed subspace $Z \subseteq X$ is complemented in $X$ if there exists a bounded linear projection $P : X \to X$ with $P(X) = Z$.

Problem. Suppose $X$ is a Plichko Banach space and $Z \subseteq X$ is a complemented closed subspace. Must $Z$ itself be a Plichko Banach space?

status_search_result: The question of whether every complemented subspace of a Plichko Banach space is again Plichko is listed as an open problem in recent surveys on norming Markushevich bases. paper_title: Norming Markushevich bases: recent results and open problems
original_question: Let X be a Banach space. (1) If X has a norming Markushevich basis, must the dual ball (B_{X*},w*) be semi-Eberlein? (2) If (B_{X*},w*) is semi-Eberlein for every equivalent renorming of X, must X be a subspace of a weakly compactly generated Banach space? (3) Are the dual balls of C([0,ω₁]) and of C(K_ρ) semi-Eberlein?
self_contained_problem:
Preliminaries. Let X be a (real) Banach space with closed unit ball B_X and topological dual X*. The weak* topology on X* is denoted w*. A biorthogonal system {(x_α, x*_α) : α ∈ Γ} ⊂ X × X* is a Markushevich basis (M-basis) of X if span{x_α : α ∈ Γ} is dense in X and {x*_α : α ∈ Γ} separates the points of X. An M-basis is called norming if the closed linear subspace span‖·‖{x*_α : α ∈ Γ} of X* is a norming subspace of X*, i.e., the formula |||x||| = sup{|x*(x)| : x* ∈ span{x*_α}, ‖x*‖ ≤ 1} defines an equivalent norm on X.

A compact Hausdorff space K is called Eberlein if it is homeomorphic to a weakly compact subset of some Banach space. K is called semi-Eberlein if there exists a set D ⊂ K which is dense in K and such that D is homeomorphic to a subset of some Σ-product of real lines that consists of points with countable support — equivalently, K contains a dense subset whose points each "depend on countably many coordinates" in a topological embedding of K into some [-1,1]^Γ. A Banach space X is weakly compactly generated (WCG) if there exists a weakly compact subset W ⊂ X with X = span‖·‖ W. Let ω_1 denote the first uncountable ordinal, equipped with the order topology on [0, ω_1], so that C([0, ω_1]) is the Banach space of continuous real functions with sup-norm. Let K_ϱ denote the following compact space: take an Aronszajn tree T (a tree of height ω_1 with countable levels and no uncountable branches or antichains) and let K_ϱ be the one-point compactification of T (with the tree-interval topology), or equivalently the standard compactification associated with the ϱ-function construction of Todorčević. 

Problem. 
(1) If X is a Banach space possessing a norming Markushevich basis, must the dual ball (B_{X*}, w*) be a semi-Eberlein compact space?
(2) Suppose that for every equivalent norm |||·||| on X the dual ball (B_{(X,|||·|||)*}, w*) is semi-Eberlein. Does it follow that X is isomorphic to a subspace of some weakly compactly generated Banach space?
(3) Are the dual balls (B_{C([0,ω_1])*}, w*) and (B_{C(K_ϱ)*}, w*) semi-Eberlein compact spaces?

No source asserts they have been solved.

original_question: Can a scattered semi-Eberlein compact space contain a copy of the ordinal interval [0,ω₂]?
self_contained_problem:
Background and definitions. All spaces are Hausdorff. A compact space $K$ is called Eberlein compact if it is homeomorphic to a weakly compact subset of some Banach space. More generally, $K$ is called semi-Eberlein if there exists a set $D \subseteq K$ such that:
(i) $D$ is dense in $K$, and
(ii) $D$ is homeomorphic to a subset of a $\Sigma$-product of real lines $\Sigma(\mathbb{R}^\Gamma) = \{x \in \mathbb{R}^\Gamma : \{\gamma \in \Gamma : x(\gamma) \neq 0\}\text{ is countable}\}$ for some index set $\Gamma$, in such a way that $D$ sits inside the $\sigma$-product $\sigma(\mathbb{R}^\Gamma) = \{x \in \mathbb{R}^\Gamma : \{\gamma \in \Gamma : x(\gamma) \neq 0\}\text{ is finite}\}$ (equivalently, $K$ embeds in some $[0,1]^\Gamma$ in a way that the points with finite support form a dense subset).

A compact space $K$ is scattered if every nonempty closed subset of $K$ has an isolated point. For an ordinal $\alpha$, the ordinal interval $[0,\alpha]$ is regarded as a compact space with the order topology.

paper_title: The Future of Primordial Black Holes: Open Questions and Roadmap
original_question: Do PBHs cluster significantly after formation, and how does clustering alter binary merger rates, gravitational-wave signals observed by LIGO/Virgo and future detectors, microlensing and cosmic microwave background constraints, PBH spins, and the extrapolation from current simulations at redshift z ≈ 10^2 down to observationally relevant lower redshifts?
self_contained_problem:
Consider a cosmological population of primordial black holes (PBHs): compact objects hypothesized to form in the early Universe from the gravitational collapse of large density fluctuations, with a possibly extended mass function and a fractional abundance f_PBH = Ω_PBH/Ω_DM relative to the dark matter density. Let the spatial distribution of PBHs at formation be characterized by a two-point correlation function ξ(r), with the Poisson case corresponding to ξ ≡ 0; deviations from Poisson are referred to as "initial clustering." After formation, gravitational dynamics modifies the spatial distribution, leads to the formation of PBH halos/clusters, alters binary formation channels (early-Universe decoupling pairs, late-Universe dynamical capture, three-body hardening), and affects the population-level distribution of PBH spins.

Address the following:

(a) Quantify whether PBHs cluster significantly after formation, beyond the initial Poisson distribution, as a function of f_PBH, the PBH mass function, and any non-Gaussianity of the primordial perturbations sourcing them. Provide a predictive analytical or semi-analytical model for the evolution of the PBH correlation function ξ(r, z) from formation to redshift z ≈ 0.

(b) Determine how clustering modifies the merger rate R(z) of PBH binaries, including the relative contributions of early- and late-Universe channels, and produce a corresponding prediction for the stochastic and resolvable gravitational-wave signal observable by current (LIGO/Virgo/KAGRA) and future (Einstein Telescope, Cosmic Explorer, LISA) detectors.

(c) Determine how PBH clustering modifies the constraints on f_PBH derived from microlensing surveys and from cosmic microwave background spectral distortions and anisotropies.

(d) Determine how clustering, through repeated hierarchical mergers and dynamical interactions inside clusters, shapes the distribution of PBH spins.

(e) Develop a controlled method to extrapolate predictions from N-body simulations of PBH systems—currently feasible only down to redshifts of order z ∼ 10^2—to the much lower redshifts z ≲ 10 relevant for observational constraints, providing analytical insight into the long-term nonlinear evolution of the PBH population.
category_tag: primordial black hole clustering and merger rates
status_search_result: The question remains an active open research problem. Multiple recent works (2024–2026) study aspects of PBH clustering, redshift evolution of merger rates, and mass-ratio-modulated initial clustering, providing partial models (e.g., merger rate scaling ℛ ∝ (1+z)^β with β ≈ 1.4–2.2) and N-body simulations of PBH clusters, but a complete, predictive framework spanning clustering evolution, GW signatures, microlensing/CMB constraints, spin distribution, and extrapolation from z ∼ 10^2 to low redshift is not yet established.

paper_title: The Future of Primordial Black Holes: Open Questions and Roadmap
context_brief: PBH fraction in observed gravitational-wave events
original_question: What fraction, if any, of the binary black-hole gravitational-wave events already observed by LIGO/Virgo/KAGRA should be attributed to primordial black holes rather than astrophysical black-hole formation channels, given that current hierarchical Bayesian analyses can only constrain a putative PBH subpopulation and decisive attribution requires reducing uncertainties in both astrophysical and primordial formation models?
self_contained_problem:
Consider the catalog of binary black-hole merger events detected by current ground-based gravitational-wave observatories operating in the audio-band frequency range (roughly 10 Hz–10 kHz). Each detection provides posterior distributions on source-frame parameters such as component masses, mass ratio, effective spin, redshift, and tidal/eccentricity bounds. Assume two competing population models for the origin of these binaries:

(A) Astrophysical formation channels, in which the black holes are remnants of stellar evolution produced through isolated binary evolution, dynamical assembly in dense stellar environments (e.g. globular clusters, nuclear clusters, AGN disks), chemically homogeneous evolution, or hierarchical mergers; these channels predict mass functions consistent with stellar collapse (with an expected upper mass gap from pulsational pair instability), spin distributions tied to stellar physics, and merger rates evolving with cosmic star formation.

(B) A primordial formation channel, in which the black holes formed in the very early universe (e.g. from the gravitational collapse of large-amplitude cosmological perturbations) and later pair up to merge; this channel predicts a broad mass spectrum extending beyond stellar limits, generically low natal spins, an isotropic spin orientation distribution, and a merger-rate density evolving roughly as (1+z)^{8/3} at high redshift, independent of star formation.

Denote by f_PBH the fraction of the observed binary black-hole gravitational-wave events that originate from channel (B). Using a hierarchical Bayesian population analysis that mixes models (A) and (B) and is conditioned on the full observed catalog (including selection effects), determine f_PBH, or equivalently provide a posterior credible interval for f_PBH and identify which (if any) individual events have a posterior probability greater than 1/2 of being of primordial origin.
category_tag: primordial black holes and gravitational-wave populations
status_search_result: Recent population analyses of LVK O3/O4 catalogs only place upper bounds or weak constraints on a possible PBH subpopulation in the BBH data; no decisive attribution of any specific event to primordial origin has been established, and the fraction remains uncertain due to degeneracies with astrophysical formation models. The question is regarded as open in the gravitational-wave and PBH communities as of 2026.

paper_title: The Future of Primordial Black Holes: Open Questions and Roadmap
original_question: Can future gravitational-wave observations identify high-redshift PBH binary mergers as a smoking-gun primordial signal by measuring merger-rate evolution at redshifts above roughly 10 and by detecting mergers at redshift z greater than about 30, where astrophysical-origin black-hole mergers are expected to switch off, despite luminosity-distance uncertainties and contamination from Population III binaries?
self_contained_problem:
Consider a cosmological population of binary black hole mergers observed via gravitational waves. Astrophysical-origin stellar black hole binaries are expected to have a merger-rate density that drops sharply (effectively switching off) at redshifts z ≳ 20–30, whereas a population of primordial black holes (PBHs) formed in the early universe would produce a binary merger-rate density that grows monotonically with redshift and persists well beyond z = 30. Let f_PBH denote the fraction of dark matter in the form of PBHs.

Question: Determine whether next-generation (3G) gravitational-wave detectors can unambiguously identify a primordial origin of compact binary mergers by:
(a) measuring the redshift evolution of the merger-rate density at redshifts z ≳ 10, and
(b) detecting individual binary black hole mergers at z ≳ 30,
under realistic conditions that include (i) large luminosity-distance measurement uncertainties arising from low signal-to-noise ratios at high redshift, and (ii) contamination from mergers originating from Population III stellar binaries.

Specifically, characterize the smallest PBH abundance f_PBH (in the solar-mass range) that can be constrained or detected through such high-redshift merger observations, and identify the statistical and observational conditions under which a detection of high-z mergers constitutes a definitive "smoking gun" signature distinguishing primordial from astrophysical black hole populations.
category_tag: Primordial black holes and gravitational-wave cosmology
status_search_result: The question concerns whether future 3G gravitational-wave detectors (Einstein Telescope, Cosmic Explorer) can use high-redshift binary black hole mergers as a smoking-gun PBH signature. Recent forecasting studies (e.g., works by Ng, Franciolini, Pujolas, Riotto, Vitale and collaborators around 2022–2024) show that measuring merger-rate evolution at z ≳ 10 could in principle constrain f_PBH down to ~10^-5 in the solar-mass range, even with Pop III contamination, but no actual observation has been performed and luminosity-distance uncertainties at low SNR remain a significant obstacle. The problem is forward-looking and remains open pending the operation of 3G detectors.

paper_title: The Future of Primordial Black Holes: Open Questions and Roadmap
original_question: Can PBHs populate the pair-instability mass gap, the predicted deficit of astrophysical black holes between roughly 50 and 120 solar masses caused by pair-instability supernovae, and would a feature in the black-hole mass spectrum reveal a new black-hole formation mechanism?
self_contained_problem:
Stellar evolution theory predicts that massive stars whose helium cores enter the pair-instability regime either undergo pulsational mass loss or are completely disrupted by pair-instability supernovae, producing a deficit (the "pair-instability mass gap") of stellar-origin black holes with masses roughly between 50 M_⊙ and 120 M_⊙. Primordial black holes (PBHs), defined as black holes formed in the early Universe from the gravitational collapse of cosmological overdensities (rather than from stellar collapse), are not subject to this stellar-evolution constraint and may in principle have any mass.

Let f_PBH(M) denote the differential mass function of a PBH population and let p_obs(M_1, M_2) denote the observed distribution of component masses in merging binary black holes inferred from gravitational-wave catalogs.

(a) Determine whether there exist physically motivated PBH formation scenarios (specifying the curvature power spectrum, equation-of-state features at QCD-like thermal transitions, or other production mechanisms) which yield a PBH abundance and mass spectrum f_PBH(M) such that mergers of PBH binaries can account for a statistically significant fraction of observed binary-black-hole events with at least one component mass in the interval [50 M_⊙, 120 M_⊙], while remaining consistent with all current cosmological, microlensing, CMB, and gravitational-wave constraints on PBHs.

(b) Identify a distinguishing feature in the binary-black-hole mass spectrum (e.g., a peak, edge, or excess inside the pair-instability gap) whose presence would constitute a "smoking-gun" indication of a non-stellar (in particular primordial) black-hole formation channel, and quantify the statistical sensitivity required to establish such a feature.
category_tag: Primordial black holes and gravitational-wave astronomy
status_search_result: The question remains open. Recent analyses of LIGO–Virgo–KAGRA GWTC-4 data report evidence of a pair-instability gap in the secondary-mass distribution with a lower edge near ~44 M_⊙, but a number of observed events still have components in or near the gap, and proposals that PBHs (often with thermal/QCD-induced features in the mass function) can populate it are actively studied. No consensus has been reached that PBHs are required or excluded as the explanation, and the proposed smoking-gun spectral feature has not been definitively identified.

paper_title: The Future of Primordial Black Holes: Open Questions and Roadmap
original_question: Can PBH mass-spin correlations induced by accretion be used to determine the primordial nature of individual gravitational-wave events or of the event population, and how can uncertainties in the accretion model be reduced enough for population-level tests?
self_contained_problem:
Consider a population of black holes that may be of primordial origin, i.e., formed in the early universe by the gravitational collapse of large cosmological overdensities, rather than from stellar evolution. Suppose that, after formation, such primordial black holes (PBHs) accrete baryonic matter from the surrounding cosmological medium according to a spherical/disk accretion model that produces a deterministic correlation between the PBH mass M and dimensionless spin χ ∈ [0,1]: there exists a function χ_acc(M; θ) depending on accretion parameters θ (e.g., accretion onset redshift, efficiency, disk geometry) such that an isolated PBH of present-day mass M is predicted to have spin χ_acc(M; θ). Astrophysical (stellar-origin) black holes follow a distinct, generically different mass–spin distribution p_astro(M, χ).

(a) Formulate precise statistical criteria — for instance, a likelihood-ratio or Bayes-factor test on the joint mass–spin posterior of a single gravitational-wave merger event — under which the observation of an individual binary black hole event with measured (M, χ) suffices to identify it as primordial via the predicted accretion-induced mass–spin correlation, accounting for the measurement covariance of current/future GW detectors.

(b) At the population level, given N gravitational-wave events with posteriors on (M_i, χ_i), derive the dependence of the discrimination power (e.g., expected log Bayes factor between a primordial+astrophysical mixture model and a purely astrophysical model) on N and on the prior uncertainty in the accretion parameters θ. Determine quantitatively how tightly θ must be constrained, and how large N must be, so that the population-level test achieves a prescribed statistical significance (e.g., 5σ) for detecting (or excluding) a primordial subpopulation obeying the χ_acc(M; θ) relation.
status_search_result: The question is part of an open research roadmap on primordial black holes. Recent literature continues to develop accretion-driven mass–spin correlations as a discriminator between primordial and astrophysical black holes (e.g., De Luca, Franciolini, Pani, Riotto; Hütsi et al.), and population-level GW analyses with LIGO–Virgo–KAGRA data have placed only weak constraints, with the accretion model itself remaining a dominant systematic. No definitive resolution has been published; the status is open.

paper_title: The Future of Primordial Black Holes: Open Questions and Roadmap
original_question: Can near-extremal, higher-dimensional, maximally rotating, charged, or memory-burden-suppressed PBHs remain stable on cosmological timescales after Hawking evaporation would otherwise remove them, and can such relics be detected directly in terrestrial detectors or indirectly through high-energy emission from occasional binary mergers?
self_contained_problem:
Consider primordial black holes (PBHs), i.e. black holes hypothesized to have formed in the early universe from large density perturbations or other mechanisms, with initial masses small enough that standard semiclassical Hawking radiation would cause them to fully evaporate on a timescale shorter than the present age of the universe.

For each of the following classes of PBHs, determine whether they can remain stable, or at least extremely long-lived (with lifetimes exceeding the current age of the universe), as cosmological relics, and determine whether such relics admit feasible direct or indirect observational signatures:

(a) Near-extremal four-dimensional Reissner–Nordström or Kerr–Newman PBHs whose charge or angular momentum is tuned close to the extremal bound, so that the Hawking temperature is parametrically small.

(b) Higher-dimensional PBHs in models with compact extra dimensions of size L: in particular, low-mass five-dimensional PBHs that initially behave as four-dimensional Schwarzschild black holes and Hawking radiate down to a horizon radius comparable to L, where their effective temperature approaches zero and the evaporation stalls.

(c) Maximally rotating PBHs or maximally charged PBHs formed at very early cosmological epochs, so that their initial spin or charge parameter saturates the extremal bound.

(d) PBHs whose evaporation is strongly suppressed by the conjectured quantum-gravitational "memory burden" effect, in which the back-reaction of stored quantum information halts or strongly slows semiclassical Hawking emission once a comparable fraction of the initial mass has been radiated.

For each class, specify the conditions (mass range, charge or spin, extra-dimension size, suppression parameter) under which the resulting object is stable on cosmological timescales. In addition, assess whether such relics—possibly down to mass scales as small as a few Planck masses for charged PBH relics—can be detected either directly in terrestrial detectors sensitive to charged or strongly-interacting massive particle-like objects, or indirectly through high-energy particle emission generated by occasional binary mergers of such relics.
status_search_result: The viability and detection of near-extremal, higher-dimensional, maximally charged/rotating, and memory-burdened PBH relics are the subject of active ongoing research (2024–2026), with multiple recent works proposing constraints and possible detection channels (high-energy neutrinos, induced gravitational waves, gamma-ray signatures, LHAASO observations, binary mergers). No definitive resolution exists; the question remains open with partial progress.

original_question: Can lunar-far-side 21 cm dark-ages telescopes such as LUSEE-Night and DSL detect PBH accretion imprints on diffuse hydrogen absorption against the cosmic microwave background out to redshifts below roughly 100, providing a high-redshift observational test of primordial black holes?
self_contained_problem:
Consider the cosmological 21 cm hydrogen absorption signal during the cosmic Dark Ages, measured as a differential brightness temperature of the diffuse neutral hydrogen against the cosmic microwave background (CMB) at redshifts in the range roughly 30 ≲ z ≲ 100. Suppose that a population of primordial black holes (PBHs) constitutes a fraction f_PBH of the dark matter, with masses in an astrophysically relevant window. Such PBHs accrete the ambient intergalactic medium and emit radiation that perturbs the gas kinetic temperature, the hydrogen spin temperature, and the ionization history, thereby imprinting a characteristic signature on the global 21 cm absorption signal and its power spectrum (including velocity acoustic oscillation features sourced by relative dark-matter–baryon streaming).

Question: Using lunar far-side radio interferometers/global-signal experiments operating in the frequency band corresponding to the redshifted 21 cm line from the Dark Ages (i.e., observing the cosmological 21 cm signal at z ≲ 100, free from Earth's ionosphere and terrestrial radio interference), is it possible to detect — at statistically significant level — the imprint of PBH accretion on the diffuse hydrogen 21 cm absorption signal against the CMB? Specifically, determine the range of PBH masses and abundances f_PBH for which such an experiment can either detect the accretion signature or place an upper limit improving on existing CMB-based constraints, accounting for instrumental sensitivity, foreground subtraction, and astrophysical uncertainties in the accretion model.

paper_title: Opportunities and open questions in modern β decay
original_question: How can soft electromagnetic final-state interactions between beta-decay final-state particles be incorporated in a single consistent renormalization and matching framework accurate at the 0.01% level? The question includes how to reconcile the traditional Fermi-function treatment of Coulomb effects and radiative-correction factors with effective-field-theory treatments of running, matching, and large-logarithm resummation for neutron and finite-nuclear-charge beta decays.
self_contained_problem:
Consider allowed nuclear beta decay processes (in particular free neutron decay and beta decay of nuclei with finite nuclear charge Z) where one wishes to compute the differential and total decay rates with a theoretical uncertainty at or below the 10^{-4} (0.01%) level. The amplitude is dressed by soft electromagnetic final-state interactions between the outgoing charged particles (electron/positron, recoiling nucleus, and, where relevant, additional charged hadrons), which traditionally are encoded by (i) the Fermi function F(Z,E) resumming the Coulomb interaction between the lepton and the daughter nucleus, and (ii) multiplicative radiative-correction factors such as the outer correction g(E,E_0) and inner correction Δ_R^V capturing virtual and real soft photons.

Develop a single consistent renormalization and matching framework, formulated in the language of effective field theory (with a tower of EFTs separating the scales m_W, m_p, m_e, and the atomic/Coulomb scale Zα m_e), that:

1. Reproduces the established Fermi-function treatment of Coulomb effects in the appropriate low-energy limit, with controlled power counting in Zα and v/c.
2. Performs the matching of Wilson coefficients across each scale and resums the resulting large logarithms (e.g. log(m_W/m_p), log(m_p/m_e)) via renormalization-group evolution, in a scheme consistent with the definition of the Fermi function.
3. Yields a total theoretical uncertainty on the inclusive and differential rates that is demonstrably ≤ 0.01% for both the neutron (Z=0 daughter charge interpreted appropriately) and finite-Z nuclear cases, with all renormalization-scheme dependencies and double-counting between the Fermi function and EFT radiative corrections explicitly resolved.

Establish the exact correspondence between the traditional factorized form rate ∝ F(Z,E) · (1 + δ_R) · |M|^2 and the EFT factorization formula at this precision, for both the neutron and finite-Z beta decays.
category_tag: Effective field theory of beta decay
status_search_result: An EFT reformulation of the Fermi function ("Field Theory of the Fermi Function", Phys. Rev. Lett. 133, 021803, 2024) provides a factorization formula, matching at successive scales, and renormalization-group resummation of large logarithms, including a three-loop anomalous dimension. This addresses parts of the program for the neutron case, but the precise correspondence with the traditional Fermi-function/radiative-correction treatment at the 0.01% level, especially for finite nuclear charge Z, remains under active investigation and is not fully established.

paper_title: Opportunities and open questions in modern β decay
original_question: Can direct measurements of superallowed beta-spectrum shapes provide useful constraints on additional energy-dependent radiative corrections in beta decay, despite historically limited sensitivity of such spectrum-shape measurements compared with integrated decay rates?
self_contained_problem:
In the theory of nuclear beta decay, a superallowed 0^+ → 0^+ Fermi transition has a differential decay rate (spectrum shape) of the schematic form

  dΓ/dE = G_V^2 |M_F|^2 F(Z,E) p E (E_0 − E)^2 [1 + δ_R(E,Z) + δ'_R(E) + ...],

where E is the electron total energy, E_0 the endpoint energy, p the electron momentum, F(Z,E) the Fermi function, M_F the Fermi matrix element, and δ_R, δ'_R denote nucleus-dependent and energy-dependent outer/inner radiative corrections. The integrated rate (ft value) determines the product G_V^2 |M_F|^2 up to overall radiative corrections, but is by construction insensitive to the energy dependence inside the bracket.

Problem. Determine whether direct measurements of the differential beta spectrum dΓ/dE for superallowed 0^+ → 0^+ transitions can provide useful, quantitative constraints on the energy-dependent radiative corrections (in particular the shape function inside the bracket beyond the leading allowed shape p E (E_0 − E)^2 F(Z,E)), given the historically limited experimental sensitivity of spectrum-shape measurements relative to integrated ft-value determinations. Specifically, quantify the precision with which the energy dependence of the radiative-correction shape function can be extracted from feasible direct spectrum-shape experiments, and compare it to the precision needed to test current theoretical predictions for these corrections.
status_search_result: This is an open experimental/theoretical question in modern beta-decay physics. Recent reviews and experimental programs (e.g., precision spectrum-shape measurements using cyclotron radiation emission spectroscopy, ion traps, and gas-filled detectors) are actively pursuing such measurements, but no definitive demonstration that direct superallowed spectrum-shape measurements yield useful constraints on energy-dependent radiative corrections has been established as of the most recent literature.

paper_title: Opportunities and open questions in modern β decay
context_brief: Enhanced isospin breaking in axial radiative corrections
original_question: How should unexpectedly large enhanced isospin-breaking effects in order-alpha axial-current radiative corrections be computed, and can dedicated lattice-QCD plus finite-photon-mass lattice-QED calculations reduce the uncertainty in the renormalization of lambda = gA/gV used to compare lattice and experimental determinations of gA?
self_contained_problem:
Consider the axial-vector coupling $g_A$ and the vector coupling $g_V$ of the nucleon that govern neutron beta decay $n \to p e^- \bar\nu_e$, and define their ratio $\lambda = g_A/g_V$. At order $\alpha$ in the electroweak Standard Model, the radiative corrections to the axial current decompose into a $\gamma W$-box contribution (which is comparatively well controlled) and additional isospin-breaking contributions arising from the difference between up and down quark masses together with electromagnetism. Recent analyses indicate that these enhanced isospin-breaking pieces produce unexpectedly large shifts in the $O(\alpha)$ renormalization factor relating $\lambda$ as defined in pure QCD (and computed on the lattice) to $\lambda$ as extracted from experimental neutron beta-decay observables.

(a) Provide a controlled theoretical computation of the enhanced isospin-breaking contributions to the $O(\alpha)$ axial-current radiative corrections, identifying all hadronic structure-dependent pieces and quantifying their parametric and numerical size.

(b) Formulate a lattice-QCD plus lattice-QED calculation (e.g., using a finite photon mass as an infrared regulator) that directly computes the relevant $O(\alpha)$ isospin-breaking correction to the renormalization of $\lambda$. Specify and carry out the necessary ingredients: finite-volume corrections for QED in a finite box, the modification of the electron propagator in the QED background, and the non-perturbative renormalization of the relevant currents. Demonstrate that the resulting uncertainty on the renormalization factor relating lattice and experimental determinations of $\lambda = g_A/g_V$ can be reduced below the precision target needed for current neutron-decay phenomenology.
status_search_result: The literature confirms that lattice QCD+QED methodology for isospin-breaking and electromagnetic corrections is actively developing (e.g., RBC/UKQCD leptonic-decay work, C* boundary-condition QCD+QED, finite-volume QED schemes), but no published lattice-QCD+QED calculation has yet delivered the dedicated $O(\alpha)$ enhanced-isospin-breaking correction to the renormalization of $\lambda = g_A/g_V$ at the required precision. The issue of unexpectedly large enhanced isospin-breaking effects in axial radiative corrections remains an outstanding problem.

paper_title: Opportunities and open questions in modern β decay
original_question: Can the small beta-energy dependence of nuclear gamma-W-box radiative corrections be measured directly, and can such measurements benchmark theoretical estimates of nuclear Nachtmann-moment contributions when the expected slope is only a few parts in 10^-4 per MeV?
self_contained_problem:
In allowed nuclear beta decay, the differential decay rate as a function of the beta particle's kinetic energy E receives an electroweak radiative correction that includes a hadronic/nuclear gamma-W box contribution. This nuclear gamma-W box contribution carries a small dependence on E that, in current theoretical estimates based on dispersion representations involving the first Nachtmann moment of the γW interference structure function F_3, produces a slope of order a few parts in 10^{-4} per MeV in the energy-dependent correction factor multiplying the spectrum.

Determine whether the following is possible:

(a) Design and analyze an experimental procedure capable of directly detecting a slope of order 10^{-4} per MeV in the beta-energy-dependent nuclear gamma-W box radiative correction to the allowed beta spectrum, specifying the required precision, kinematic range, and systematic-error budget.

(b) Show how such a direct measurement of the energy-dependent slope can be used to benchmark (i.e., constrain or falsify) theoretical estimates of the nuclear Nachtmann-moment contributions that enter the dispersive computation of the gamma-W box, and quantify the level at which a measurement can discriminate between competing nuclear-structure inputs.

Equivalently: does there exist (in principle and in practice) a beta-spectrum measurement strategy whose statistical and systematic sensitivity is better than a few parts in 10^{-4} per MeV across the relevant beta endpoint range, sufficient to test current theoretical predictions for the energy slope of nuclear gamma-W box corrections?
category_tag: Electroweak radiative corrections in beta decay
status_search_result: Recent literature on radiative corrections to neutron and superallowed nuclear beta decay (e.g., dispersive analyses via Nachtmann moments of F_3, and updates of Δ_R^V) actively discuss the gamma-W box contribution and its uncertainties, but no published experiment has directly measured the predicted few-parts-in-10^{-4}-per-MeV beta-energy slope of the nuclear gamma-W box correction. The challenge is repeatedly described as extremely difficult, and no benchmarking measurement of the Nachtmann-moment-based estimates appears to exist as of 2026.

paper_title: Opportunities and open questions in modern β decay
original_question: How should nuclear-structure and isospin-breaking corrections to the Gamow-Teller-to-Fermi mixing ratio rho be computed for mirror beta decays, rather than assuming that the corrected rho entering the integrated decay-rate formula is the same effective rho extracted from angular-correlation measurements?
self_contained_problem:
Consider an allowed nuclear beta decay between mirror nuclei (isospin doublet, T = 1/2). The decay rate has both a vector (Fermi) and an axial-vector (Gamow-Teller) contribution, parametrized by the Fermi matrix element M_F and the Gamow-Teller matrix element M_GT. Define the mixing ratio

  ρ = (C_A M_GT) / (C_V M_F),

where C_V and C_A are the vector and axial-vector coupling constants. The integrated decay rate (used in extractions of the CKM matrix element V_ud from mirror transitions) depends on a "corrected" mixing ratio ρ_corr that should incorporate nuclear-structure and isospin-symmetry-breaking corrections (analogous to the δ_C and δ_NS corrections in superallowed 0+ → 0+ Fermi transitions). On the other hand, angular-correlation observables (such as the β–ν angular correlation coefficient a_βν) yield an experimentally extracted effective ratio ρ_exp.

Provide a first-principles or systematic theoretical framework for computing the nuclear-structure and isospin-breaking corrections that relate ρ_corr to the bare ρ, and quantify the difference ρ_corr − ρ_exp for T = 1/2 mirror beta decays. In particular, determine to what extent the approximation ρ_corr = ρ_exp, commonly assumed in the integrated decay-rate formula for mirror transitions, is justified, and compute the leading corrections that must be applied to ρ_exp before its use in V_ud extractions.

paper_title: Opportunities and open questions in modern β decay
original_question: Do isospin-breaking corrections induced by weak magnetism in nuclear beta decays add coherently over all nucleons, and can they become sizeable in final-state correlations when leading-order contributions cancel, such as in neon-19 mirror observables where a_beta_nu and A_beta are close to 4%?
self_contained_problem:
In allowed nuclear β decay, the hadronic current receives recoil-order corrections, among which the weak-magnetism term plays a prominent role. The Standard Model prediction for the weak-magnetism form factor assumes exact isospin symmetry between the initial and final nuclear states; in reality, isospin symmetry is broken by the proton–neutron mass difference, electromagnetic interactions, and charge-symmetry-breaking components of the strong interaction. For a given nucleus with A nucleons, let δb_i denote the isospin-breaking correction to the weak-magnetism contribution associated with nucleon i, and let δb_total = Σ_i δb_i be the total correction entering the nuclear matrix element governing the β–ν angular correlation coefficient a_{βν} and the β-asymmetry parameter A_β.

(a) Determine whether the individual contributions δb_i add coherently across all A nucleons (so that δb_total scales with the number of nucleons or with a collective nuclear quantity) or whether they add incoherently (so that cancellations or stochastic-like scaling occur).

(b) For the mirror transition of ^{19}Ne, where the leading-order Standard Model predictions for a_{βν} and A_β are both close to 4% in magnitude and large cancellations between Fermi and Gamow–Teller contributions occur, quantify the size of the weak-magnetism isospin-breaking corrections to a_{βν} and A_β and determine whether these corrections are sizeable compared to the leading-order values.
status_search_result: Recent literature on β-decay correlations and recoil corrections, including studies of mirror transitions and weak-magnetism form factors, acknowledges that recoil and isospin-breaking corrections cannot be neglected at the ~1% precision now reached experimentally, and treats ^{19}Ne as a special case where leading-order suppression enhances the relative importance of such corrections. No source found provides a definitive answer to whether weak-magnetism isospin-breaking corrections add coherently across nucleons, indicating the question remains open.

paper_title: Opportunities and open questions in modern β decay
context_brief: Novel detector technologies for precision beta decay
original_question: How can Cyclotron Radiation Emission Spectroscopy, quantum-sensor recoil spectroscopy, Superconducting Tunnel Junction detectors, and high-efficiency atom or ion traps be combined or developed to overcome detector non-linearities, backscattering, bremsstrahlung losses, and simulation-validation limits in future precision beta-decay searches for exotic physics?
self_contained_problem:
Precision measurements of nuclear beta decay aim to detect signatures of physics beyond the Standard Model by characterizing the energy and angular distributions of emitted electrons (or positrons), recoiling daughter nuclei, and any accompanying neutrals. Traditional scintillator and semiconductor electron spectrometers are limited by three principal sources of systematic uncertainty: (i) detector non-linearities in the energy response, (ii) electron backscattering from detector surfaces, and (iii) bremsstrahlung energy losses in source and detector materials; additionally, the validation of Monte Carlo simulations modeling these effects is limited by available calibration data.

Several emerging detection technologies aim to circumvent these limitations:

1. Cyclotron Radiation Emission Spectroscopy (CRES): measures the frequency of cyclotron radiation emitted by a charged particle gyrating in a uniform magnetic field B, with frequency ω = eB/(γ m_e), thereby inferring its Lorentz factor γ and kinetic energy non-destructively.

2. Quantum-sensor recoil spectroscopy: uses cryogenic calorimetric sensors (e.g., transition-edge sensors, magnetic microcalorimeters) to measure the kinetic energy of the recoiling daughter ion or atom with eV-scale resolution.

3. Superconducting Tunnel Junction (STJ) detectors: cryogenic devices in which deposited energy breaks Cooper pairs, providing high-resolution spectroscopy of low-energy particles.

4. High-efficiency atom or ion traps: confine the parent nucleus in a near-massless, near-backing-free environment, enabling clean coincidence detection of the beta particle and recoil daughter.

Problem. Design a conceptual experimental scheme that integrates two or more of the above techniques (CRES, quantum-sensor recoil spectroscopy, STJ detectors, atom/ion traps) into a single coincidence apparatus for precision beta-decay measurements (e.g., a measurement of the beta-neutrino angular correlation coefficient a_βν, the Fierz interference term b, or related observables sensitive to scalar/tensor exotic currents). The scheme should (a) eliminate or dramatically reduce the dominant systematic uncertainties of traditional spectrometers (detector non-linearities, backscattering, bremsstrahlung losses), (b) provide internal calibration channels that constrain Monte Carlo simulation uncertainties at the level required for a fractional sensitivity to exotic couplings below 10^{-3}, and (c) achieve a usable rate and acceptance compatible with statistics-limited operation. Quantify expected systematic budgets and identify the technological developments required to realize such a combined apparatus.
status_search_result: This is a forward-looking experimental program rather than a mathematically posed conjecture. Active R&D efforts (e.g., Project 8 for CRES, He6-CRES, BeEST for STJ, and various MOT/Paul-trap based beta-decay experiments such as TRINAT, WISArD, and St. Benedict) are ongoing as of 2026, but no integrated apparatus combining these technologies at the precision required for definitive exotic-physics searches has been demonstrated. The question therefore remains open.

paper_title: Protocols for Observational Studies: Methods and Open Problems
original_question: In matched observational studies, when researchers must decide whether to specify the study protocol before or after matching treated and control units, what methods besides prespecifying important matching covariates before matching can reduce researcher hope bias, where researcher hope bias means understating uncertainty or declining to match on possible confounders because the researcher hopes the matched study will retain enough power to be informative?
self_contained_problem:
Consider a matched observational study in which a researcher matches treated units to control units on observed covariates and then performs outcome analysis to test a causal hypothesis. The researcher must decide whether to fully specify the study protocol (including the choice of matching covariates, calipers, balance constraints, test statistics, and inference procedures) before performing the matching or after inspecting the matched sample. Define "researcher hope bias" as the tendency, when specifying (or revising) a protocol after matching, to understate uncertainty or to decline to match on possible confounders because the researcher hopes that the resulting matched study will retain enough statistical power to be informative.

One known mitigation is the following: before matching, the researcher specifies a list of covariates believed to be important to match on, and in the final protocol provides explicit reasons for any deviations from this initial list.

Problem: Devise and rigorously justify additional methodologies — beyond prespecification of an initial covariate list with documented deviations — that provably reduce researcher hope bias in matched observational studies, while still allowing the researcher to use information learned from the matched sample (e.g., about unmeasured confounding) when finalizing the protocol. A satisfactory answer should describe the procedure, the statistical guarantees it provides (for example, on Type I error, coverage, or sensitivity-analysis validity), and the assumptions required.
status_search_result: The question is posed as an explicit open methodological problem in the literature on protocols for matched observational studies. A brief web search did not surface a definitive subsequent methodology that comprehensively addresses researcher hope bias beyond the prespecified-covariate-list approach. Related work on preregistration, sample splitting, and design-based sensitivity analysis exists but does not appear to claim resolution of this problem.

paper_title: Protocols for Observational Studies: Methods and Open Problems
original_question: For sample-splitting methods in observational study protocols, where data are randomly divided into a planning sample used to choose hypotheses, outcomes, or subgroups and an analysis sample used for confirmatory testing with appropriate multiplicity correction, how should researchers choose a good fraction of the data to allocate to the planning sample as a function of the total sample size?
self_contained_problem:
Consider an observational study with a total of $n$ units, and suppose that the data are to be analyzed by a sample-splitting procedure: a random subset of size $n_P = \lfloor f \cdot n \rfloor$ (the "planning sample") is used to explore the data and select a collection of hypotheses, outcomes, and/or subgroups for confirmatory testing, while the remaining $n_A = n - n_P$ observations (the "analysis sample") are used to test the selected hypotheses with a familywise-error-rate–controlling procedure (e.g., Bonferroni–Holm) applied to the number of hypotheses chosen from the planning sample.

Determine a principled rule for choosing the planning-sample fraction $f = f(n) \in (0,1)$ as a function of the total sample size $n$ that optimizes the resulting confirmatory inference. Specifically, formulate a criterion (for instance, maximizing expected power of the analysis-sample test, or minimizing design sensitivity to unmeasured confounding under a Rosenbaum-style sensitivity model) and identify the value $f^*(n)$ that optimizes this criterion, including its asymptotic behavior as $n \to \infty$ and its dependence on relevant problem parameters (number of candidate hypotheses/outcomes, effect-size structure, and bias magnitude).
status_search_result: Recent work has begun to address this question. "Planning for gold: Hypothesis screening with split samples for valid powerful testing in matched observational studies" (arXiv:2406.00866, 2024) provides empirically recommended splitting fractions, and "Optimal Sample Splitting for Observational Studies" (arXiv:2601.22782) proposes a numerical procedure for choosing an optimal split fraction adaptive to low- and high-dimensional outcome spaces. These results give practical and partial answers (e.g., small planning fractions such as around 15% often perform well), but a fully general theoretical rule giving $f^*(n)$ as a function of $n$ across all settings has not been established.
