paper_title: Open Problems in Topology II
context_brief: Perfect GO-spaces and sigma-closed-discrete dense sets
original_question: Let kappa be a cardinal greater than omega_1. A generalized ordered space, or GO-space, is a linearly ordered set equipped with a Hausdorff topology having a base of order-convex sets; a linearly ordered topological space, or LOTS, is the special case where the topology is the open-interval topology of the order. Is it consistent with ZFC that every perfect GO-space with local density at most kappa has a sigma-closed-discrete dense set? Equivalently, is it consistent with ZFC that every perfect non-Archimedean space with local density at most kappa is metrizable, or that every perfect GO-space with local density at most kappa and a point-countable base is metrizable?
self_contained_problem:
Definitions. A generalized ordered space (GO-space) is a triple $(X,\tau,<)$ where $(X,<)$ is a linearly ordered set and $\tau$ is a Hausdorff topology on $X$ that has a base consisting of order-convex sets (a set $C\subseteq X$ is order-convex if $a,b\in C$ and $a<x<b$ imply $x\in C$). A linearly ordered topological space (LOTS) is a GO-space whose topology coincides with the open-interval topology induced by $<$. A topological space is perfect if every closed subset is a $G_\delta$. A space has local density at most $\kappa$ if every point has a neighborhood of density at most $\kappa$. A subset $D\subseteq X$ is $\sigma$-closed-discrete if it is a countable union of subsets each of which is closed and discrete in $X$. A topological space is non-Archimedean if it has a base $\mathcal B$ such that any two members of $\mathcal B$ are either disjoint or one contains the other. A space has a point-countable base if it admits a base $\mathcal B$ such that every point belongs to at most countably many members of $\mathcal B$.

Question. Let $\kappa$ be a cardinal with $\kappa>\omega_1$. Is it consistent with ZFC that every perfect GO-space of local density at most $\kappa$ has a $\sigma$-closed-discrete dense subset? Equivalently, is it consistent with ZFC that every perfect non-Archimedean space of local density at most $\kappa$ is metrizable, and is it consistent with ZFC that every perfect GO-space of local density at most $\kappa$ admitting a point-countable base is metrizable?
status_search_result: The question is part of a known program of Bennett and Lutzer on perfect GO-spaces with $\sigma$-closed-discrete dense subsets. It is known that the property is axiom-sensitive (independent of ZFC for small cardinalities), and there is no published evidence that the consistency question for $\kappa>\omega_1$ has been resolved. The problem appears still open.

paper_title: Open Problems in Topology II
original_question: Let S denote the class of all separable metrizable spaces. A GO-space X is cleavable over S when, for each subset A of X, there is a continuous map f_A from X into a member of S that separates A from its complement, meaning f_A(x) is not equal to f_A(y) whenever x is in A and y is in X minus A. Characterize exactly which GO-spaces are cleavable over S without assuming restrictions on cardinal functions such as cellularity.
self_contained_problem:
A GO-space (generalized ordered space) is a triple $(X,\tau,<)$ where $<$ is a linear order on $X$ and $\tau$ is a Hausdorff topology on $X$ that has a base consisting of order-convex sets and is finer than (or equal to) the open-interval topology induced by $<$. Let $\mathcal{S}$ denote the class of all separable metrizable topological spaces. A topological space $X$ is said to be cleavable over $\mathcal{S}$ if for every subset $A\subseteq X$ there exist a space $Y_A\in\mathcal{S}$ and a continuous map $f_A:X\to Y_A$ such that $f_A(x)\neq f_A(y)$ whenever $x\in A$ and $y\in X\setminus A$.

Provide an intrinsic characterization of those GO-spaces $X$ that are cleavable over $\mathcal{S}$, without imposing any restriction on the cardinal functions of $X$ (such as cellularity, density, weight, etc.).
status_search_result: Partial results on cleavability of GO-spaces over separable metrizable spaces are known (e.g., Bennett–Byerly–Lutzer, "Cleavability in Ordered Spaces", Order 2001), giving characterizations under cardinal-function restrictions such as bounded cellularity. A full intrinsic characterization without such restrictions does not appear in the literature, and the problem is posed as open.

paper_title: Open Problems in Topology II
original_question: For a GO-space X, characterize exactly when X is cleavable over the real line R, meaning that for every subset A of X there is a continuous real-valued map f_A on X such that f_A(x) is not equal to f_A(y) whenever x is in A and y is in X minus A.
self_contained_problem:
Definitions. A linearly ordered topological space (LOTS) is a triple (X, <, τ) where < is a linear order on X and τ is the topology on X generated by the open intervals with respect to <. A generalized ordered space (GO-space) is a triple (X, <, τ) where < is a linear order on X and τ is a topology on X that has a base of order-convex sets and that refines the open interval topology induced by <.

Let M be a class of topological spaces. A topological space X is said to be cleavable over M if for every subset A ⊆ X there exist a space Y ∈ M and a continuous map f_A : X → Y such that f_A(x) ≠ f_A(y) whenever x ∈ A and y ∈ X \ A. When M = {ℝ} (the real line with its usual topology), this means: for every A ⊆ X there is a continuous function f_A : X → ℝ with f_A(x) ≠ f_A(y) for all x ∈ A and all y ∈ X \ A.

paper_title: Open Problems in Topology II
original_question: If X is a perfect monotonically Lindelof GO-space and Y is any subspace of X, must Y itself be monotonically Lindelof, where monotonically Lindelof means that open covers admit monotone choices of countable open refinements?
self_contained_problem:
A generalized ordered space (GO-space) is a triple $(X,\tau,<)$ where $<$ is a linear order on $X$ and $\tau$ is a Hausdorff topology on $X$ having a base consisting of order-convex sets (sets $C$ such that $a,b\in C$ and $a<x<b$ imply $x\in C$). Question: Let $X$ be a perfect monotonically Lindelöf GO-space, and let $Y\subseteq X$ be an arbitrary subspace (equipped with the induced order and the subspace topology). Must $Y$ be monotonically Lindelöf?

original_question: If X is a first-countable LOTS and X squared minus the diagonal is hereditarily paracompact, must X have a point-countable base? Also, can a Souslin space have the property that its square minus the diagonal is hereditarily paracompact?

context_brief: Bases of countable order in countably compact GO-spaces
original_question: Suppose X is a GO-space that is countably compact but not compact, and every compact subset of X is a metrizable G_delta subspace of X. Must X have a base of countable order?
self_contained_problem:
A generalized ordered space (GO-space) is a triple $(X,\tau,\le)$, where $\le$ is a linear order on $X$ and $\tau$ is a Hausdorff topology on $X$ having a base consisting of order-convex sets (sets $C\subseteq X$ such that whenever $a,b\in C$ and $a\le c\le b$, also $c\in C$). A space $X$ is countably compact if every countably infinite subset of $X$ has an accumulation point in $X$. A space $X$ has a base of countable order if there is a sequence $(\mathcal B_n)_{n\in\mathbb N}$ of bases for the topology of $X$ such that, for every $x\in X$ and every decreasing sequence $(B_n)$ with $x\in B_n\in\mathcal B_n$ for each $n$, the family $\{B_n:n\in\mathbb N\}$ is a local base at $x$. A subspace $Y\subseteq X$ is a $G_\delta$-subspace of $X$ if $Y=\bigcap_{n\in\mathbb N}U_n$ for some sequence of open subsets $U_n$ of $X$.

Question: Let $X$ be a GO-space that is countably compact but not compact, and assume that every compact subset of $X$ is a metrizable $G_\delta$-subspace of $X$. Must $X$ have a base of countable order?

paper_title: Open Problems in Topology II
context_brief: Branch-space representations of ordered real subsets
original_question: Let < be the usual ordering of the real line. For which subsets X of R does there exist a tree T, together with linear orderings of the nodes of T, such that no node of T contains an order-isomorphic copy of (X,<), while (X,<) itself is order-isomorphic to the branch space of T? In particular, which F_sigma_delta subsets of R are order-isomorphic to the branch space of some countable tree?
self_contained_problem:
Let $<$ denote the usual ordering of the real line $\mathbb{R}$. A tree is a partially ordered set $(T,\le_T)$ in which, for every $t\in T$, the set of predecessors $\{s\in T : s<_T t\}$ is well-ordered by $<_T$. A node of $T$ is a maximal antichain consisting of elements that all have the same set of strict predecessors (equivalently, the set of immediate successors of a fixed element together with the set of minimal elements forms the nodes). A branch of $T$ is a maximal linearly ordered subset of $T$. Suppose each node of $T$ is endowed with a linear ordering; then the set $B(T)$ of all branches of $T$ carries the lexicographic linear ordering induced by these node orderings, in which two distinct branches $b_1,b_2$ are compared by looking at the unique node containing both their splitting elements and using the linear order on that node. This linearly ordered set $B(T)$ is called the branch space of $T$.

(a) Characterize those subsets $X\subseteq \mathbb{R}$ for which there exists a tree $T$ together with linear orderings of the nodes of $T$ such that:
 (i) no node of $T$ contains, as a linearly ordered subset, a copy order-isomorphic to $(X,<)$; and
 (ii) $(X,<)$ is order-isomorphic to the branch space $B(T)$ of $T$.

(b) In particular, characterize precisely which $F_{\sigma\delta}$-subsets of $\mathbb{R}$ (i.e., subsets that are countable intersections of $F_\sigma$ sets in $\mathbb{R}$) are order-isomorphic to the branch space of some countable tree $T$ (with linearly ordered nodes).

It is known that both $\mathbb{R}$ and the space of irrationals $\mathbb{P}$ admit such representations, while the rationals $\mathbb{Q}$ do not.

paper_title: Some open problems in the theory of infinite dimensional algebras
original_question: Does there exist a finitely presented infinite torsion group, where a torsion group means a group in which every element has finite order?
self_contained_problem:
A group $G$ is called a torsion group (or periodic group) if every element $g \in G$ has finite order, i.e., there exists an integer $n = n(g) \geq 1$ such that $g^n = 1$. A group is finitely presented if it admits a presentation $\langle x_1, \dots, x_k \mid r_1, \dots, r_m \rangle$ with finitely many generators and finitely many defining relations.

Question: Does there exist an infinite, finitely presented torsion group?
status_search_result: The existence of an infinite finitely presented torsion group is a well-known long-standing open problem in combinatorial/geometric group theory. While infinite finitely generated torsion groups have been constructed (Golod–Shafarevich, Aleshin, Grigorchuk; and the Burnside groups B(m,n) for large n by Novikov–Adian, Ol'shanskii, Ivanov, Lysenok), no example is known to be finitely presented, and the problem still appears in current problem lists (e.g., Baumslag's open problems in combinatorial group theory).

   1 − m t_0 + H_R(t_0) < 0.

The Gelfand–Kirillov (GK) dimension of a finitely generated K-algebra B with generating subspace V is GKdim(B) = lim sup_{n→∞} log_n dim_K(V^n), and it is independent of the chosen finite-dimensional generating subspace.

paper_title: Some open problems in the theory of infinite dimensional algebras
original_question: Does there exist a division algebra that is finitely generated, algebraic, and infinite-dimensional?
self_contained_problem:
Let $K$ be a field. A $K$-algebra $D$ is called a division algebra if $D$ is an associative (not necessarily commutative) $K$-algebra with $1$ in which every nonzero element has a two-sided multiplicative inverse. We say $D$ is finitely generated (as a $K$-algebra) if there exist finitely many elements $d_1,\dots,d_n \in D$ such that $D$ is generated by $d_1,\dots,d_n$ together with $1$ under the operations of addition, scalar multiplication by $K$, and multiplication. We say $D$ is algebraic over $K$ if every element of $D$ is a root of some nonzero polynomial with coefficients in $K$. Finally, $D$ is infinite-dimensional if $\dim_K D = \infty$.

Does there exist a field $K$ and a $K$-algebra $D$ such that $D$ is simultaneously a division algebra, finitely generated as a $K$-algebra, algebraic over $K$, and infinite-dimensional over $K$?
status_search_result: This is the Kurosh problem for division rings, posed by A. G. Kurosh in 1941. While Golod–Shafarevich (1964) gave finitely generated infinite-dimensional algebraic (nil) algebras, the division-algebra case remains open: a finitely generated algebraic division ring is not known to be centrally finite. Recent work (e.g., the "Quantitative Kurosh Problem" in Forum of Mathematics Sigma and works on algebraicity of bounded degree in division rings, 2022) explicitly refers to it as still open.

original_question: Using the same Lie algebra generated by v_1 and v_2 from the self-similar derivation construction over the truncated polynomial algebra T, let U be its universal associative enveloping algebra and let Z be the center of U. Because powers of elements of the Lie algebra fall into Z, form the ring of fractions D = (Z \ {0})^{-1} U. Is D an algebraic division algebra?

  T = F[t_i : i ≥ 0] / (t_i^2 : i ≥ 0)
be the truncated polynomial algebra in countably many variables. For each i ≥ 0 let ∂_i denote the F-linear derivation of T determined by ∂_i(t_j) = δ_{ij}. Define two derivations of T recursively by the self-similar formulas
  v_1 = ∂_0 + t_1 · v_2',   v_2 = ∂_1 + t_2 · v_1',
where v_1' and v_2' are obtained from v_1 and v_2, respectively, by shifting all indices up by 1 (i.e. by replacing each t_i with t_{i+1} and each ∂_i with ∂_{i+1}). Equivalently, v_1 and v_2 are the unique derivations of T satisfying these self-similar identities.

  D = (Z \ {0})^{-1} U.

paper_title: Some Properties of and Open Problems on Hessian Nilpotent Polynomials
context_brief: Whether self-inverting series are automatically Hessian nilpotent
original_question: Let P(z) be a formal power series in C[[z]] with order at least 2 and with (Hes P)(0) nilpotent. Define its symmetric formal map F(z) = z - grad P(z); when the inverse has the form G(z) = z + grad Q(z), call Q(z) the inversion pair of P(z). If P is self-inverting, meaning Q(z) = P(z), must every such self-inverting polynomial or formal power series be Hessian nilpotent?
self_contained_problem:
Work over the formal power series ring $\mathbb{C}[[z]] = \mathbb{C}[[z_1, \dots, z_n]]$. For $P(z) \in \mathbb{C}[[z]]$, let $o(P)$ denote the order (lowest degree of a nonzero monomial), $\nabla P = (\partial P/\partial z_1, \dots, \partial P/\partial z_n)$ the gradient, and $\mathrm{Hes}(P) = (\partial^2 P/\partial z_i \partial z_j)$ the Hessian matrix. Call $P$ Hessian nilpotent (HN) if $\mathrm{Hes}(P)$ is a nilpotent matrix over $\mathbb{C}[[z]]$.

Assume $P(z) \in \mathbb{C}[[z]]$ satisfies $o(P) \ge 2$ and $(\mathrm{Hes}\,P)(0)$ is nilpotent. Define the symmetric formal map
$$F(z) = z - \nabla P(z).$$
Under these hypotheses one can show that $F$ has a formal inverse $G(z)$ and that $G(z)$ can be uniquely written in the form
$$G(z) = z + \nabla Q(z)$$
for some $Q(z) \in \mathbb{C}[[z]]$ with $o(Q) \ge 2$. The series $Q(z)$ is called the inversion pair of $P(z)$.

Say that $P(z)$ is self-inverting if $Q(z) = P(z)$.

Question: must every self-inverting polynomial (or, more generally, every self-inverting formal power series) $P(z) \in \mathbb{C}[[z]]$ necessarily be Hessian nilpotent?
status_search_result: A search returned the original problem listing and related work on Hessian nilpotent polynomials and the Jacobian conjecture, but no source was found that resolves whether every self-inverting polynomial or formal power series must be Hessian nilpotent. The problem appears to remain unresolved, but no definitive recent statement was located.

paper_title: Some Properties of and Open Problems on Hessian Nilpotent Polynomials
context_brief: Possible failure of the Vanishing Conjecture for non-polynomial Hessian nilpotent series
original_question: Does there exist a Hessian nilpotent formal power series P(z) in C[[z]] that is not a polynomial and for which the Vanishing Conjecture fails? Equivalently, can one find a non-polynomial Hessian nilpotent formal power series over C for which Delta^m(P(z)^(m+1)) does not vanish for all sufficiently large m, or prove that no such example exists?
self_contained_problem:
Let $\mathbb{C}[[z]]=\mathbb{C}[[z_1,\dots,z_n]]$ denote the ring of formal power series in $n$ variables over $\mathbb{C}$, and let $\Delta=\sum_{i=1}^n \partial^2/\partial z_i^2$ denote the Laplace operator. A formal power series $P(z)\in\mathbb{C}[[z]]$ is called Hessian nilpotent (HN) if its Hessian matrix $\mathrm{Hess}(P)=(\partial^2 P/\partial z_i\partial z_j)$ is nilpotent as a matrix over $\mathbb{C}[[z]]$. The Vanishing Conjecture (VC) for $P(z)$ asserts that
$$\Delta^m\!\bigl(P(z)^{m+1}\bigr)=0\quad\text{for all sufficiently large }m\ge 1.$$

Determine whether there exists a Hessian nilpotent formal power series $P(z)\in\mathbb{C}[[z]]\setminus\mathbb{C}[z]$ (i.e., not a polynomial) for which the Vanishing Conjecture fails — that is, $\Delta^m(P^{m+1})\ne 0$ for infinitely many $m$ — or, alternatively, prove that no such non-polynomial counterexample exists.
status_search_result: A literature search shows the Vanishing Conjecture for Hessian nilpotent series is an active reduction of the Jacobian Conjecture, and no counterexample (polynomial or non-polynomial) appears in the available sources. The problem of finding a non-polynomial HN formal power series violating the VC, or proving none exists, does not appear to have been resolved.

paper_title: Some Properties of and Open Problems on Hessian Nilpotent Polynomials
original_question: Let C^n carry the standard C-bilinear form <., .>, and let X(C^n) be the set of isotropic vectors alpha with <alpha, alpha> = 0. Let P(z) be a homogeneous harmonic polynomial of degree d >= 2 over C written as P(z) = sum_{i=1}^k h_{alpha_i}(z)^d, where h_alpha(z) = <alpha, z> and each alpha_i lies in X(C^n). Define the graph G(P) to have vertex set {1, 2, ..., k}, with vertices i and j joined by an edge exactly when <alpha_i, alpha_j> is nonzero; regard G(P) as labeled when an edge i--j is assigned the value <alpha_i, alpha_j>, and in the even-degree variant when the edge label is h_{alpha_i}(z)^((d-2)/2) <alpha_i, alpha_j> h_{alpha_j}(z)^((d-2)/2). What necessary or sufficient conditions on this labeled graph G(P) ensure that P(z) is Hessian nilpotent?
self_contained_problem:
Equip $\mathbb{C}^n$ with the standard symmetric $\mathbb{C}$-bilinear form $\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle$ given by $\langle u,v\rangle=\sum_{i=1}^n u_i v_i$, and let $X(\mathbb{C}^n)=\{\alpha\in\mathbb{C}^n:\langle\alpha,\alpha\rangle=0\}$ denote the set of isotropic vectors. For $\alpha\in\mathbb{C}^n$ set $h_\alpha(z)=\langle\alpha,z\rangle\in\mathbb{C}[z_1,\dots,z_n]$. A polynomial $P(z)\in\mathbb{C}[z_1,\dots,z_n]$ is called Hessian nilpotent if its Hessian matrix $\mathrm{Hess}(P)=\bigl(\partial^2 P/\partial z_i\partial z_j\bigr)$ is a nilpotent matrix over $\mathbb{C}[z_1,\dots,z_n]$.

Fix an integer $d\geq 2$ and let $P(z)$ be a homogeneous harmonic polynomial of degree $d$ (i.e., $\Delta P=0$ where $\Delta=\sum_i\partial^2/\partial z_i^2$) written in the form
$$P(z)=\sum_{i=1}^{k} h_{\alpha_i}(z)^{d}, \qquad \alpha_1,\dots,\alpha_k\in X(\mathbb{C}^n).$$

Associate to $P$ the labeled graph $G(P)$ with vertex set $[k]=\{1,2,\dots,k\}$ defined by: vertices $i\neq j$ are joined by an edge if and only if $\langle\alpha_i,\alpha_j\rangle\neq 0$. Consider two labelings of the edges of $G(P)$:

(i) the scalar labeling, where edge $i\text{--}j$ is labeled by $\langle\alpha_i,\alpha_j\rangle\in\mathbb{C}$;

(ii) for even $d$, the polynomial labeling, where edge $i\text{--}j$ is labeled by $h_{\alpha_i}(z)^{(d-2)/2}\,\langle\alpha_i,\alpha_j\rangle\,h_{\alpha_j}(z)^{(d-2)/2}\in\mathbb{C}[z_1,\dots,z_n]$.

Find necessary or sufficient conditions, formulated purely in terms of the combinatorics of the labeled graph $G(P)$ (under either labeling), which ensure that $P(z)$ is Hessian nilpotent.
status_search_result: The question is presented as an open problem in the study of Hessian nilpotent polynomials, motivated by the Jacobian conjecture. Partial results exist (e.g., complete descriptions of the graphs of HN polynomials when the span of the isotropic vectors has dimension at most 2 or at least s−2), but a full graph-theoretic characterization in general remains unresolved.

paper_title: Topological Open Problems in the Geometry of Banach Spaces
context_brief: Nonlinear transfer of Kadec and strictly convex norms
original_question: Let X and Y be normed spaces. Characterize the nonlinear maps Φ:X→Y with the following transfer property: whenever Y admits a Kadec norm, X also admits a Kadec norm; and whenever Y admits a strictly convex norm, X also admits a strictly convex norm. Here a Kadec norm is a norm for which the weak topology and the norm topology coincide on the unit sphere, and a strictly convex norm is one whose unit sphere contains no nontrivial line segment.
self_contained_problem:
Let $X$ and $Y$ be (real) normed linear spaces. A norm $\|\cdot\|$ on a normed space $Z$ is called a Kadec norm if the weak topology and the norm topology coincide on the unit sphere $S_Z = \{z \in Z : \|z\| = 1\}$. The norm is called strictly convex (or rotund) if its unit sphere contains no nontrivial line segment, equivalently, if $\|z_1\| = \|z_2\| = 1$ and $z_1 \neq z_2$ imply $\|\tfrac{1}{2}(z_1 + z_2)\| < 1$.

Say that a (not necessarily linear) map $\Phi : X \to Y$ has the Kadec transfer property if, whenever $Y$ admits an equivalent Kadec norm, then $X$ also admits an equivalent Kadec norm. Similarly, $\Phi$ has the strictly convex transfer property if, whenever $Y$ admits an equivalent strictly convex norm, then $X$ admits an equivalent strictly convex norm.

Problem. Give an intrinsic characterization of those nonlinear maps $\Phi : X \to Y$ that possess the Kadec transfer property, and of those that possess the strictly convex transfer property. In particular, identify natural classes of nonlinear maps (for example, uniform homeomorphisms, Lipschitz maps, coarse equivalences, or maps satisfying a prescribed modulus of continuity) that ensure these renorming properties pass from $Y$ to $X$.
status_search_result: No published characterization of nonlinear maps transferring Kadec or strictly convex renormings was found. Related work establishes preservation of such renorming properties under linear isomorphisms and certain uniform/Lipschitz equivalences, but a general characterization in the nonlinear setting appears to remain unresolved.

paper_title: Topological Open Problems in the Geometry of Banach Spaces
original_question: Are descriptive Banach spaces exactly the σ-fragmented Banach spaces, or is one of these two classes strictly larger? In this setting, a descriptive Banach space is a Banach space whose norm topology has a network that is the countable union of subfamilies which are isolated or discrete in their union for the weak topology.
self_contained_problem:
Let $(X, \|\cdot\|)$ be a Banach space, and let $\tau$ denote its norm topology and $w$ its weak topology. A family $\mathcal{N}$ of subsets of $X$ is called a network for $\tau$ if every $\tau$-open set is a union of members of $\mathcal{N}$. A family $\mathcal{F}$ of subsets of $X$ is said to be isolated (or discrete in its union) for the weak topology if, equipping $Y := \bigcup\{F : F \in \mathcal{F}\}$ with the relative weak topology, every point of $Y$ has a $w$-open neighborhood meeting at most one member of $\mathcal{F}$.

Call $X$ a descriptive Banach space if $\tau$ admits a network $\mathcal{N} = \bigcup_{n=1}^{\infty} \mathcal{N}_n$ such that, for each $n$, the subfamily $\mathcal{N}_n$ is isolated for the weak topology in its union.

Call $X$ a $\sigma$-fragmented Banach space (with respect to the norm) if for every $\varepsilon > 0$ there is a decomposition $X = \bigcup_{n=1}^{\infty} X_n^\varepsilon$ such that, for each $n$ and each nonempty subset $A \subseteq X_n^\varepsilon$, there exists a weakly open set $U \subseteq X$ with $U \cap A \neq \emptyset$ and $\|\cdot\|$-diameter of $U \cap A$ less than $\varepsilon$.

Question: Does the class of descriptive Banach spaces coincide with the class of $\sigma$-fragmented Banach spaces, or is one of these classes strictly larger than the other?
status_search_result: Web searches surface the standard literature on σ-fragmentability and descriptive Banach spaces (Jayne–Namioka–Rogers, Cascales–Namioka, Oncina–Raja) and various surveys of open problems in Banach space geometry, but no source found explicitly settles whether the two classes coincide. The status appears to remain unresolved, but no definitive source was located confirming it as still open as of the search date.

paper_title: Topological Open Problems in the Geometry of Banach Spaces
context_brief: Radon-Nikodym property and Kadec or rotund renorming
original_question: Let X be a Banach space with the Radon-Nikodym property, meaning every bounded closed convex subset of X has slices of arbitrarily small diameter. Must X admit an equivalent Kadec norm? Must X admit an equivalent rotund, equivalently strictly convex, norm?
self_contained_problem:
A Banach space $X$ is said to have the Radon–Nikodým property (RNP) if every bounded closed convex subset of $X$ admits slices of arbitrarily small diameter (where a slice of a bounded convex set $C$ is a nonempty intersection of $C$ with an open half-space).

An equivalent norm $|\!|\!|\cdot|\!|\!|$ on $X$ is called:
- a Kadec norm if on the unit sphere $\{x\in X:|\!|\!|x|\!|\!|=1\}$ the weak topology and the norm topology coincide;
- rotund (equivalently, strictly convex) if whenever $|\!|\!|x|\!|\!|=|\!|\!|y|\!|\!|=1$ and $x\neq y$, then $|\!|\!|(x+y)/2|\!|\!|<1$.

Question: Must every Banach space $X$ with the Radon–Nikodým property admit an equivalent Kadec norm? Must every such $X$ admit an equivalent rotund norm?
status_search_result: The question of whether every Banach space with the Radon–Nikodým property admits an equivalent rotund (and equivalently a Kadec) renorming appears to still be open. Survey-style sources note that for RNP spaces, the existence of equivalent LUR, Kadec, and rotund norms is known to be equivalent, but no general construction is known. A positive answer is known in the dual case (every dual space with RNP admits an equivalent LUR norm), but the general non-dual case remains unresolved.

paper_title: Topological Open Problems in the Geometry of Banach Spaces
original_question: If a Banach space X has a Fréchet differentiable norm, must X admit an equivalent locally uniformly rotund norm? A norm is locally uniformly rotund when, for every sequence x_n and point x, the condition 2||x||^2+2||x_n||^2−||x+x_n||^2→0 implies ||x−x_n||→0.
self_contained_problem:
Let X be a real Banach space. A norm ‖·‖ on X is said to be Fréchet differentiable if at every nonzero point x ∈ X the limit
  lim_{t→0} (‖x+th‖ − ‖x‖)/t
exists uniformly for h in the unit sphere of X. A norm ‖·‖ on X is called locally uniformly rotund (LUR) if for every x ∈ X and every sequence (x_n) in X,
  lim_{n→∞} (2‖x‖² + 2‖x_n‖² − ‖x + x_n‖²) = 0   ⟹   lim_{n→∞} ‖x − x_n‖ = 0.
Two norms on X are called equivalent if they induce the same topology.

Question: Suppose X admits an equivalent Fréchet differentiable norm. Does X necessarily admit an equivalent locally uniformly rotund norm?
status_search_result: The implication "Fréchet differentiable renorming ⇒ LUR renorming" is a well-known open problem in the geometry of Banach spaces. Partial positive results exist (e.g., when the dual norm is also Gâteaux differentiable, or when X has an unconditional basis), but the general question remains unresolved in the literature available through 2026.

paper_title: Topological Open Problems in the Geometry of Banach Spaces
context_brief: Pointwise Borel structure and LUR renorming for Baire-one compacta
original_question: Let Γ be a Polish space and let K⊂R^Γ be a compact set of Baire-one functions such that every function in K has at most countably many discontinuities. For C(K), do the Borel sets generated by the pointwise topology and by the supremum norm topology coincide? Is the identity map from C(K) with the pointwise topology to C(K) with the supremum norm σ-continuous? Does C(K) admit an equivalent locally uniformly rotund norm?
self_contained_problem:
Let Γ be a Polish space, and let K ⊂ ℝ^Γ be a pointwise compact set of Baire-one functions on Γ such that every function f ∈ K has at most countably many points of discontinuity. Let C(K) denote the Banach space of continuous real-valued functions on K endowed with the supremum norm ‖·‖_∞, and let C_p(K) denote the same vector space endowed with the topology of pointwise convergence on K. Answer the following three questions:

(a) Do the σ-algebras of Borel subsets of C(K) generated by the pointwise topology and by the norm topology coincide?

(b) Is the identity map Id : C_p(K) → (C(K), ‖·‖_∞) σ-continuous, i.e., can C(K) be written as a countable union of sets on each of which the identity is continuous from the pointwise to the norm topology?

(c) Does C(K) admit an equivalent locally uniformly rotund (LUR) norm? (A norm ‖·‖ is LUR if, whenever x_n, x ∈ C(K) satisfy 2‖x‖² + 2‖x_n‖² − ‖x + x_n‖² → 0, then ‖x_n − x‖ → 0.)

paper_title: Tensegrity frameworks: Dynamic analysis review and open problems
original_question: For a tensegrity structure whose feasible configurations are embedded in a lower-dimensional subspace of the chosen parameterization space, how can one compute a shape-control or path-planning trajectory between two feasible configurations, taking into account environmental and internal constraints such as non-intersecting bars and the robot kinematic and dynamic models?
status_search_result: Partial solutions exist for specific classes: analytic identification of the prestressable equilibrium manifold for symmetric prism tensegrities with search-based feasible-path generation, RRT-Connect-based collision-free planners for tensegrity shape control, and a semidefinite-programming formulation for flying tensegrity robots that restricts deformations to the cone of positive-definite matrices. A fully general algorithm handling arbitrary topologies, bar non-intersection, and full kinematic/dynamic feasibility on the lower-dimensional feasible manifold remains open.

paper_title: Open Problems in Algebraic Statistics
original_question: Does the collection of known polynomial invariants of degree at most 9 cut out the algebraic variety of 4×4×4 contingency tables (pijk) over C that have tensor rank at most 4, equivalently tables admitting a decomposition pijk = ρAi·σAj·θAk + ρCi·σCj·θCk + ρGi·σGj·θGk + ρTi·σTj·θTk for i, j, k ∈ {A, C, G, T}?
self_contained_problem:
Work over the complex numbers. Let $I=\{A,C,G,T\}$ and consider the 64-dimensional space $\mathbb{C}^4\otimes\mathbb{C}^4\otimes\mathbb{C}^4$ of $4\times 4\times 4$ tables $(p_{ijk})_{i,j,k\in I}$. Define the variety $X\subset\mathbb{C}^{4\times 4\times 4}$ to be the Zariski closure of the set of tensors of tensor rank at most $4$, i.e. tables admitting a decomposition
$$p_{ijk}=\rho^A_i\sigma^A_j\theta^A_k+\rho^C_i\sigma^C_j\theta^C_k+\rho^G_i\sigma^G_j\theta^G_k+\rho^T_i\sigma^T_j\theta^T_k$$
for vectors $\rho^a,\sigma^a,\theta^a\in\mathbb{C}^4$, $a\in I$. Three families of homogeneous polynomials are known to vanish on $X$:
(i) the degree-$5$ "Strassen commutativity" polynomials,
(ii) the degree-$6$ Landsberg–Manivel polynomials, and
(iii) certain degree-$9$ symmetrization polynomials.
Question: Do these known polynomials of degree at most $9$ cut out $X$ set-theoretically; that is, is $X$ equal to the common zero locus in $\mathbb{C}^{4\times 4\times 4}$ of these polynomials?
status_search_result: This is the set-theoretic version of Allman's "salmon conjecture" for the fourth secant variety of the Segre embedding of $\mathbb{P}^3\times\mathbb{P}^3\times\mathbb{P}^3$. paper_title: Open Problems in Algebraic Statistics
original_question: Which projective varieties M in projective space P^n have maximum likelihood degree 1, meaning that for generic data vector (u0, u1, ..., un) the restriction of the likelihood function L(p0, p1, ..., pn) = p0^u0 · p1^u1 · ... · pn^un / (p0 + p1 + ··· + pn)^(u0 + u1 + ··· + un) to M has exactly one complex critical point after excluding singular points of M and points where L has poles or zeros?
self_contained_problem:
Let $M \subseteq \mathbb{P}^n$ be an irreducible complex projective variety, and consider the likelihood function
$$L(p_0,p_1,\dots,p_n) = \frac{p_0^{u_0}\, p_1^{u_1} \cdots p_n^{u_n}}{(p_0+p_1+\cdots+p_n)^{u_0+u_1+\cdots+u_n}},$$
where $u=(u_0,u_1,\dots,u_n)$ is a generic integer (or complex) data vector. The maximum likelihood degree (ML degree) of $M$ is defined as the number of complex critical points of the restriction $L|_M$, where one excludes the singular locus of $M$ and the points where $L$ has a zero or a pole (i.e., points lying on the divisor $\{p_0 p_1 \cdots p_n (p_0+\cdots+p_n)=0\}$).

Problem: Give a geometric characterization of all projective varieties $M \subseteq \mathbb{P}^n$ whose ML degree equals $1$, i.e., those varieties on which, for generic $u$, the restricted likelihood function has exactly one complex critical point.
status_search_result: June Huh (2013/2014, "Varieties with maximum likelihood degree one") established a geometric characterization: a projective variety has ML degree one if and only if it is the image of a reduced A-discriminantal variety under a monomial map with finite fibers, with the maximum likelihood estimator given explicitly by Kapranov's Horn uniformization. This resolves the question as originally posed.

paper_title: Open Problems in Algebraic Statistics
original_question: What relationship, if any, does the maximum likelihood degree of an algebraic statistical model have to the convergence properties of numerical statistical algorithms such as iterative proportional scaling and the EM algorithm?
self_contained_problem:
Let M be an algebraic statistical model, i.e. a statistical model whose parameter space (or whose set of probability distributions) is described as the intersection of an algebraic variety with the probability simplex. Given i.i.d. data, the maximum likelihood estimation problem on M consists of maximizing the log-likelihood function over M. The maximum likelihood degree (ML degree) of M is defined as the number of complex critical points of the likelihood function on the Zariski closure of M, for generic data.

Two standard numerical procedures used to compute maximum likelihood estimates on such models are:
(i) iterative proportional scaling (IPS), used for hierarchical log-linear models on contingency tables, which cyclically rescales the current estimate to match observed marginal totals; and
(ii) the expectation–maximization (EM) algorithm, an iterative method that alternates between computing expected sufficient statistics under current parameter values and re-maximizing the complete-data log-likelihood.

Establish a precise relationship between the ML degree of M and the convergence behavior (e.g., rate of convergence, number of limit points, dependence on starting values, occurrence of local maxima, or computational complexity) of IPS and the EM algorithm when applied to M. In particular, determine whether and how the ML degree quantitatively governs or bounds the convergence properties of these algorithms.
status_search_result: Web searches turned up extensive literature on convergence of EM and on iterative proportional scaling (including modern optimization perspectives), and on the ML degree as an algebraic invariant, but no systematic results directly linking the ML degree of an algebraic statistical model to convergence rates or behavior of EM or IPS. The question appears to remain open, with no published comprehensive study addressing this specific relationship.

paper_title: Open Problems in Algebraic Statistics
original_question: For the DNA alignment example whose model M is the set of positive 4×4 matrices (pij) of rank at most 2 and whose likelihood function is L = (∏i pii)^4 · (∏i≠j pij)^2 · (∑i,j pij)^−40, is the matrix (1/40)·[[3,3,2,2],[3,3,2,2],[2,2,3,3],[2,2,3,3]] a global maximum of L?
self_contained_problem:
Let $M$ denote the set of all positive $4\times 4$ matrices $P=(p_{ij})_{1\le i,j\le 4}$ (i.e., $p_{ij}>0$) of rank at most $2$. Consider the likelihood function $L:M\to\mathbb{R}_{>0}$ defined by
$$L(P) \;=\; \Bigl(\prod_{i=1}^{4} p_{ii}\Bigr)^{4} \cdot \Bigl(\prod_{i\ne j} p_{ij}\Bigr)^{2} \cdot \Bigl(\sum_{i,j=1}^{4} p_{ij}\Bigr)^{-40}.$$
Decide whether the matrix
$$\widehat{P} \;=\; \frac{1}{40}\begin{pmatrix} 3 & 3 & 2 & 2 \\ 3 & 3 & 2 & 2 \\ 2 & 2 & 3 & 3 \\ 2 & 2 & 3 & 3 \end{pmatrix}$$
is a global maximum of $L$ on $M$.

paper_title: Open Problems in Algebraic Statistics
original_question: For a centered multivariate Gaussian random vector X = (X1, ..., Xn) on R^n with positive-definite covariance matrix Σ, which collections of conditional independence statements of the form Xi is independent of Xj given X_K, where i and j are distinct indices and K is a subset of the remaining indices, can be realized? Equivalently, characterize the Gaussian conditional independence models: semi-algebraic subsets of the cone PD_n of real positive-definite symmetric n×n matrices defined by equations det(Σ_{{i}∪K,{j}∪K}) = 0, where this determinant is the almost-principal minor associated with the conditional independence statement Xi independent of Xj given X_K.
self_contained_problem:
Let $X = (X_1, \dots, X_n)$ be a centered Gaussian random vector on $\mathbb{R}^n$ with positive-definite covariance matrix $\Sigma \in \mathrm{PD}_n$, where $\mathrm{PD}_n$ denotes the cone of real symmetric positive-definite $n\times n$ matrices. For distinct indices $i,j \in \{1,\dots,n\}$ and a subset $K \subseteq \{1,\dots,n\}\setminus\{i,j\}$, the conditional independence statement "$X_i \perp\!\!\!\perp X_j \mid X_K$" holds if and only if the almost-principal minor
$$[i \perp\!\!\!\perp j \mid K] \;:=\; \det\bigl(\Sigma_{\{i\}\cup K,\;\{j\}\cup K}\bigr) \;=\; 0,$$
where $\Sigma_{A,B}$ denotes the submatrix of $\Sigma$ with row indices $A$ and column indices $B$.

Define a Gaussian conditional independence (GCI) model to be any semi-algebraic subset of $\mathrm{PD}_n$ that can be cut out by polynomial equations of the form $[i \perp\!\!\!\perp j \mid K] = 0$.

Problem: Characterize all collections $\mathcal{C}$ of conditional independence statements $\{i \perp\!\!\!\perp j \mid K\}$ that are realizable in the sense that there exists $\Sigma \in \mathrm{PD}_n$ for which the set of CI statements holding for $\Sigma$ equals $\mathcal{C}$. Equivalently, give a description of the GCI models as semi-algebraic subsets of $\mathrm{PD}_n$.
status_search_result: The general characterization of realizable Gaussian conditional independence structures is open. It is known there is no finite complete axiomatization of Gaussian CI relations (Šimeček; Sullivant), and the CI implication problem is undecidable. Realizability of gaussoids has been characterized only for small $n$ (e.g., $n=4$); no general forbidden-minor or finite characterization is known for larger ground sets.

paper_title: Open Problems in Algebraic Statistics
context_brief: Rational points on strict CI models
original_question: Does every strict conditional independence model for discrete random variables have a Q-rational point? Here a strict conditional independence model is the intersection of the positive orthant with the constructible set of tables for which a specified collection of conditional independence statements Xi ⊥⊥ Xj | XK holds and all other such statements do not hold.
self_contained_problem:
Let $X_1, \ldots, X_n$ be discrete random variables with $X_i$ taking values in a finite set of cardinality $d_i$. A joint distribution is represented by a nonnegative tensor $p = (p_{x_1,\ldots,x_n}) \in \mathbb{R}_{\geq 0}^{d_1 \times \cdots \times d_n}$ with $\sum p_{x_1,\ldots,x_n} = 1$. For disjoint subsets $i, j \in \{1,\ldots,n\}$ and $K \subseteq \{1,\ldots,n\} \setminus \{i,j\}$, the conditional independence (CI) statement $X_i \perp\!\!\!\perp X_j \mid X_K$ corresponds to a system of polynomial (quadratic) equations in the entries of $p$ (vanishing of certain $2\times 2$ minors of suitable flattenings).

Fix a collection $\mathcal{C}$ of CI statements among $\{X_1, \ldots, X_n\}$. The strict CI variety associated with $\mathcal{C}$ is the constructible subset of $\mathbb{R}^{d_1 \times \cdots \times d_n}$ consisting of all tensors $p$ such that every CI statement in $\mathcal{C}$ holds and every CI statement not in $\mathcal{C}$ fails. The strict CI model is the intersection of this constructible set with the strictly positive orthant (equivalently, the set of strictly positive probability tensors realizing exactly the CI statements in $\mathcal{C}$).

Question: Does every nonempty strict CI model (over all choices of $n$, dimensions $d_1, \ldots, d_n$, and collections $\mathcal{C}$) contain a point with all coordinates in $\mathbb{Q}$?
status_search_result: The question is posed as a "bonus problem" in a list of open problems in algebraic statistics. A web search did not reveal any subsequent paper resolving the existence of $\mathbb{Q}$-rational points on every strict CI model for discrete random variables; related literature on CI ideals, primary decompositions, and graphical model geometry does not address this specific rationality question. The problem appears to remain open.

paper_title: Eight Open Problems in Distributed Computing
original_question: For randomized wait-free consensus against a weak adversary that cannot observe private coin flips before they are made public, where an O(log n) per-process work protocol is known using multi-writer registers, can one prove a nontrivial lower bound, ideally an Omega(log n) lower bound, for multi-writer registers or even for stronger objects such as unit-cost snapshots?
self_contained_problem:
Consider the standard asynchronous shared-memory model with n processes that communicate via atomic registers. The (binary or multi-valued) consensus problem requires each process to start with an input value, eventually decide a value, such that all decisions agree (Agreement), every decided value was some process's input (Validity), and every nonfaulty process eventually decides (Termination, here in the wait-free sense: any number of processes may fail by crashing). Algorithms may be randomized, with each process tossing private local coins, and the cost measure is per-process work (i.e., the worst-case expected number of shared-memory steps performed by a single process). The scheduling is controlled by an adversary; here the adversary is "weak" in the sense that it cannot observe the outcome of a coin flip until that outcome has been written to a shared register (i.e., made public).

It is known that under such a weak adversary, randomized wait-free consensus is solvable with O(log n) expected work per process using multi-writer atomic registers. 

Problem: Prove a nontrivial lower bound on the per-process expected work for randomized wait-free consensus among n processes against a weak adversary that cannot observe coin flips before they are made public, in the shared-memory model with multi-writer atomic registers (and, more generally, with stronger primitives such as unit-cost atomic snapshot objects). Ideally, establish a matching Ω(log n) per-process lower bound, or otherwise show any superconstant lower bound in these models.
category_tag: distributed computing / randomized consensus lower bounds
status_search_result: Existing lower bounds for randomized consensus under weak/oblivious adversaries (Attiya–Censor; later work) address termination-probability versus total step complexity tradeoffs and Ω(n) register-count bounds, but no nontrivial per-process work lower bound (let alone Ω(log n)) for multi-writer registers or unit-cost snapshots against a weak adversary appears in the literature. Upper bounds have actually improved (e.g., O(log log n) per step expected with multi-writer registers under an oblivious adversary), widening the gap. The problem appears to remain open.

paper_title: Eight Open Problems in Distributed Computing
context_brief: Oblivious routing C plus D objective
original_question: In oblivious routing, let C be congestion and D be the maximum path length produced by the routing. Which classes of networks admit oblivious routing algorithms for which C + D is close to the offline optimum, so that packet delivery can be scheduled in time proportional to C + D?
self_contained_problem:
Consider packet routing in an undirected network $G=(V,E)$. A routing instance consists of a multiset of source-destination pairs $\{(s_i,t_i)\}_{i=1}^k$, one packet per pair. A routing scheme assigns to each pair $(s_i,t_i)$ a path $P_i$ from $s_i$ to $t_i$ in $G$. Given such an assignment, define
- the congestion $C = \max_{e \in E} |\{ i : e \in P_i \}|$,
- the dilation $D = \max_i |P_i|$ (the maximum hop-length of any chosen path).

It is known that, given the paths, the packets can then be scheduled and delivered in time $O(C+D)$. A routing scheme is called oblivious if the path $P_i$ chosen for the pair $(s_i,t_i)$ depends only on $(s_i,t_i)$ (and possibly private randomness) and not on the other source-destination pairs in the instance.

The offline optimum for an instance is $\mathrm{OPT}(G,\{(s_i,t_i)\}) = \min (C^* + D^*)$, where the minimum is over all path assignments and $C^*, D^*$ are the corresponding congestion and dilation.

Problem. Characterize, or exhibit, classes of networks $G$ that admit an oblivious routing algorithm $\mathcal{A}$ such that for every routing instance the resulting congestion $C$ and dilation $D$ satisfy
$$ C + D \;\le\; f(|V|) \cdot \mathrm{OPT}(G,\{(s_i,t_i)\}) $$
for some small (e.g. polylogarithmic) factor $f$, so that packets can be delivered in time proportional to $C+D$ that is close to the offline optimum.
status_search_result: Ghaffari, Haeupler, and Zuzic (STOC 2021, "Hop-Constrained Oblivious Routing") proved that every undirected network admits an oblivious routing scheme whose (congestion + dilation) is within a poly(log n) factor of the offline optimum, resolving this question affirmatively for general undirected graphs. Earlier work had given matching results for specific classes (e.g. d-dimensional meshes within an O(d^2) factor). Subsequent work (Haeupler–Hershkowitz–Zuzic STOC 2022; electrical-flow based schemes, ITCS 2024) refines the bounds and gives efficient constructions.

paper_title: Eight Open Problems in Distributed Computing
context_brief: Stability bounds for memoryless symmetric consensus
original_question: For memoryless symmetric ongoing consensus functions, where the function output is invariant under permutations of input positions, how can the approximately factor-2 gap between known upper and lower bounds on the number of output changes be closed, and how should non-geodesic input-change paths be analyzed to distinguish and evaluate the performance of different consensus functions?
self_contained_problem:
Consider the long-lived consensus problem in the following abstract form. Let $n \ge 1$ and let $f : \{0,1\}^n \to \{0,1\}$ be a Boolean function that is symmetric, i.e. invariant under all permutations of its $n$ input coordinates: $f(x_{\sigma(1)}, \dots, x_{\sigma(n)}) = f(x_1, \dots, x_n)$ for every permutation $\sigma \in S_n$. The function $f$ is interpreted as a memoryless consensus rule: at each time step $t$, given an input vector $x^{(t)} \in \{0,1\}^n$, the system outputs $f(x^{(t)})$, with no dependence on past inputs or outputs.

Given an input path, that is a sequence $x^{(0)}, x^{(1)}, \dots, x^{(T)} \in \{0,1\}^n$ in which consecutive vectors differ in at most one coordinate, define the number of output changes along the path as
$$ \mathrm{OC}(f; x^{(0)},\dots,x^{(T)}) \;=\; \#\bigl\{\, t \in \{1,\dots,T\} : f(x^{(t)}) \neq f(x^{(t-1)}) \,\bigr\}. $$
A path is called geodesic if it realizes the Hamming distance between its endpoints, i.e. $T = \|x^{(T)} - x^{(0)}\|_1$ and no coordinate is flipped more than once.

The "instability" of $f$ is the worst-case rate of output changes over admissible input paths. Known results provide an upper bound $U(n)$ and a lower bound $L(n)$ on this instability for symmetric memoryless rules, valid uniformly over $f$, with $U(n)/L(n)$ tending to a constant approximately equal to $2$ as $n \to \infty$.

(a) Determine the exact asymptotic instability of memoryless symmetric consensus, thereby closing the factor-$2$ gap between $U(n)$ and $L(n)$.

(b) Extend the analysis to non-geodesic input paths (paths in which coordinates may be flipped repeatedly) and develop quantitative measures based on such paths that distinguish and rank different symmetric consensus functions $f$ according to their output-change behavior.
status_search_result: Related work (e.g., Davidovitch–Dolev–Rajsbaum on stability of long-lived consensus and a 2011 arXiv preprint "Geodesic stability for memoryless binary long-lived consensus") addresses bounds on output changes for symmetric memoryless consensus, but no source found indicates the factor-2 gap has been closed or that a non-geodesic-path framework for separating consensus functions has been developed. The question therefore appears to remain open.

paper_title: Eight Open Problems in Distributed Computing
original_question: For wait-free linearizable implementations of an m-component atomic snapshot object from shared registers, where SCAN returns a consistent view of all components and UPDATE changes one component, what are the tight space-time tradeoffs for SCAN time beyond the known space-optimal lower bound and the best known upper bounds? In particular, can the gap between existing lower bounds for implementations using a fixed number of registers and the known O(n)-time implementations using many or unbounded registers be closed?
self_contained_problem:
Consider the asynchronous shared-memory model in which n processes communicate via atomic single-writer or multi-writer read/write registers. An m-component atomic snapshot object stores a vector of m values and supports two operations: UPDATE(i, v), which sets the i-th component to value v, and SCAN, which returns the entire vector of m component values consistent with a single instantaneous moment. An implementation of such an object from base registers is required to be wait-free (every operation terminates in a finite number of its own steps regardless of the behavior of other processes) and linearizable (each operation appears to take effect atomically at some point during its execution).

The time complexity of a SCAN is measured by the worst-case number of steps performed by a process executing a SCAN. The space complexity is the number of base registers used. It is known that any implementation using exactly m base registers requires Ω(mn) steps for SCAN in the worst case, while implementations using a larger (possibly unbounded) number of registers can achieve SCAN time O(n).

Determine the tight space-time tradeoff between the number of base registers used and the worst-case SCAN step complexity for wait-free linearizable implementations of an m-component atomic snapshot object. In particular, close the gap between the known Ω(mn) lower bound for implementations restricted to m registers and the O(n)-time upper bound for implementations using many registers: for each value r ≥ m of the number of registers, identify matching upper and lower bounds on the worst-case SCAN time.
status_search_result: The literature shows tight Ω(mn) bounds for space-optimal (m-register) implementations and O(n)-time implementations using many registers, but no result closing the full tradeoff across intermediate register counts has been found. Recent work (e.g., on single-scanner and CAS-based variants, and asynchronous latency improvements through 2024) addresses related but distinct settings, leaving the general space-time tradeoff for multi-writer snapshots from registers open.

paper_title: Eight Open Problems in Distributed Computing
original_question: For wait-free linearizable register implementations of atomic snapshot objects, what are the full tradeoffs among the number of registers used, the worst-case time complexity of SCAN operations, and the worst-case time complexity of UPDATE operations?
self_contained_problem:
Consider the shared-memory model of asynchronous distributed computing with $n$ processes communicating through atomic read/write registers. An *atomic snapshot object* with $m$ components supports two operations: $\mathrm{UPDATE}(i,v)$, which writes value $v$ to component $i$, and $\mathrm{SCAN}$, which returns a vector of the current values of all $m$ components. An implementation is *linearizable* if every concurrent execution is equivalent to one in which each operation appears to take effect instantaneously at some point between its invocation and response, and *wait-free* if every process that begins an operation completes it in a finite number of its own steps, regardless of the behavior of the other processes.

For wait-free linearizable implementations of an atomic snapshot object from atomic read/write registers, determine the complete set of achievable tradeoffs among the three quantities
\[
(R,\ T_{\mathrm{SCAN}},\ T_{\mathrm{UPDATE}}),
\]
where $R$ is the number of registers used by the implementation, $T_{\mathrm{SCAN}}$ is the worst-case step complexity of a $\mathrm{SCAN}$ operation, and $T_{\mathrm{UPDATE}}$ is the worst-case step complexity of an $\mathrm{UPDATE}$ operation. Specifically, characterize, as a function of $n$ and $m$, the set of triples $(R, T_{\mathrm{SCAN}}, T_{\mathrm{UPDATE}})$ that are simultaneously realizable, with matching upper and lower bounds.
status_search_result: Partial results are known: space-optimal single-scanner implementations have a tight Ω(m²) SCAN bound, and space-optimal multi-writer snapshots admit a tight Θ(mn) bound; implementations using unbounded registers achieve O(1) UPDATE and O(m) SCAN. However, a complete characterization of the three-way tradeoff among register count, SCAN time, and UPDATE time has not been established.

paper_title: Eight Open Problems in Distributed Computing
context_brief: Pure Nash equilibria with link-capacity beliefs
original_question: In the incomplete-information extension of the KP selfish-routing model, where n selfish users route unsplittable traffic over m parallel links, links may have several possible capacities, and each user's belief about link capacities is a probability distribution that may differ from the beliefs of other users, does every instance admit a Pure Nash Equilibrium, or can the conjecture that such equilibria always exist be disproved?
self_contained_problem:
Consider the following routing game with incomplete information about link capacities. There are $n$ selfish users and $m$ parallel links connecting a common source to a common destination. Each user $i \in \{1,\dots,n\}$ controls an unsplittable amount of traffic $w_i > 0$ that must be routed entirely on a single link. Each link $\ell \in \{1,\dots,m\}$ has a capacity drawn from a finite set $C_\ell = \{c_\ell^{(1)}, c_\ell^{(2)}, \dots, c_\ell^{(k_\ell)}\}$ of possible positive real values. For every user $i$ and every link $\ell$, user $i$ holds a subjective probability distribution $p_{i,\ell}$ on $C_\ell$ representing $i$'s belief about the capacity of link $\ell$; these beliefs may differ across users (the users' priors need not be common nor consistent). 

A (pure) strategy of user $i$ is a choice of one link $s_i \in \{1,\dots,m\}$. Given a pure strategy profile $s = (s_1,\dots,s_n)$, the expected cost (latency) experienced by user $i$ on link $\ell = s_i$, under $i$'s own belief, is
$$\mathrm{cost}_i(s) \;=\; \mathbb{E}_{c \sim p_{i,\ell}}\!\left[\frac{\sum_{j:\, s_j = \ell} w_j}{c}\right].$$
A pure strategy profile $s^*$ is a Pure Nash Equilibrium if, for every user $i$ and every alternative link $\ell' \in \{1,\dots,m\}$,
$$\mathrm{cost}_i(s^*) \;\le\; \mathrm{cost}_i(s^*_{-i}, \ell').$$

Question: Does every instance of this game (for arbitrary $n$, $m$, weights $w_i$, capacity sets $C_\ell$, and user-specific belief distributions $p_{i,\ell}$) admit a Pure Nash Equilibrium? Either prove existence in full generality, or exhibit an instance with no Pure Nash Equilibrium.
status_search_result: Available literature on selfish routing under network uncertainty with user-specific (subjective) beliefs about link capacities indicates that existence of a Pure Nash Equilibrium in the general case is an open problem; negative results known for related models with three users do not apply here. Related Bayesian routing models with uncertainty about other users' traffic (not capacities) admit a potential-function argument guaranteeing pure Bayesian Nash equilibria, but this does not resolve the capacity-belief variant. No definitive proof or counterexample for the general capacity-belief KP model was located.

paper_title: Eight Open Problems in Distributed Computing
original_question: For the asynchronous deterministic shared-memory Write-All problem with p processors and t memory locations under adversarial failures or delays, is it possible to achieve optimal total work O(t) while using p = t^delta processors for some delta greater than 1/2?
self_contained_problem:
The asynchronous deterministic Write-All problem is defined as follows. There are $t$ shared memory locations, each initialized to $0$, and $p$ asynchronous processors operating on this shared memory. The processors execute a common deterministic algorithm and must cooperate so that every one of the $t$ memory locations is set to $1$ at least once before the algorithm terminates. Processors are subject to an adversary that may impose arbitrary asynchrony (including delays, halting, or crash failures of any subset of processors), provided that at least one processor remains live until termination. The total work of an execution is the sum, over all processors, of the number of basic shared-memory steps each processor performs while still active; the worst-case work of an algorithm is the maximum of this quantity over all admissible adversarial schedules. An algorithm is called work-optimal if its worst-case total work is $O(t)$.

Question: Does there exist a constant $\delta > 1/2$ and a deterministic algorithm solving the asynchronous Write-All problem with $t$ memory locations and $p = t^{\delta}$ processors whose total work is $O(t)$?
status_search_result: Known deterministic asynchronous Write-All algorithms achieve work-optimal $O(t)$ only for processor counts well below $t^{1/2}$. Kowalski–Shvartsman obtained work optimality for $p = O(t^{1/(2+\varepsilon)})$, and later improvements still stay below the $t^{1/2}$ threshold (e.g. $p = O((t/\log t)^{1/(3+\varepsilon)})$). No deterministic work-optimal algorithm is known for any $\delta > 1/2$, and the problem appears to remain open.

paper_title: Eight Open Problems in Distributed Computing
original_question: In a distributed Stackelberg-style selfish routing problem, where each node i wants to send flow x_i to a destination, the total flow is r, a subset L of non-selfish nodes can coordinate under a leader, and the remaining nodes selfishly route their flows to avoid high delay, can one find distributed algorithms by which the nodes in L choose their flows so that the Nash Equilibrium reached by the selfish nodes is close to an optimal flow routing such as minimum total latency?
self_contained_problem:
Consider a network in which each node $i$ wishes to route a flow of rate $x_i$ to a common destination, with total demand $r = \sum_i x_i$. Edges of the network have load-dependent latency functions, and each unit of flow experiences a delay equal to the sum of the latencies along its chosen path. Let $L$ be a designated subset of nodes (the "coordinated" or "leader" nodes) which can cooperate (for instance, under an elected leader) and route their portion of the flow according to a jointly chosen strategy. The remaining nodes (the "selfish" followers) independently choose routes for their own flows so as to minimize the delay they experience, eventually reaching a Nash equilibrium given the routing committed to by the nodes in $L$.

The total cost of a flow assignment is the total latency, $\sum_e f_e \cdot \ell_e(f_e)$, where $f_e$ is the flow on edge $e$ and $\ell_e$ is its latency function. An optimal routing minimizes this total latency over all feasible flows.

Design a distributed algorithm — to be executed by the nodes in $L$ using only local communication and information — that chooses the flows of the coordinated nodes so that the resulting Nash equilibrium induced among the selfish nodes has total latency provably close to that of the optimal routing. Equivalently: provide distributed Stackelberg strategies for $L$ achieving a bounded approximation ratio (or additive guarantee) to the minimum-total-latency flow, together with the associated convergence and complexity guarantees.
status_search_result: Centralized Stackelberg routing strategies (e.g., LLF and SCALE) and their approximation guarantees with respect to optimal latency are well studied for parallel-link and general multicommodity networks. However, the specific question of designing fully distributed algorithms by which a subset L of cooperating nodes computes its Stackelberg strategy so that the Nash equilibrium induced on selfish followers approximates the minimum-latency routing does not appear to be conclusively resolved in the literature. Status remains unclear.

paper_title: Eight Open Problems in Distributed Computing
context_brief: Local algorithms on unit disk graphs
original_question: For geometric graph models motivated by wireless sensor networks, especially unit disk graphs where geometry constrains node placement and wireless links, what is the local complexity of typical coordination tasks such as computing a dominating set under k-local communication?
self_contained_problem:
A unit disk graph (UDG) is a graph $G=(V,E)$ obtained from a finite set $V\subset \mathbb{R}^2$ of points in the plane by joining two points $u,v$ by an edge if and only if their Euclidean distance satisfies $\|u-v\|\le 1$. A distributed algorithm on $G$ operates in synchronous rounds: each node $v\in V$ starts with a unique identifier and (possibly) its coordinates, and in each round every node may send a message to each neighbor and update its local state. After $k$ rounds, the output of $v$ may depend only on information gathered within its $k$-hop neighborhood; such an algorithm is called $k$-local, and the local complexity of a task is the smallest $k=k(n,\varepsilon,\dots)$ for which a correct (or $(1+\varepsilon)$-approximate) algorithm exists.

Determine the local complexity, as a function of the number of nodes $n$ and the desired approximation parameter $\varepsilon>0$, of fundamental coordination tasks on unit disk graphs under $k$-local communication. As a concrete benchmark, establish matching upper and lower bounds on the number of communication rounds required for a deterministic distributed algorithm to compute a $(1+\varepsilon)$-approximation to a minimum dominating set of a unit disk graph, both in the location-aware model (where each node knows its coordinates) and in the connectivity-only model (where nodes know only the graph structure and unique IDs).
category_tag: Distributed local algorithms on unit disk graphs
status_search_result: Substantial progress has been made: local constant-factor approximation algorithms for dominating and connected dominating sets in UDGs are known, and local PTAS results exist for location-aware UDGs (Wattenhofer et al., Czyzowicz et al.). Lenzen, Pignolet, and Wattenhofer established asymptotically tight bounds on the time/approximation tradeoff for deterministic distributed algorithms on UDGs, showing in particular that $o(\log^* n)$ rounds do not suffice for a $(1+\varepsilon)$-approximate minimum dominating set. However, a complete characterization of the local complexity of all typical coordination tasks on UDGs remains open, so the broad question is only partially resolved.

paper_title: Nine open problems on conjunctive and Boolean grammars
original_question: Do conjunctive grammars over a one-letter alphabet generate only regular languages, or can a conjunctive grammar generate a nonregular unary language? A conjunctive grammar is a context-free grammar extended with explicit conjunction in rule bodies, without the explicit negation operation available in Boolean grammars.
self_contained_problem:
A conjunctive grammar is a quadruple $G=(\Sigma,N,R,S)$, where $\Sigma$ is a finite alphabet, $N$ is a finite set of nonterminal symbols, $S\in N$ is the start symbol, and $R$ is a finite set of rules of the form
$$A \to \alpha_1 \,\&\, \alpha_2 \,\&\, \cdots \,\&\, \alpha_n,$$
with $A\in N$, $n\ge 1$, and each $\alpha_i\in(\Sigma\cup N)^*$. The language generated by such a rule consists of all strings $w\in\Sigma^*$ that can be derived from each of the conjuncts $\alpha_i$; formally, the languages $L_G(A)\subseteq\Sigma^*$ for $A\in N$ are defined as the least solution of the system of equations
$$L_G(A) \;=\; \bigcup_{A\to\alpha_1\&\cdots\&\alpha_n\in R}\; \bigcap_{i=1}^{n} \widehat{\alpha_i}, \qquad A\in N,$$
where $\widehat{\alpha}$ denotes the language obtained from $\alpha$ by concatenation, with each nonterminal $B$ replaced by $L_G(B)$. The language generated by $G$ is $L(G)=L_G(S)$. Negation is not permitted.

Question: Does there exist a conjunctive grammar $G$ over a one-letter alphabet $\Sigma=\{a\}$ such that $L(G)\subseteq\{a\}^*$ is not a regular language? Equivalently, are all unary languages generated by conjunctive grammars regular?
status_search_result: The problem was solved by Artur Jeż, who constructed a conjunctive grammar generating the non-regular unary language $\{a^{4^n}: n\ge 0\}$, first announced in 2007 (DLT) and published in International Journal of Foundations of Computer Science (2008). Subsequent work generalized this to broader classes of unary languages generated by conjunctive grammars.

paper_title: Nine open problems on conjunctive and Boolean grammars
original_question: Are all languages generated by Boolean grammars contained in deterministic space DSPACE(n^(1-epsilon)) for some positive epsilon, thereby improving the known linear-space upper bound for recognizing Boolean grammar languages?
self_contained_problem:
A Boolean grammar is a quadruple G = (Σ, N, R, S), where Σ is a finite alphabet of terminal symbols, N is a finite set of nonterminal symbols, S ∈ N is a start symbol, and R is a finite set of rules of the form
   A → α₁ & … & α_m & ¬β₁ & … & ¬β_n,
with m ≥ 1, n ≥ 0, and each α_i, β_j ∈ (Σ ∪ N)*. The language L(G) ⊆ Σ* generated by G is defined as the unique (or, in general, the chosen well-founded) solution of the associated system of language equations
   A = ⋂_i α_i ∩ ⋂_j ¬β_j (for each A ∈ N),
and L(G) is the component corresponding to S. Conjunctive grammars are the special case with n = 0.

It is known that every language generated by a Boolean grammar is recognizable in deterministic space O(n), i.e., lies in DSPACE(n).

Question: Does there exist a constant ε > 0 such that every language generated by a Boolean grammar lies in DSPACE(n^{1−ε})? Equivalently, can the linear deterministic space upper bound for recognition of Boolean grammar languages be improved to a sublinear deterministic space bound?
status_search_result: The best known deterministic space upper bound for languages generated by Boolean grammars remains DSPACE(n) (linear space). No sublinear deterministic space algorithm has been reported in the literature, and the question of whether such an improvement is possible appears to remain open. Related work notes that conjunctive grammars can express P-complete languages, which suggests substantial obstacles to drastic improvements but does not resolve the sublinear-space question.

paper_title: Nine open problems on conjunctive and Boolean grammars
original_question: Is the class of languages generated by conjunctive grammars closed under complementation? Equivalently, for every conjunctive grammar G over a fixed alphabet, is the complement of the language L(G) also generated by some conjunctive grammar?
self_contained_problem:
A conjunctive grammar over a finite alphabet Σ is a tuple G = (Σ, N, R, S), where N is a finite set of nonterminals, S ∈ N is the start symbol, and R is a finite set of rules of the form A → α₁ & α₂ & ⋯ & αₘ with m ≥ 1 and each αᵢ ∈ (Σ ∪ N)*. The semantics is given by the least fixed point of language equations: each nonterminal A is interpreted as a language L(A) ⊆ Σ*, where for every rule A → α₁ & ⋯ & αₘ in R, L(α₁) ∩ ⋯ ∩ L(αₘ) ⊆ L(A), with concatenation of languages extended to strings of terminals and nonterminals in the usual way. The language generated by G is L(G) = L(S). Let 𝓛_conj denote the class of all languages of the form L(G) for some conjunctive grammar G.

Question: Is 𝓛_conj closed under complementation? Equivalently, for every conjunctive grammar G over an alphabet Σ, does there exist a conjunctive grammar G' over Σ such that L(G') = Σ* ∖ L(G)?
status_search_result: The complement closure problem for the class of conjunctive languages appears to remain open. Closure under complement is known for the linear subfamily (linear conjunctive grammars, e.g. via trellis automata), but no resolution of the question for general conjunctive grammars is found in the literature; recent surveys and overviews continue to list it as unresolved.

paper_title: Nine open problems on conjunctive and Boolean grammars
original_question: Does the hierarchy of Boolean LL(k) grammar languages collapse at a finite lookahead length? More precisely, is there a number k0 > 0 such that, for every k >= k0, Boolean LL(k) grammars generate exactly the same family of languages as Boolean LL(k0) grammars? A Boolean LL(k) grammar is a Boolean grammar satisfying a uniqueness condition for generalized recursive-descent parsing with k-symbol lookahead: for each nonterminal, lookahead string of length at most k, and possible surrounding sequence of conjuncts, at most one rule can apply.
self_contained_problem:
A Boolean grammar is a quadruple G = (Σ, N, R, S) where Σ is a finite alphabet of terminals, N is a finite set of nonterminals, S ∈ N is the start symbol, and R is a finite set of rules of the form
    A → α₁ & … & αₘ & ¬β₁ & … & ¬βₙ ,
with m ≥ 1, n ≥ 0, and αᵢ, βⱼ ∈ (Σ ∪ N)*. The language L(G) ⊆ Σ* is defined as the least solution (or, equivalently, by any of the standard equivalent semantics) of the corresponding language equations interpreting concatenation, intersection (&), and complementation (¬) in the usual way.

For a positive integer k, a Boolean grammar G is called Boolean LL(k) if it satisfies the following uniqueness condition for generalized recursive-descent parsing with k-symbol lookahead: for every nonterminal A ∈ N, every lookahead string w ∈ Σ^{≤k}, and every admissible surrounding sequence of conjuncts that may arise during a generalized recursive-descent parse, at most one rule of A is applicable.

Let 𝓛_BLL(k) denote the family of languages generated by Boolean LL(k) grammars.

Question: Does the hierarchy {𝓛_BLL(k)}_{k ≥ 1} collapse at some finite lookahead? That is, does there exist an integer k₀ ≥ 1 such that, for every k ≥ k₀,
    𝓛_BLL(k) = 𝓛_BLL(k₀) ?
status_search_result: No source was located establishing a collapse or strict-hierarchy result for general Boolean LL(k) grammars. Related collapse results are known for restricted subclasses (e.g., LL(k)-linear conjunctive grammars can be reduced to LL(1)-linear, and the Boolean closure of linear context-free languages collapses at a finite level), but these do not address the full Boolean LL(k) hierarchy. The problem appears to remain open.

paper_title: Feynman integrals as generalized functions on path space: things done and open problems
original_question: Within the white-noise generalized-function approach to Feynman path integrals, can the construction of non-perturbative Feynman integrals be extended by weakening the requirement that the expression inside the relevant expectation be integrable, while still yielding a valid T-transform and hence a well-defined generalized white-noise functional?
self_contained_problem:
Background and setup. Let $(\mathcal{S}'(\mathbb{R}), \mathcal{B}, \mu)$ be the white noise probability space, where $\mu$ is the standard Gaussian (white noise) measure on the space $\mathcal{S}'(\mathbb{R})$ of tempered distributions. Let $(\mathcal{S}) \subset L^2(\mu) \subset (\mathcal{S})^*$ be the Hida triple of test and generalized white noise functionals. For $\Phi \in (\mathcal{S})^*$, the T-transform is defined by
$$ (T\Phi)(\xi) \;=\; \langle\!\langle \Phi,\; \exp(i\langle \cdot,\xi\rangle) \rangle\!\rangle, \qquad \xi \in \mathcal{S}(\mathbb{R}),$$
where $\langle\!\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle\!\rangle$ is the dual pairing. A functional $\Phi \in (\mathcal{S})^*$ is uniquely determined by $T\Phi$, and the characterization theorem states that $F:\mathcal{S}(\mathbb{R})\to\mathbb{C}$ equals $T\Phi$ for some $\Phi \in (\mathcal{S})^*$ if and only if $F$ is ray-entire of second order growth and locally uniformly bounded on $\mathcal{S}(\mathbb{R})$.

In the white-noise formulation of quantum mechanics, for suitable potentials $V$ and times $0<t_0<t$, the Feynman integrand for a particle moving from $x_0$ to $x$ in $\mathbb{R}^d$ is formally
$$ I_V \;=\; N \exp\!\Big(\tfrac{i+1}{2}\!\int_{t_0}^{t}\!\!\dot{B}(s)^2\, ds\Big)\,\exp\!\Big(-i\!\int_{t_0}^{t} V(B(s)+x)\, ds\Big)\,\delta(B(t)+x-x_0),$$
and one seeks to realize $I_V$ as an element of $(\mathcal{S})^*$ by verifying that a candidate T-transform $T I_V(\xi)$ exists and satisfies the characterization theorem. In the standard non-perturbative construction (e.g.\ via a Doss-type formula), this verification proceeds by demonstrating integrability of an associated expectation expression that defines $T I_V(\xi)$.

Problem. Determine whether the class of potentials $V$ for which $I_V$ can be rigorously constructed as a generalized white noise functional in $(\mathcal{S})^*$ in a non-perturbative manner can be enlarged by replacing the current pointwise/absolute integrability requirement on the integrand defining the candidate T-transform with a strictly weaker condition (for example, a conditional or oscillatory-integral notion, an analytic continuation, or a distributional limit), in such a way that the resulting $\xi \mapsto T I_V(\xi)$ still satisfies the white-noise characterization theorem and hence defines a unique element of $(\mathcal{S})^*$ whose generalized expectation provides the Green's function of the corresponding Schrödinger equation. Identify explicitly such a weakened integrability condition and the resulting larger class of admissible potentials, or prove that no such weakening is possible while preserving a valid T-transform.
category_tag: White noise analysis and Feynman path integrals
status_search_result: Recent literature on white-noise Feynman integrals (including work on phase-space and QFT extensions through 2024–2025) continues to construct non-perturbative Feynman integrands under explicit integrability hypotheses on the relevant expectation (e.g. via Doss-type formulas, finite signed measures of bounded support, and Laplace-transformable potentials). No source located states that the integrability requirement has been replaced by a strictly weaker general condition extending the admissible class of potentials. The problem therefore appears to remain open.

$$(Th)(u_2)=\int_{V_1} h(u_1)\,F(u_1+u_2)\,dm_1(u_1),\qquad u_2\in V_2,$$
maps $H_1$ into $H_2$.
