paper_title: Open Problems in the Function Theory of the Bergman Space
original_question: For an inner divisor G of L2_a(D), let Phi_G be the Green-potential function associated with |G|^2 - 1. Theorem 1.6 gives the isometry ||Gf||^2_L2 = ||f||^2_L2 + integral_D |f'(z)|^2 Phi_G(z) dS(z) for all f in the Hardy space H2(D). Does this isometry extend to every f in L2_a(D)? If it does not always extend, for exactly which inner divisors G does the extension hold?
self_contained_problem:
Let $\mathbb{D}=\{z\in\mathbb{C}:|z|<1\}$ be the open unit disk and let $dS$ denote normalized area measure on $\mathbb{D}$. The Bergman space $L^2_a(\mathbb{D})$ consists of all holomorphic functions $f:\mathbb{D}\to\mathbb{C}$ with $\|f\|_{L^2}^2=\int_{\mathbb{D}}|f(z)|^2\,dS(z)<\infty$, and the Hardy space $H^2(\mathbb{D})$ consists of holomorphic $f$ with $\sup_{0<r<1}\int_0^{2\pi}|f(re^{i\theta})|^2\,\frac{d\theta}{2\pi}<\infty$.

A function $G\in L^2_a(\mathbb{D})$ is called an inner divisor for $L^2_a(\mathbb{D})$ if there exists a (closed, $z$-invariant) subspace $M\subset L^2_a(\mathbb{D})$ such that $G$ is the extremal solution (of unit norm) to the corresponding extremal problem; equivalently, $G$ satisfies the orthogonality relation $\int_{\mathbb{D}}(|G(z)|^2-1)q(z)\,dS(z)=0$ for every bounded holomorphic $q$ in a natural class. For such a $G$, define the Green-potential function
$$\Phi_G(z)=\int_{\mathbb{D}}\log\Big|\frac{1-\bar w z}{z-w}\Big|^2\,(|G(w)|^2-1)\,dS(w),\qquad z\in\mathbb{D}.$$
It is known that $0\le \Phi_G(z)\le 1-|z|^2$ on $\mathbb{D}$ and that the isometry
$$\|Gf\|_{L^2}^2=\|f\|_{L^2}^2+\int_{\mathbb{D}}|f'(z)|^2\,\Phi_G(z)\,dS(z)$$
holds for every $f\in H^2(\mathbb{D})$.

Question: Does this isometry extend to every $f\in L^2_a(\mathbb{D})$? If it does not hold for all inner divisors $G$, characterize precisely those inner divisors $G$ of $L^2_a(\mathbb{D})$ for which the identity above is valid for every $f\in L^2_a(\mathbb{D})$.
status_search_result: A web search located the broader literature on contractive zero-divisors, biharmonic Green functions, and Bergman inner functions (Hedenmalm, Duren–Khavinson–Shapiro, Aleman–Richter–Sundberg, Olofsson, Shimorin), but did not turn up a definitive published resolution of the specific question of whether the $H^2$-isometry extends to all of $L^2_a(\mathbb{D})$, nor a precise characterization of the inner divisors for which the extension holds. Status appears unknown based on the available search evidence.

paper_title: Open Problems in the Function Theory of the Bergman Space
original_question: For finite zero sequences A and B in L2_a(D), let Phi_A and Phi_B be the Green-potential functions associated with the zero divisors G_A and G_B. If A is contained in B, is Phi_A(z) ≤ Phi_B(z) for every z in D?
self_contained_problem:
Let $\mathbb{D}$ denote the open unit disk in $\mathbb{C}$ and let $L^2_a(\mathbb{D})$ denote the Bergman space of holomorphic functions $f$ on $\mathbb{D}$ with $\|f\|^2 = \int_{\mathbb{D}} |f(z)|^2\, dA(z) < \infty$, where $dA$ is normalized area measure. A finite sequence $A = (a_1,\dots,a_n)$ of points in $\mathbb{D}$ (with multiplicities) is called a zero sequence for $L^2_a(\mathbb{D})$. To such a finite zero sequence one associates the canonical (contractive) zero divisor $G_A \in L^2_a(\mathbb{D})$: the unique extremal function solving $\sup\{\operatorname{Re} f(0) : f \in L^2_a(\mathbb{D}),\ \|f\|=1,\ f \text{ vanishes on } A \text{ with the prescribed multiplicities}\}$ (equivalently, $G_A$ is the reproducing-kernel-based contractive divisor of the zero-based invariant subspace generated by $A$). Define the Green-potential function $\Phi_A : \mathbb{D} \to \mathbb{R}$ associated with $G_A$ by
$$\Phi_A(z) \;=\; \int_{\mathbb{D}} \log|G_A(w)|^2 \, G(z,w)\, dA(w),$$
where $G(z,w)$ is the Green function of $\mathbb{D}$ for the Laplacian (so that $\Delta_z \Phi_A(z) = \log|G_A(z)|^2$ in the distributional sense, with zero boundary values).

Question: If $A$ and $B$ are two finite zero sequences for $L^2_a(\mathbb{D})$ with $A \subset B$ (as multisets), does the inequality
$$\Phi_A(z) \;\le\; \Phi_B(z)$$
hold for every $z \in \mathbb{D}$?
status_search_result: A targeted web search did not surface any publication that resolves the monotonicity conjecture $\Phi_A \le \Phi_B$ for $A \subset B$ in $L^2_a(\mathbb{D})$. The conjecture appears in Hedenmalm's open-problems survey and is referenced in subsequent surveys on the Bergman space, but no proof or counterexample was located. Status is reported as unknown.

paper_title: Open Problems in the Function Theory of the Bergman Space
original_question: For the weighted biharmonic operator Delta (1 - |z|^2)^{-alpha} Delta on the unit disk D, is its Green function U_alpha(z, zeta) positive on D x D for every real parameter alpha with -1 < alpha ≤ 1?
self_contained_problem:
Let $\mathbb{D}=\{z\in\mathbb{C}:|z|<1\}$ denote the open unit disk. For a real parameter $\alpha$ with $-1<\alpha\le 1$, consider the weighted biharmonic operator
$$L_\alpha u(z) \;=\; \Delta\!\left((1-|z|^2)^{-\alpha}\,\Delta u(z)\right), \qquad z\in\mathbb{D},$$
where $\Delta$ is the Euclidean Laplacian. Let $U_\alpha(z,\zeta)$ denote the Green function of $L_\alpha$ on $\mathbb{D}$ with Dirichlet (clamped-plate) boundary conditions; that is, for each fixed $\zeta\in\mathbb{D}$, the function $z\mapsto U_\alpha(z,\zeta)$ satisfies
$$\Delta\!\left((1-|z|^2)^{-\alpha}\,\Delta_z U_\alpha(z,\zeta)\right) \;=\; \delta_\zeta(z) \quad \text{on } \mathbb{D},$$
together with the boundary conditions $U_\alpha(z,\zeta)=0$ and $\partial_{n} U_\alpha(z,\zeta)=0$ for $z\in\partial\mathbb{D}$.

Determine whether, for every real $\alpha$ with $-1<\alpha\le 1$,
$$U_\alpha(z,\zeta) \;>\; 0 \qquad \text{for all } (z,\zeta)\in \mathbb{D}\times\mathbb{D}.$$
status_search_result: The positivity of the Green function for the weighted biharmonic operator $\Delta(1-|z|^2)^{-\alpha}\Delta$ on the unit disk has been established. Shimorin obtained an explicit integral formula proving positivity for $\alpha\in(-1,0)$, and constructive existence/positivity results were given for $\alpha\ge 0$, with $\alpha=1$ corresponding to Hedenmalm's earlier explicit formula. More generally, positivity holds whenever the weight is radial, logarithmically subharmonic, and area integrable, which covers $(1-|z|^2)^\alpha$ for $-1<\alpha\le 1$.

paper_title: Open Problems in the Function Theory of the Bergman Space
context_brief: Adding a zero to a Bergman zero divisor
original_question: For every zero sequence A of L2_a(D), does the quotient G_{A union {0}} / G_A belong to the Smirnov space on D, where the Smirnov space consists of quotients f/g with f and g bounded analytic functions on D and g outer?
self_contained_problem:
Let $\mathbb{D}=\{z\in\mathbb{C}:|z|<1\}$ denote the open unit disk, and let $L^2_a(\mathbb{D})$ be the (unweighted) Bergman space of analytic functions $f$ on $\mathbb{D}$ for which $\|f\|^2=\int_{\mathbb{D}}|f(z)|^2\,dA(z)<\infty$, where $dA$ is normalized area measure. A sequence $A=\{a_j\}\subset\mathbb{D}$ (with multiplicities) is called a zero sequence for $L^2_a(\mathbb{D})$ if there exists a non-trivial function in $L^2_a(\mathbb{D})$ whose zero set, counted with multiplicities, equals $A$. For such a zero sequence $A$, let $I_A$ denote the closed subspace of $L^2_a(\mathbb{D})$ consisting of all functions vanishing on $A$ (with multiplicities), and let $G_A$ denote the canonical (contractive) zero divisor associated with $A$, i.e. the unique extremal solution to the problem
$$\sup\{\mathrm{Re}\,f(0)/z_A : f\in I_A,\ \|f\|=1\},$$
suitably normalized, so that $G_A$ is the canonical Bergman zero divisor.

Define the Smirnov space on $\mathbb{D}$ to be
$$N^+(\mathbb{D}) = \{f/g : f,g\in H^\infty(\mathbb{D}),\ g\text{ is outer}\},$$
where $H^\infty(\mathbb{D})$ is the algebra of bounded analytic functions on $\mathbb{D}$ and a function $g\in H^\infty(\mathbb{D})$ is outer if $\log|g(0)|=\int_0^{2\pi}\log|g(e^{i\theta})|\,\frac{d\theta}{2\pi}$.

Question: For every zero sequence $A$ of $L^2_a(\mathbb{D})$ (with $0\notin A$), does the quotient $G_{A\cup\{0\}}/G_A$ belong to the Smirnov space $N^+(\mathbb{D})$?
status_search_result: Web searches did not reveal a published resolution of this specific question concerning whether quotients of canonical Bergman zero divisors $G_{A\cup\{0\}}/G_A$ always lie in the Smirnov class. Closely related works by Hedenmalm, Aleman, Duren–Khavinson–Shapiro–Sundberg study contractive divisors and their multiplier/expansive properties, but none located here state a definitive answer to this particular quotient-membership question. Current status could not be confirmed from the available sources.

paper_title: Open Problems in the Function Theory of the Bergman Space
context_brief: Carathéodory-type theorem for Bergman zero divisors
original_question: Is every analytic function f on D satisfying ||f phi||_L2 ≤ ||phi||_H2 for every phi in H2(D) the normal limit of finite zero divisors for the Bergman space?
self_contained_problem:
Let $\mathbb{D}$ denote the open unit disk in the complex plane. The Hardy space $H^2(\mathbb{D})$ consists of analytic functions $\varphi(z)=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty} a_n z^n$ on $\mathbb{D}$ with $\|\varphi\|_{H^2}^2 := \sum_{n=0}^\infty |a_n|^2 < \infty$. The Bergman space $L^2_a(\mathbb{D})$ consists of analytic functions $g$ on $\mathbb{D}$ with $\|g\|_{L^2}^2 := \int_{\mathbb{D}} |g(z)|^2\, dA(z) < \infty$, where $dA$ is normalized area measure on $\mathbb{D}$.

For a finite set of points $\{z_1,\dots,z_n\}\subset \mathbb{D}$ (counted with multiplicities), the associated finite Bergman zero divisor is the unique extremal function $G \in L^2_a(\mathbb{D})$ of unit norm that vanishes exactly on this set and maximizes $\operatorname{Re} G^{(k)}(0)$ at the lowest-order nonvanishing derivative; equivalently, it is the canonical contractive divisor associated with that zero set. Call an analytic function on $\mathbb{D}$ a "normal limit of finite zero divisors" if it is the limit, uniformly on compact subsets of $\mathbb{D}$, of a sequence of such finite Bergman zero divisors.

Question: Is it true that every analytic function $f$ on $\mathbb{D}$ satisfying
$$\|f\varphi\|_{L^2} \le \|\varphi\|_{H^2} \quad \text{for every } \varphi \in H^2(\mathbb{D})$$
is a normal limit of finite Bergman zero divisors?
status_search_result: A web search did not find a published resolution of this specific conjecture concerning the characterization of normal limits of finite Bergman zero divisors via a contractive multiplier condition from $H^2$ into the Bergman space. Related work on contractive divisors and extremal functions in Bergman spaces by Hedenmalm, Duren, Khavinson, Shapiro, and Sundberg exists, but no source clearly settles this exact statement, so the status appears unknown.

paper_title: Open Problems in the Function Theory of the Bergman Space
original_question: Does there exist an absolute constant epsilon with 0 < epsilon < 2^{-1/2} such that, whenever f and g are in L2_a(D) and |f(z)| ≤ |g(z)| throughout the annulus epsilon < |z| < 1, the Bergman L2 norm inequality ||f||_L2 ≤ ||g||_L2 follows?
self_contained_problem:
Let $\mathbb{D}=\{z\in\mathbb{C}:|z|<1\}$ be the open unit disk, and let $L^2_a(\mathbb{D})$ denote the Bergman space of holomorphic functions $f:\mathbb{D}\to\mathbb{C}$ with
$$\|f\|_{L^2}^2 = \int_{\mathbb{D}} |f(z)|^2\, dA(z) < \infty,$$
where $dA$ is normalized area measure on $\mathbb{D}$.

Question: Does there exist an absolute constant $\varepsilon$ with $0<\varepsilon<2^{-1/2}$ having the following property? For every pair $f,g\in L^2_a(\mathbb{D})$ such that
$$|f(z)|\le |g(z)| \quad\text{for all } z\text{ with } \varepsilon<|z|<1,$$
one has
$$\|f\|_{L^2} \le \|g\|_{L^2}.$$
status_search_result: The existence question (Korenblum's conjecture for $L^2_a$) was settled affirmatively by W. K. Hayman, who proved that an absolute constant $\varepsilon$ exists (with an explicit small value). Subsequent work by Hinkkanen extended the result to $L^p_a$ for $p\ge 1$ with improved constants, while Schuster, Wang and others further refined the admissible value of $\varepsilon$. The sharp (largest) value of $\varepsilon$ remains unknown, but the existence question posed here is solved. For $0<p<1$, Božin and Karapetrović showed the analogous principle fails.

paper_title: Open Problems in the Function Theory of the Bergman Space
context_brief: Cyclic vectors in the Bergman space
original_question: A function f in L2_a(D) is cyclic if the functions f, zf, z^2 f, and so on span a dense subspace of L2_a(D). Which functions in L2_a(D) are cyclic?
self_contained_problem:
Let $\mathbb{D} = \{z \in \mathbb{C} : |z| < 1\}$ denote the open unit disk, and let $L^2_a(\mathbb{D})$ be the Bergman space of holomorphic functions $f : \mathbb{D} \to \mathbb{C}$ such that
$$\|f\|^2 = \int_{\mathbb{D}} |f(z)|^2 \, dA(z) < \infty,$$
where $dA$ is the normalized area measure on $\mathbb{D}$. A function $f \in L^2_a(\mathbb{D})$ is called cyclic if the linear span of $\{f, zf, z^2 f, z^3 f, \dots\}$ is dense in $L^2_a(\mathbb{D})$ with respect to the norm above (equivalently, $f$ is a cyclic vector for the operator of multiplication by $z$ on $L^2_a(\mathbb{D})$).

Provide a complete characterization of the cyclic elements of $L^2_a(\mathbb{D})$: give necessary and sufficient conditions on $f \in L^2_a(\mathbb{D})$ that determine whether $f$ is cyclic.
status_search_result: The problem of characterizing cyclic vectors in the Bergman space $L^2_a(\mathbb{D})$ remains open. While necessary conditions and various sufficient conditions are known, no complete characterization exists, in contrast to the Hardy space case. Recent surveys and research papers on cyclicity in Bergman, Dirichlet, and de Branges–Rovnyak spaces continue to treat it as an unresolved problem, with related conjectures (e.g., Brown–Shields for the Dirichlet space) also open.

paper_title: Open Problems in the Function Theory of the Bergman Space
original_question: Suppose f belongs to L2_a(D) and satisfies the lower bound |f(z)| ≥ epsilon (1 - |z|^2)^N for every z in D, for some positive constants epsilon and N. Must f be cyclic in L2_a(D)?
self_contained_problem:
Let $\mathbb{D} = \{z \in \mathbb{C} : |z| < 1\}$ denote the open unit disk, and let $dA$ denote normalized area measure on $\mathbb{D}$. Define the Bergman space
$$L^2_a(\mathbb{D}) = \Big\{ f : \mathbb{D} \to \mathbb{C} \text{ holomorphic} : \|f\|^2 = \int_{\mathbb{D}} |f(z)|^2 \, dA(z) < \infty \Big\}.$$
A function $f \in L^2_a(\mathbb{D})$ is called cyclic if the closed linear span in $L^2_a(\mathbb{D})$ of the set $\{p \cdot f : p \text{ a polynomial}\}$ equals $L^2_a(\mathbb{D})$ (equivalently, the smallest closed subspace of $L^2_a(\mathbb{D})$ containing $f$ that is invariant under multiplication by $z$ is all of $L^2_a(\mathbb{D})$).

Suppose $f \in L^2_a(\mathbb{D})$ satisfies the pointwise lower bound
$$|f(z)| \;\geq\; \varepsilon\,(1 - |z|^2)^N \quad \text{for every } z \in \mathbb{D},$$
for some positive constants $\varepsilon > 0$ and $N > 0$. Must $f$ be cyclic in $L^2_a(\mathbb{D})$?
status_search_result: Searches indicate this is a long-standing open question (Shapiro's cyclicity problem for the Bergman space). Related results (Borichev–Hedenmalm, Brown–Korenblum, and work in large/weighted Bergman spaces) show that in some weighted Bergman spaces invertible non-cyclic elements exist, but no resolution for the standard $L^2_a(\mathbb{D})$ under the stated lower bound was found. Status appears to remain open.

original_question: Call an invariant subspace I of L2_a(D) maximal if every invariant subspace containing I is either I itself or the whole space L2_a(D). Must every maximal invariant subspace of L2_a(D) have codimension 1?
self_contained_problem:
Let $\mathbb{D}=\{z\in\mathbb{C}:|z|<1\}$ denote the open unit disk, and let $L^2_a(\mathbb{D})$ be the Bergman space, that is, the Hilbert space of analytic functions $f:\mathbb{D}\to\mathbb{C}$ satisfying
$$\|f\|^2 = \int_{\mathbb{D}} |f(z)|^2\, dA(z) < \infty,$$
where $dA$ is normalized Lebesgue area measure on $\mathbb{D}$. A closed subspace $I\subseteq L^2_a(\mathbb{D})$ is called invariant if $z\cdot I\subseteq I$, i.e., $zf\in I$ whenever $f\in I$. Call an invariant subspace $I$ of $L^2_a(\mathbb{D})$ maximal if every invariant subspace $J$ with $I\subseteq J\subseteq L^2_a(\mathbb{D})$ satisfies either $J=I$ or $J=L^2_a(\mathbb{D})$.

Question: Must every maximal invariant subspace of $L^2_a(\mathbb{D})$ have codimension $1$?
status_search_result: The problem has been solved affirmatively. Hedenmalm proved that every maximal invariant subspace of the Bergman space $L^2_a(\mathbb{D})$ has codimension 1. Aleman–Richter and later authors extended the codimension-1 property to broader settings (including Bergman spaces over planar regions), and Guo et al. generalized it to abstract Hilbert space settings.

paper_title: Variation Structures: Results and Open Problems
original_question: For an invariant i of isolated hypersurface germs f:(C^{n+2},0)->(C,0) that can be written as f=p∘ϕ with ϕ:(C^{n+2},0)->(C^2,0) an isolated complete intersection singularity and p:(C^2,0)->(C,0) a curve singularity, what category C(i) of supplementary coefficient structures on (C^2,0) or on the local complement of the discriminant germ Δ⊂(C^2,0) should be used so that ϕ determines an element S(ϕ)∈C(i) and i(f) can be computed from p and S(ϕ)? In particular, can one define a generalized Dynkin diagram D(p,S), for an isolated curve singularity p and S∈C(i), such that D(p,S(ϕ)) is the Dynkin diagram of f=p∘ϕ whenever f has an isolated singularity?
self_contained_problem:
Let $f:(\mathbb{C}^{n+2},0)\to(\mathbb{C},0)$ be a holomorphic germ defining an isolated hypersurface singularity. Assume $f$ admits a factorization $f = p\circ\varphi$, where:

(a) $\varphi:(\mathbb{C}^{n+2},0)\to(\mathbb{C}^{2},0)$ is an isolated complete intersection singularity (ICIS), with discriminant germ $\Delta\subset(\mathbb{C}^{2},0)$; and

(b) $p:(\mathbb{C}^{2},0)\to(\mathbb{C},0)$ is a reduced plane curve singularity.

Fix an invariant $i$ of isolated hypersurface singularities (such as the Milnor number, the geometric genus, the spectrum, the monodromy representation, the Seifert form, the Hodge or mixed Hodge structure on vanishing cohomology, or the Coxeter–Dynkin diagram).

The problem is to construct a category $\mathcal{C}(i)$ of "supplementary coefficient structures" on the germ $(\mathbb{C}^{2},0)$, or equivalently on the complement of the discriminant $\Delta$ in $(\mathbb{C}^{2},0)$ (for instance: local systems, perverse sheaves, variation structures, or some enriched analogue), satisfying the following two properties.

(1) Every ICIS $\varphi$ as above functorially determines an element $S(\varphi)\in\mathcal{C}(i)$.

(2) For every reduced plane curve singularity $p$ and every object $S\in\mathcal{C}(i)$, one can define a "generalized Dynkin diagram" $D(p,S)$, in a way that depends only on $p$ and $S$, such that whenever $f=p\circ\varphi$ has isolated singularity one has the equality
$$ D(p,S(\varphi)) = \text{(the Coxeter–Dynkin diagram of }f\text{)},$$
and more generally $i(f)$ can be recovered from $p$ and $S(\varphi)$ alone.

For which invariants $i$ (beyond those for which it is already known) does such a category $\mathcal{C}(i)$ and such an assignment $D(p,S)$ exist, and how can it be constructed?

Web searches did not turn up any subsequent work providing a general categorical answer or a general construction of $D(p,S)$ for invariants beyond the cases originally known (e.g. the Seifert/variation structure case). The problem appears to remain open in its general form.

paper_title: Variation Structures: Results and Open Problems
original_question: Classify all ε-hermitian variation structures for G=Z, writing a structure as (U;b,h,V) with h=ρ(1) and V=V(1), beyond the already classified simple structures. The classification should include degenerate and non-simple cases such as indecomposable variation structures whose monodromy h has more than one Jordan block, identify natural restrictions that occur for simple structures V(f) coming from isolated hypersurface singularities, and classify the structures satisfying those restrictions, including a class containing the structures produced by hypersurface singularities with one-dimensional singular locus.
self_contained_problem:
Fix ε ∈ {+1,−1} and let G = Z. An ε-hermitian variation structure (HVS) over Z is a quadruple V = (U; b, h, V) where:
- U is a finite-dimensional complex vector space;
- b : U × U → C is a non-degenerate ε-hermitian form (i.e. b(y,x) = ε·conj(b(x,y))), allowed to be degenerate in the generalized sense considered below;
- h : U → U is a b-isometric automorphism (the monodromy), so b(h x, h y) = b(x,y);
- V : U → U is a C-linear endomorphism (the variation operator) satisfying the compatibility b(V x, y) + ε·conj(b(x, V y)) + b(V x, V y) = ... encoded by the standard relation V = h − I composed with the duality induced by b on the non-degenerate part, in such a way that V determines (and is determined by) h on the non-degenerate part of U.
Two such structures are isomorphic via b-isometries that intertwine h and V. The structure is called simple when b is non-degenerate; otherwise it is degenerate. It is indecomposable if it is not isomorphic to an orthogonal direct sum of two non-trivial ε-HVS.

The simple ε-hermitian variation structures over Z (equivalently, with monodromy h whose every generalized eigenspace forms a single Jordan block of fixed size) have a known complete classification into indecomposable building blocks.

Problem. Classify all ε-hermitian variation structures (U; b, h, V) for G = Z beyond the simple case. In particular:

(a) Classify the indecomposable ε-HVS whose monodromy h has more than one Jordan block (so that even the associated isometric structure (b, h), which may be degenerate, is indecomposable).

(b) Identify the natural restrictions on (U; b, h, V) that are forced when V = V(f) arises from the Milnor fibration / variation operator of an isolated hypersurface singularity f : (C^{n+1}, 0) → (C, 0), and classify all ε-HVS satisfying these restrictions.

(c) Classify a class of ε-HVS large enough to include every variation structure produced by a germ of a hypersurface singularity with one-dimensional singular locus.

The status of the problem as a whole appears unresolved based on available evidence.

paper_title: Variation Structures: Results and Open Problems
original_question: For an isolated complete intersection singularity ϕ with two-dimensional base space and the embedded-resolution local setup that restricts V(ϕ) to a Z^2-variation structure near a point P on the exceptional divisor, a natural limit mixed Hodge structure carries a Z^2 action via the semisimple part of the monodromy representation. Can the isolated-hypersurface theorem connecting the topological invariant V(f) with the Hodge-theoretical primitive invariants pλ^{a,b}(f), and in particular showing that Hodge numbers determine the real Seifert form, be extended to this Z^2 limit mixed-Hodge setting?
self_contained_problem:
Setup. Let $\phi:(\mathbb{C}^{n+2},0)\to(\mathbb{C}^2,0)$ be the germ of an isolated complete intersection singularity with two-dimensional base. Choose an embedded resolution of the discriminant and fix a point $P$ on the exceptional divisor where two smooth components meet transversally. Restricting the geometric vanishing data of $\phi$ to a small bidisc transverse to the exceptional divisor at $P$ yields a $\mathbb{Z}^2$-variation structure $V(\phi)$ on the local vanishing cohomology, in the sense of Némethi: a free $\mathbb{Z}$-module equipped with two commuting monodromy automorphisms, two variation maps, an intersection form and a Seifert-type form, satisfying the usual compatibility relations.

Hodge side. The two commuting monodromies $h_1,h_2$ act on the vanishing cohomology, and one has a natural limit mixed Hodge structure (a polarized bigraded $\mathbb{Z}^2$-equivariant analog of Steenbrink's limit mixed Hodge structure) on which the semisimple parts of $h_1,h_2$ act, decomposing the cohomology into joint eigenspaces indexed by pairs of eigenvalues $\lambda=(\lambda_1,\lambda_2)\in(\mathbb{C}^*)^2$. From this one extracts primitive Hodge numbers $p^{a,b}_\lambda(\phi)$ ($a,b\in\mathbb{Z}_{\ge0}$, $\lambda\in(\mathbb{C}^*)^2$) refining Steenbrink's spectrum.

Hypersurface model. In the one-parameter (isolated hypersurface singularity $f$) case, the following is known: the integral $\mathbb{Z}$-variation structure $V(f)$, after tensoring with $\mathbb{R}$, is completely determined by the primitive equivariant Hodge numbers $p^{a,b}_\lambda(f)$; in particular these Hodge numbers determine the real Seifert form of $f$.

Problem. Prove or disprove the analogous statement for $\phi$: do the primitive equivariant Hodge numbers $p^{a,b}_\lambda(\phi)$ of the $\mathbb{Z}^2$-equivariant limit mixed Hodge structure determine the real $\mathbb{Z}^2$-variation structure $V(\phi)\otimes\mathbb{R}$, and in particular the real Seifert form attached to $\phi$ at $P$?
category_tag: Variation structures and limit mixed Hodge structures of singularities
status_search_result: Recent works (e.g., Kulikov–Némethi and Hertling–Stahlke on real Seifert forms and Steenbrink mixed Hodge structures, 2017–2020) confirm and refine the hypersurface theorem relating Hodge numbers to the real Seifert form, but no search result explicitly establishes the analogous statement for the $\mathbb{Z}^2$-equivariant limit mixed Hodge structure of an isolated complete intersection singularity with two-dimensional base. The status of the extension to this $\mathbb{Z}^2$ setting could not be confirmed.

paper_title: Variation Structures: Results and Open Problems
original_question: For ε-hermitian variation structures of a group G, form the Witt group WVε(G) by quotienting isomorphism classes under direct sum by hyperbolic structures. For G=Z^k, the known classification decomposes WVε(G) over unitary characters χ and has summand Z for χ≠1 and Z2 for χ=1. How can this Witt-group classification be extended to more general groups, ideally to local fundamental groups of complements of curve singularities p^{-1}(0)⊂(C^2,0)?
self_contained_problem:
Let $\varepsilon \in \{+1,-1\}$ and let $G$ be a group. An $\varepsilon$-hermitian variation structure over $G$ is a quadruple $(U; b, h, V)$ where $U$ is a finite-dimensional complex vector space, $b: U \times U \to \mathbb{C}$ is a non-degenerate $\varepsilon$-hermitian form, $h: G \to \mathrm{Aut}(U,b)$ is a representation by $b$-isometries, and $V: U \to U$ is a $\mathbb{C}$-linear endomorphism satisfying the compatibility conditions making $(U;b,h,V)$ an $\varepsilon$-hermitian variation structure in the sense of Némethi. A variation structure is called hyperbolic if it is isomorphic to a standard hyperbolic model on $U \oplus U^*$. Direct sum $\oplus$ endows the set of isomorphism classes with the structure of a commutative monoid, and the quotient
$$WV_\varepsilon(G) := \{\text{iso. classes of }\varepsilon\text{-hermitian variation structures over }G\}/\{\text{hyperbolic structures}\}$$
is an abelian group, called the Witt group of $\varepsilon$-hermitian variation structures of $G$.

For $G = \mathbb{Z}^k$, $WV_\varepsilon(\mathbb{Z}^k)$ decomposes as a direct sum indexed by unitary characters $\chi \in \widehat{G}$, and
$$WV_\varepsilon(\mathbb{Z}^k)_\chi \cong \begin{cases} \mathbb{Z} & \text{if } \chi \neq 1, \\ \mathbb{Z}/2 & \text{if } \chi = 1, \end{cases}$$
with explicit generators $(\mathbb{C}; \pm i^{(1-\varepsilon)/2}, \chi, \pm(\chi-1)i^{(\varepsilon-1)/2})$ for $\chi \neq 1$ and $(\mathbb{C}; 0, 1, 0)$ for $\chi = 1$.

Problem: Extend this classification of $WV_\varepsilon(G)$ to more general groups $G$. In particular, obtain a classification theorem when $G$ is the local fundamental group $\pi_1(B \setminus p^{-1}(0))$ of the complement of a plane curve singularity germ $p^{-1}(0) \subset (\mathbb{C}^2, 0)$, where $B$ is a small ball around the origin.
status_search_result: The question is posed as an open problem in a problem list on variation structures. Web search reveals continued research on hermitian variation structures (e.g., work relating real Seifert forms, Hodge numbers and Blanchfield pairings) but no general classification theorem of $WV_\varepsilon(G)$ for arbitrary $G$, nor for local fundamental groups of plane curve singularity complements. The problem appears to remain open.

paper_title: Variation Structures: Results and Open Problems
original_question: Let ηV(g) be the eta-invariant of an ε-hermitian variation structure V evaluated at g∈G, and let σ(V;Ke,Kg,Kh) be Wall's cocycle built from the kernels Kg={(φ,u):V(g)φ=u}. For which variation structures V, or for which groups G, does the eta-invariant satisfy the coboundary identity δ(η)=-σ, i.e. σ(V;Ke,Kg,Kh)=-η(g)-η(g^{-1}h)+η(h), as is known when G is finitely generated abelian?
self_contained_problem:
Fix a sign ε ∈ {+1, −1} and a group G. An ε-hermitian variation structure V over G consists of a finite-dimensional complex vector space H with an ε-hermitian non-degenerate form, together with, for each g ∈ G, a linear endomorphism V(g): H → H satisfying the standard axioms of an ε-hermitian variation structure (so that V decomposes into Hodge-type pieces V_χ indexed by characters χ, and to each piece one associates a signature-type invariant). For g ∈ G, define the eta-invariant η_V(g) as the sum over the Hodge decomposition of the signatures of the pieces:
   η_V(g) = Σ_χ η_V(g)_χ.

For three elements e (identity), g, h ∈ G, define the kernels
   K_g = {(φ, u) ∈ H ⊕ H : V(g)φ = u},
and analogously K_e, K_h. Let σ(V; K_e, K_g, K_h) denote Wall's non-additivity cocycle (the signature of the triple intersection form) associated with the triple (K_e, K_g, K_h).

It is known that whenever G is a finitely generated abelian group, the identity
   σ(V; K_e, K_g, K_h) = −η_V(g) − η_V(g^{-1} h) + η_V(h)
holds for every variation structure V over G; equivalently, δ(η) = −σ as a 2-coboundary relation on G.

Problem: Characterize all variation structures V (respectively, all groups G) for which the coboundary identity
   σ(V; K_e, K_g, K_h) = −η_V(g) − η_V(g^{-1} h) + η_V(h),
i.e. δ(η) = −σ, holds for all g, h ∈ G.
status_search_result: A targeted search did not surface any subsequent work explicitly characterizing the variation structures or groups beyond the finitely generated abelian case for which δ(η) = −σ. The current status appears unresolved in the available literature.

paper_title: Variation Structures: Results and Open Problems
context_brief: Eta invariant from limit Hodge data
original_question: For an isolated complete intersection singularity ϕ with two-dimensional base and an embedded-resolution local model (U,E)->(B,Δ), the restriction of V(ϕ) near P=Δ~0∩E gives a Z^2-variation structure. Compute the eta-invariant of this Z^2-variation structure in terms of the natural limit mixed Hodge structure with Z^2 action via the semisimple monodromy representation.
self_contained_problem:
Let $\phi:(X,0)\to(\mathbb{C}^2,0)$ be the germ of an isolated complete intersection singularity with two-dimensional base, and let $(U,E)\to(B,\Delta)$ be an embedded-resolution local model in which $\Delta=\Delta_1\cup\Delta_2\subset B$ is the discriminant (a normal-crossing curve) and $E\subset U$ is the exceptional divisor of the resolution. Fix a point $P\in\widetilde{\Delta}_0\cap E$, where $\widetilde{\Delta}_0$ denotes the strict transform of $\Delta$, and let $U_P$ be a small neighborhood of $P$. The fundamental group $\pi_1(U_P\setminus E)\cong\mathbb{Z}^2$ is generated by two commuting monodromies around the local branches meeting at $P$.

To this data one associates a $\mathbb{Z}^2$-variation structure $V(\phi)$ on the local vanishing cohomology near $P$: namely a finite-dimensional $\mathbb{Q}$-vector space $H$ equipped with a non-degenerate hermitian/$(-1)^n$-symmetric form, two commuting monodromy automorphisms $h_1,h_2$ preserving the form, and variation maps $\mathrm{Var}_i:H\to H$ satisfying $h_i=\mathrm{id}+\mathrm{Var}_i\circ b$ (with $b$ the form), as in the Nemethi theory of variation structures. The associated $\eta$-invariant $\eta(V(\phi);P)$ is the signature-type invariant defined for such $G=\mathbb{Z}^2$ variation structures.

On the other hand, the same local data carry a canonical limit mixed Hodge structure (the two-variable Steenbrink limit MHS at the corner $P$) on $H$, with weight filtration $W_\bullet$ and Hodge filtration $F^\bullet$, and with a commuting $\mathbb{Z}^2$-action by the semisimple parts of the two monodromies.

Problem. Give an explicit formula expressing the $\eta$-invariant of the $\mathbb{Z}^2$-variation structure $V(\phi)$ at $P$ in terms of the Hodge numbers $h^{p,q}_{\lambda_1,\lambda_2}$ of the eigenspace decomposition of this limit mixed Hodge structure under the semisimple $\mathbb{Z}^2$-monodromy action.
status_search_result: Web searches turned up the general framework of spectral pairs and limit mixed Hodge structures for isolated complete intersection singularities (e.g. work of Ebeling–Steenbrink) and Némethi's theory of variation structures, but no source explicitly providing the requested formula for the η-invariant of the $\mathbb{Z}^2$-variation structure in terms of the two-variable limit MHS at a corner. No resolution of this specific problem was located.

paper_title: Quadratic Stochastic Operators: Results and Open Problems
original_question: A quadratic stochastic operator (QSO) on S^{m-1} is determined by heredity coefficients P_{ij,k} satisfying P_{ij,k} >= 0, P_{ij,k} = P_{ji,k}, and sum_k P_{ij,k} = 1, via x'_k = sum_{i,j} P_{ij,k} x_i x_j. For Volterra QSOs, transversality means that the associated skew-symmetric matrix A has all even-order leading principal minors nonzero. How should transversality be defined for an arbitrary QSO, and what necessary and sufficient conditions on the full heredity-coefficient tensor P = (P_{ij,k}) characterize arbitrary QSOs that are transversal under that definition?
self_contained_problem:
Let $S^{m-1}=\{x=(x_1,\dots,x_m)\in\mathbb{R}^m : x_i\ge 0,\ \sum_{i=1}^m x_i=1\}$ denote the $(m-1)$-dimensional standard simplex. A quadratic stochastic operator (QSO) $V:S^{m-1}\to S^{m-1}$ is a mapping of the form
$$x'_k=(Vx)_k=\sum_{i,j=1}^m P_{ij,k}\, x_i x_j,\qquad k=1,\dots,m,$$
where the heredity coefficients $P_{ij,k}$ satisfy
$$P_{ij,k}\ge 0,\quad P_{ij,k}=P_{ji,k},\quad \sum_{k=1}^m P_{ij,k}=1\ \ \text{for all }i,j.$$

A QSO is called Volterra if $P_{ij,k}=0$ whenever $k\notin\{i,j\}$; in this case the operator can be written as
$$(Vx)_k=x_k\Big(1+\sum_{i=1}^m a_{ki} x_i\Big),$$
with a skew-symmetric matrix $A=(a_{ki})$ satisfying $a_{ki}=-a_{ik}$, $|a_{ki}|\le 1$. A skew-symmetric matrix $A$ is called transversal if all of its even-order leading principal minors are nonzero, and a Volterra QSO is called transversal when its associated $A$ is transversal.

Problem. Formulate a definition of transversality for an arbitrary (not necessarily Volterra) QSO, expressed in terms of the heredity tensor $P=(P_{ij,k})$, that reduces to the above notion in the Volterra case. Then determine necessary and sufficient conditions on the tensor $P$ that characterize when an arbitrary QSO is transversal under the proposed definition.
status_search_result: No published resolution was located. The problem is posed as an open problem in the survey on quadratic stochastic operators, and existing literature on QSOs (including studies of Volterra, F-, and permutation-type QSOs) does not appear to provide a definition of transversality for arbitrary QSOs together with necessary and sufficient conditions on the heredity tensor.

paper_title: Quadratic Stochastic Operators: Results and Open Problems
context_brief: Ergodicity for the three-parameter Volterra family
original_question: Consider the Volterra quadratic stochastic operator on S^2 defined by x' = x(1 + ay - bz), y' = y(1 - ax + cz), and z' = z(1 + bx - cy), with a, b, c in [-1, 1]. The known result states that when a, b, and c are all nonzero and have the same sign, the Cesaro averages (1/n) sum_{k=0}^{n-1} V^k(x) fail to converge for this operator. Determine the exact role of this parameter condition for the ergodic theorem: in particular, is the stated condition sufficient to decide when the ergodic theorem holds or fails for this family?
self_contained_problem:
Let S^2 = {(x,y,z) ∈ ℝ^3 : x,y,z ≥ 0, x+y+z = 1} denote the two-dimensional standard simplex. For parameters a, b, c ∈ [−1, 1], define the Volterra quadratic stochastic operator V : S^2 → S^2 by
  x' = x(1 + ay − bz),
  y' = y(1 − ax + cz),
  z' = z(1 + bx − cy).
Say that the ergodic theorem holds for V if, for every initial point x ∈ S^2, the Cesàro averages
  A_n(x) = (1/n) ∑_{k=0}^{n−1} V^k(x)
converge as n → ∞. It is known that whenever a, b, c are all nonzero and all have the same sign, the ergodic theorem fails for V (i.e. there exists x ∈ S^2 for which A_n(x) does not converge).

Question: Is the condition "a, b, c are all nonzero and have the same sign" also necessary for the failure of the ergodic theorem? Equivalently, does the ergodic theorem hold for V for every choice of (a,b,c) ∈ [−1,1]^3 not satisfying this condition (i.e. when at least one of a,b,c is zero, or when they do not all share the same sign)?
status_search_result: Subsequent work has addressed the ergodicity of Volterra quadratic stochastic operators on the two-dimensional simplex. In particular, a 2012 preprint claims to give a full description of the ergodic properties of three-dimensional Volterra QSOs, and a 2025 chapter "Ergodic Volterra Quadratic Mappings of the Simplex" presents a complete analysis of asymptotic behavior on the three-dimensional simplex, which would resolve the question of necessity for this three-parameter family. However, since I could not directly verify a precise statement matching the claimed converse, the status is recorded as partially_solved.

paper_title: Quadratic Stochastic Operators: Results and Open Problems
original_question: Let V be a Volterra quadratic stochastic operator on S^{m-1}, and let tau be a permutation of {1, ..., m}. Define the permuted Volterra operator V_tau by permuting the output coordinates of V according to tau; when tau is not the identity this operator is non-Volterra. For arbitrary tau, determine the asymptotic behavior of trajectories of V_tau, including convergence, periodic behavior, omega-limit sets, and other possible long-term dynamics.
self_contained_problem:
Let $S^{m-1} = \{x = (x_1, \ldots, x_m) \in \mathbb{R}^m : x_i \geq 0, \ \sum_{i=1}^m x_i = 1\}$ denote the standard $(m-1)$-simplex. A quadratic stochastic operator (QSO) $V : S^{m-1} \to S^{m-1}$ is a map of the form
\[
(V(x))_k = \sum_{i,j=1}^m p_{ij,k}\, x_i x_j, \qquad k = 1, \ldots, m,
\]
where the coefficients satisfy $p_{ij,k} = p_{ji,k} \geq 0$ and $\sum_{k=1}^m p_{ij,k} = 1$ for all $i, j$. The QSO $V$ is called Volterra if $p_{ij,k} = 0$ whenever $k \notin \{i, j\}$; equivalently, $(V(x))_k = x_k\bigl(1 + \sum_{i=1}^m a_{ki} x_i\bigr)$ for some skew-symmetric matrix $(a_{ki})$ with $|a_{ki}| \leq 1$.

Given a permutation $\tau$ of $\{1, \ldots, m\}$, define the permuted operator $V_\tau : S^{m-1} \to S^{m-1}$ by
\[
(V_\tau(x))_k = (V(x))_{\tau(k)}, \qquad k = 1, \ldots, m.
\]
When $\tau$ is not the identity, $V_\tau$ is in general a non-Volterra QSO.

For an arbitrary Volterra QSO $V$ and an arbitrary permutation $\tau$, describe the asymptotic behavior of the trajectories $\{V_\tau^n(x)\}_{n \geq 0}$ for $x \in S^{m-1}$: determine convergence/divergence, fixed and periodic points, $\omega$-limit sets, and any other long-term dynamical features.
status_search_result: The problem remains broadly open in full generality. Partial results have been established for specific subclasses: superpositions of Volterra and permuted Volterra QSOs on the two-dimensional simplex have been analyzed (trajectories shown to converge to periodic orbits or diverge), and certain classes of permuted Volterra QSOs in low dimensions have been investigated. However, the asymptotic behavior of permuted $\ell$-Volterra QSOs and the general case for arbitrary $m$ and arbitrary $\tau$ has not been resolved.

paper_title: Quadratic Stochastic Operators: Results and Open Problems
original_question: Develop a general dynamical-systems theory for ell-Volterra quadratic stochastic operators. The theory should include Lyapunov functions, descriptions of limit-point sets of trajectories, and other structural results governing the asymptotic behavior of the iterates of an ell-Volterra QSO.
self_contained_problem:
Let $S^{m-1}=\{x=(x_1,\dots,x_m)\in\mathbb{R}^m:x_i\ge 0,\ \sum_{i=1}^m x_i=1\}$ be the (m−1)-dimensional standard simplex. A quadratic stochastic operator (QSO) is a mapping $V:S^{m-1}\to S^{m-1}$ defined by
$$(Vx)_k=\sum_{i,j=1}^m p_{ij,k}\,x_i x_j,\qquad k=1,\dots,m,$$
where the coefficients satisfy $p_{ij,k}=p_{ji,k}\ge 0$ and $\sum_{k=1}^m p_{ij,k}=1$ for all $i,j$.

Fix an integer $\ell\in\{0,1,\dots,m\}$ and a subset $I\subseteq\{1,\dots,m\}$ with $|I|=\ell$. The QSO $V$ is called an $\ell$-Volterra operator (with respect to $I$) if
$$p_{ij,k}=0\quad\text{whenever }k\notin\{i,j\}\text{ and }\{i,j\}\cap I=\varnothing,$$
i.e., the operator behaves as a classical Volterra QSO on the indices outside $I$ while allowing arbitrary stochastic coefficients on pairs involving an index in $I$. (For $\ell=0$ one recovers the classical Volterra QSOs; for $\ell=m$ one recovers all QSOs.)

For an initial point $x^{(0)}\in S^{m-1}$, the trajectory is the sequence $x^{(n+1)}=V(x^{(n)})$, $n\ge 0$, and its $\omega$-limit set $\omega(x^{(0)})$ is the set of limit points of $\{x^{(n)}\}_{n\ge 0}$ in $S^{m-1}$.

Problem. Develop a general dynamical-systems theory for $\ell$-Volterra quadratic stochastic operators on $S^{m-1}$. In particular:
(a) Construct Lyapunov functions $\varphi:S^{m-1}\to\mathbb{R}$ (i.e., continuous functions for which $\varphi\circ V$ compares monotonically with $\varphi$) suitable for arbitrary $\ell$-Volterra QSOs.
(b) Describe the set of fixed points and periodic points of $V$.
(c) Describe the structure of $\omega(x^{(0)})$ for every $x^{(0)}\in S^{m-1}$, including conditions ensuring convergence to a fixed point, convergence to a periodic orbit, or more complicated asymptotic behavior.
(d) Establish further structural results governing the asymptotic dynamics of the iterates of an $\ell$-Volterra QSO.
status_search_result: The problem appears partially solved. For specific subclasses of ℓ-Volterra QSOs, Lyapunov functions have been constructed and used to obtain upper estimates of ω-limit sets, and the fixed-point sets have been characterized. However, a complete general dynamical-systems theory for arbitrary ℓ-Volterra QSOs—covering all Lyapunov functions and full descriptions of limit sets—remains open, and the broader question of asymptotic behavior of QSOs is still considered open in general.

Let $E=\{1,2,\dots,m\}$ be a finite set ("species set") and let $S^{m-1}=\{x=(x_1,\dots,x_m)\in\mathbb{R}^m: x_i\geq 0,\ \sum_i x_i=1\}$ be the standard simplex. A quadratic stochastic operator (QSO) on $S^{m-1}$ is a map $V:S^{m-1}\to S^{m-1}$ defined by

where the coefficients satisfy $P_{ij,k}\geq 0$, $P_{ij,k}=P_{ji,k}$, and $\sum_{k=1}^m P_{ij,k}=1$ for all $i,j$.

\[

\]
where the heredity coefficients $P_{ij,k}$ satisfy $P_{ij,k}=P_{ji,k}\ge 0$ and $\sum_{k=1}^m P_{ij,k}=1$ for all $i,j$. The operator $V$ is called regular if for every initial point $x^{(0)}\in S^{m-1}$ the iterates $x^{(n+1)}=V(x^{(n)})$ converge to a single fixed point of $V$ that does not depend on $x^{(0)}$.

original_question: Classify all surjective quadratic stochastic operators on the simplex S^{m-1} in every dimension m >= 5.
self_contained_problem:
Let $m\ge 2$ and let $S^{m-1}=\{x=(x_1,\dots,x_m)\in\mathbb{R}^m: x_i\ge 0,\ \sum_{i=1}^m x_i=1\}$ denote the standard $(m-1)$-dimensional simplex. A quadratic stochastic operator (QSO) on $S^{m-1}$ is a map $V:S^{m-1}\to S^{m-1}$ of the form
$$(Vx)_k=\sum_{i,j=1}^m p_{ij,k}\,x_i x_j,\qquad k=1,\dots,m,$$
where the coefficients $\{p_{ij,k}\}$ satisfy
$$p_{ij,k}=p_{ji,k}\ge 0\quad\text{for all }i,j,k,\qquad \sum_{k=1}^m p_{ij,k}=1\quad\text{for all }i,j.$$
The QSO $V$ is called surjective if $V(S^{m-1})=S^{m-1}$.

For every dimension $m\ge 5$, give a complete description (classification) of the set of all surjective quadratic stochastic operators on $S^{m-1}$, including a description of the extreme points of this set.

paper_title: Quadratic Stochastic Operators: Results and Open Problems
context_brief: Effect of phase transitions on QSO dynamics
original_question: When a quadratic stochastic operator is generated by a Gibbs measure associated with a Hamiltonian H on a continuous state space, and the Gibbs measure may be non-unique because the corresponding physical system has a phase transition, how does the thermodynamic phase transition affect the behavior of the trajectories of the associated QSO?
self_contained_problem:
Let $(E,\mathcal{B})$ be a measurable space (the state space, taken to be a continuum). Let $S(E,\mathcal{B})$ denote the set of all probability measures on $(E,\mathcal{B})$. A quadratic stochastic operator (QSO) is a map $V: S(E,\mathcal{B})\to S(E,\mathcal{B})$ defined by
$$(V\lambda)(A) \;=\; \int_E\!\!\int_E P(x,y,A)\,d\lambda(x)\,d\lambda(y), \qquad A\in\mathcal{B},$$
where $P(\cdot,\cdot,\cdot)$ is a measurable family of probability kernels satisfying $P(x,y,\cdot)=P(y,x,\cdot)$ for all $x,y\in E$. The trajectory of an initial measure $\lambda^{(0)}\in S(E,\mathcal{B})$ is the sequence $\lambda^{(n)} = V^n\lambda^{(0)}$, $n\ge 0$.

Suppose now that the kernel $P$ is constructed from a Gibbs measure $\mu$ on $E$ associated with a Hamiltonian $H:E\to\mathbb{R}$ at temperature $T>0$, so that the QSO $V=V_{H,T}$ is generated by this Gibbs measure. For Hamiltonians $H$ and temperatures $T$ at which the system exhibits a phase transition (i.e. the Gibbs measure associated with $(H,T)$ is non-unique), describe how this non-uniqueness/phase transition manifests itself in the dynamical behavior of the trajectories $\{V_{H,T}^n\lambda^{(0)}\}_{n\ge 0}$. In particular, determine the relationship between the set of limit points (or fixed points, periodic orbits, ergodic averages) of the QSO dynamics and the simplex of Gibbs measures for $(H,T)$, and show how crossing a phase-transition threshold changes the asymptotic behavior of trajectories.

paper_title: Quadratic Stochastic Operators: Results and Open Problems
context_brief: Non-product measures still tractable by QSO theory
original_question: In the graph-based construction of QSOs, a product measure over the maximal connected components of the graph yields a non-Volterra QSO reducible to separate Volterra QSOs. Find a probability measure mu on the configuration space that is not such a product measure, but whose corresponding non-Volterra QSO can still be investigated within an established theory of quadratic stochastic operators.
self_contained_problem:
Setup. Let $G=(V,L)$ be a (possibly infinite) graph with vertex set $V$ and edge set $L$, and consider a finite "spin" set $\Phi$. The configuration space is $\Omega=\Phi^{V}$, equipped with its product $\sigma$-algebra. For each probability measure $\mu$ on $\Omega$ one can define a quadratic stochastic operator (QSO) $V_\mu$ on the simplex of probability measures on $\Phi$ associated with the graph $G$ as follows: given two independent configurations sampled from a product distribution determined by a state $x$ on $\Phi$, one applies a local "crossover" rule along the edges of $G$ governed by $\mu$, and $V_\mu(x)$ is the law of the resulting single-site marginal. A QSO is called Volterra if its quadratic coefficients $p_{ij,k}$ satisfy $p_{ij,k}=0$ whenever $k\notin\{i,j\}$, and non-Volterra otherwise.

Reference (product) measure. Suppose the graph $G$ decomposes into maximal connected components $G_1,\dots,G_q$, and let
$$\mu_{\mathrm{prod}}=\bigotimes_{s=1}^{q}\mu_s,$$
where each $\mu_s$ is a probability measure on $\Phi^{V(G_s)}$. It is known that the non-Volterra QSO $V_{\mu_{\mathrm{prod}}}$ generated by such a product measure is reducible to $q$ separate Volterra QSOs, one for each component, and hence its dynamics can be analyzed by the existing theory of Volterra QSOs.

Problem. Exhibit a probability measure $\mu$ on the configuration space $\Omega=\Phi^{V}$ that is not of the product form $\mu_{\mathrm{prod}}$ described above, yet such that the corresponding non-Volterra QSO $V_\mu$ can still be analyzed within an established framework of quadratic stochastic operators (e.g. reduction to Volterra, permuted Volterra, $\ell$-Volterra, or other previously studied classes of QSOs). Describe such a $\mu$ explicitly and indicate the framework in which the associated non-Volterra QSO $V_\mu$ is tractable.

paper_title: Quadratic Stochastic Operators: Results and Open Problems
context_brief: Finite complete indicator systems for conjugacy
original_question: For the topological conjugacy classification of QSOs, an indicator is a polynomial in the heredity coefficients whose bounded range is forced by topological conjugacy, and a complete system of indicators is one whose bounds imply topological conjugacy. Does there exist a finite complete system of indicators for QSOs, and if so, what is a basis, meaning a minimal complete system, for these indicators?
self_contained_problem:
Let $S^{m-1} = \{x = (x_1,\dots,x_m) \in \mathbb{R}^m : x_i \ge 0,\ \sum_{i=1}^m x_i = 1\}$ be the $(m-1)$-dimensional simplex. A quadratic stochastic operator (QSO) on $S^{m-1}$ is a map $V : S^{m-1} \to S^{m-1}$ of the form
$$(Vx)_k = \sum_{i,j=1}^m P_{ij,k}\, x_i x_j, \qquad k=1,\dots,m,$$
where the heredity coefficients $P_{ij,k}$ satisfy $P_{ij,k} = P_{ji,k} \ge 0$ and $\sum_{k=1}^m P_{ij,k} = 1$ for all $i,j$. Two QSOs $V_1, V_2$ are said to be topologically conjugate if there exists a homeomorphism $h : S^{m-1}\to S^{m-1}$ with $h\circ V_1 = V_2\circ h$.

Call a polynomial $f$ in the variables $\{P_{ij,k}\}$ an indicator (for topological conjugacy of QSOs) if topological conjugateness of any two QSOs $V_1$ and $V_2$, with heredity coefficient arrays $P^{(1)}$ and $P^{(2)}$ respectively, forces the values $f(P^{(1)})$ and $f(P^{(2)})$ to lie in a common bounded subset of $\mathbb{R}$ (equivalently, the range of $f$ on each topological-conjugacy class is bounded). A family $\mathcal F$ of indicators is called a complete system of indicators if, whenever every $f \in \mathcal F$ satisfies the corresponding bound on two QSOs $V_1, V_2$, the operators $V_1$ and $V_2$ are topologically conjugate. A minimal (under inclusion) complete system of indicators is called a basis.

Question: Does there exist a finite complete system of indicators for QSOs on $S^{m-1}$? If yes, exhibit a basis (a minimal complete system of indicators).

paper_title: On some open problems in Diophantine approximation
original_question: Let Lambda be a full-rank lattice in R^(n+1). Define its homogeneous minimum N(Lambda) as the infimum of |z_0 z_1 ... z_n| over all nonzero z = (z_0, z_1, ..., z_n) in Lambda. Call a lattice algebraic when it is obtained from the embeddings of a basis 1, theta_1, ..., theta_n of a totally real algebraic field of degree n+1, followed by multiplication by a diagonal matrix with nonzero diagonal entries. For n >= 2, must every lattice Lambda with N(Lambda) > 0 be algebraic?
self_contained_problem:
For an integer n ≥ 2, let Λ ⊂ ℝ^(n+1) be a full-rank lattice. Define its homogeneous minimum by
   N(Λ) = inf { |z_0 z_1 ⋯ z_n| : z = (z_0, z_1, …, z_n) ∈ Λ, z ≠ 0 }.

Call Λ an algebraic lattice if there exist a totally real algebraic number field K of degree n+1 over ℚ, with elements 1, θ_1, …, θ_n forming a ℚ-basis of K, and (real) embeddings σ_0, σ_1, …, σ_n : K → ℝ such that, setting
   Ω = ( σ_i(θ_j) )_{0 ≤ i,j ≤ n}   (with θ_0 := 1),
one has Λ = G · Ω · ℤ^(n+1), where G is a diagonal (n+1)×(n+1) matrix with nonzero real diagonal entries.

Question: Is it true that every full-rank lattice Λ ⊂ ℝ^(n+1) with N(Λ) > 0 must be an algebraic lattice?
category_tag: Oppenheim conjecture on product of linear forms / algebraic lattices
status_search_result: This is the classical Oppenheim conjecture on products of linear forms (the lattice/algebraic-form version, distinct from the quadratic-form Oppenheim conjecture proved by Margulis). It is closely related to the Littlewood conjecture and is widely regarded as still open for every n ≥ 2; only partial results (e.g., Einsiedler–Katok–Lindenstrauss-type measure rigidity, bounds on Hausdorff dimension of exceptions) are known.

paper_title: On some open problems in Diophantine approximation
original_question: Let M >= 2 and let (t_j) be a sequence of positive real numbers satisfying t_{j+1}/t_j >= 1 + 1/M for all positive integers j. Peres and Schlag proved that there is an absolute constant gamma > 0 such that every such sequence admits a real alpha with ||alpha t_j|| >= gamma/(M log M) for all j. What is the correct optimal order, as a function of M, of the largest universal lower bound that can be forced in this homogeneous problem? In particular, can the gamma/(M log M) bound be improved?
self_contained_problem:
Fix a real number $M\ge 2$ and consider sequences $(t_j)_{j\ge 1}$ of positive real numbers satisfying the lacunarity condition
$$\frac{t_{j+1}}{t_j}\ \ge\ 1+\frac{1}{M}\qquad\text{for every }j\ge 1.$$
For a real number $x$, let $\|x\|$ denote the distance from $x$ to the nearest integer. Define
$$F(M)\ :=\ \inf_{(t_j)}\ \sup_{\alpha\in\mathbb{R}}\ \inf_{j\ge 1}\ \|\alpha\, t_j\|,$$
where the outer infimum is taken over all sequences $(t_j)$ satisfying the above lacunarity condition.

It is known that there is an absolute constant $\gamma>0$ such that for every such sequence $(t_j)$ there exists $\alpha\in\mathbb{R}$ with $\|\alpha t_j\|\ge \gamma/(M\log M)$ for all $j\ge 1$; equivalently, $F(M)\ge \gamma/(M\log M)$. It is also known that $F(M)\le C/M$ for some absolute constant $C$.

Determine the correct order of magnitude of $F(M)$ as $M\to\infty$. In particular, can the lower bound $\gamma/(M\log M)$ be replaced by $\gamma'/M$ (possibly with extra factors smaller than $\log M$), i.e., is the logarithmic factor necessary?
status_search_result: The Peres–Schlag bound $\gamma/(M\log M)$ is known to be sharp only up to the logarithmic factor, and the original authors note that their probabilistic construction does not generally give optimal bounds. Subsequent literature on lacunary sequences and Diophantine approximation (including work on the dispersion of dilated lacunary sequences and density-modulo-1 results applying Peres–Schlag's construction) continues to treat the homogeneous optimal order as an open problem; no improvement removing the $\log M$ factor in this generality has been located.

paper_title: On some open problems in Diophantine approximation
original_question: Fix alpha,beta in (0,1) with alpha + beta = 1. For theta = (theta_1,theta_2), consider the set of shifts eta = (eta_1,eta_2) in R^2 for which inf over q of max(q^alpha ||q theta_1 - eta_1||, q^beta ||q theta_2 - eta_2||) is positive. Harrap proved that this shift set has full Hausdorff dimension when theta belongs to BAD(alpha,beta). Does the same full-Hausdorff-dimension statement, and even the Schmidt-game winning property, hold without assuming theta belongs to BAD(alpha,beta)?
self_contained_problem:
Let $\alpha,\beta\in(0,1)$ satisfy $\alpha+\beta=1$. For $q\in\mathbb{N}$ and $x\in\mathbb{R}$, let $\|x\|$ denote the distance from $x$ to the nearest integer. Define the weighted badly approximable set
$$\mathrm{BAD}(\alpha,\beta)=\Big\{(\theta_1,\theta_2)\in\mathbb{R}^2:\inf_{q\in\mathbb{N}}\max\!\big(q^{\alpha}\|q\theta_1\|,\ q^{\beta}\|q\theta_2\|\big)>0\Big\}.$$
For a fixed $\theta=(\theta_1,\theta_2)\in\mathbb{R}^2$, consider the shift set
$$S(\theta)=\Big\{(\eta_1,\eta_2)\in\mathbb{R}^2:\inf_{q\in\mathbb{N}}\max\!\big(q^{\alpha}\|q\theta_1-\eta_1\|,\ q^{\beta}\|q\theta_2-\eta_2\|\big)>0\Big\}.$$
It is known that whenever $\theta\in\mathrm{BAD}(\alpha,\beta)$, the set $S(\theta)$ has full Hausdorff dimension $2$ in $\mathbb{R}^2$.

Question: Without the assumption $\theta\in\mathrm{BAD}(\alpha,\beta)$, is it true that for every $\theta\in\mathbb{R}^2$ (with $\theta_1,\theta_2$ irrational, say) the set $S(\theta)$ still has full Hausdorff dimension $2$? Moreover, is $S(\theta)$ a winning set for Schmidt's game?
status_search_result: Searches turn up Harrap's original full-dimension result for $\theta\in\mathrm{BAD}(\alpha,\beta)$ and various subsequent advances on weighted/twisted inhomogeneous badly approximable sets (including winning properties on nondegenerate curves and inhomogeneous Schmidt's conjecture in arbitrary dimensions), but no source clearly resolves the full-dimension/winning question for arbitrary $\theta$ outside $\mathrm{BAD}(\alpha,\beta)$. Status remains unclear from the available evidence.

paper_title: On some open problems in Diophantine approximation
original_question: Let theta_1 and theta_2 be real numbers linearly independent over Z together with 1. For positive integers x_1,x_2, define psi_+(t) as the minimum of ||theta_1 x_1 + theta_2 x_2|| over 0 < max(x_1,x_2) <= t, and define omega_+(theta_1,theta_2) as the supremum of gamma such that lim inf as t tends to infinity of t^gamma psi_+(t) is finite. What is the optimal value of inf omega_+(theta_1,theta_2) over linearly independent pairs? Is it the golden ratio phi, the exponent sigma discussed in the same setting, or some value between them?
self_contained_problem:
For real numbers $\theta_1,\theta_2$ such that $1,\theta_1,\theta_2$ are linearly independent over $\mathbb{Z}$, and for $t\ge 1$, define
$$\psi_+(t)=\psi_{+;\Theta}(t)=\min_{\substack{x_1,x_2\in\mathbb{Z}_{>0}\cup\{0\},\; (x_1,x_2)\ne(0,0)\\ \max(x_1,x_2)\le t,\; x_1,x_2\ge 0}}\|\theta_1 x_1+\theta_2 x_2\|,$$
where $\|\cdot\|$ denotes the distance to the nearest integer and the minimum is taken over pairs of nonnegative integers $x_1,x_2$ (positive integers in the strict sense) with $0<\max(x_1,x_2)\le t$. Set
$$\omega_+(\theta_1,\theta_2)=\sup\{\gamma\ge 0:\liminf_{t\to\infty} t^{\gamma}\psi_+(t)<\infty\}.$$
Let $\phi=\tfrac{1+\sqrt 5}{2}$ denote the golden ratio, and let $\sigma$ denote the unique real root greater than $1$ of $x^3-x-1=0$ (the "plastic" constant), which arises as a known upper bound in this context.

Determine the exact value of
$$\inf_{\theta_1,\theta_2}\omega_+(\theta_1,\theta_2),$$
the infimum being taken over all pairs $(\theta_1,\theta_2)$ with $1,\theta_1,\theta_2$ linearly independent over $\mathbb{Z}$. In particular, decide whether this infimum equals $\phi$, equals $\sigma$, or takes some intermediate value in $(\sigma,\phi)$ (or $(\phi,\sigma)$).
status_search_result: The question of the optimal value of the exponent $\inf_\Theta \omega_+(\Theta)$ for a linear form in two positive integer variables appears in Moshchevitin's list of open problems in Diophantine approximation and is referenced in his work on Schmidt's theorem with positive integers. No published resolution determining whether the optimal value equals $\phi$, $\sigma$, or an intermediate value was found; the problem appears to remain open.

paper_title: On some open problems in Diophantine approximation
original_question: Does there exist an absolute constant k such that for every positive integer q there is an integer a coprime to q whose finite continued fraction expansion a/q = [b_0; b_1, ..., b_s] has all partial quotients b_j, for j >= 1, bounded by k? Zaremba's original stronger guess is that k = 5 suffices.
self_contained_problem:
For a rational number a/q in lowest terms with q a positive integer, write its finite continued fraction expansion as
   a/q = [b_0; b_1, b_2, …, b_s] := b_0 + 1/(b_1 + 1/(b_2 + 1/(… + 1/b_s))),
where b_0 ∈ ℤ and b_1, …, b_s are positive integers (the partial quotients).

Question: Does there exist an absolute constant k (independent of q) such that for every positive integer q there exists an integer a with gcd(a, q) = 1 whose continued fraction expansion a/q = [b_0; b_1, …, b_s] satisfies
   max_{1 ≤ j ≤ s} b_j ≤ k ?

The stronger form of the question asks whether k = 5 suffices.
status_search_result: Zaremba's conjecture remains open. Significant progress was made by Bourgain and Kontorovich (2014), who proved that the set of denominators q admitting such an a with partial quotients bounded by an absolute constant has density 1, and subsequent work by Huang, Kan, Frolenkov–Kan, and others has improved various aspects, but the full conjecture (and the stronger k = 5 form) is not established.

paper_title: On some open problems in Diophantine approximation
original_question: Let p be prime, U a multiplicative subgroup of Z_p^*, v a nonzero residue class, and R = vU. A known result assumes #R >= 10^8 p^(7/8) log^(5/2) p and then finds an element a in R whose continued-fraction partial quotients for a/p have sum at most 500 log p log log p, yielding D(a,p) << log p log log p. Can the exponent 7/8 in the subgroup-size hypothesis be replaced by a smaller exponent while retaining such a conclusion?
self_contained_problem:
Let $p$ be a prime, let $U$ be a multiplicative subgroup of $(\mathbb{Z}/p\mathbb{Z})^*$, let $v\in(\mathbb{Z}/p\mathbb{Z})^*$, and set $R = vU \subset \mathbb{Z}/p\mathbb{Z}$. For an integer $a$ with $1\le a<p$ and $\gcd(a,p)=1$, write the (finite) regular continued fraction expansion
$$\frac{a}{p}=[b_1,b_2,\dots,b_l],\qquad b_i=b_i(a),\ l=l(a),$$
and define the discrepancy-type quantity $D(a,p)$ as the discrepancy of the sequence $\{ka/p\}_{k=1}^{p-1}$ modulo $1$ (so that $D(a,p)\ll \frac{1}{p}\sum_{i=1}^{l(a)} b_i$).

It is known that there exists an absolute constant such that whenever
$$\#R \;\ge\; 10^8\, p^{7/8}\,\log^{5/2} p,$$
one can find an element $a\in R$ with
$$\sum_{i=1}^{l(a)} b_i(a) \;\le\; 500\,\log p\,\log\log p,$$
and consequently $D(a,p)\ll \log p\,\log\log p$.

Problem: Determine whether the exponent $7/8$ in the size hypothesis $\#R\ge 10^8 p^{7/8}\log^{5/2}p$ can be replaced by a strictly smaller exponent $\theta<7/8$ (possibly with a different implicit constant and a different power of $\log p$) while still guaranteeing the existence of an element $a\in R$ whose continued-fraction partial quotients for $a/p$ satisfy $\sum_i b_i(a)\ll \log p\,\log\log p$ (so that $D(a,p)\ll \log p\,\log\log p$).
status_search_result: A targeted web search did not surface a paper explicitly improving the exponent 7/8 in the stated subgroup-size hypothesis for the continued-fraction / discrepancy bound on cosets of multiplicative subgroups of $\mathbb{Z}/p\mathbb{Z}$. No source clearly establishing the improvement (or its impossibility) was located, so the current status is taken as unknown.

paper_title: On some open problems in Diophantine approximation
context_brief: Salem problem for question mark function
original_question: For Minkowski's question mark function ?(x), define its Fourier-Stieltjes coefficients d_n by d_n = integral from 0 to 1 of cos(2 pi n x) d?(x). Does d_n tend to 0 as n tends to infinity?
self_contained_problem:
Let ?(x) denote Minkowski's question mark function on [0,1], defined as follows: for x = [0; a_1, a_2, a_3, ...] ∈ [0,1] written as a regular continued fraction with positive integer partial quotients a_i, set
  ?(x) = 2 · Σ_{k≥1} (-1)^{k+1} · 2^{-(a_1 + a_2 + ... + a_k)}.
The function ? is continuous and strictly increasing on [0,1], with ?(0)=0 and ?(1)=1, and it induces a Borel probability measure d? on [0,1] (singular with respect to Lebesgue measure). Define the Fourier–Stieltjes coefficients of ? by
  d_n = ∫_0^1 cos(2π n x) d?(x),   n ∈ ℕ.
Determine whether
  d_n → 0   as n → ∞.
category_tag: Minkowski question mark function / Salem's problem
status_search_result: Salem's 1943 problem on the decay of the Fourier–Stieltjes coefficients of Minkowski's question mark function has been resolved affirmatively. Yakubovich (2011, C. R. Math.) gave an affirmative answer using the Kontorovich–Lebedev transform, and Jordan and Sahlsten later established polynomial decay of the Fourier transform of the Minkowski measure, in particular implying d_n → 0.

paper_title: On some open problems in Diophantine approximation
original_question: Let F_n be the Stern-Brocot sequence at level n, written in increasing order as 0 = xi_{0,n} < xi_{1,n} < ... < xi_{2^n,n} = 1. Define R_n by the identity sum_{j=1}^{2^n} (xi_{j,n} - j/2^n)^2 = 2^n integral from 0 to 1 of (?(x)-x)^2 dx + R_n, where ? is Minkowski's question mark function. Is R_n -> 0 as n -> infinity?
self_contained_problem:
Let ?: [0,1] → [0,1] denote Minkowski's question mark function, the strictly increasing continuous function characterized by ?(0)=0, ?(1)=1, and the functional relation that sends a number with continued fraction expansion [0; a_1, a_2, a_3, …] to 2·∑_{k≥1} (−1)^{k+1} 2^{−(a_1+a_2+…+a_k)}.

Define the Stern-Brocot sequences F_n ⊂ [0,1] recursively as follows. Set F_0 = {0/1, 1/1}. Given F_n listed in increasing order, F_{n+1} is obtained by inserting between every two consecutive entries a/b < c/d the mediant (a+c)/(b+d). Then F_n has exactly 2^n + 1 elements; write them in increasing order as
   0 = ξ_{0,n} < ξ_{1,n} < … < ξ_{2^n, n} = 1.

For each integer n ≥ 0 define the remainder R_n by the identity
   ∑_{j=1}^{2^n} (ξ_{j,n} − j/2^n)^2  =  2^n ∫_0^1 (?(x) − x)^2 dx + R_n.

(It is known that |R_n| ≤ 4 for all n.)

Question: Does R_n → 0 as n → ∞?

paper_title: Trimer Covers in the Triangular Grid: Twenty Mostly Open Problems
original_question: Consider the finite triangular-grid regions called (a,b)-benzels, tiled by five trihex prototiles: a right-pointing stone, a left-pointing stone, and three bone orientations. Let T003(a,b) count tilings that allow no stones and all three bone orientations. For k >= 2, what exact formula governs T003(k(3k-1)/2, k(3k+1)/2)? More weakly, is there a recurrence or other counting method that is substantially more efficient than brute-force enumeration for these bone-only benzels?
self_contained_problem:
Work in the triangular lattice and consider the following setup. Let $\omega = e^{2\pi i/3}$ and let $L = \mathbb{Z} + \mathbb{Z}\omega$ be the triangular lattice in the complex plane. For nonnegative integers $a,b$, the $(a,b)$-benzel is the (finite) region consisting of all unit triangular cells lying entirely within the hexagon whose vertices are $\omega^j(a\omega + b)$ and $-\omega^j(a + b\omega)$ for $j \in \{0,1,2\}$. The unit triangles come in two orientations (up-pointing and down-pointing).

Five trihex prototiles are allowed, each formed by three mutually adjacent triangular cells: a right stone, a left stone, and three bone orientations (vertical bone, rising bone, falling bone). A bone consists of three triangles whose centers are collinear; a stone consists of three triangles whose centers form a small triangle.

Let $T_{003}(a,b)$ denote the number of tilings of the $(a,b)$-benzel that use no stones (neither right nor left) and may use any of the three bone orientations. It is known that an $(a,b)$-benzel admits a tiling by bones alone only if $\{a,b\} = \{k(3k-1)/2,\; k(3k+1)/2\}$ for some integer $k \geq 2$.

(a) Find an exact closed-form formula for
$$T_{003}\!\left(	frac{k(3k-1)}{2},\; 	frac{k(3k+1)}{2}ight), \qquad k \geq 2.$$
(b) Failing an exact formula, exhibit a recurrence or other method of computing $T_{003}(k(3k-1)/2,\, k(3k+1)/2)$ that is substantially more efficient than brute-force enumeration of all tilings.
status_search_result: Jim Propp's benzel problems page explicitly lists Problem 1 as "Open." The recent paper "Tilings of benzels via generalized compression" (2024) and "A pentagonal number theorem for tribone tilings" (Kim–Propp) establish the pentagonal-number existence criterion for bone-only tilability but do not provide an exact enumeration formula or efficient recurrence for $T_{003}$.

paper_title: Trimer Covers in the Triangular Grid: Twenty Mostly Open Problems
context_brief: left stones two bones offset formula
original_question: Let T012(a,b) denote the number of tilings of the (a,b)-benzel in which left stones are allowed, right stones are forbidden, and exactly two of the three bone orientations are allowed. Is it true that T012(3n+1, 3n+2) = 2^n n! for every n >= 1?
self_contained_problem:
Consider the triangular grid and the hexagonal (honeycomb) lattice dual to it. For positive integers $a,b$, the $(a,b)$-benzel is a specific finite region of the hexagonal grid (a hexagonal analogue of the Aztec diamond) whose precise definition is the following: take all hexagonal cells whose centers $(x,y)$ satisfy the four inequalities $b \le 2x+y$, $2x+y \le 2a+b-1$, $-a \le x-y \le a+b-1$ (after a suitable normalization of axes). The prototiles considered here are "trihexes" (connected unions of three hexagonal cells), grouped into two classes:
- Stones: a "left stone" and a "right stone" (the two mirror-image triangular arrangements of three hexagons meeting at a vertex);
- Bones: three straight trihexes obtained by gluing three hexagons in a row, occurring in three possible orientations (vertical, rising, and falling).

For $i,j \in \{0,1\}$ and $k \in \{0,1,2,3\}$, let $T_{ijk}(a,b)$ denote the number of tilings of the $(a,b)$-benzel by translates of the prototiles, where the right stone is allowed iff $i=1$, the left stone is allowed iff $j=1$, and exactly $k$ of the three bone orientations are allowed (when $k=2$, the count is summed/considered over the relevant choice of which two bone orientations are permitted, in accordance with the standard convention that makes $T_{ijk}$ well-defined as in the formulation of the conjecture).

Prove or disprove: for every integer $n \ge 1$,
$$T_{012}(3n+1,\,3n+2) \;=\; 2^n\, n!.$$

original_question: Let T103(a,b) denote the number of tilings of the (a,b)-benzel in which right stones are allowed, left stones are forbidden, and all three bone orientations are allowed. Whenever the Conway-Lagarias invariant of the (a,b)-benzel is positive or zero, must a type-103 tiling exist?
self_contained_problem:
Work in the triangular lattice. A "stone" is a trimer consisting of three unit triangles meeting at a common vertex; there are two chiralities, called the right stone and the left stone. A "bone" is a trimer consisting of three unit triangles in a row; bones come in three rotational orientations. For positive integers a, b, the (a,b)-benzel is a certain hexagonally symmetric region of the triangular lattice (a hexagonal region with corners trimmed so as to be tileable by trimers, as introduced in the study of Propp's benzels).

For indices i, j ∈ {0,1} and k ∈ {0,1,2,3}, let T_{ijk}(a,b) denote the number of tilings of the (a,b)-benzel using the prototile set that includes the right stone iff i=1, includes the left stone iff j=1, and includes exactly k of the three bone orientations (chosen in the standard rotation-symmetric way when k<3, otherwise all three). 

The Conway–Lagarias invariant CL(a,b) of the (a,b)-benzel is defined (following Conway–Lagarias) by: for any tiling of a simply-connected region of the triangular lattice by stones and bones, the total area of right stones minus the total area of left stones depends only on the region; this common value is CL(a,b).

Question: Is it true that whenever CL(a,b) ≥ 0, we have T_{103}(a,b) > 0? Equivalently, whenever the Conway–Lagarias invariant of the (a,b)-benzel is nonnegative, must there exist a tiling of the (a,b)-benzel using only right stones and bones (in any of the three orientations), with left stones forbidden?

original_question: Let T112(a,b) count tilings of the (a,b)-benzel when both stone orientations are allowed and exactly two of the three bone orientations are allowed. What formula governs T112(3n-1, 3n) for n >= 1?

For positive integers $a, b$, define the $(a,b)$-benzel as the region obtained from the triangular grid by removing all unit triangles whose centroid lies "too far" in a specified way (the standard benzel region with parameters $a, b$, having three-fold rotational symmetry, used in the study of trimer tilings on the hexagonal lattice). There are two stone orientations (left stone and right stone, each formed by three triangles meeting at a vertex) and three bone orientations (each a row of three triangles aligned along one of the three lattice directions).

For $i, j \in \{0,1\}$ and $k \in \{0,1,2,3\}$, let $T_{ijk}(a,b)$ denote the number of tilings of the $(a,b)$-benzel using only prototiles drawn from the following allowed set: the right stone is allowed iff $i = 1$, the left stone is allowed iff $j = 1$, and exactly $k$ of the three bone orientations are allowed (with the choice of which $k$ bone orientations being fixed by convention up to symmetry).

Define
$$T(n) = T_{112}(3n-1, 3n) \quad \text{for } n \geq 1.$$

self_contained_problem:
Consider the triangular grid in the plane viewed as a tessellation by unit upward- and downward-pointing triangular cells. For positive integers a and b with appropriate parity, the (a,b)-benzel is a certain centrally symmetric hexagonal region of this grid (formed by removing three pairs of corner triangles from a large equilateral triangle so that the resulting region has 60°/120° angles and side lengths controlled by a and b).

The allowed prototiles for tiling are the following five trimers (each a union of three cells of the triangular grid):
- the right stone and the left stone (the two orientations of a triangle made of three pairwise-adjacent cells),
- three bones (the three orientations of a straight strip of three collinear cells): the vertical bone, the rising bone, and the falling bone.

For i,j ∈ {0,1} and k ∈ {0,1,2,3}, let T_{ijk}(a,b) denote the number of tilings of the (a,b)-benzel using only prototiles from the following set: the right stone is allowed iff i = 1, the left stone is allowed iff j = 1, and exactly k of the three bones are allowed (the choice of which k bones is fixed by a standard convention symmetric in the bone orientations, and T_{ijk} is well-defined up to this symmetry).

In particular T_{112}(a,b) counts the tilings in which both stones are allowed and exactly two of the three bone orientations are allowed.

Separately, the "number of royal paths in a lattice of order n" is the standard combinatorial sequence R(n) counting lattice paths from (0,0) to (n,n) using steps (1,0), (0,1), and (1,1), where each step has a weight depending on direction in the manner of the classical royal-path / Delannoy-type weighted count (the specific sequence starts 1, 6, 50, 518, 5870, ...).

   T_{112}(n+2, 2n) = R(n) ?

- A right stone is the union of one ▵ and two adjacent ▿'s forming an isoceles trapezoid of one orientation, and a left stone is its mirror image.

paper_title: Trimer Covers in the Triangular Grid: Twenty Mostly Open Problems
original_question: For tilings of a finite simply-connected region in the hexagonal grid by stones and bones, there are two natural local 2-flip moves: one replaces two oppositely oriented stones by two bones, and the other replaces a stone-and-bone pair by a stone of the same orientation together with a bone of a different orientation. Can every such tiling be transformed into every other such tiling by a finite succession of these 2-flips?
self_contained_problem:
Consider the hexagonal grid (the regular tiling of the plane by unit hexagons). A "stone" is a tile consisting of three pairwise-adjacent hexagonal cells meeting at a common vertex; there are two orientations of stones (the "left" stone and the "right" stone, related by 180° rotation). A "bone" is a tile consisting of three hexagonal cells arranged in a straight line; there are three orientations of bones (horizontal, rising at 60°, and falling at -60°). Together stones and bones constitute the five "stones-and-bones" prototiles, each covering three cells of the hexagonal grid.

Let R be a finite simply-connected region of the hexagonal grid, and consider tilings of R by congruent copies of the five prototiles above. Define two local "2-flip" moves on such tilings:

(F1) Replace two stones of opposite orientations (one left and one right) that together occupy six cells forming a region tilable by two bones, by two bones covering the same six cells; or perform the reverse replacement.

(F2) Replace a pair consisting of one stone and one bone, occupying six cells, by another pair consisting of a stone of the same orientation and a bone of a different orientation covering the same six cells.

Two tilings of R are said to be "2-flip equivalent" if one can be obtained from the other by a finite sequence of moves of types (F1) and (F2). Question: For every finite simply-connected region R of the hexagonal grid, is it the case that any two tilings of R by stones and bones are 2-flip equivalent?
status_search_result: The general question appears to remain open. A restricted case — when one of the three bone orientations is forbidden (type 112) — is known to follow from Sheffield's connectivity theorem for ribbon tilings. Recent work (2025) on tilability of the hexagonal grid by stones, bones, and snakes via dimer models extends related results but does not resolve the full 2-flip connectivity question.
