paper_title: Neutrino-nucleus interactions: open questions and future projects
original_question: How can a larger set of experimental neutrino-nucleus data strengthen the interpolation between low-energy neutrino-nucleus models, such as Elementary Particle Theory, Effective Field Theories, the shell model, and the Random-Phase Approximation, and high-energy descriptions based on the Fermi Gas, while also improving extrapolations to neutron-rich nuclei of astrophysical interest that are not experimentally accessible?
self_contained_problem:
Consider the theoretical modeling of neutrino-nucleus scattering across a wide range of incident neutrino energies. In the low-energy regime (roughly below a few tens of MeV), the cross sections are typically computed using approaches such as Elementary Particle Theory (treating the nucleus as a single object whose form factors are constrained by symmetries), Effective Field Theories of the strong and weak interactions, the nuclear shell model, and the Random-Phase Approximation (RPA), which builds correlated particle-hole excitations on top of a mean-field ground state. In the high-energy regime (roughly above a few hundred MeV), the standard description is the Relativistic Fermi Gas model, in which the target nucleus is treated as a degenerate gas of non-interacting nucleons with momenta filling a Fermi sphere.

Formulate and answer the following question. Given a (hypothetical) enlarged set of measured neutrino-nucleus cross sections σ(Eν, A, Z) on a variety of nuclei (A, Z) over a broad range of neutrino energies Eν spanning the transition region between the two regimes:

(a) Construct a quantitative interpolation scheme that smoothly matches the low-energy nuclear-structure-based predictions (EPT/EFT/shell model/RPA) to the high-energy Fermi-Gas predictions, in a way that is consistent with all the measured data and respects exact symmetry constraints (CVC, PCAC, current conservation, sum rules).

(b) Using this scheme, give controlled extrapolations of σ(Eν, A, Z) to neutron-rich nuclei of astrophysical relevance (e.g. those participating in r-process nucleosynthesis or core-collapse supernova environments) that are not currently accessible experimentally, together with rigorous theoretical uncertainty estimates.

Does there exist such an interpolation/extrapolation framework that is simultaneously consistent with all available data, respects the relevant nuclear and electroweak symmetries, and provides quantitatively reliable predictions for neutron-rich nuclei?
status_search_result: Neutrino-nucleus cross section modeling across the transition between low- and high-energy regimes remains an active and unresolved area, as documented in recent reviews (NuSTEC white papers, Snowmass reports). Tensions between data and models persist for medium-energy quasi-elastic and resonance regions, and extrapolations to neutron-rich nuclei for astrophysics still carry large theoretical uncertainties. No unified, fully validated framework currently exists.

original_question: Can a low-energy beta-beam facility, either at a future exotic-ion laboratory such as GSI, GANIL, EURISOL, or RIA or as part of the high-energy CERN beta-beam facility, meet the essential requirements of attainable ion intensity and an available storage ring for ions?
self_contained_problem:
Consider the proposal of a low-energy beta-beam facility, in which radioactive ions that undergo beta decay are produced, accelerated to (relatively low) Lorentz boost factors, and stored in a circulating ring so that the resulting pure (anti-)electron-neutrino beam emerging from beta decay can be directed toward a low-energy neutrino-nucleus experiment. Two architectural scenarios are envisaged:

(a) the facility is embedded in a dedicated exotic-ion laboratory (such as a high-intensity radioactive ion beam facility of GSI/GANIL/EURISOL/RIA type), or

(b) the facility is appended to a high-energy beta-beam complex at a large hadron laboratory (CERN-type), with an additional low-energy storage ring downstream.

For either scenario, the two essential technical requirements are:
(i) the attainable production intensity of suitable beta-unstable ions (e.g., 6He, 18Ne) must be sufficient to yield a useful neutrino flux at the detector; and
(ii) a storage ring capable of accumulating and circulating these ions at the desired (low) gamma factor must be available.

Problem: Determine whether either of the scenarios (a) or (b) can simultaneously meet requirements (i) and (ii) at a level sufficient to make a low-energy beta-beam facility feasible for neutrino-nucleus interaction studies.
status_search_result: Subsequent design studies (EURISOL Design Study under FP6, beta-beam Letter of Intent, and HIE-ISOLDE storage ring technical design report) have continued to investigate the feasibility of a low-energy beta-beam, addressing both ion intensity targets and storage ring concepts. However, no low-energy beta-beam facility has been built, and the question of whether the required ion intensities and a dedicated storage ring can be realized in practice remains an open feasibility/design question rather than a settled result.

context_brief: Low-energy beta-beam sensitivity to neutrino magnetic moment
original_question: Can a low-energy beta-beam source at rest, combined with very low-threshold detectors and accurately calculated neutrino fluxes, improve current direct limits on the neutrino magnetic moment by almost an order of magnitude, and what precise sensitivity remains after detailed detector-response simulation?
self_contained_problem:
Consider a hypothetical neutrino source consisting of radioactive ions decaying at rest, which produces a pure flavor neutrino flux (a "beta-beam at rest") whose energy spectrum is determined by the known beta-decay kinematics of the parent isotope and can therefore be computed with high precision. Suppose this source is coupled to a detector with a very low recoil-energy threshold (well below 1 keV scale), so that elastic neutrino–electron (and/or neutrino–nucleus) scattering events at small energy transfer can be recorded. The differential cross section for such scattering receives a Standard Model weak contribution plus an additional contribution proportional to the square of the neutrino magnetic moment μ_ν (in units of the Bohr magneton μ_B), the latter being strongly enhanced as the recoil energy tends to zero.

Question: Determine whether such a configuration can improve the current direct experimental upper limits on the neutrino magnetic moment μ_ν by close to an order of magnitude, and compute the precise sensitivity on μ_ν (in units of μ_B) that remains achievable after a detailed simulation of the detector response, including realistic energy resolution, threshold effects, and background subtraction.
status_search_result: Feasibility studies indicate that a low-energy beta-beam source combined with low-threshold detectors could in principle probe neutrino magnetic moments at the level of a few × 10⁻¹¹ μ_B, comparable to or slightly better than current direct limits, but this requires very high ion production rates (≳ 10¹⁵ s⁻¹) and no such facility has been realized. Current best direct laboratory limits on μ_ν come from reactor and dark-matter direct-detection experiments (e.g., CONUS, XENONnT), with the precise achievable beta-beam sensitivity depending on detector-response simulations that have not been definitively settled. The status of the specific claim of nearly an order-of-magnitude improvement therefore remains unresolved.

paper_title: Open Problems in Heavy Quarkonium Physics
original_question: Are the approximately equal radial spacings seen in the low-lying bottomonium spectrum merely a numerical coincidence of perturbative calculations with leading-order renormalon cancellation, or do they genuinely reflect that these states are Coulombic or quasi-Coulombic bound states? Resolving this requires further theoretical and phenomenological study of higher bottomonium levels and their fine splittings.
self_contained_problem:
In the framework of non-relativistic QCD applied to heavy quarkonium, consider the low-lying bottomonium spectrum (the b\bar b bound states such as the Υ(nS) family for n=1,2,3, together with their χ_b and η_b partners). Empirically, the radial level spacings between successive S-wave states are observed to be approximately equal. In perturbative computations of the static QCD potential, the leading u=1/2 infrared renormalon of the potential cancels against the renormalon of twice the heavy-quark pole mass when one expresses the pole mass in terms of a short-distance mass (e.g. the MS-bar, PS, or MSR mass); after this leading-order renormalon cancellation, the perturbative predictions for radial spacings come out close to the observed values.

Determine whether this near-equality of radial spacings in bottomonium is:
(a) merely a numerical coincidence arising from perturbative calculations after leading-order renormalon cancellation (potentially due to large NLL/NNLO corrections analogous to those in 1S hyperfine splittings, or to sizeable non-perturbative corrections hidden within current error bands), or
(b) a genuine reflection of the fact that these bottomonium states are Coulombic or quasi-Coulombic bound states (i.e. dominated by the perturbative one-gluon-exchange Coulomb-like interaction, with non-perturbative contributions subleading).

Provide a theoretical and phenomenological resolution by analysing higher bottomonium levels and their fine splittings in a manner that decisively distinguishes (a) from (b).
status_search_result: Recent N3LO NRQCD analyses of the bottomonium spectrum (e.g. global fits at N3LO around 2018, and N3LO bottom-mass extractions) report that n=1,2 bottomonium levels are well described perturbatively after renormalon cancellation, while n=3 states show poor perturbative convergence, leaving the Coulombic-versus-coincidence interpretation of the regular radial spacings unresolved. No conclusive demonstration favoring (a) or (b) has appeared, so the question remains open.

paper_title: Open Problems in Heavy Quarkonium Physics
original_question: Why do Tevatron measurements of high-transverse-momentum charmonium production fail to show the transverse polarization expected from standard NRQCD gluon-fragmentation dynamics? In the scenario described in the paper, large-pT production is dominated by a transversely polarized gluon fragmenting into a color-octet 3S1 heavy-quark pair, and standard NRQCD power counting predicts that this transverse polarization should survive into the observed S-wave quarkonium state. The open problem is whether the discrepancy is due to experimental uncertainty, alternative power counting, or higher-order effects that dilute the polarization.
self_contained_problem:
In the framework of non-relativistic QCD (NRQCD) factorization for inclusive heavy quarkonium hadroproduction, the production cross section for an S-wave charmonium H (e.g. J/ψ or ψ(2S)) is written as a sum over intermediate heavy quark–antiquark Fock states n = ^{2S+1}L_J^{[1,8]} of short-distance partonic coefficients times long-distance NRQCD matrix elements ⟨O^H[n]⟩, with a power counting in the heavy-quark velocity v. At transverse momenta p_T much larger than the quarkonium mass, the leading short-distance mechanism is gluon fragmentation into a color-octet ^3S_1 c c̄ pair, and the fragmenting gluon is, to leading order in α_s, almost on-shell and therefore transversely polarized. Within standard v-power counting, the heavy-quark spin symmetry of NRQCD then predicts that the produced S-wave charmonium should inherit a sizable transverse polarization at large p_T, quantified by the polar angular distribution coefficient α → +1 (where dN/dcosθ ∝ 1 + α cos^2 θ in a suitable reference frame) as p_T → ∞.

Hadron-collider measurements of prompt J/ψ and ψ(2S) polarization at large p_T do not show this strong transverse polarization; instead α is observed to be small, and in some cases slightly longitudinal.

Problem: Determine, within NRQCD factorization (or a controlled modification of its power counting), the mechanism that resolves this discrepancy. Concretely:
(i) compute the polarization α(p_T) of prompt J/ψ and ψ(2S) at large p_T including all contributions (color-singlet and color-octet ^1S_0^{[8]}, ^3S_1^{[8]}, ^3P_J^{[8]}) consistently to higher orders in α_s and v, including effects such as soft-gluon emission off the intermediate color-octet pair, feed-down from heavier charmonia, and possible alternative power countings;
(ii) decide whether the observed lack of transverse polarization can be reconciled with NRQCD predictions while simultaneously describing the measured unpolarized p_T spectra of these states with a single, universal set of long-distance matrix elements ⟨O^H[n]⟩.
status_search_result: As of 2024–2025, the charmonium polarization puzzle remains unresolved. Recent reviews and LHC measurements (CMS, LHCb, ALICE) continue to report tension between NRQCD predictions—both LO and NLO—and the observed small/longitudinal polarization of prompt J/ψ and ψ(2S) at large p_T. No single set of long-distance matrix elements has been shown to simultaneously describe cross sections and polarizations across experiments; modified NRQCD approaches incorporating soft-gluon effects are being explored but the problem is still open.

paper_title: Open Problems in Hydrodynamical Approach to Relativistic Heavy Ion Collisions
context_brief: Model degeneracy in hydrodynamic interpretation of QGP observables
original_question: How can hydrodynamical modeling of relativistic heavy-ion collisions be used to extract quantitative properties of quark-gluon plasma and the bulk QCD phase transition when very different model scenarios, including continuous emission, sudden freeze-out, final-state cascade calculations, and simplified blast-wave solutions, can reproduce the same observables after suitable parameter choices?
self_contained_problem:
Consider the relativistic hydrodynamical description of the hot, dense matter produced in high-energy heavy-ion collisions, in which the evolution of the fireball is modeled by the conservation laws \(\partial_\mu T^{\mu\nu}=0\) (with optional shear and bulk viscous corrections) supplemented by a QCD-motivated equation of state \(p=p(\varepsilon)\) that encodes a transition between a quark-gluon plasma phase and a hadronic phase, together with a prescription for converting fluid cells into observable hadrons. Several inequivalent prescriptions are in common use, including: (i) continuous emission throughout the evolution, (ii) sudden freeze-out on a sharp hypersurface (Cooper–Frye on an isothermal or isochronous surface), (iii) hybrid schemes in which the hydrodynamic stage is matched to a hadronic transport cascade (e.g. an rQMD-type afterburner), and (iv) drastically simplified parametrizations such as blast-wave solutions characterized by a few thermal and flow parameters. Empirically, all of these scenarios, after suitable choices of their free parameters (initial conditions, equation of state, transport coefficients, freeze-out temperature and time, flow profile, etc.), can reproduce the same set of bulk observables (single-particle transverse-momentum spectra, anisotropic flow harmonics \(v_n(p_T)\), Hanbury Brown–Twiss radii, particle ratios) within experimental accuracy.

Problem: Develop a quantitative framework that breaks this degeneracy. Specifically, identify a finite set of observables, or functionals of the hydrodynamic solution, whose values are sensitive to the differences among scenarios (i)–(iv) in a way that allows one to extract, in a model-independent manner, intrinsic properties of the underlying QCD matter — in particular the equation of state \(p(\varepsilon)\) in the transition region, the order/nature of the bulk QCD phase transition, and the transport coefficients (shear viscosity to entropy density ratio \(\eta/s\) and bulk viscosity \(\zeta/s\)) — together with rigorous error estimates that account for parameter ambiguities in the freeze-out/hadronization stage.
status_search_result: The interpretive degeneracy among hydrodynamic freeze-out/hadronization prescriptions remains an active research problem. Modern hybrid frameworks (e.g., MUSIC+UrQMD, Trajectum, JETSCAPE Bayesian analyses) and global Bayesian inference studies (2019–2024) have made substantial progress in constraining the QGP equation of state and transport coefficients, but the precise extraction of bulk properties continues to depend on the choice of particlization scheme and viscous corrections, and competing scenarios still fit data comparably well. No definitive resolution of the model-degeneracy problem has been established.

paper_title: Open Problems in Hydrodynamical Approach to Relativistic Heavy Ion Collisions

status_search_result: The fast thermalization (or hydrodynamization) of the quark–gluon plasma produced in heavy-ion collisions remains an open problem. Isotropization is generally recognized as insufficient for thermalization, and the precise degree to which hydrodynamic success requires local equilibrium is still under active investigation.

paper_title: Open Problems in Hydrodynamical Approach to Relativistic Heavy Ion Collisions
original_question: Which observables can serve as signals of genuine hydrodynamic behavior in relativistic heavy-ion collisions, beyond successful fits by hydrodynamical models, and how can candidates such as shock-wave propagation be identified in order to reduce the remaining conceptual and quantitative uncertainties?
self_contained_problem:
In the hydrodynamical description of relativistic heavy-ion collisions, the system created shortly after impact is modeled as a strongly interacting fluid governed by the local conservation laws ∂_μ T^{μν} = 0 (and ∂_μ j^μ_B = 0 for conserved charges), closed by an equation of state p = p(ε, n_B) and supplemented by initial conditions, a freeze-out prescription, and possibly transport coefficients (shear viscosity η, bulk viscosity ζ). Many measured observables in such collisions — single-particle transverse momentum spectra, elliptic flow v_2 and higher harmonics v_n, HBT radii, etc. — can be fit by hydrodynamical models, but successful fitting alone does not establish that the matter truly behaves as a hydrodynamic fluid, since other (e.g. transport or parton-cascade) descriptions can also reproduce many of these features.

Problem: Identify a set of experimentally measurable observables in relativistic heavy-ion collisions whose presence (or quantitative behavior) would constitute a direct signal of genuine hydrodynamic evolution of the produced matter, as opposed to mere agreement of fits with hydrodynamical models. In particular:

(a) Formulate precise criteria, derivable from the relativistic hydrodynamic equations, that distinguish genuine fluid behavior from non-hydrodynamic dynamics.

(b) Determine whether shock-wave propagation excited by a fast parton traversing the medium — for example, the conical "Mach-cone" structure characterized by a Mach angle cos θ_M = c_s/v, where c_s is the medium speed of sound and v is the source velocity — can be unambiguously identified in two- and three-particle azimuthal correlations triggered by high-p_T particles, and specify under what experimental and theoretical conditions such an identification is robust against backgrounds (deflected jets, Cherenkov gluon radiation, medium-induced bremsstrahlung).

(c) Propose additional candidate signatures (e.g., sound-mode propagation imprinted on flow harmonics, response to localized initial-state perturbations, ridge-like structures, characteristic dependence of v_n on c_s and viscosity) and quantify how they reduce the conceptual and quantitative uncertainties of the hydrodynamic picture.
status_search_result: The identification of unambiguous signals of genuine hydrodynamic behavior in heavy-ion collisions — and in particular the experimental observation of a Mach-cone shock wave — remains an active and unresolved research problem. Subsequent literature has shown that the originally-claimed Mach-cone signal in three-particle correlations is strongly model-dependent and can be mimicked by deflected jets and other mechanisms, while shock-wave studies in viscous and anisotropic relativistic hydrodynamics continue to appear. No consensus signature has been established.

paper_title: SOFT PHYSICS AND INTERMITTENCY : OPEN QUESTION(S) in KRAKOW
original_question: After very high energy collisions, can domains of disordered chiral condensate form in an effective pion-and-sigma field theory, and would such domains produce observable bunches of particles with a definite charge, such as neutral-particle bunches?
self_contained_problem:
Consider an effective field theory of low-energy hadrons formulated as a linear sigma model whose dynamical fields are the pion isotriplet π=(π¹,π²,π³) and a scalar σ field, with a chirally symmetric potential whose vacuum spontaneously breaks SU(2)_L × SU(2)_R down to the diagonal isospin SU(2) and selects a preferred direction in the (σ,π) order-parameter space. Suppose that following a very high-energy hadronic or nuclear collision the system is initially driven into a hot, approximately chirally symmetric configuration and then rapidly cooled (quenched), so that long-wavelength modes of the chiral order parameter (σ,π) may temporarily relax along directions misaligned with the true vacuum direction, forming spatial regions ("domains") of disoriented chiral condensate (DCC).

(a) Within this effective field theory, determine whether such DCC domains can form as a dynamical consequence of the quench, and characterize their typical size, lifetime, and number distribution.

(b) Determine whether the decay of these domains produces observable bunches of pions with anomalous isospin composition — in particular, events containing a definite charge fraction such as bunches of nearly all neutral pions — and predict the resulting event-by-event distribution of the neutral-pion fraction f = N(π⁰)/N(π), to be contrasted with the binomial baseline f-distribution expected from isospin-symmetric independent emission.
status_search_result: Theoretical mechanisms for DCC formation in a quenched linear sigma model are well developed and predict anomalous neutral-pion fraction distributions. However, dedicated experimental searches (MiniMax at the Tevatron, WA98 at CERN SPS, and subsequent RHIC/LHC analyses) have not produced a confirmed DCC signal, and reviews as recent as Mohanty–Serreau (2005) and later describe DCC observation as still eluding experiment. The question of whether DCC domains genuinely form and yield observable neutral bunches therefore remains open.

paper_title: SOFT PHYSICS AND INTERMITTENCY : OPEN QUESTION(S) in KRAKOW
original_question: Can nuclei be used as sub-10-fermi microdetectors to obtain information about the first stages of hadron production, while reliably distinguishing nuclear effects from particle-production effects?
self_contained_problem: Consider hadron-nucleus and nucleus-nucleus collisions at high energies, in which the target (or projectile) nucleus has a spatial extent of less than 10 fermis and the constituent nucleons act as a spatially distributed array of scatterers probing the developing hadronic system. Treating such a nucleus as a "microdetector," determine whether it is possible, in principle and in practice, to extract reliable information about the earliest stages of hadron production (i.e., the space-time evolution of the partonic/pre-hadronic system on sub-fermi to few-fermi scales) from observables of the final-state particles, in such a way that genuine particle-production dynamics can be unambiguously disentangled from purely nuclear effects (such as Fermi motion, nuclear absorption, rescattering of produced hadrons in nuclear matter, collective nuclear flow, and shadowing). Formulate observables and a separation procedure, or prove obstructions to such a separation.
status_search_result: This is an open-ended methodological question in high-energy nuclear/particle phenomenology rather than a precise mathematical conjecture. Nuclei are routinely used as probes of hadronization (e.g., in nuclear DIS, RHIC and LHC heavy-ion programs), but a fully reliable and general separation of nuclear effects from genuine particle-production effects on the earliest hadron-formation stages remains an active research program with no definitive resolution.

paper_title: SOFT PHYSICS AND INTERMITTENCY : OPEN QUESTION(S) in KRAKOW
original_question: In intermittency studies of hadron-induced reactions, do same-sign-particle correlations at very small Lorentz-invariant momentum distance q² reproduce the same effects as analyses in full three-dimensional phase space, and can conventional Bose-Einstein interference between identical particles explain, or at least determine the influence on, the intermittency phenomenon?
self_contained_problem:
Consider the phenomenon of intermittency in multiparticle production from hadron–hadron collisions, where one studies the scaling behaviour of normalised factorial moments F_q(δ) of the multiplicity distribution with respect to the size δ of phase-space cells, the empirical fact being that F_q(δ) grows as a power of 1/δ when δ becomes small.

For pairs of same-charge final-state particles, define the Lorentz-invariant squared momentum distance
  q² = −(p₁ − p₂)²,
and consider the correlation integral built from same-sign particle pairs at very small q². Compare this with the analysis performed in the full three-dimensional phase space parametrised by rapidity y, azimuthal angle φ, and transverse momentum p_T.

(a) Do the same-sign-particle correlations at very small q² in hadron-induced reactions reproduce quantitatively the intermittent behaviour observed in the three-dimensional (y, φ, p_T) phase-space analysis?

(b) Can conventional Bose–Einstein interference between identical bosons, modelled e.g. by a two-particle correlation function C₂(q) = 1 + λ exp(−R² q²) (or its analogue), account for the intermittency phenomenon in hadron-induced reactions, and if not, to what extent does it determine or contribute to the observed scaling of factorial moments?
status_search_result: Subsequent experimental and theoretical work (e.g. NA22 correlation-integral analyses and reviews of intermittency/Bose-Einstein correlations) has established that in hadron-induced reactions same-sign pair correlations dominate the intermittent rise at small q², that correlation integrals show power-law behaviour in Q² consistent with the (y,φ,p_T) analysis, and that Bose-Einstein correlations are a major, though not exclusive, source of the intermittency signal in hadronic collisions. The qualitative answer is therefore largely affirmative, but a fully quantitative decomposition remains a matter of ongoing modelling.

paper_title: SOFT PHYSICS AND INTERMITTENCY : OPEN QUESTION(S) in KRAKOW
original_question: Does intermittency in multiparticle final states have a direct connection with fundamental perturbative QCD, given that perturbative calculations predict intermittent behavior for emitted gluons but hadronization may change the strength of the effect observed for hadrons?
self_contained_problem:
Consider high-energy multiparticle production processes, in which the final state consists of many hadrons distributed in phase space. For a phase-space variable (such as rapidity), divide an interval of size $\Delta$ into $M$ equal bins of size $\delta = \Delta/M$ and, for each event, let $n_m$ denote the multiplicity in bin $m$. The normalized factorial moments of order $q \ge 2$ are defined by
$$F_q(\delta) = \frac{1}{M}\sum_{m=1}^{M} \frac{\langle n_m(n_m-1)\cdots(n_m-q+1)\rangle}{\langle n_m\rangle^q},$$
where $\langle\cdot\rangle$ denotes the event average. The system is said to exhibit intermittency if, as $\delta \to 0$, $F_q(\delta)$ grows as a power law $F_q(\delta) \propto \delta^{-\phi_q}$ with strictly positive intermittency exponents $\phi_q > 0$.

Within perturbative QCD (for instance, in the axial gauge using the double-leading-log or modified leading-log approximation for parton cascades), factorial moments of the emitted gluon multiplicity distribution in small angular or rapidity windows can be computed and are known to display intermittent behavior of the form above, with calculable exponents $\phi_q^{\text{parton}}$. Hadronization (the non-perturbative transition from partons to hadrons) is expected to modify these exponents, so that the measured hadronic exponents $\phi_q^{\text{hadron}}$ may differ in magnitude (though not necessarily in qualitative form) from $\phi_q^{\text{parton}}$.

Question: Does the intermittency phenomenon observed in hadronic multiparticle final states admit a direct, quantitative derivation from perturbative QCD? More precisely, is there a controlled theoretical framework — incorporating both perturbative parton branching and a model of hadronization (e.g., local parton–hadron duality or a definite fragmentation scheme) — that reproduces the experimentally measured intermittency exponents $\phi_q^{\text{hadron}}$ for all $q \ge 2$ in high-energy hadronic, leptonic, and nuclear collisions, and that explains why the strength of the effect differs between gluon-level and hadron-level distributions?
status_search_result: Web sources confirm that intermittency in multiparticle final states is widely interpreted as a consequence of QCD parton cascading, with local parton–hadron duality (LPHD) used to connect parton- and hadron-level distributions. Perturbative QCD calculations reproduce the qualitative form of intermittency for gluons, but a complete, quantitatively predictive derivation of the measured hadronic intermittency exponents from first-principles QCD (including a controlled treatment of hadronization) does not appear to be established. The status of the precise question remains unclear from the available literature.

paper_title: SOFT PHYSICS AND INTERMITTENCY : OPEN QUESTION(S) in KRAKOW
original_question: Can phase-transition or statistical-mechanics models explain intermittent fluctuations in multiparticle production when it is uncertain whether such reactions satisfy the requirements for a pure equilibrium phase transition, and when heavy-ion fluctuations may differ from those expected from quark-gluon plasma formation and decay?
self_contained_problem:
In high-energy multiparticle production, "intermittency" denotes the power-law growth of normalized factorial moments $F_q(\delta) = \langle n(n-1)\cdots(n-q+1)\rangle/\langle n\rangle^q \sim \delta^{-\phi_q}$ of particle multiplicity counts as the size $\delta$ of a phase-space bin (in rapidity, azimuthal angle, or transverse momentum) is decreased. These scaling fluctuations have been observed in hadron-hadron, lepton-hadron, and heavy-ion collisions.

One proposed theoretical explanation interprets the observed intermittent fluctuations as critical fluctuations (both dynamical and geometrical) associated with a phase transition, by analogy with statistical-mechanics systems near a second-order critical point — in particular the deconfinement / chiral transition between a quark-gluon plasma and a hadronic gas.

Question: Determine whether a phase-transition or equilibrium statistical-mechanics framework can quantitatively account for the empirically observed intermittency exponents $\phi_q$ in multiparticle production, given that:
(a) it is not established that multiparticle production reactions satisfy the conditions (equilibration, well-defined order parameter, scaling near criticality) required for a pure equilibrium phase transition; and
(b) the intermittency patterns observed in heavy-ion collisions appear to differ from those predicted for the formation and decay of an equilibrium quark-gluon plasma.

Specifically, identify a statistical-mechanics or phase-transition model (thermal or non-thermal) whose predicted moment-scaling exponents $\phi_q$ match those measured across hadronic and nuclear reactions, or otherwise rule out such an explanation.
status_search_result: The literature reports partial progress: Lévy stable-law analyses classify intermittency patterns into thermal ($\mu<1$, QGP-like) and non-thermal ($\mu>1$, cascading) phase transitions, and heavy-ion data have been interpreted as showing non-thermal rather than thermal critical behavior. However, no single equilibrium-phase-transition model has been established as quantitatively reproducing the observed exponents across reactions, and the question of whether intermittency genuinely originates from a phase transition remains unsettled.

paper_title: SOFT PHYSICS AND INTERMITTENCY : OPEN QUESTION(S) in KRAKOW
original_question: When factorial analyses in different phase-space dimensions reveal different dynamical excitations, how should lower-dimensional intermittency be interpreted if Bose-Einstein correlations dominate most three-dimensional studies, and how should Ochs-Wosiek moments-over-moments scaling in one- and two-dimensional NA22 studies be explained?
self_contained_problem:
Setup. In multiparticle production experiments one studies scaled factorial moments
   F_q(δ) = ⟨ n(n−1)···(n−q+1) ⟩ / ⟨ n ⟩^q
of charged-particle multiplicities n in cells of size δ obtained by partitioning a D-dimensional phase-space region (D = 1, 2, 3, with variables such as rapidity, azimuthal angle, and transverse momentum). "Intermittency" denotes a power-law growth F_q(δ) ∝ δ^{−φ_q} as δ → 0. The Ochs–Wosiek relation is the empirical "moments-over-moments" scaling
   ln F_q(δ) = c_q · ln F_2(δ) + d_q,
observed (in particular in the NA22 π⁺p and K⁺p data at √s = 22 GeV) in one- and two-dimensional analyses, with slope ratios c_q that depend on the dimensionality D in which the moments are computed.

It is widely accepted that in three-dimensional phase space the intermittency signal is dominated by Bose–Einstein correlations between identical bosons (the two-particle correlator C_2(Q) being well described by a function of the four-momentum difference Q only in 3D).

Problem. Provide a dynamical interpretation of the lower-dimensional (D = 1 and D = 2) intermittency signal that is consistent with Bose–Einstein correlations being the dominant source of the three-dimensional signal. Concretely:

(a) Identify the physical mechanism(s) producing the observed power-law growth of F_q(δ) when phase space is projected onto one or two dimensions, given that the genuine identical-particle Bose–Einstein correlation acts in the full three-dimensional Q-space and is partially washed out under projection.

(b) Derive, within this mechanism, the dependence of the Ochs–Wosiek slope ratios c_q = φ_q/φ_2 on the dimension D, and reproduce quantitatively the c_q values observed in the one- and two-dimensional NA22 factorial-moment analyses.

(c) Explain why factorial-moment analyses performed in different phase-space dimensions can reveal apparently different dynamical excitations (the "wall-and-tower" effect), and specify under what conditions lower-dimensional intermittency cannot be reduced to a kinematic projection of a purely three-dimensional Bose–Einstein dynamics.
category_tag: Intermittency and Bose-Einstein correlations in multiparticle production
status_search_result: Searches indicate continued analysis by NA22 and theoretical work attributing 3D intermittency largely to Bose–Einstein correlations, while lower-dimensional Ochs–Wosiek scaling has been fitted phenomenologically (e.g., by Lévy stable laws with index μ≈1.6). No definitive, generally accepted dynamical derivation reconciling the 1D/2D Ochs–Wosiek scaling with a Bose–Einstein-dominated 3D picture was located, so the question appears to remain unresolved at the level of a first-principles explanation.

paper_title: SOFT PHYSICS AND INTERMITTENCY : OPEN QUESTION(S) in KRAKOW
original_question: Why do three-dimensional factorial moments, especially the second factorial cumulant K_2 = F_2 - 1, show similar scale-invariant behavior across lepton-hadron, hadron-hadron, and heavy-ion reactions; is this universality caused by a common Bose-Einstein origin of the fluctuations, and should such a large scale-invariant range occur in all cases?
self_contained_problem:
Consider multiparticle production in high-energy collisions of three different reaction classes: lepton–hadron, hadron–hadron, and heavy-ion (nucleus–nucleus) reactions. For each event, partition a three-dimensional phase-space region (for example the cube spanned by rapidity, azimuthal angle, and transverse momentum, or by three components of momentum) into M equal cells, and let n_m be the number of produced charged particles in cell m. Define the normalized scaled factorial moments of order q by
   F_q(M) = ⟨ (1/M) Σ_{m=1}^M n_m(n_m−1)···(n_m−q+1) ⟩ / ⟨ (1/M) Σ_{m=1}^M n_m ⟩^q,
and the second factorial cumulant by K_2(M) = F_2(M) − 1.

Empirically, when log F_q(M) is plotted against log M in three-dimensional phase space, K_2(M) shows an approximately power-law (scale-invariant) increase, K_2(M) ∼ M^{φ_2}, with very similar exponent φ_2 across lepton–hadron, hadron–hadron, and heavy-ion reactions, differing essentially only by an additive constant attributable to long-range correlations, and persisting over a range from M = 1 up to about M = 10^4 subdivisions.

Provide a theoretical explanation of this approximate universality. In particular: (i) determine whether the common scale-invariant behaviour of K_2 in these three reaction classes can be derived from a common Bose–Einstein origin of the short-range two-particle correlations, and (ii) decide whether a scale-invariant range as wide as 1 ≤ M ≤ 10^4 should be expected on this basis in all three reaction classes.
category_tag: Factorial moments and intermittency in multiparticle production
status_search_result: Searches indicate active and ongoing investigation of the universality of three-dimensional factorial moments and their connection to Bose–Einstein correlations across lepton–hadron, hadron–hadron, and heavy-ion reactions. While partial explanations linking the short-range part of K_2 to Bose–Einstein correlations have been advanced and intermittency exponents are being measured in current heavy-ion programs (e.g., searches for the QCD critical point), no single decisive derivation establishes the observed cross-reaction universality and the extent of its scale-invariant range. The status is best described as unresolved/unknown in a definitive sense.

paper_title: SOFT PHYSICS AND INTERMITTENCY : OPEN QUESTION(S) in KRAKOW
original_question: In deep-inelastic lepton-hadron reactions at HERA, can final-hadron fluctuation and correlation measurements separate or exploit the competition between Bose-Einstein-type correlations and perturbative-QCD-induced mechanisms, thereby revealing properties such as improved perturbative expansions, gluon coherence in the space-like region, or parton saturation beyond the perturbative regime?
self_contained_problem:
Consider deep-inelastic lepton–hadron scattering at high energy (such as at a collider with proton beam energies of order hundreds of GeV against electron/positron beams of tens of GeV). In the final hadronic state of such reactions, two distinct dynamical mechanisms are expected to generate non-trivial multiplicity fluctuations and rapidity (or pseudorapidity) correlations:

(a) Bose–Einstein correlations among identical bosons in the final state, producing an enhancement of like-sign pairs at small relative four-momentum;

(b) Perturbative QCD parton-cascade mechanisms (gluon bremsstrahlung, branching, color coherence/angular ordering), producing intermittent self-similar fluctuations characterized by power-law growth of normalized scaled factorial moments
   F_q(δ) = ⟨ n(n−1)⋯(n−q+1) ⟩ / ⟨ n ⟩^q  ∝  δ^{−φ_q}   as the bin size δ in rapidity (or in higher-dimensional phase space) shrinks.

Formulate observables built from multiparticle correlation functions and factorial-moment intermittency exponents φ_q of charged final-state hadrons in deep-inelastic events, and determine whether (and how) such observables can:

  (i) cleanly separate the contribution of mechanism (a) from that of mechanism (b);
  (ii) be used to probe quantitative features of the underlying perturbative QCD dynamics, specifically:
        – the regime of improved (resummed) perturbative expansions of BFKL/Lipatov type at small Bjorken x,
        – the coherence of soft-gluon emission in the space-like (initial-state) parton cascade,
        – the onset of non-linear parton-saturation effects beyond the linear perturbative regime.

Provide either an explicit construction of such discriminating observables together with predictions for their behavior in each regime, or a rigorous argument that no such separation/exploitation is possible within the standard framework of perturbative QCD plus a final-state symmetrization prescription for identical bosons.
category_tag: Intermittency and multiparticle correlations in DIS
status_search_result: The question is a programmatic research challenge posed in the early 1990s about using intermittency and correlation measurements in DIS to probe BFKL dynamics, gluon coherence, and parton saturation. ZEUS and H1 at HERA have published factorial-moment/intermittency and Bose–Einstein correlation analyses, but no single result definitively disentangles the two mechanisms or settles the use of intermittency as a probe of small-x resummation, coherence, or saturation. The status is therefore best characterized as an ongoing research direction rather than a closed mathematical problem.

paper_title: SOFT PHYSICS AND INTERMITTENCY : OPEN QUESTION(S) in KRAKOW
original_question: Is the proposed micro-universe picture of multiparticle production correct, in which dynamical fluctuations originate from partons structuring themselves during scattering into colorless clusters through rearrangements until hadrons form in the new vacuum structure?
self_contained_problem:
In high-energy hadronic and nuclear collisions, the final state consists of a large number of produced hadrons whose multiplicity distributions exhibit non-trivial dynamical (non-statistical) fluctuations, often quantified by scaled factorial moments F_q(δ) = ⟨n(n-1)...(n-q+1)⟩/⟨n⟩^q computed in phase-space bins of size δ. An "intermittent" behaviour corresponds to a power-law growth F_q(δ) ∝ δ^{-φ_q} as δ → 0, with positive intermittency exponents φ_q.

Consider the following proposed dynamical mechanism (the "micro-universe parton-structuration picture") for the origin of these dynamical fluctuations:

(i) During a scattering process, partons (quarks and gluons) created from the vacuum undergo a self-structuration phase, forming transient fluctuating color configurations.
(ii) These fluctuating structures undergo successive rearrangements, organizing partons into colorless clusters.
(iii) The process terminates when colorless clusters condense into hadrons, consistent with the asymptotic (confining) vacuum structure of QCD.
(iv) The dynamical fluctuations observed in factorial moments (intermittency, multifractal scaling of hadron multiplicities in phase-space) arise precisely from this parton structuration / rearrangement / hadronization cascade in the vacuum.

Question: Is this proposed mechanism a correct description of the origin of dynamical multiplicity fluctuations and intermittency observed in soft multiparticle production? Specifically, can one derive (or rule out) the observed power-law scaling of factorial moments and multifractal spectra from a dynamical model based on parton structuration into colorless clusters and rearrangement towards hadrons in a non-perturbative vacuum?
status_search_result: The question concerns the physical correctness of a conjectured picture of soft multiparticle production. No definitive verification or refutation appears in the literature; intermittency in soft hadron production remains an active topic and competing models (cascading, QCD parton showers, Bose–Einstein correlations, critical-fluctuation pictures) coexist without consensus.

paper_title: Open Questions in Charm Decays Deserving an Answer
original_question: Is the lifetime ratio tau(D_s)/tau(D^0) equal to 1 up to very small corrections, or does it differ at the approximately 1% level because weak-annihilation contributions and SU(3) flavor breaking have a measurable impact on charm decays?
self_contained_problem:
Let $\tau(D^0)$ and $\tau(D_s)$ denote the total lifetimes of the neutral charm meson $D^0$ (quark content $c\bar u$) and the strange-charmed meson $D_s^+$ (quark content $c\bar s$), respectively. In the heavy-quark expansion for inclusive nonleptonic decays of charm hadrons, the leading contribution is universal and predicts equal lifetimes, while subleading effects — in particular weak-annihilation (WA) diagrams (in which the valence quark and antiquark of the meson annihilate through a $W$ exchange) and breaking of $SU(3)$ flavor symmetry between $u$ and $s$ quarks — generate a difference between $\tau(D_s)$ and $\tau(D^0)$.

Determine the value of the ratio
$$ R \;=\; \frac{\tau(D_s)}{\tau(D^0)} $$
to roughly $1\%$ precision and decide between the following two qualitative scenarios:
(i) $R = 1$ up to very small corrections (i.e. WA and $SU(3)$-breaking effects are negligible in charm decays), or
(ii) $R$ deviates from $1$ at approximately the $1\%$ level or more, indicating a measurable impact of weak annihilation and $SU(3)$ flavor breaking on inclusive charm decay widths.
status_search_result: Experimental measurements (E791, CLEO, SELEX, and subsequent experiments compiled by the PDG) firmly establish that τ(Ds)/τ(D0) differs from unity well beyond the 1% level. Current world averages give a ratio of roughly 1.2, many standard deviations above 1, demonstrating that weak-annihilation contributions and SU(3) flavor breaking have a clearly measurable impact on charm decays. Thus scenario (ii) is realized.

paper_title: Open Questions in Charm Decays Deserving an Answer
original_question: What are the absolute branching ratios of D_s, Lambda_c, and Xi_c decays to precision far better than the current tens-of-percent level, so that charm-hadron final states can be used reliably as normalization inputs in beauty-decay measurements and in determinations of |V(cb)|?
self_contained_problem:
In the Standard Model of particle physics, the charmed hadrons $D_s^+$ (a meson with quark content $c ar s$), $\Lambda_c^+$ (a baryon with content $udc$), and $\Xi_c$ (baryons with content $usc$ or $dsc$) decay weakly via the charm quark transition $c	o s$ (or $c	o d$). For each ground-state charmed hadron $H_c\in\{D_s^+,\Lambda_c^+,\Xi_c^0,\Xi_c^+\}$, and for each exclusive hadronic decay mode $H_c	o f$ (e.g., $D_s^+	o\phi\pi^+$, $\Lambda_c^+	o pK^-\pi^+$, $\Xi_c^+	o\Xi^-\pi^+\pi^+$), determine the absolute branching fraction $\mathcal{B}(H_c	o f)$, defined as the partial decay width to $f$ divided by the total width of $H_c$, to a fractional precision substantially better than the order of tens of percent that was available historically. The required precision is that needed so that these branching fractions serve as reliable normalization inputs in measurements of beauty-hadron semileptonic decays $B	o\ell
u D^{(*)}$, $B_s	o\ell
u D_s^{(*)}$, and $\Lambda_b	o\ell
u\Lambda_c$ used in the extraction of the Cabibbo–Kobayashi–Maskawa matrix element $|V_{cb}|$.
status_search_result: The problem has been substantially advanced since the original question. BESIII, CLEO-c, Belle, and LHCb have measured absolute branching fractions of $D_s^+$ and $\Lambda_c^+$ decays at the few-percent level: e.g., BESIII determined $\mathcal{B}(\Lambda_c^+\to pK^-\pi^+)=(6.61\pm 0.11\pm 0.12)\%$, a 2–3-fold precision improvement. Comparable progress has been made for many $D_s^+$ modes. For $\Xi_c^{0,+}$, absolute branching fractions have only recently begun to be measured (e.g., Belle's $\Xi_c^+\to\Xi^-\pi^+\pi^+$ and $\Xi_c^0\to\Xi^-\pi^+$) and remain less precise. Thus the problem is partially solved.

paper_title: Open Questions in Charm Decays Deserving an Answer
original_question: What are the branching fractions for the radiative and rare charm decays D -> gamma K^*, D -> gamma rho/omega, D_s -> gamma phi, D_s -> gamma rho/omega, and related D -> l^+ l^- K/K^*/rho/omega modes, and does the ratio BR(D -> gamma rho/omega)/BR(D -> gamma K^*) differ from tan^2 theta_c in a way that would signal New Physics in c -> u gamma rather than ordinary weak-annihilation dynamics?
self_contained_problem:
Consider the radiative and rare charm-meson decays
  D → γ K*,  D → γ ρ/ω,  D_s → γ φ,  D_s → γ ρ/ω,
together with the related rare leptonic-pair modes
  D → ℓ⁺ℓ⁻ K,  D → ℓ⁺ℓ⁻ K*,  D → ℓ⁺ℓ⁻ ρ,  D → ℓ⁺ℓ⁻ ω,
where ℓ ∈ {e, μ}. Let θ_c denote the Cabibbo angle, so that tan²θ_c ≈ 0.05.

(a) Determine the Standard-Model branching fractions of each of the above decay modes, including a reliable theoretical treatment of long-distance contributions (in particular weak-annihilation/exchange dynamics) and short-distance c → u γ and c → u ℓ⁺ℓ⁻ amplitudes.

(b) Predict the ratio
  R := BR(D → γ ρ/ω) / BR(D → γ K*)
within the Standard Model, and establish quantitatively whether, and by how much, the inequality R ≠ tan²θ_c can arise from ordinary weak-annihilation dynamics alone, versus serving as a clean signal of New Physics (for example non-minimal supersymmetric contributions) entering c → u γ. Identify the threshold of deviation of R from tan²θ_c above which a New-Physics interpretation becomes unavoidable.
status_search_result: Several of the branching fractions have been measured: BaBar measured BR(D⁰ → K̄*⁰γ) and BR(D⁰ → φγ) (Phys. Rev. D 78, 071101, 2008), and Belle observed D⁰ → ρ⁰γ with BR ≈ 1.77×10⁻⁵ (Phys. Rev. Lett. 118, 051801, 2017). However, robust Standard-Model predictions for the radiative modes are still hampered by large long-distance/weak-annihilation uncertainties (see e.g. JHEP 08 (2017) 091, "Rare radiative charm decays within the SM and beyond"), so the clean separation of New Physics in c → u γ from weak-annihilation dynamics via the ratio R = BR(D → γρ/ω)/BR(D → γK*) remains unresolved. Several of the rare D → ℓ⁺ℓ⁻ (K,K*,ρ,ω) modes have not yet been observed. Thus the program is partially completed.

paper_title: Open Questions in Charm Decays Deserving an Answer
original_question: Do Cabibbo-suppressed charm decays such as D^0 -> K^+ K^-, D^0 -> pi^+ pi^-, D^+ -> K^+ K^- pi^+, and D^+ -> phi pi^+ show direct CP violation or T-odd final-state correlations at the 10^-3 level, which is roughly the upper size expected within the Standard Model but could be enhanced to about the 1% level by New Physics?
self_contained_problem:
Consider singly Cabibbo-suppressed decays of charmed mesons, in particular the two-body modes $D^0 \to K^+ K^-$ and $D^0 \to \pi^+ \pi^-$, the three-body mode $D^+ \to K^+ K^- \pi^+$ (including its $\phi\pi^+$ resonant component), and four-body modes such as $D^\pm \to K^+ K^- \pi^\pm \pi^0$. For a decay $D \to f$ with CP-conjugate $\bar D \to \bar f$, define the direct CP asymmetry
$$A_{CP}(f) = \frac{\Gamma(D \to f) - \Gamma(\bar D \to \bar f)}{\Gamma(D \to f) + \Gamma(\bar D \to \bar f)},$$
and for the four-body mode define the T-odd triple-product correlation
$$C_T = \langle \vec p_{\pi^\pm} \cdot (\vec p_{K^+} \times \vec p_{K^-}) \rangle,$$
with the CP-violating observable $A_T = \tfrac{1}{2}(C_T - \bar C_T)$ (where $\bar C_T$ is the analogous quantity for the CP-conjugate decay). Within the Standard Model these direct CP asymmetries and T-odd correlations are estimated to be at most of order $10^{-3}$, while New Physics could plausibly enhance them to about the $1\%$ level.

Determine experimentally whether any of these singly Cabibbo-suppressed charm decays exhibits a nonzero direct CP asymmetry $A_{CP}$ or a nonzero T-odd correlation $A_T$ at the $10^{-3}$ sensitivity level, and decide whether the observed effects are consistent with the Standard Model expectation of $\lesssim 10^{-3}$ or instead indicate enhancement (e.g. to the $\sim 1\%$ level) characteristic of New Physics.
category_tag: CP violation in charm meson decays
status_search_result: LHCb has reached the $10^{-3}$ sensitivity for direct CP asymmetries in singly Cabibbo-suppressed charm decays, and in 2019 reported the first observation of CP violation in charm via $\Delta A_{CP}$ between $D^0\to K^+K^-$ and $D^0\to\pi^+\pi^-$. Individual asymmetries (e.g. $a^d_{K^+K^-}=(6\pm6)\times10^{-4}$, $a^d_{\pi^+\pi^-}=(22\pm6)\times10^{-4}$) are now measured at this level, and dedicated searches in $D^+\to K^+K^-\pi^+$ and T-odd correlations in $D\to KK\pi\pi$ have been performed without conclusive evidence of New Physics. Whether the observed level is fully Standard-Model or contains a New Physics contribution remains debated, so the underlying question is only partially resolved.

paper_title: Twenty Open Questions in Supersymmetric Particle Physics
context_brief: MSSM baryon/lepton violation and matter parity
original_question: In the Minimal Supersymmetric Standard Model, the most general renormalizable superpotential allows baryon-number-violating and lepton-number-violating interactions that together would mediate very rapid proton decay through squark-suppressed operators. What exact symmetry or mechanism forbids the dangerous simultaneous baryon and lepton violation, can that symmetry be understood as a gauge-protected discrete symmetry rather than an ad hoc global rule, and how should higher-dimension proton-decay operators and lightest-superpartner stability be controlled at the same time?
self_contained_problem:
Consider the Minimal Supersymmetric Standard Model (MSSM) with chiral matter superfields Q, u^c, d^c, L, e^c (in the usual Standard-Model gauge representations) and Higgs doublet superfields H_u, H_d. The most general renormalizable gauge-invariant superpotential admits the baryon-number-violating couplings λ''_{ijk} u^c_i d^c_j d^c_k and the lepton-number-violating couplings λ_{ijk} L_i L_j e^c_k, λ'_{ijk} L_i Q_j d^c_k, and μ_i L_i H_u. Simultaneously turning on a baryon-violating coupling λ'' and a lepton-violating coupling λ' generates an effective four-fermion operator (QudL-type) that mediates proton decay suppressed only by squark masses, producing a proton lifetime grossly inconsistent with experiment.

(a) Determine a discrete symmetry imposed on the MSSM superfields that simultaneously forbids all of the dangerous renormalizable B- and L-violating couplings while permitting all phenomenologically required Yukawa interactions and the μ-term.

(b) Determine whether such a discrete symmetry can be realized as the unbroken subgroup of a spontaneously broken continuous gauge symmetry (i.e. a discrete gauge symmetry, free of mixed gauge–discrete anomalies), so that it is protected against violation by quantum-gravity effects, rather than being imposed as an ad hoc global rule.

(c) Identify a discrete symmetry (or combination of symmetries) that, in addition to forbidding the dangerous dimension-four operators, also forbids or sufficiently suppresses the dimension-five proton-decay operators QQQL and u^c u^c d^c e^c, while still guaranteeing the absolute stability of the lightest superpartner so as to provide a viable dark-matter candidate.

However, no single uniquely preferred symmetry has been established experimentally, and the question of the "correct" discrete gauge symmetry of the MSSM remains a topic of ongoing model-building work, so the broader question is best regarded as partially solved.

paper_title: Twenty Open Questions in Supersymmetric Particle Physics
original_question: The MSSM contains many physical CP-violating phases beyond the single Standard Model phase, and these phases can contribute to neutron electric dipole moments and kaon CP violation without the strong suppressions present in the Standard Model. Why are large supersymmetric CP-violating effects not ubiquitous in present experiments, and are the phases small, the relevant superpartners heavy, the scalar masses degenerate or decoupled, or the supersymmetry-breaking mechanism specially structured?
self_contained_problem:
Consider the Minimal Supersymmetric Standard Model (MSSM), a supersymmetric extension of the Standard Model of particle physics in which every Standard Model fermion is paired with a bosonic superpartner (and vice versa), and which contains two Higgs doublets together with their fermionic superpartners. After eliminating phases removable by field redefinitions, the MSSM Lagrangian contains 43 physical CP-violating phases in addition to the single Cabibbo–Kobayashi–Maskawa phase of the Standard Model. Among these are the phases φ_μ of the supersymmetric Higgs mass parameter μ and φ_A of the trilinear soft-breaking couplings A, as well as phases in the gaugino masses and the squark/slepton mass matrices. Generic O(1) values of such phases, with superpartner masses around the electroweak scale (∼100 GeV), lead to contributions to the electric dipole moment of the neutron and to CP-violating observables in the neutral kaon system (such as ε_K and ε'/ε) that exceed current experimental bounds by several orders of magnitude, without the GIM-type suppression operative in the Standard Model. Phenomenological viability therefore requires one of: (i) the new CP-violating phases are universally small (e.g. |φ_{A,B}| ≲ 10^{-2}); (ii) the relevant superpartners are heavy (squarks and sleptons of the first two generations above ∼1 TeV); (iii) the soft scalar mass matrices are nearly degenerate or aligned so as to suppress flavor-changing and CP-violating effects; or (iv) the underlying mechanism of supersymmetry breaking has a special structure (such as gauge mediation, anomaly mediation, or specific flavor symmetries) that automatically produces small or aligned phases.

Problem. Determine, within the framework of the MSSM (or any well-motivated extension), the mechanism that naturally reconciles the presence of generic supersymmetric CP-violating phases with the stringent experimental upper bounds on the neutron and electron electric dipole moments and on CP violation in the kaon and B-meson systems. Specifically, identify which combination of the alternatives above (small phases, heavy superpartners, scalar degeneracy/decoupling, or structured supersymmetry breaking) is realized in nature, and construct an explicit, predictive model of supersymmetry breaking and mediation in which the suppression of supersymmetric CP-violating effects follows from symmetry or dynamics rather than fine tuning.
status_search_result: The supersymmetric CP problem remains an open question in particle physics. As of 2026, despite many proposed solutions (heavy first/second-generation sfermions, alignment, gauge/anomaly mediation, approximate CP symmetries), no superpartners have been discovered at the LHC, and tightening EDM bounds (notably ACME and neutron EDM experiments) continue to constrain supersymmetric phases without selecting a definitive mechanism. Recent reviews continue to list the SUSY CP problem as unresolved.

paper_title: Twenty Open Questions in Supersymmetric Particle Physics
original_question: The MSSM contains many charged and colored scalar fields, not only Higgs fields, and its scalar potential has D-flat and F-flat directions along which charge- or color-breaking minima or unbounded-from-below behavior can arise. Why does the physical MSSM vacuum preserve QCD color and electromagnetic charge, what constraints on soft parameters are required, and if deeper charge- or color-breaking vacua exist, what cosmological history keeps the universe in the observed Standard-Model-like vacuum?
self_contained_problem:
Consider the Minimal Supersymmetric Standard Model (MSSM): a four-dimensional N=1 supersymmetric gauge theory with gauge group SU(3)_C × SU(2)_L × U(1)_Y, two Higgs doublet superfields H_u and H_d, three generations of quark and lepton chiral superfields, the MSSM superpotential with Yukawa couplings y_u, y_d, y_e and μ-term μ H_u H_d, and explicit soft supersymmetry-breaking terms consisting of scalar mass-squared matrices for all sfermions and Higgses, gaugino masses M_1, M_2, M_3, trilinear A-terms (A_u, A_d, A_e), and the bilinear Higgs soft term B μ.

The full tree-level scalar potential V(φ) on the space of all charged and colored scalar fields (squarks, sleptons, and Higgses) generically possesses:
(a) D-flat and F-flat directions along which V can become unbounded from below (UFB);
(b) charge- and/or color-breaking (CCB) stationary points at which squark or slepton VEVs are nonzero, possibly forming minima deeper than the standard electroweak-symmetry-breaking minimum in which only the neutral Higgs components acquire VEVs.

Address the following:

1. Determine necessary and sufficient analytic conditions on the soft-breaking parameters (sfermion mass-squareds, A-terms, gaugino masses, μ, B) such that the global minimum of V preserves SU(3)_C color and U(1)_em electric charge, i.e. such that no CCB minimum is deeper than the standard vacuum and V is bounded from below along all UFB directions.

2. Provide a theoretical explanation of why the physical MSSM vacuum realized in nature preserves color and electromagnetic charge.

3. In the case where the standard electroweak vacuum is only a local (metastable) minimum and deeper CCB or UFB regions exist, determine the cosmological conditions (thermal history, tunneling rates, inflationary initial conditions) under which the universe is dynamically selected into, and remains in, the standard-model-like vacuum on timescales longer than the age of the universe.
status_search_result: Analytic necessary/sufficient tree-level constraints on MSSM soft parameters from CCB and UFB directions have been derived (Casas–Lleyda–Muñoz and follow-ups in the 1990s), and post-Higgs-discovery analyses (e.g. JHEP 2014) have updated these bounds and incorporated metastability via vacuum tunneling rate computations. Thus the parameter-space constraint aspect is largely solved at the level of tree-plus-loop analyses, but the deeper conceptual question of why nature selects the color/charge-preserving vacuum and the full cosmological selection mechanism (including non-thermal initial conditions and inflationary history) remains open.

paper_title: Twenty Open Questions in Supersymmetric Particle Physics
original_question: If supersymmetry is broken in a hidden sector, the visible Standard Model sector must still acquire soft masses that violate the tree-level supertrace relation without reintroducing unacceptable flavor violation. By what channel does the visible sector learn that supersymmetry has been broken—supergravity mediation through Planck-suppressed operators, gauge mediation through loops of messenger fields, pseudo-anomalous U(1) mediation, or another mechanism—and what experimental signatures can distinguish the mediation mechanism?
status_search_result: As of 2026, no superpartners have been observed at the LHC or any other experiment, so the empirical question of which mediation mechanism (if any) is realized in nature remains open. Theoretical model-building has produced detailed predictions for gravity, gauge, anomaly, and U(1) mediation scenarios, and characteristic signatures (e.g., gravitino LSP with NLSP decays for gauge mediation) are well understood, but the lack of a discovered SUSY spectrum prevents experimental discrimination.

paper_title: Twenty Open Questions in Supersymmetric Particle Physics
original_question: Additional abelian U(1) gauge factors arise naturally in many MSSM extensions, but visible-sector U(1)′ breaking is constrained by supersymmetric scalar potentials and hidden-sector U(1) factors can communicate large D-term supersymmetry breaking through gauge kinetic mixing. How can extra U(1) gauge symmetries be incorporated into supersymmetric models without predicting unobserved weak-scale interactions or destabilizing the MSSM gauge hierarchy?
self_contained_problem:
Consider supersymmetric extensions of the Standard Model (the MSSM) augmented by one or more additional abelian gauge factors U(1)′. Such extra U(1)′ symmetries may live in the visible sector, in which case their spontaneous breaking is governed by a supersymmetric scalar potential involving MSSM-charged or singlet fields, or they may live in a hidden sector that is coupled to the visible sector only gravitationally and through the gauge-invariant kinetic mixing operator

  L_mix = -(ε/2) F^Y_{μν} F'^{μν},

where F^Y is the hypercharge field strength and F' is the field strength of the hidden U(1)′. In a supersymmetric context this mixing extends to the superfield level and, when the hidden U(1)′ has a nonzero D-term from supersymmetry breaking, induces visible-sector soft mass-squared contributions of order ε times the hidden D-term, which generically destabilize the electroweak hierarchy.

Problem. Construct (or prove obstructions to constructing) a consistent supersymmetric model containing one or more additional U(1) gauge factors, beyond the MSSM gauge group SU(3)_c × SU(2)_L × U(1)_Y, satisfying all of the following:
1. Anomaly cancellation, including mixed anomalies with the MSSM gauge factors, is achieved with a phenomenologically acceptable matter content.
2. The extra U(1) symmetry is spontaneously broken, with the associated Z′ boson (and any accompanying matter or interactions) either sufficiently heavy or sufficiently weakly coupled to evade all current experimental bounds on weak-scale gauge interactions.
3. Any gauge kinetic mixing ε between the extra U(1) factors and U(1)_Y, together with the associated D-term contributions to visible-sector scalar masses, does not destabilize the MSSM gauge hierarchy, i.e. soft masses for MSSM scalars remain near the electroweak scale.
4. The model is compatible with standard mechanisms of supersymmetry breaking and mediation.

Either exhibit such a model explicitly, or prove a no-go statement delimiting which combinations of U(1) charge assignments, breaking scales, and kinetic-mixing parameters are admissible.
status_search_result: The question of how extra U(1) gauge factors can be consistently embedded in supersymmetric models without unobserved weak-scale phenomena or destabilization of the MSSM hierarchy remains an active area of research. Foundational work on kinetic mixing and the SUSY gauge hierarchy (Dienes–Kolda–March-Russell, 1996) established the destabilization problem, and subsequent work through 2025 (string-theoretic kinetic mixing, dark gauge mediation, singlet portals) continues to propose partial solutions in specific frameworks (e.g. low-scale gauge mediation, particular string compactifications), but no general resolution has been established.

paper_title: Twenty Open Questions in Supersymmetric Particle Physics
original_question: The MSSM gauge couplings appear to meet near 2 × 10^16 GeV when evolved with the minimal supersymmetric particle content, suggesting a single unified gauge coupling and possibly a simple GUT group such as SU(5), SO(10), SU(6), or E6. Does the MSSM truly unify into a supersymmetric grand unified theory, and can such a theory simultaneously explain charge quantization, matter representations, baryon-number violation, and the observed low-energy couplings?
self_contained_problem:
Consider the Minimal Supersymmetric Standard Model (MSSM): a quantum field theory extending the Standard Model gauge group G_SM = SU(3)_C × SU(2)_L × U(1)_Y by adding, for every Standard Model fermion, a scalar superpartner of the same gauge quantum numbers, and, for every gauge boson, a fermionic gaugino superpartner, together with two Higgs doublet chiral superfields H_u and H_d and their higgsino partners, with soft supersymmetry breaking terms at the TeV scale. Let g_1(μ), g_2(μ), g_3(μ) denote the running U(1)_Y (in GUT normalization), SU(2)_L, and SU(3)_C gauge couplings, evolved via the two-loop renormalization group equations of the MSSM from the electroweak scale upward.

(a) Determine whether there exists a scale M_GUT (near 2 × 10^16 GeV) at which g_1(M_GUT) = g_2(M_GUT) = g_3(M_GUT) once experimental uncertainties and threshold corrections from supersymmetric and heavy particle spectra are taken into account, and characterize precisely the spectrum constraints required for exact unification.

(b) Decide whether the MSSM is the low-energy limit of a four-dimensional supersymmetric grand unified theory based on a simple gauge group G ⊇ G_SM (such as SU(5), SO(10), SU(6), or E_6) in which:
  (i) one full generation of MSSM matter fits into a (small set of) irreducible representations of G, explaining the observed hypercharge assignments and charge quantization;
  (ii) the proton decay rate induced by baryon-number-violating dimension-5 and dimension-6 operators is consistent with current experimental lower bounds on the proton lifetime;
  (iii) the unified gauge coupling, the running yielding the measured low-energy values of (g_1, g_2, g_3) at the Z-boson mass, and the doublet–triplet splitting problem are all simultaneously and naturally accommodated.

Provide either an explicit construction satisfying (i)–(iii) or a no-go result excluding such a theory.
status_search_result: No supersymmetric grand unified theory has been experimentally confirmed. Proton decay searches (Super-Kamiokande, Hyper-Kamiokande) continue to constrain and exclude minimal SUSY SU(5) variants, while LHC searches have not observed superpartners at the TeV scale, tightening but not refuting MSSM-based unification scenarios. Gauge coupling unification in the MSSM remains a strong hint, with various SUSY GUT models (flipped SU(5), SO(10), E_6, orbifold GUTs) still viable. The question of whether the MSSM truly arises from a SUSY GUT explaining all the listed features is still open.

paper_title: Twenty Open Questions in Supersymmetric Particle Physics
original_question: A supersymmetric GUT relates quarks and leptons in unified multiplets and therefore constrains Yukawa couplings and fermion mass matrices. Can a self-consistent SUSY GUT explain the observed quark and lepton masses, GUT-scale relations such as the Georgi-Jarlskog factors, inter-generation hierarchies, up-type quark masses, and small neutrino masses while respecting the representation and coupling constraints imposed by realistic model building and string theory?
self_contained_problem:
Consider a supersymmetric grand unified theory (SUSY GUT) based on a simple gauge group G (such as SU(5), SO(10), or E6) that contains the Standard Model gauge group SU(3)_c × SU(2)_L × U(1)_Y, and in which the quarks and leptons of each Standard Model generation are embedded into a small number of irreducible representations of G. The matter Yukawa couplings of the Minimal Supersymmetric Standard Model (MSSM), which produce the up-type quark mass matrix M_u, the down-type quark mass matrix M_d, the charged-lepton mass matrix M_e, and (after introducing right-handed neutrinos and/or a seesaw mechanism) the neutrino mass matrix M_ν, are then determined at the unification scale M_GUT by a smaller set of Yukawa couplings of G-invariant superpotential operators (possibly including higher-dimensional operators suppressed by powers of M_GUT/M_Pl and/or contributions from Higgs fields in non-fundamental representations). Running these boundary conditions down to the electroweak scale via the MSSM renormalization group equations yields the physical fermion masses and mixings.

Construct, or prove the existence (or non-existence) of, a self-consistent SUSY GUT model satisfying all of the following requirements simultaneously:

1. The representation content, superpotential, and symmetry-breaking pattern are fully specified, use only fields and couplings that can arise in a controlled ultraviolet completion (in particular, are compatible with known constraints from perturbative heterotic or other string-theory constructions, including level, anomaly, and modular-invariance constraints on the allowed representations and Yukawa couplings).

2. After renormalization-group evolution from M_GUT to the electroweak scale, the model reproduces the measured charged-fermion masses (m_u, m_c, m_t, m_d, m_s, m_b, m_e, m_μ, m_τ) and CKM mixing angles within experimental uncertainties.

3. The model produces the Georgi–Jarlskog-type GUT-scale mass relations m_b ≈ m_τ, m_μ ≈ 3 m_s, m_e ≈ (1/3) m_d (or a comparably successful pattern of charged-fermion mass ratios at M_GUT) as consequences of the chosen group-theoretic structure rather than as fine-tuned input.

4. The inter-generation mass hierarchies m_u : m_c : m_t and m_d : m_s : m_b and m_e : m_μ : m_τ, and in particular the largeness of the top-quark Yukawa coupling relative to the other up-type Yukawas, are explained by a symmetry principle (e.g., a flavor symmetry, texture zeros, or geometric/string selection rules) within the model rather than imposed by hand.

5. Neutrinos acquire masses small enough to be compatible with current bounds while reproducing observed neutrino mass-squared differences and lepton mixing angles, via a mechanism (such as a seesaw) that is consistent with the chosen GUT representations.

Either exhibit such a model explicitly and verify the above, or prove that no SUSY GUT meeting the stated string-theoretic and model-building constraints can simultaneously satisfy conditions 1–5.
status_search_result: The problem of constructing a fully realistic SUSY GUT that explains all fermion mass and mixing data (including Georgi–Jarlskog-type relations, hierarchies, and neutrino masses) from a string-theory–consistent UV completion remains an active area of research with many partial proposals (SO(10) flavor models, F-theory GUTs, orbifold/heterotic constructions) but no universally accepted complete solution. The question is generally regarded as open.

paper_title: Twenty Open Questions in Supersymmetric Particle Physics
original_question: Why should supersymmetric particle physics be embedded in string theory: can a theory whose fundamental objects are one-dimensional strings simultaneously provide quantized gravity through a massless spin-two excitation, improve ultraviolet finiteness relative to point-particle field theory, require gauge symmetry and gauge coupling unification, and explain why supersymmetry should appear at high energies?
self_contained_problem:
Consider a candidate theory of fundamental physics whose elementary objects are one-dimensional extended strings of characteristic length on the order of 10^{-33} cm, whose distinct vibrational/excitation modes are postulated to give rise to all known elementary particles and gauge bosons. Provide a rigorous account that establishes the following four properties of such a string-based framework, and explain in what precise sense each property follows from the one-dimensional nature of the fundamental objects:

1. (Quantized gravity.) Show that the spectrum of excitations of a closed string necessarily contains a massless spin-two state, and explain why this state can be consistently identified with the graviton of a quantum theory of gravity.

2. (Ultraviolet behavior.) Demonstrate that perturbative scattering amplitudes built from string worldsheets exhibit improved ultraviolet behavior compared with the corresponding amplitudes in point-particle quantum field theory, and characterize the mechanism (e.g. modular invariance, soft high-energy behavior) responsible for this improvement.

3. (Gauge symmetry and unification.) Show that consistency of the string theory (anomaly cancellation, modular invariance, tadpole cancellation, etc.) forces the appearance of non-abelian gauge symmetries, and analyze whether and how the gauge couplings of these symmetries are predicted to unify at a high scale.

4. (Necessity of supersymmetry.) Establish under what consistency conditions a string theory containing spacetime fermions must be spacetime supersymmetric, and explain the sense in which supersymmetry is therefore predicted to be present at sufficiently high energies, motivating its relevance for particle physics below the string scale.

The problem is to give a coherent and mathematically precise justification — within a single string-theoretic framework — of all four features simultaneously, identifying the minimal assumptions required and the logical implications among them.
status_search_result: This is a foundational motivational/conceptual question about why string theory is a natural setting for supersymmetric particle physics. While many of its individual components (massless spin-2 in closed string spectra, improved UV behavior, gauge symmetries from heterotic/Type I constructions, spacetime supersymmetry from worldsheet supersymmetry and GSO projection) are well-established results in string theory, the overarching question of whether string theory is the correct embedding for supersymmetric particle physics — and whether it leads to testable predictions such as gauge coupling unification and low-energy supersymmetry — remains open as of recent reviews.
