paper_title: Selection Principles and Special Sets of Reals
original_question: For a set of reals X, the δ-property means that for every open ω-cover U of X, the space X belongs to the closure of U under the lim inf operation. The property (Ω over Γ) means that every open ω-cover of X contains an open γ-subcover. Are these two properties equivalent?
self_contained_problem:
Let X be a set of real numbers (equivalently, a separable metrizable zero-dimensional space). 

Recall the following definitions:
- An open cover U of X is an ω-cover if X is not a member of U and every finite subset of X is contained in some U ∈ U.
- An open cover U of X is a γ-cover if U is infinite and every x ∈ X belongs to all but finitely many members of U.
- The lim inf operator on a family U of subsets of X is defined by liminf(U) = ⋃_{V ⊆ U infinite} ⋂ V; equivalently, x ∈ liminf(U) iff x belongs to all but finitely many members of some infinite V ⊆ U. The closure of U under the lim inf operation is the smallest family containing U that is closed under taking lim inf of its infinite subfamilies.
- X has the δ-property if for every open ω-cover U of X, the set X belongs to the closure of U under the lim inf operation (i.e., X can be obtained from U by iterated applications of the lim inf operator).
- X has the property (Ω over Γ) (sometimes denoted ⟨Ω, Γ⟩, also known as the γ-property) if every open ω-cover of X contains a γ-subcover (i.e., an infinite subfamily that is a γ-cover of X).

Question: Are the δ-property and the property (Ω over Γ) equivalent for every set of real numbers X?
status_search_result: It is known that the property (Ω over Γ) coincides with being a γ-set, and the δ-property defines δ-sets. Orenshtein and Tsaban showed (consistently, under the set-theoretic assumption p = c) that there exists a δ-set that is not a γ-set, by constructing a set of reals A for which C_p(A) has the Pytkeev property but is not Fréchet–Urysohn. Thus the two properties are consistently not equivalent. Whether ZFC alone refutes the equivalence (i.e., whether a δ-set that is not a γ-set can be constructed without additional axioms) appears to remain open.

original_question: For a set of reals X, let O be the family of open covers of X, Ω the family of open ω-covers (every finite subset of X is contained in some member), and Γ the family of open γ-covers (infinite covers in which each point belongs to all but finitely many members). Suppose X and Y each satisfy S1(O, O), and X additionally satisfies Ufin(O, Γ). Must the product X × Y also satisfy S1(O, O)?
self_contained_problem:
Let X and Y be sets of real numbers (regarded as topological subspaces of R). For a topological space Z, let:
• O(Z) denote the family of all open covers of Z;
• Ω(Z) denote the family of open ω-covers of Z, i.e. open covers U of Z such that Z ∉ U and every finite subset of Z is contained in some member of U;
• Γ(Z) denote the family of open γ-covers of Z, i.e. infinite open covers U of Z such that every point of Z belongs to all but finitely many members of U.

For classes A, B of covers, define the following selection principles:
• S1(A, B): for every sequence (Un : n ∈ N) with each Un ∈ A, there exist Un ∈ Un such that {Un : n ∈ N} ∈ B.
• Sfin(A, B): for every sequence (Un : n ∈ N) with each Un ∈ A, there exist finite Fn ⊆ Un such that ∪n Fn ∈ B.
• Ufin(A, B): for every sequence (Un : n ∈ N) of elements of A with no finite subcover, there exist finite Fn ⊆ Un such that {∪Fn : n ∈ N} ∈ B.

The property S1(O, O) is the Rothberger property and Ufin(O, Γ) is the Hurewicz property.

Suppose that X and Y both satisfy S1(O, O), and that X additionally satisfies Ufin(O, Γ). Does it necessarily follow that the product space X × Y satisfies S1(O, O)?

- S_fin(A, B): For every sequence (U_n : n ∈ ω) with each U_n ∈ A, there exist finite F_n ⊆ U_n such that ⋃_{n∈ω} F_n ∈ B.
- U_fin(A, B): For every sequence (U_n : n ∈ ω) with each U_n ∈ A and no U_n containing a finite subcover of X, there exist finite F_n ⊆ U_n such that { ⋃ F_n : n ∈ ω } ∈ B.

A property P of topological spaces is said to be preserved under finite products if whenever X and Y satisfy P, the product X × Y satisfies P.

paper_title: Selection Principles and Special Sets of Reals
original_question: Is it consistent that there exists a subgroup G ≤ Z^N having strong measure zero and satisfying Sfin(O, O), while still being unbounded and failing S1(O, O)?
self_contained_problem:
Let $\mathbb{Z}^{\mathbb{N}}$ denote the Baer–Specker group, equipped with its standard Polish group topology (the product topology with $\mathbb{Z}$ discrete). For an open cover $\mathcal{U}$ of a topological space $X$, recall the Scheepers selection principles:
- $\mathsf{S}_1(\mathcal{O},\mathcal{O})$: for every sequence $(\mathcal{U}_n)_{n\in\mathbb{N}}$ of open covers of $X$ there exist $U_n\in\mathcal{U}_n$ such that $\{U_n:n\in\mathbb{N}\}$ is an open cover of $X$ (Rothberger's property).
- $\mathsf{S}_{\mathrm{fin}}(\mathcal{O},\mathcal{O})$: for every sequence $(\mathcal{U}_n)_{n\in\mathbb{N}}$ of open covers of $X$ there exist finite $\mathcal{F}_n\subseteq\mathcal{U}_n$ such that $\bigcup_n \mathcal{F}_n$ is an open cover of $X$ (Menger's property).

A set $X$ in a Polish group $(G,\cdot)$ with a left-invariant metric has strong measure zero if for every sequence $(\varepsilon_n)_{n\in\mathbb{N}}$ of positive reals there exist sets $A_n\subseteq G$ of diameter at most $\varepsilon_n$ with $X\subseteq\bigcup_n A_n$.

A subset $X\subseteq\mathbb{Z}^{\mathbb{N}}$ is unbounded if it is unbounded with respect to the eventual-domination order $\le^*$ on $\mathbb{Z}^{\mathbb{N}}$ (equivalently, on $\mathbb{N}^{\mathbb{N}}$ after taking absolute values).

Question: Is it consistent with ZFC that there exists a subgroup $G\le\mathbb{Z}^{\mathbb{N}}$ such that
1. $G$ has strong measure zero,
2. $G$ satisfies $\mathsf{S}_{\mathrm{fin}}(\mathcal{O},\mathcal{O})$,
3. $G$ is unbounded in $(\mathbb{Z}^{\mathbb{N}},\le^*)$, and
4. $G$ does not satisfy $\mathsf{S}_1(\mathcal{O},\mathcal{O})$?
status_search_result: A 2008 note titled "A note on unbounded strongly measure zero subgroups of the Baer–Specker group" (Topology and its Applications) addresses exactly this question, establishing the consistency of unbounded strongly measure zero subgroups of $\mathbb{Z}^{\mathbb{N}}$ with the relevant Menger-type / Rothberger-type selection properties separated. The problem is therefore reported as solved (consistency established).

paper_title: Selection Principles and Special Sets of Reals
original_question: Let p* be the minimal size of a centered family of infinite subsets of N that is not linearly refinable modulo finite sets. Is p equal to p*?
self_contained_problem:
Work in ZFC. Let ω denote the natural numbers, and for A,B ⊆ ω write A ⊆* B (A is almost contained in B) when A \ B is finite. A family F ⊆ [ω]^ω of infinite subsets of ω is called centered if every finite subfamily has infinite intersection. A pseudo-intersection of F is an infinite set A ⊆ ω with A ⊆* B for every B ∈ F. A family L ⊆ [ω]^ω is said to linearly refine F (modulo finite) if L is linearly ordered by ⊆*, and for every B ∈ F there exists A ∈ L with A ⊆* B.

Define:
 • p = the minimal cardinality of a centered family F ⊆ [ω]^ω which has no pseudo-intersection (the pseudo-intersection number);
 • p* = the minimal cardinality of a centered family F ⊆ [ω]^ω which is not linearly refinable modulo finite, i.e. admits no linearly (⊆*-) ordered refining family.

Decide whether p = p* is provable in ZFC.
status_search_result: The cardinal p* was renamed lr (the linear refinement number). Machura, Shelah and Tsaban (Fundamenta Mathematicae, "The linear refinement number and selection theory", 2014) proved that it is consistent that p < lr < c, and in particular that p < p*. Hence p = p* is not a theorem of ZFC; the question is resolved in the negative.

paper_title: Selection Principles and Special Sets of Reals
original_question: If X and Y are meager-additive subsets of R, must X × Y be meager-additive? Likewise, if X and Y are null-additive, must X × Y be null-additive?
self_contained_problem:
Work in the real line $\mathbb{R}$ with its usual topology and Lebesgue measure. A set $X\subseteq\mathbb{R}$ is called:

- meager-additive if for every meager set $M\subseteq\mathbb{R}$, the algebraic sum $X+M=\{x+m:x\in X,\,m\in M\}$ is again meager;
- null-additive if for every Lebesgue null set $N\subseteq\mathbb{R}$, the algebraic sum $X+N$ is again Lebesgue null.

A subset of $\mathbb{R}^2$ is called meager-additive (respectively null-additive) if the same definition holds with $\mathbb{R}$ replaced by $\mathbb{R}^2$, addition being coordinate-wise, and meagerness (respectively Lebesgue nullness) taken in $\mathbb{R}^2$.

Question. Suppose $X,Y\subseteq\mathbb{R}$.

(a) If $X$ and $Y$ are both meager-additive, must the Cartesian product $X\times Y\subseteq\mathbb{R}^2$ be meager-additive?

(b) If $X$ and $Y$ are both null-additive, must $X\times Y\subseteq\mathbb{R}^2$ be null-additive?

The null-additive analogue does not appear to have been settled in the literature consulted, so the problem appears partially solved overall.

original_question: For a connected simple algebraic group G, let Cay(G) denote the minimum degree of a dominant rational G-equivariant map from G, with G acting by conjugation, to its Lie algebra Lie G, with G acting via the adjoint representation. What are the Cayley degrees Cay(G) of the connected simple algebraic groups?
self_contained_problem:
Let $k$ be an algebraically closed field of characteristic zero, and let $G$ be a connected simple algebraic group over $k$ with Lie algebra $\mathrm{Lie}(G)$. Consider $G$ as a $G$-variety via the conjugation action, and consider $\mathrm{Lie}(G)$ as a $G$-variety via the adjoint representation. A dominant rational map $\varphi\colon G \dashrightarrow \mathrm{Lie}(G)$ is called $G$-equivariant if $\varphi(g x g^{-1}) = \mathrm{Ad}(g)\,\varphi(x)$ as rational maps. The degree of such a $\varphi$ is the degree of the induced extension of function fields $[k(G):\varphi^*k(\mathrm{Lie}(G))]$. Define the Cayley degree
$$\mathrm{Cay}(G) \;=\; \min\{\deg(\varphi) : \varphi\colon G \dashrightarrow \mathrm{Lie}(G)\text{ dominant rational }G\text{-equivariant}\}.$$
Determine $\mathrm{Cay}(G)$ for every connected simple algebraic group $G$.
status_search_result: Lemire, Popov, and Reichstein (2006) classified which simple algebraic groups are Cayley (i.e., have Cay(G)=1), and the stably Cayley case has been settled in characteristic zero (Borovoi–Kunyavskii–Lemire–Reichstein, 2014). However, no general formula for the Cayley degree Cay(G) of arbitrary connected simple algebraic groups appears in the literature; the problem of computing Cay(G) in all cases remains open.

context_brief: Existence of groups with large Cayley degree
original_question: Does there exist an algebraic group G with Cayley degree Cay(G) > 2? If so, does there exist a simple algebraic group with Cay(G) > 2?
self_contained_problem:
Let $k$ be an algebraically closed field of characteristic zero and let $G$ be a connected linear algebraic group over $k$ with Lie algebra $\mathfrak{g} = \mathrm{Lie}(G)$. Consider the action of $G$ on itself by conjugation and the adjoint action of $G$ on $\mathfrak{g}$. Define the Cayley degree $\mathrm{Cay}(G)$ to be the smallest positive integer $d$ such that there exists a $G$-equivariant dominant rational map $\varphi\colon G \dashrightarrow \mathfrak{g}$ (with respect to the conjugation and adjoint actions) of degree $d$; equivalently, $\mathrm{Cay}(G) = [k(G) : \varphi^*k(\mathfrak{g})]$ minimized over all such $\varphi$. (Thus $\mathrm{Cay}(G) = 1$ if and only if $G$ is a Cayley group, i.e.\ admits a $G$-equivariant birational isomorphism with its Lie algebra.)

(a) Does there exist a connected linear algebraic group $G$ over $k$ with $\mathrm{Cay}(G) > 2$?

(b) Does there exist a connected simple algebraic group $G$ over $k$ with $\mathrm{Cay}(G) > 2$?
status_search_result: The notion of Cayley degree was introduced by Lemire, Popov, and Reichstein, and at the time of its introduction no examples were known of (simple) algebraic groups with Cayley degree exceeding 2. Subsequent work has focused on classifying Cayley and stably Cayley simple groups (Cay(G)=1), but a web search did not produce any source establishing the existence of an algebraic group, simple or otherwise, with Cayley degree strictly greater than 2, nor a proof that none exists. The status therefore appears to remain unresolved.

original_question: Let f_lambda(z) = lambda z + z^2 with lambda = exp(2 pi i theta), and suppose theta is irrational so that f_lambda is a Cremer polynomial, meaning it is not analytically conjugate to a rotation near 0. In the Julia set of such a Cremer polynomial, is there an arc joining the fixed point 0 to its preimage -lambda?
self_contained_problem:
For $\lambda = e^{2\pi i \theta}$ with $\theta \in \mathbb{R}$, consider the quadratic polynomial $f_\lambda(z) = \lambda z + z^2$, which fixes the origin with multiplier $\lambda$. Assume $\theta$ is irrational and that $f_\lambda$ is not analytically (equivalently, topologically) conjugate to the rotation $z \mapsto \lambda z$ in any neighborhood of $0$; such an $f_\lambda$ is called a Cremer polynomial, and $0$ is its Cremer fixed point. Let $J(f_\lambda) \subset \mathbb{C}$ denote the Julia set of $f_\lambda$, i.e. the closure of the set of repelling periodic points (equivalently, the complement of the Fatou set). Note that $-\lambda$ is the unique other preimage of $0$ under $f_\lambda$, and both $0$ and $-\lambda$ belong to $J(f_\lambda)$.

Question: For every Cremer polynomial $f_\lambda$, does the Julia set $J(f_\lambda)$ contain an arc (a homeomorphic image of the closed interval $[0,1]$) whose endpoints are $0$ and $-\lambda$?
status_search_result: The question about the existence of an arc joining the Cremer fixed point 0 to its preimage -λ in the Julia set of a quadratic Cremer polynomial appears to remain open. Subsequent work by Blokh, Childers, Oversteegen, Sørensen and others has established striking topological properties of Cremer Julia sets (non-local connectivity, examples with positive area, degenerate impressions, external rays accumulating on both 0 and -λ), but no result fully resolving the existence (or nonexistence) of such an arc for all Cremer polynomials was found.

original_question: Construct a convincing computer visualization of the Julia set of a Cremer polynomial f_lambda(z) = lambda z + z^2, where theta is irrational and the map is not analytically conjugate to a rotation near 0.
self_contained_problem:
For $\lambda = e^{2\pi i \theta}$ with $\theta \in \mathbb{R}\setminus\mathbb{Q}$, consider the quadratic polynomial
$$f_\lambda(z) = \lambda z + z^2,$$
which fixes $0$ with multiplier $\lambda$. The map $f_\lambda$ is called a Siegel polynomial if it is analytically conjugate, in some neighborhood of $0$, to the rigid rotation $z \mapsto \lambda z$; otherwise (still with $\theta$ irrational) it is called a Cremer polynomial. Recall that the (filled) Julia set of $f_\lambda$ is the set of points whose forward orbit under iteration of $f_\lambda$ is bounded, and its Julia set $J(f_\lambda)$ is the topological boundary of this set.

Produce a convincing, mathematically faithful computer-generated picture of the Julia set $J(f_\lambda)$ for some choice of irrational $\theta$ for which $f_\lambda$ is a Cremer polynomial. Equivalently, exhibit an effective algorithm which, given a precision $\varepsilon > 0$, outputs an image approximating $J(f_\lambda)$ in the Hausdorff metric to within $\varepsilon$, together with the resulting picture.
status_search_result: Significant progress has been made but the problem in its strongest form is not fully resolved. Braverman and Yampolsky proved that there exist computable irrational rotation numbers $\theta$ for which the Cremer Julia set $J(f_\lambda)$ is not computable, i.e., no algorithm can produce arbitrarily accurate pictures — a strong obstruction to "convincing visualization" in general. Conversely, for certain restricted classes of Cremer rotation numbers, computable approximations and partial visualizations have been achieved (work of Binder, Braverman, Yampolsky and others on computational complexity of Cremer Julia sets). Thus the question is partially solved: some Cremer Julia sets are provably non-visualizable, while others can be drawn with rigorous guarantees.

original_question: For which Cremer polynomials f_lambda(z) = lambda z + z^2 is the critical point accessible from the complement of the Julia set?
self_contained_problem:
For a complex parameter $\lambda = \exp(2\pi i \theta)$ with $\theta \in \mathbb{R}$, consider the quadratic polynomial
$$f_\lambda(z) = \lambda z + z^2,$$
which has a fixed point at $0$ with multiplier $\lambda$ and a unique critical point at $z = -\lambda/2$. The filled Julia set $K(f_\lambda)$ is the set of points whose forward orbits under $f_\lambda$ remain bounded, and the Julia set $J(f_\lambda) = \partial K(f_\lambda)$. Call $f_\lambda$ a Cremer polynomial if $\theta$ is irrational and $f_\lambda$ is not analytically conjugate to a rotation in any neighborhood of $0$ (equivalently, $0$ is not a Siegel fixed point). For a Cremer polynomial the critical point lies in $J(f_\lambda)$. A point $p \in J(f_\lambda)$ is said to be accessible (from the complement of the Julia set) if there exists a continuous path $\gamma: [0,1] \to \mathbb{C}$ with $\gamma([0,1)) \subset \mathbb{C} \setminus K(f_\lambda)$ and $\gamma(1) = p$.

Characterize precisely those Cremer polynomials $f_\lambda$ (equivalently, those irrational rotation numbers $\theta$ producing a Cremer fixed point) for which the critical point $-\lambda/2$ is accessible from the complement of the Julia set.
status_search_result: Kiwi proved that a Cremer polynomial whose Cremer periodic orbit is approximated by small cycles has a non-accessible critical point. This provides a broad sufficient condition for non-accessibility, but a full characterization of which Cremer rotation numbers yield an accessible critical point has not been established. The general classification problem appears to remain open.

original_question: Does there exist a Siegel polynomial f_lambda(z) = lambda z + z^2, with theta irrational and f_lambda analytically conjugate to a rotation near 0, whose Siegel disk has boundary that is not a Jordan curve?
self_contained_problem:
For $\lambda = e^{2\pi i \theta}$ with $\theta \in \mathbb{R}\setminus\mathbb{Q}$, consider the quadratic polynomial
$$f_\lambda(z) = \lambda z + z^2.$$
Suppose that $f_\lambda$ is analytically conjugate to the rigid rotation $z \mapsto \lambda z$ in some neighborhood of the fixed point $0$; that is, there exists an analytic conjugacy $\varphi$ defined on a neighborhood $U$ of $0$ with $\varphi(0)=0$, $\varphi'(0)\neq 0$, satisfying $\varphi(f_\lambda(z)) = \lambda\,\varphi(z)$ on $U$. The Siegel disk $\Delta_\lambda$ of $f_\lambda$ is the maximal such linearization domain containing $0$; it is a simply connected open subset of $\mathbb{C}$ on which $f_\lambda$ is conjugate to an irrational rotation. Such a polynomial $f_\lambda$ is called a Siegel polynomial.

Question: Does there exist an irrational $\theta$ for which $f_\lambda$ is a Siegel polynomial and the boundary $\partial \Delta_\lambda$ of its Siegel disk is not a Jordan curve?
status_search_result: The question appears to remain open in general. Strong partial results are known: Petersen–Zakeri (Acta Math. 2004) proved that for almost every irrational rotation number the boundary of the Siegel disk of $\lambda z + z^2$ is a Jordan curve; bounded-type rotation numbers give quasicircle boundaries (Douady–Ghys–Herman–Shishikura); and Yang (J. Eur. Math. Soc., 2016/preprint 1608.04106) showed the same for sufficiently high-type rotation numbers. No example of a quadratic Siegel polynomial with non-Jordan Siegel-disk boundary is known, and no proof covering all irrational $\theta$ is known.

original_question: For the quadratic polynomial P_c(z) = z^2 + c with connected Julia set, is the Julia set locally connected whenever the parameter c is real?
self_contained_problem: For a complex parameter $c \in \mathbb{C}$, let $P_c : \mathbb{C} \to \mathbb{C}$ be the quadratic polynomial $P_c(z) = z^2 + c$. The filled Julia set $K(P_c)$ is the set of points $z \in \mathbb{C}$ whose forward orbit $\{P_c^n(z)\}_{n \ge 0}$ is bounded, and the Julia set $J(P_c) = \partial K(P_c)$ is its topological boundary. Restrict attention to those parameters $c$ for which $J(P_c)$ is connected (equivalently, the critical orbit of $0$ under $P_c$ is bounded).\n\nProve or disprove: for every real parameter $c \in \mathbb{R}$ such that $J(P_c)$ is connected, the Julia set $J(P_c)$ is locally connected.
status_search_result: The question was answered affirmatively. Levin and van Strien (Annals of Mathematics, 1998) proved that the Julia set of a real polynomial with only real critical points is locally connected whenever it is connected; in particular, $J(P_c)$ is locally connected for every real $c$ in the Mandelbrot set. Independent proofs in the quadratic case were also obtained via complex bounds (Lyubich, Graczyk–Świątek).

original_question: Suppose one could prove that whenever two quadratic polynomials P_c1 and P_c2 are topologically conjugate, they are also quasiconformally conjugate. Would that implication force local connectivity of the quadratic connectedness locus, that is, the Mandelbrot set of parameters c for which the Julia set of P_c(z) = z^2 + c is connected?
self_contained_problem:
For each complex parameter c ∈ ℂ, consider the quadratic polynomial P_c(z) = z^2 + c acting on ℂ. The filled Julia set K_c is the set of points whose forward orbit under P_c is bounded, and the Julia set J_c = ∂K_c. The Mandelbrot set M is the set of parameters c ∈ ℂ for which J_c is connected (equivalently, the orbit of 0 under P_c is bounded).

Two polynomials P_{c_1} and P_{c_2} are said to be topologically conjugate on ℂ if there is an orientation-preserving homeomorphism h: ℂ → ℂ such that h ∘ P_{c_1} = P_{c_2} ∘ h, and quasiconformally conjugate if such an h can be chosen to be a quasiconformal homeomorphism.

Suppose one knew the following implication:

(∗) For every pair c_1, c_2 ∈ ℂ, if P_{c_1} and P_{c_2} are topologically conjugate, then they are quasiconformally conjugate.

Question: Does the validity of (∗) imply that the Mandelbrot set M is locally connected?
status_search_result: Local connectivity of the Mandelbrot set (MLC) remains an open central conjecture in holomorphic dynamics as of 2026. While Yoccoz established MLC at all finitely renormalizable parameters and recent work (Dudko–Lyubich and others) has extended it to broad classes including Feigenbaum-type parameters, the general implication from topological-to-quasiconformal rigidity to MLC has not been established, and MLC itself is not resolved.

original_question: If the quadratic polynomial P_c is nonrecurrent, does there exist a conformal metric of the form rho(z)|dz| with integrable singularities for which P_c is expanding on its Julia set?
self_contained_problem:
Let $P_c(z) = z^2 + c$ be a quadratic polynomial on the complex plane, and let $J(P_c)$ denote its Julia set. Assume that $P_c$ is nonrecurrent, meaning that the critical point $0$ is not in the $\omega$-limit set of its own forward orbit under $P_c$.

A conformal metric on a neighborhood $U$ of $J(P_c)$ is an expression of the form $\rho(z)\,|dz|$, where $\rho$ is a non-negative measurable function whose singularities are integrable (i.e. $\rho$ may vanish or blow up, but $\int_K \rho^2\,dA < \infty$ on compact sets, and more generally the singularities give finite length to short curves). The map $P_c$ is said to be expanding with respect to $\rho(z)\,|dz|$ on $J(P_c)$ if there exist constants $\lambda > 1$ and $n_0 \ge 1$ such that for every $z$ in $J(P_c)$,
$$\rho(P_c^{n_0}(z))\,|(P_c^{n_0})'(z)| \;\ge\; \lambda\,\rho(z).$$

Question: Does the nonrecurrence of $P_c$ imply the existence of such a conformal metric $\rho(z)\,|dz|$ with integrable singularities for which $P_c$ is expanding on $J(P_c)$?
status_search_result: The question is answered affirmatively by the work of Carleson, Jones and Yoccoz ("Julia and John", 1994) and subsequent results in the theory of semi-hyperbolic rational maps. A quadratic polynomial is nonrecurrent (with no parabolic cycle) precisely when it is semi-hyperbolic, and semi-hyperbolic rational maps are known to be expanding with respect to a conformal metric with integrable singularities (an orbifold-type metric) on a neighborhood of the Julia set. This is standard in the theory of conformal fractals (Przytycki–Urbański).

original_question: Can the mating construction for two monic polynomials of the same degree be realized by quasiconformal surgery?
self_contained_problem:
Let $f$ and $g$ be two monic complex polynomials of the same degree $d \geq 2$, each acting on the Riemann sphere $\widehat{\mathbb{C}}$. The formal (topological) mating of $f$ and $g$ is defined as follows. Compactify the dynamical plane of $f$ by attaching the circle at infinity $S^1_f = \{\infty \cdot e^{2\pi i\theta} : \theta \in \mathbb{R}/\mathbb{Z}\}$, on which $f$ acts as $\theta \mapsto d\theta$, and do the same for $g$. Glue the two compactified planes along their circles at infinity by identifying the point at angle $\theta$ on $S^1_f$ with the point at angle $-\theta$ on $S^1_g$, obtaining a topological 2-sphere $\Sigma$ carrying a continuous self-map $f \sqcup_\partial g : \Sigma \to \Sigma$ of degree $d$.

One says that $f$ and $g$ are mateable, and that the geometric mating exists, if there exists a rational map $R : \widehat{\mathbb{C}} \to \widehat{\mathbb{C}}$ of degree $d$ and a semiconjugacy $\Phi : \Sigma \to \widehat{\mathbb{C}}$ from $f \sqcup_\partial g$ to $R$ that is conformal on the interiors of the filled-in dynamical planes.

Question: For every pair of monic polynomials $f, g$ of the same degree $d \geq 2$ for which the geometric mating exists, can the rational map $R$ realizing the mating be constructed by a quasiconformal surgery procedure (i.e., by cutting and pasting the dynamics of $f$ and $g$ along suitable curves and applying the measurable Riemann mapping theorem to a quasiregular model with a forward-invariant bounded-dilatation Beltrami coefficient)?
status_search_result: Quasiconformal surgery has been used successfully to construct matings in many specific settings—most notably Shishikura's surgery for postcritically finite hyperbolic polynomials, and various extensions to higher-degree and primitive tuning cases. However, a fully general quasiconformal-surgery construction of mating for all mateable pairs of monic polynomials of equal degree is not established; the surgery approach is known to apply broadly but not universally.

original_question: Let P1 be a polynomial with a periodic critical point omega of period k such that no other critical points lie in the basin of that superattracting cycle, and let P2 be a polynomial with one critical point of the same local degree, with both Julia sets connected. In the topological tuning construction, one replaces the immediate basin of omega by a copy of the dynamical plane of P2, matches external angles of P2 with internal angles of the basin, shrinks external rays of P2 to points, and makes analogous modifications at each preimage. Does this tuning construction always produce a map conjugate to a polynomial?
self_contained_problem:
Let P1 be a complex polynomial of degree at least 2 with connected Julia set, having a superattracting periodic cycle that contains a critical point ω of period k, and such that no other critical points of P1 lie in the basin of this superattracting cycle. Let P2 be a complex polynomial with a single critical point whose local degree at that critical point equals the local degree of P1 at ω, and assume P2 also has connected Julia set.

Form a new dynamical system P3 by the following topological tuning construction: remove the immediate basin U of ω together with each strict preimage of U under iteration of P1, and into each removed component glue in a copy of the filled Julia set of P2 (the dynamical plane of P2), in such a way that the external angles of P2 are matched with the internal angles of the corresponding basin component of P1, the external rays of P2 are collapsed to points, and the gluing is performed coherently at all preimages so that the new dynamics on the modified plane extends P1 outside the basins and agrees with P2 (up to the boundary identifications) on each inserted copy.

Question: Is the resulting dynamical system P3 always topologically conjugate to a polynomial of the same degree as P1?
status_search_result: The quadratic case is classical (Douady–Hubbard). Recent work using quasiconformal surgery (e.g., Inou–Mukherjee–Shen type results, arXiv:2010.05199, 2021) has established that any primitive postcritically-finite hyperbolic polynomial can be tuned with an arbitrary generalized polynomial with non-escaping critical points, extending the Douady–Hubbard tuning theorem to higher degrees in primitive cases. The general (non-primitive, satellite) higher-degree situation is not fully settled in the same generality, so the question is best described as partially solved.

original_question: In the polynomial tuning construction, does the resulting polynomial depend continuously on P2?
self_contained_problem:
Setup (polynomial tuning). Let $P_1:\mathbb{C}\to\mathbb{C}$ be a monic polynomial of degree $d_1\geq 2$ with connected Julia set, and suppose $P_1$ has a superattracting periodic cycle of period $p\geq 2$ passing through a critical point. The filled Julia set $K(P_1)$ then contains a "little filled Julia set" $K'\subset K(P_1)$ associated to the renormalization of $P_1^p$ about this cycle: there exist topological disks $U'\Subset V'$ such that $P_1^p:U'\to V'$ is a polynomial-like map of some degree $d_2\geq 2$ with filled Julia set $K'$.

Let $P_2:\mathbb{C}\to\mathbb{C}$ be any monic polynomial of degree $d_2$ with connected Julia set. The Douady–Hubbard tuning construction produces a new polynomial $P_1\perp P_2$ of degree $d_1$ (well-defined up to affine conjugacy) obtained, roughly, by replacing the dynamics of $P_1^p$ on the small filled Julia set $K'$ with a polynomial-like copy of $P_2$, and gluing this back into $P_1$ via the straightening theorem.

Question. Fix $P_1$ as above. Does the tuned polynomial $P_1\perp P_2$ depend continuously on $P_2$? More precisely, regarding $P_2$ as varying in the connectedness locus of monic centered polynomials of degree $d_2$, is the map $P_2\mapsto P_1\perp P_2$ (taking values in monic centered polynomials of degree $d_1$, modulo affine conjugacy) continuous?

(It is known that the answer is "yes" in the case where both $P_1$ and $P_2$ are quadratic.)
status_search_result: A search turned up the standard Douady–Hubbard framework for tuning and the parameter version of the straightening theorem (which gives continuity in the unicritical/quadratic-like setting), but no clear reference resolving continuous dependence of the tuned polynomial on $P_2$ in the general higher-degree case. Status appears unresolved in the general case.

original_question: If a sequence of source polynomials P_{1,k} tends to a limit, do the corresponding tunings of P_{1,k} with a fixed polynomial P2 converge to a limit that is independent of P2?
self_contained_problem:
Let $P_1$ and $P_2$ be monic polynomials of degree at least $2$ in one complex variable, each with connected filled Julia set, and assume that $P_1$ admits a renormalization slot in which the tuning operation $P_1 \boxplus P_2$ is well defined; here the tuning $P_1 \boxplus P_2$ denotes the polynomial obtained from $P_1$ by replacing the dynamics on a small Mandelbrot-like copy associated with a periodic critical cycle of $P_1$ by a quasi-conformally inserted copy of $P_2$, in the sense of Douady–Hubbard. 

Suppose $\{P_{1,k}\}_{k \ge 1}$ is a sequence of such "source" polynomials, all tunable by polynomials of the type of $P_2$, and assume that $P_{1,k} \to P_{1,\infty}$ as $k \to \infty$ (uniformly on compact subsets of $\mathbb{C}$, with the corresponding combinatorial data stabilizing).

Question: Does the sequence of tunings $P_{1,k} \boxplus P_2$ converge as $k \to \infty$, and if so, is the limit independent of the choice of the fixed polynomial $P_2$?
status_search_result: Web search did not return any source that explicitly resolves this specific question about convergence of tunings P_{1,k} ⊞ P_2 and independence of the limit from P_2. While related Douady–Hubbard tuning theory and convergence results for external rays and renormalizations are well developed, no direct confirmation of a solution or open status for this precise question was found.

original_question: Can the intertwining construction for polynomials be implemented by quasiconformal surgery?
self_contained_problem:
Let $f_1, f_2: \mathbb{C} \to \mathbb{C}$ be two monic polynomials of degrees $d_1, d_2 \geq 2$ each having a fixed point with prescribed multiplier (e.g., a common repelling or parabolic fixed point with matching combinatorial data along external rays landing there). An "intertwining" of $f_1$ and $f_2$ is a polynomial $F$ of degree $d_1 + d_2 - 1$ together with a decomposition of the filled Julia set $K(F)$ into two invariant pieces on which $F$ is conjugate to $f_1$ and $f_2$ respectively, glued along the orbit of the chosen fixed point so that the external ray combinatorics of $f_1$ and $f_2$ are matched.

Question: Can such an intertwining polynomial $F$ always be produced by quasiconformal surgery? Concretely, does there exist a construction that builds a quasiregular model map by cutting and pasting $f_1$ and $f_2$ along chosen ray pairs, equips $\mathbb{C}$ with an $F$-invariant Beltrami coefficient of norm strictly less than $1$, and then applies the measurable Riemann mapping theorem to straighten this model to a holomorphic polynomial $F$ realizing the intertwining of $f_1$ and $f_2$?
status_search_result: The question of realizing the intertwining construction for polynomials via quasiconformal surgery was answered affirmatively by Epstein and Yampolsky in "Geography of the cubic connectedness locus I: Intertwining surgery" (Annales Scientifiques de l'ENS, 1999), where intertwining surgery is implemented as a quasiconformal surgery in the spirit of Branner–Douady, producing cubic (and more generally higher-degree) polynomials by intertwining two lower-degree ones.

original_question: Consider the space of monic polynomials z maps to z^n + a_{n-1} z^{n-1} + ... + a_1 z with |a_1| >= 1, so that the origin is an unattractive fixed point, and do not assume the Julia set is connected. If at least one external ray lands at the origin, there is a rotation number for these rays under theta maps to n theta mod 1. Does this rotation number extend uniquely to a continuous map from this space of polynomials to R/Z, taking the value theta when a_1 = e^{2 pi i theta}?
self_contained_problem:
Let $n \geq 2$ be a fixed integer, and consider the space
$$\mathcal{P}_n = \{\, P(z) = z^n + a_{n-1} z^{n-1} + \cdots + a_2 z^2 + a_1 z \;:\; a_j \in \mathbb{C},\ |a_1| \geq 1\,\},$$
of monic polynomials of degree $n$ that fix the origin with multiplier $a_1$ of modulus at least $1$, so that $0$ is a non-attracting fixed point. For each such $P$, the basin of infinity carries external rays $R_\theta$ parametrized by angles $\theta \in \mathbb{R}/\mathbb{Z}$, and the dynamics on these angles is given by $\theta \mapsto n\theta \pmod 1$. (The Julia set is not assumed to be connected, in which case external rays are defined via the Böttcher coordinate near $\infty$ and may not all extend to $\infty$ on the parameter level, but those that land at the fixed point $0$ are well defined.)

Suppose that for some $P \in \mathcal{P}_n$ at least one external ray lands at the origin. Then the set of angles of rays landing at $0$ is invariant under $\theta \mapsto n\theta \pmod 1$, and the restriction of this map to that set is conjugate to a rigid rotation by some $\rho(P) \in \mathbb{R}/\mathbb{Z}$, called the combinatorial rotation number at $0$.

Question: Does $\rho$ extend uniquely to a continuous map
$$\rho : \mathcal{P}_n \longrightarrow \mathbb{R}/\mathbb{Z}$$
defined on the entire space $\mathcal{P}_n$, with the property that $\rho(P) = \theta$ whenever $a_1 = e^{2\pi i \theta}$?
status_search_result: A targeted web search located the foundational Goldberg–Milnor work on fixed point portraits and related papers on external rays and rotation numbers at fixed points of polynomial maps, but no source clearly resolves the question of unique continuous extension of the combinatorial rotation number to the full parameter space considered. The status appears to remain unverified in the literature accessible by search.

original_question: Instead of lifting by polynomials in Thurston’s algorithm for interval maps, consider the family p(x) = -|x|^alpha + c with alpha > 1, equivalently after affine rescaling the family x maps to k - k|2x - 1|^alpha from the unit interval to itself with 0 < k <= 1. Given an initial map f0 with preperiodic or periodic kneading sequence, does Thurston’s algorithm converge for this specific nonpolynomial lifting family?
self_contained_problem:
For a real parameter $\alpha>1$ and a parameter $k\in(0,1]$, consider the one-parameter family of unimodal interval maps
$$ p_{k,\alpha}:[0,1]\to[0,1],\qquad p_{k,\alpha}(x)=k-k\,|2x-1|^{\alpha}, $$
each of which has a unique critical point at $x=1/2$ and sends the boundary $\{0,1\}$ to $0$. (When $\alpha$ is an even integer, $p_{k,\alpha}$ is, after an affine change of coordinates, the real polynomial $x\mapsto -|x|^{\alpha}+c$.)

To any unimodal map $f:[0,1]\to[0,1]$ with critical point $c=1/2$ one associates its kneading sequence, the itinerary of the critical value under $f$ with respect to the partition $[0,c)$, $\{c\}$, $(c,1]$. Call $f$ admissible if its kneading sequence is either eventually periodic (preperiodic) or periodic.

Thurston's pull-back algorithm in this setting is defined as follows. Given an initial admissible unimodal map $f_0$ with kneading sequence $K$, recursively choose, for each $n\ge 0$, the parameter $k_{n+1}\in(0,1]$ so that $p_{k_{n+1},\alpha}$ realises the same combinatorial pull-back data as $f_n$ on its (pre)periodic critical orbit, and set $f_{n+1}=p_{k_{n+1},\alpha}$ (equivalently, lift $f_n$ through the family $\{p_{k,\alpha}\}_{k\in(0,1]}$ via the prescribed kneading data $K$).

Question: For every $\alpha>1$ and every initial admissible unimodal map $f_0$ whose kneading sequence is preperiodic or periodic, does the sequence $(f_n)_{n\ge 0}$ produced by this Thurston-type algorithm converge to a map in the family $\{p_{k,\alpha}:k\in(0,1]\}$ with kneading sequence equal to that of $f_0$?

It is known that convergence holds when $\alpha$ is an even integer (the polynomial case). The problem asks whether convergence persists for all real $\alpha>1$.

No source was found that specifically resolves convergence of the Thurston-type lifting algorithm for the non-polynomial family $x\mapsto k-k|2x-1|^{\alpha}$ for general real $\alpha>1$. Status appears unresolved beyond the polynomial (even-integer) case.

original_question: Find a general property of a lifting family in the interval version of Thurston’s algorithm that guarantees convergence for arbitrary kneading sequences, not only preperiodic or periodic ones.
self_contained_problem:
Consider the interval version of Thurston's algorithm for unimodal (or, more generally, piecewise monotone) self-maps of a compact interval. Let f: I → I be a piecewise monotone interval map with a designated set of critical (turning) points, and let K(f) denote its kneading sequence (the symbolic itinerary of the critical orbit relative to the laps of f). Given an admissible kneading sequence κ, Thurston's algorithm produces a sequence of maps {f_n} obtained by iteratively "lifting" along a chosen one-parameter family F = {f_t} of piecewise monotone maps (a "lifting family") so that, in good cases, f_n converges to a piecewise monotone map realizing κ.

It is known that the algorithm converges when κ is periodic or preperiodic (i.e., when the critical orbit is finite), but convergence may fail for general kneading sequences.

Problem. Identify and prove a general structural property of a lifting family F = {f_t} which is sufficient to guarantee that Thurston's algorithm, when applied with F as the lifting family, converges to a piecewise monotone interval map realizing κ for every admissible kneading sequence κ — not merely for periodic or preperiodic ones.
status_search_result: Subsequent work (e.g., on Thurston's method for real polynomials and on tower/metric algorithms for interval maps) has established convergence results in various restricted settings — for unimodal maps of high entropy and for periodic/preperiodic kneading data — while counterexamples are known at low entropy. No source found provides a single general property of the lifting family that guarantees convergence for arbitrary kneading sequences, so the question appears to remain open.

original_question: In the same setting of a polynomial diffeomorphism of C^2 with an invariant interior component U and limiting map g: U -> C^2, suppose g has a fixed point in U and rank one, so that g is a retraction onto a Siegel disk. Can g instead be a retraction onto a Herman ring, or onto a punctured Siegel disk?
self_contained_problem:
Let $f:\mathbb{C}^2\to\mathbb{C}^2$ be a polynomial diffeomorphism (i.e., a polynomial automorphism of $\mathbb{C}^2$) with positive dynamical degree, and let $U\subset\mathbb{C}^2$ be a periodic Fatou (interior) component which is invariant under $f$. Assume that the family of iterates $\{f^n|_U\}$ is normal, and let $g:U\to\mathbb{C}^2$ be a limit map of a convergent subsequence $f^{n_k}|_U \to g$. Suppose that $g$ has rank one at every point of $U$ (so the image $\Sigma=g(U)$ is a one-dimensional complex submanifold of $U$, and $g$ is a holomorphic retraction $U\to\Sigma$ such that $f|_\Sigma:\Sigma\to\Sigma$ is a conformal automorphism). It is known that if $g$ has a fixed point in $U$, then $\Sigma$ must be a Siegel disk (i.e., $f|_\Sigma$ is conformally conjugate to an irrational rotation of the unit disk).

Question: Can the situation instead occur in which $\Sigma$ is a Herman ring (a doubly connected Riemann surface, conformally an annulus $\{1<|z|<R\}$, on which $f$ acts as an irrational rotation), or in which $\Sigma$ is a punctured Siegel disk (a once-punctured disk on which $f$ acts as an irrational rotation)? Equivalently, determine whether such rank-one limit retractions onto a Herman ring or onto a punctured Siegel disk are possible for polynomial diffeomorphisms of $\mathbb{C}^2$.

The classification of recurrent Fatou components by Bedford–Smillie (and subsequent work) treats Siegel-disk retractions, but the existence/nonexistence of Herman-ring or punctured-Siegel-disk retractions in this dissipative-automorphism setting does not appear to have been settled in the literature located.

original_question: In the spaces Rat_d and Poly_d of rational and polynomial maps of degree d with the topology of uniform convergence, is the subset of expanding maps dense? Equivalently, is every rational or polynomial map approximable by maps for which some iterate uniformly expands the spherical metric on the Julia set?
self_contained_problem:
Let $\widehat{\mathbb{C}}$ denote the Riemann sphere equipped with the spherical metric. For an integer $d\geq 2$, let $\mathrm{Rat}_d$ be the space of rational maps $f:\widehat{\mathbb{C}}\to\widehat{\mathbb{C}}$ of degree $d$, and let $\mathrm{Poly}_d\subset\mathrm{Rat}_d$ be the subspace of polynomial maps of degree $d$. Endow both spaces with the topology of uniform convergence with respect to the spherical metric.

For $f\in\mathrm{Rat}_d$, let $J(f)\subset\widehat{\mathbb{C}}$ denote the Julia set of $f$ (the closure of the set of repelling periodic points), and let $P(f)$ denote the postcritical set, i.e. the closure of $\bigcup_{n\geq 1}f^n(C(f))$ where $C(f)$ is the set of critical points of $f$. The map $f$ is called expanding (equivalently hyperbolic, or Axiom A) if $P(f)\cap J(f)=\emptyset$; equivalently, there exist constants $C>0$ and $\lambda>1$ such that some iterate $f^n$ satisfies $\|(f^n)'(z)\|_{\mathrm{sph}}\geq C\lambda^n$ uniformly for all $z\in J(f)$.

Question: Is the set of expanding maps dense in $\mathrm{Rat}_d$? Is the set of expanding maps dense in $\mathrm{Poly}_d$?
category_tag: Density of hyperbolicity in complex dynamics
status_search_result: This is the classical Fatou density-of-hyperbolicity conjecture, still open in full generality for $\mathrm{Rat}_d$ and $\mathrm{Poly}_d$ with $d\geq 2$. It has been established in important special cases: for real polynomials of any degree (Kozlovski–Shen–van Strien, 2007), for real quadratic polynomials (Lyubich; Graczyk–Świątek), and for rational maps with Cantor Julia sets (Peng–Yin–Zhai and subsequent work). The general complex case remains a central open problem in holomorphic dynamics.

original_question: For every geometrically finite rational map f, is every connected component of its Julia set locally connected?
self_contained_problem:
Let $f:\widehat{\mathbb{C}}\to\widehat{\mathbb{C}}$ be a rational map of degree at least $2$ acting on the Riemann sphere. Denote by $J(f)$ its Julia set and by $F(f)$ its Fatou set. Recall that $f$ is called geometrically finite if every critical point of $f$ that lies in the Julia set has a finite forward orbit (equivalently, every critical point is either preperiodic or its forward orbit is contained in the union of basins of attracting and parabolic periodic cycles).

Prove or disprove: for every geometrically finite rational map $f$, every connected component of the Julia set $J(f)$ is locally connected.
status_search_result: The local connectivity of every connected component of the Julia set of a geometrically finite rational map was established by Tan Lei and Yin Yongcheng. Their work, building on earlier results for hyperbolic and subhyperbolic maps, proves local connectivity by constructing expanding conformal metrics in neighborhoods of Julia components. The result is now standard in complex dynamics.

original_question: Extend Thurston’s combinatorial theory of critically finite rational maps, where the post-critical set P is finite, to all geometrically finite rational maps. That is, describe such a map f up to combinatorial equivalence relative to P by finite topological data, and characterize which combinatorial types are realized by rational maps.
self_contained_problem:
Let $f:\widehat{\mathbb{C}}\to\widehat{\mathbb{C}}$ be a rational map of degree at least two on the Riemann sphere. Let $C_f$ denote the set of critical points of $f$, and let
$$P_f = \overline{\bigcup_{n\geq 1} f^n(C_f)}$$
be the post-critical set. The map $f$ is called critically finite (post-critically finite) if $P_f$ is finite, and geometrically finite if $P_f \cap J(f)$ is finite, where $J(f)$ is the Julia set (equivalently, every critical point in $J(f)$ has a finite forward orbit, while critical points in the Fatou set may have infinite orbits contained in attracting basins).

Two branched coverings $f,g:S^2\to S^2$ with marked sets $P_f, P_g$ are combinatorially equivalent rel $P$ if there exist orientation-preserving homeomorphisms $\varphi_0,\varphi_1:(S^2,P_f)\to(S^2,P_g)$ with $\varphi_0\circ f=g\circ\varphi_1$ and $\varphi_0$ isotopic to $\varphi_1$ rel $P_f$.

Thurston's theorem classifies critically finite rational maps up to combinatorial equivalence by finite topological data (a critically finite branched self-cover of $S^2$ together with the marked post-critical set), and characterizes which such combinatorial classes are realized by rational maps via the absence of a Thurston obstruction.

Problem: Extend Thurston's combinatorial theory to all geometrically finite rational maps. Specifically:
(a) Define a notion of finite topological data describing a geometrically finite rational map up to combinatorial equivalence rel $P_f$, allowing for critical points with infinite orbits in attracting Fatou components.
(b) Determine necessary and sufficient combinatorial conditions on such topological data so that the corresponding combinatorial class is realized by a geometrically finite rational map on $\widehat{\mathbb{C}}$.
status_search_result: Partial progress has been made. Cui, Jiang, and Sullivan extended Thurston's characterization to sub-hyperbolic semi-rational branched coverings, and Cui–Tan gave a characterization of hyperbolic rational maps via similar combinatorial obstructions. Further extensions cover rational maps with disconnected Julia sets and parabolic orbifolds. However, a complete combinatorial classification covering all geometrically finite rational maps (including the parabolic cycles case in full generality) does not appear to be fully settled as a single uniform theorem.

context_brief: Critically finite maps on projective space
original_question: Let f: P^n -> P^n be a critically finite rational map in the sense that there exist hypersurfaces V subset W subset P^n such that f maps P^n - W to P^n - V as a covering map. Are there nontrivial examples for which P^n - V is Kobayashi hyperbolic, and if so how do such maps behave dynamically?
self_contained_problem:
A rational self-map $f:\mathbb{P}^n\to\mathbb{P}^n$ (with $n\ge 2$) is called critically finite if there exist (possibly reducible) hypersurfaces $V\subset W\subset\mathbb{P}^n$ such that the restriction $f:\mathbb{P}^n\setminus W\to\mathbb{P}^n\setminus V$ is a covering map. A complex space $X$ is said to be Kobayashi hyperbolic if its Kobayashi pseudodistance is a genuine distance (equivalently, every holomorphic map $\mathbb{C}\to X$ is constant).

Construct nontrivial examples of critically finite maps $f:\mathbb{P}^n\to\mathbb{P}^n$ for which the complement $\mathbb{P}^n\setminus V$ is Kobayashi hyperbolic, and describe the dynamical behavior of such maps (e.g., structure of their Fatou and Julia sets, behavior of critical orbits, ergodic properties).
status_search_result: Subsequent work has produced nontrivial examples of critically (post-critically) finite endomorphisms of $\mathbb{P}^n$ whose post-critical complement is Kobayashi hyperbolic, and has analyzed their dynamics: for instance, it is known that when $\mathbb{P}^k\setminus P(f)$ is Kobayashi hyperbolic, the only Fatou components are basins of superattracting cycles. However, a full classification and dynamical description in arbitrary dimension is not complete, so the question is partially addressed rather than fully resolved.

original_question: Let M be a smooth real hypersurface in C^n with defining function r. Let p0 be a point in M, and let U be a neighborhood in C^n of p0 . When do C-R functions on M ∩ U extend to {r > 0}?
self_contained_problem:
Let $M$ be a smooth real hypersurface in $\mathbb{C}^n$ ($n \geq 2$) with smooth defining function $r$, so that locally $M = \{z \in \mathbb{C}^n : r(z) = 0\}$ with $dr \neq 0$ on $M$. Fix a point $p_0 \in M$ and a neighborhood $U \subset \mathbb{C}^n$ of $p_0$. A continuous function $f$ on $M \cap U$ is called a CR function if it satisfies the tangential Cauchy–Riemann equations $\bar{L} f = 0$ (in the distributional sense) for every smooth section $\bar{L}$ of $T^{0,1} M$ over $M \cap U$.

Give geometric conditions on $M$ at $p_0$ (in terms of the Levi form, finite-type conditions, or other local invariants of the CR structure of $M$) that are necessary and sufficient so that, for every CR function $f$ on $M \cap U$, there exists a (possibly smaller) neighborhood $V \subset U$ of $p_0$ and a holomorphic function $F$ on $V \cap \{r > 0\}$ such that $F$ extends continuously to $V \cap (\{r > 0\} \cup M)$ with $F|_{V \cap M} = f|_{V \cap M}$.
status_search_result: Classical sufficient conditions for one-sided holomorphic extension of CR functions are known: if the Levi form of $r$ has a negative eigenvalue at $p_0$, then all CR functions extend to the side $\{r>0\}$ (Lewy-type theorems). More generally, results of Trépreau, Tumanov, Baouendi–Treves, and others give extension under minimality and finite-type hypotheses. A complete necessary-and-sufficient geometric characterization for one-sided extension to a fixed side in the smooth (non-real-analytic) case remains an active research topic, so the problem as posed is partially solved.

original_question: If D is a strictly pseudoconvex domain in C^2 diffeomorphic to R4 and A is an embedded analytic disc outside D with bA ⊂ bD, then there is an embedded smooth disc M in D, with bM=bA, and such that M is totally real except at one elliptic point. context_brief: Locally Stein open subsets of Stein spaces
original_question: Let M be a compact complex manifold. Find some appropriate conditions on M such that if U is an open subset of M which is locally Stein, then U is Stein.
self_contained_problem:
A complex manifold $X$ is called Stein if it is holomorphically convex, holomorphically separable, and admits global holomorphic coordinates near every point (equivalently, it admits a strictly plurisubharmonic exhaustion function). An open subset $U$ of a complex manifold $M$ is called locally Stein (or locally pseudoconvex) in $M$ if every point $p \in \partial U \cap M$ has an open neighborhood $V$ in $M$ such that $U \cap V$ is a Stein open subset of $V$.

Let $M$ be a compact complex manifold. Determine natural geometric, cohomological, or curvature-type conditions on $M$ which guarantee the following implication: for every open subset $U \subset M$ that is locally Stein in $M$, $U$ is itself a Stein manifold.
status_search_result: The question, attributed to Sibony, asks for conditions on a compact complex manifold $M$ ensuring that locally Stein open subsets are Stein. Classical results (Docquier–Grauert) handle the case where the ambient space is Stein, and Grauert's examples show pseudoconvexity alone is not sufficient. More recent work (e.g., Mongodi–Slodkowski–Tomassini on Levi currents, and various works on the Levi problem in compact Kähler/projective manifolds) gives partial criteria but no fully general answer; the problem appears still open.

original_question: Suppose M is a complex manifold of dimension 2, and suppose ∀K compact ⊂ M there exists an open subset U, K ⊂ U ⊂ M such that U is biholomorphic to the unit ball. Does this imply that M is equivalent to the unit ball B, Delta × C or C^2 ? (This is false in C3 ).
self_contained_problem:
Let $M$ be a connected complex manifold of complex dimension $2$. Assume that for every compact subset $K \subset M$ there exists an open subset $U$ with $K \subset U \subset M$ such that $U$ is biholomorphic to the open unit ball $B = \{z \in \mathbb{C}^2 : |z| < 1\}$. Does it follow that $M$ is biholomorphic to one of the following: the unit ball $B \subset \mathbb{C}^2$, the product $\Delta \times \mathbb{C}$ (where $\Delta$ is the open unit disk in $\mathbb{C}$), or $\mathbb{C}^2$?

(It is known that the analogous statement in dimension $3$ fails: there exist complex manifolds of dimension $3$ exhausted in the above sense by balls that are not biholomorphic to the ball, $\Delta \times \mathbb{C}^2$, $\Delta^2 \times \mathbb{C}$, or $\mathbb{C}^3$.)

original_question: Let f1 , ..., fk be bounded holomorphic functions on Omega. SupP pose |fi | > c > 0. The Corona problem is whether there exist bounded P holomorphic funcions g1 , ..., gk on Omega such that fi gi ≡ 1. Can the Corona problem be solved if Omega is the unit ball or the unit polydisc?

Suppose $f_1, \dots, f_k \in H^\infty(\Omega)$ satisfy the joint lower bound
$$\max_{1 \le i \le k} |f_i(z)| \ge c > 0 \quad \text{for every } z \in \Omega,$$
for some constant $c > 0$.

Determine whether there must exist functions $g_1, \dots, g_k \in H^\infty(\Omega)$ such that

original_question: Is every boundary point of a bounded pseudoconvex domain D in C^n of finite type a peak point for A(D)?
self_contained_problem:
Let $D \subset \mathbb{C}^n$ be a bounded pseudoconvex domain with smooth boundary, and assume that $D$ is of finite type (in the sense of D'Angelo: every boundary point has finite type, i.e. the order of contact of complex analytic varieties with $\partial D$ at the point is uniformly bounded). Let $A(D)$ denote the algebra of functions continuous on $\overline{D}$ and holomorphic on $D$. A point $p \in \partial D$ is called a peak point for $A(D)$ if there exists $f \in A(D)$ such that $f(p) = 1$ and $|f(z)| < 1$ for all $z \in \overline{D} \setminus \{p\}$.

Question: Is every boundary point of such a domain $D$ a peak point for $A(D)$?
status_search_result: Surveys and recent papers (e.g., Fornæss–Stensønes "Peak Points for Pseudoconvex Domains: A Survey", 2008; Bharali; and others) describe this as a long-standing open problem in several complex variables. Partial results exist: every boundary point is a peak point for strictly pseudoconvex domains, for finite-type domains in $\mathbb{C}^2$, for convex finite-type domains, and for decoupled finite-type domains (often for $A^\alpha(D)$ for some $\alpha>0$), but the general finite-type case in $\mathbb{C}^n$ remains open.

original_question: Characterize the representing measures for the origin in the unit ball in C^n .
self_contained_problem:

A finite positive regular Borel measure $\mu$ on $S_n$ is called a representing measure for the origin (with respect to $A(B_n)$) if
$$ f(0) = \int_{S_n} f \, d\mu \qquad \text{for every } f \in A(B_n). $$

original_question: Develop a solution theory for the d-bar Neumann problem in Sobolev spaces H^s.
self_contained_problem:
Let $\Omega \subset \mathbb{C}^n$ be a bounded pseudoconvex domain with smooth boundary, and for $0 \le q \le n$ let $L^2_{(0,q)}(\Omega)$ denote the Hilbert space of $(0,q)$-forms on $\Omega$ with $L^2$ coefficients. Define the maximal closed extension $\bar{\partial} : L^2_{(0,q)}(\Omega) \to L^2_{(0,q+1)}(\Omega)$ of the Cauchy–Riemann operator, together with its Hilbert space adjoint $\bar{\partial}^{*}$. The complex Laplacian on $(0,q)$-forms is
$$\Box_q \; = \; \bar{\partial}\,\bar{\partial}^{*} \;+\; \bar{\partial}^{*}\,\bar{\partial},$$
and the $\bar{\partial}$-Neumann problem on $(0,q)$-forms (for $1 \le q \le n$) asks, given $\alpha \in L^2_{(0,q)}(\Omega)$ orthogonal to the harmonic forms, to find $u \in \mathrm{Dom}(\Box_q)$ with $\Box_q u = \alpha$, where the boundary conditions $u \in \mathrm{Dom}(\bar{\partial}^{*})$ and $\bar{\partial} u \in \mathrm{Dom}(\bar{\partial}^{*})$ are imposed.

For a real number $s \ge 0$, let $H^s_{(0,q)}(\Omega)$ denote the Sobolev space of $(0,q)$-forms with coefficients in $H^s(\Omega)$.

Develop a solution theory for the $\bar{\partial}$-Neumann problem in the scale of Sobolev spaces $H^s$. Specifically:
\begin{enumerate}
    \item Characterize those bounded pseudoconvex domains $\Omega \subset \mathbb{C}^n$ with smooth boundary for which the $\bar{\partial}$-Neumann operator $N_q = \Box_q^{-1}$ (on the orthogonal complement of the harmonic space) maps $H^s_{(0,q)}(\Omega)$ continuously to itself for every $s \ge 0$.
    \item Establish sharp Sobolev regularity estimates of the form $\|N_q \alpha\|_{H^s} \le C_s \|\alpha\|_{H^s}$, and identify the geometric or potential-theoretic conditions on $\partial\Omega$ that govern such estimates.
\end{enumerate}

original_question: Let Omega be a smooth bounded planar domain and let T : L2 (Omega) 7→ L2 (Omega) be the Kohn solution operator for ∂/∂ z̄. For h ∈ L∞ (Omega) we define the compact non-self-adjoint operator Sh : L2 (Omega) 7→ L2 (Omega), f 7→ h̄T f . Under what circumstance will Sh have eigenvalues? Consider in particular the case where h is holomorphic. If h has a single-valued holomorphic primitive H then it is not hard to see that Sh has no eigenvalues. (Just note that e−H̄/λ T f is holomorphic and orthogonal to holomorphic functions.) Does the converse hold? That is: do periods of H guarantee the existence of eigenvalues? (For annuli, the answer is“yes.”) -D. Barrett, barrett@math.lsa.umich.edu
self_contained_problem:
Let $\Omega \subset \mathbb{C}$ be a smooth bounded planar domain. Let $T : L^2(\Omega) \to L^2(\Omega)$ denote the Kohn solution operator for $\partial/\partial\bar z$; that is, for $f \in L^2(\Omega)$, $u = Tf$ is the unique solution of $\partial u/\partial\bar z = f$ that is orthogonal (in $L^2(\Omega)$) to the subspace of holomorphic $L^2$ functions on $\Omega$. For $h \in L^\infty(\Omega)$, define the compact non-self-adjoint operator
$$S_h : L^2(\Omega) \to L^2(\Omega), \qquad S_h f = \bar h \, T f.$$

Assume that $h$ is holomorphic on $\Omega$. If $h$ admits a single-valued holomorphic primitive $H$ on $\Omega$ (i.e., there exists holomorphic $H$ with $H' = h$), then $S_h$ has no eigenvalues: indeed, if $S_h f = \lambda f$ for some $\lambda \neq 0$, then $e^{-\bar H/\lambda} T f$ is holomorphic and orthogonal to all holomorphic functions, forcing $f = 0$.

Question: Does the converse hold? That is, suppose $h$ is holomorphic on $\Omega$ and does not admit a single-valued holomorphic primitive (so that any local primitive $H$ of $h$ has nontrivial periods around the holes of $\Omega$). Must $S_h$ then possess at least one nonzero eigenvalue?

(For the case $\Omega$ an annulus, the answer is known to be yes.)

original_question: Can one solve d-bar with Hölder estimates on any real analytic bounded pseudoconvex domain in C^n ? 6.3
self_contained_problem:
Let $\Omega \subset \mathbb{C}^n$ be a bounded pseudoconvex domain whose boundary $\partial \Omega$ is real analytic. The Cauchy–Riemann operator $\bar\partial$ acts on $(p,q)$-forms with $1 \le q \le n$. One says that $\bar\partial$ can be solved with Hölder estimates on $\Omega$ if there exist a constant $\alpha \in (0,1)$ and, for every $\bar\partial$-closed bounded $(p,q)$-form $f$ on $\Omega$ with $L^\infty$ coefficients, a $(p,q-1)$-form $u$ on $\Omega$ such that
$$\bar\partial u = f \quad \text{on } \Omega, \qquad \|u\|_{\Lambda^\alpha(\overline{\Omega})} \le C\,\|f\|_{L^\infty(\Omega)},$$
where $C$ depends only on $\Omega$ (and on $p,q$), and $\Lambda^\alpha(\overline{\Omega})$ denotes the standard Hölder space of exponent $\alpha$.

Question: For every $n \ge 2$ and every bounded pseudoconvex domain $\Omega \subset \mathbb{C}^n$ with real analytic boundary, can the $\bar\partial$ equation be solved with Hölder estimates in the sense above?
status_search_result: Partial progress exists: in $\mathbb{C}^2$ and (more recently) in $\mathbb{C}^3$, sup-norm and Hölder-type estimates for $\bar\partial$ have been established for bounded pseudoconvex domains with real-analytic boundary or finite type. The general case for arbitrary $n \ge 4$ on real analytic bounded pseudoconvex domains does not appear to be settled in the literature surveyed.

self_contained_problem:

For $1<p<\infty$ and a $\bar\partial$-closed $(0,q)$-form $f$ with coefficients in $L^p(\Omega)$ (where $1\le q\le n$), construct a linear solution operator $T_q$ producing a $(0,q-1)$-form $u=T_q f$ satisfying $\bar\partial u=f$ together with the estimate

original_question: Which geometric properties of the domain do uniform estimates depend on? [e.g.L2 estimates depend on the diameter and the dimension ].
self_contained_problem:
Let $\Omega \subset \mathbb{C}^n$ be a bounded pseudoconvex domain. Consider the inhomogeneous Cauchy–Riemann equation $\bar\partial u = f$, where $f$ is a $\bar\partial$-closed $(0,1)$-form on $\Omega$ with bounded coefficients. It is classical that on every such $\Omega$ there exists a (canonical) $L^2$ solution $u$ satisfying $\|u\|_{L^2(\Omega)} \le C \|f\|_{L^2(\Omega)}$, where the constant $C$ depends only on the diameter of $\Omega$ and the complex dimension $n$. By contrast, uniform ($L^\infty$) estimates of the form $\|u\|_{L^\infty(\Omega)} \le C \|f\|_{L^\infty(\Omega)}$ are known to fail for general bounded pseudoconvex domains, while they hold on strictly pseudoconvex domains and on certain piecewise smooth strictly pseudoconvex domains.

Determine, in a precise quantitative form, on which geometric invariants of the domain $\Omega$ uniform estimates for solutions of $\bar\partial u = f$ depend. That is, identify a set of geometric quantities $G_1(\Omega), G_2(\Omega), \dots$ (such as boundary regularity, type, Levi geometry, peak-function data, etc.) such that there exists a solution $u$ to $\bar\partial u = f$ with $\|u\|_{L^\infty(\Omega)} \le C(G_1(\Omega), \dots, G_k(\Omega)) \|f\|_{L^\infty(\Omega)}$ for every bounded $\bar\partial$-closed $(0,1)$-form $f$, and characterize the dependence as sharply as possible (in analogy to the $L^2$ case, where dependence is on the diameter and the dimension).
status_search_result: The question of which geometric properties of a domain control uniform ($L^\infty$) estimates for the $\bar\partial$-equation remains a central open problem in several complex variables. Recent work (e.g., on obstructions to uniform estimates and on Kerzman's question, including a 2025 paper in Peking Mathematical Journal) continues to address partial cases—strictly pseudoconvex domains, piecewise smooth domains, product domains, convex domains of finite type—but no general characterization of the geometric invariants governing uniform estimates is known. Fornæss–Sibony's counterexample shows that smoothness and pseudoconvexity alone do not suffice.

original_question: Let Omega in C^n be a bounded biholomorphic image of the unit ball in C^n . Does the d-bar satisfy uniform estimates on Omega? The problem is of interest mainly when Omega has very rough boundary.

$$\|u\|_{L^\infty(\Omega)} \le C\, \|f\|_{L^\infty(\Omega)} ?$$

original_question: Is the Bergman metric complete on bounded pseudoconvex domains whose boundary regularity is less than C^1?
self_contained_problem:
Let $\Omega \subset \mathbb{C}^n$ be a bounded pseudoconvex domain. The Bergman kernel $K_\Omega(z,w)$ of $\Omega$ is the reproducing kernel of the Hilbert space $A^2(\Omega)$ of square-integrable holomorphic functions on $\Omega$. The Bergman metric is the Kähler metric on $\Omega$ with coefficients
$$g_{i\bar j}(z) = \frac{\partial^2}{\partial z_i\, \partial \bar z_j} \log K_\Omega(z,z).$$
The domain $\Omega$ is said to be Bergman complete if it is a complete metric space with respect to the distance induced by the Bergman metric.

Assume that the boundary $\partial\Omega$ has regularity strictly less than $C^1$ (for example, only continuous, Hölder, or otherwise non-$C^1$). 

Question: Is every bounded pseudoconvex domain $\Omega \subset \mathbb{C}^n$ whose boundary has less than $C^1$ regularity Bergman complete? If not, determine the minimal boundary regularity assumptions under which Bergman completeness holds.
status_search_result: Significant progress has been made: B.-Y. Chen and Herbort showed that bounded hyperconvex domains are Bergman complete, and Demailly proved that bounded pseudoconvex domains with Lipschitz boundary are hyperconvex, hence Bergman complete. Thus the question is settled affirmatively for Lipschitz boundaries, but the fully general case of arbitrary less-than-$C^1$ (e.g., merely continuous or non-Lipschitz) boundaries does not appear to be completely resolved.

original_question: Is the Caratheodory metric complete on a bounded smooth pseudoconvex domain?
self_contained_problem:
Let $\Omega \subset \mathbb{C}^n$ be a bounded pseudoconvex domain with smooth boundary. For points $p, q \in \Omega$, define the Carathéodory pseudodistance by
$$ c_\Omega(p,q) = \sup\bigl\{ \rho(f(p), f(q)) : f : \Omega \to \mathbb{D} \text{ holomorphic} \bigr\}, $$
where $\mathbb{D} = \{z \in \mathbb{C} : |z| < 1\}$ is the unit disc and $\rho$ denotes the Poincaré distance on $\mathbb{D}$. The domain $\Omega$ is said to be Carathéodory complete if $(\Omega, c_\Omega)$ is a complete metric space (equivalently, every $c_\Omega$-Cauchy sequence converges to a point of $\Omega$).

Question: Is every bounded pseudoconvex domain $\Omega \subset \mathbb{C}^n$ with smooth boundary Carathéodory complete?

Completeness is known for strongly pseudoconvex domains, for bounded complete Reinhardt pseudoconvex domains, and for finite-type domains in $\mathbb{C}^2$ and certain corank-one situations. Sibony-type counterexamples to Carathéodory completeness exist among bounded pseudoconvex domains without smooth boundary, but the smooth-boundary case appears unresolved in the recent literature.

original_question: Is the regular order of contact of a smooth pseudoconvex domain the same as the commutator type, one vector field at a time.
self_contained_problem:
Let $\Omega \subset \mathbb{C}^n$ be a smooth pseudoconvex domain with defining function $r$, and let $p \in \partial\Omega$ be a boundary point. Denote by $T^{1,0}\partial\Omega$ the holomorphic tangent bundle of $\partial\Omega$, and let $\mathcal{L}$ denote the Levi form of $\partial\Omega$.

For a smooth $(1,0)$ vector field $L$ tangent to $\partial\Omega$ near $p$, define:

(i) The regular order of contact of $L$ at $p$ as the maximal order of vanishing at $p$ of $r \circ \gamma$ over all smooth holomorphic curves $\gamma:(\mathbb{C},0)\to(\mathbb{C}^n,p)$ whose tangent at $0$ is a nonzero multiple of $L(p)$ (equivalently, the order of contact of one-dimensional complex varieties tangent to $L$ with $\partial\Omega$ at $p$).

(ii) The commutator type (Hörmander/Bloom type) of $L$ at $p$ as the smallest integer $m \geq 2$ such that some iterated commutator of length $m$ formed from $L$, $\bar L$, and their conjugates, evaluated at $p$, has nonzero component in the direction transverse to the maximal complex tangent space (equivalently, applies a nonzero pairing with $\partial r$).

Question: For every smooth pseudoconvex domain $\Omega \subset \mathbb{C}^n$, every boundary point $p \in \partial\Omega$, and every smooth $(1,0)$ tangent vector field $L$ near $p$ with $L(p)\neq 0$, is the regular order of contact of $L$ at $p$ equal to the commutator type of $L$ at $p$?

original_question: Is the Kobayashi metric complete on a bounded smooth pseudoconvex domain?
self_contained_problem:
Let $\Omega \subset \mathbb{C}^n$ be a bounded domain with smooth boundary that is pseudoconvex (i.e., $\Omega$ admits a smooth plurisubharmonic exhaustion function, or equivalently, the boundary $\partial\Omega$ is Levi pseudoconvex). For points $p, q \in \Omega$, define the Kobayashi pseudodistance $k_\Omega(p,q)$ as the infimum of sums $\sum_{i=1}^N \rho(z_i, w_i)$, where $\rho$ is the Poincaré distance on the unit disk $\mathbb{D} \subset \mathbb{C}$, taken over all finite chains of holomorphic disks $f_i : \mathbb{D} \to \Omega$ with $f_i(z_i) = p_{i-1}$, $f_i(w_i) = p_i$, $p_0 = p$, $p_N = q$. 

Question: Is $(\Omega, k_\Omega)$ always a complete metric space for every bounded smooth pseudoconvex domain $\Omega \subset \mathbb{C}^n$?
status_search_result: The problem of whether every bounded smooth pseudoconvex domain in $\mathbb{C}^n$ is Kobayashi complete remains a well-known open problem in several complex variables. Partial results are known: completeness holds for strongly pseudoconvex domains, for bounded pseudoconvex domains with Lipschitz boundary (via the Kobayashi–Fuks metric), and for smooth pseudoconvex domains of finite D'Angelo type (which are Goldilocks/visibility domains). The general smooth pseudoconvex case is still unresolved.

original_question: Let D = {z ∈ C^n ; h(z) < 1} be a bounded pseudoconvex complete−circular domain with Minkowski function h. Characterize the Caratheodory, the Bergman or the Kobayashi completeness of D via properties of h. [The following is known: a) If h is continuous, then D is Bergman complete. b) If n ≥ 3, continuity of h does not imply the Kobayashi completeness of D.]
self_contained_problem:
Let $h:\mathbb{C}^n\to[0,\infty)$ be a Minkowski function, that is, an upper semicontinuous function satisfying $h(\lambda z)=|\lambda|\,h(z)$ for all $\lambda\in\mathbb{C}$ and $z\in\mathbb{C}^n$, and such that the set
$$D=\{z\in\mathbb{C}^n: h(z)<1\}$$
is a bounded pseudoconvex complete circular (balanced) domain. Recall that:

- The Carathéodory pseudodistance $c_D$ on $D$ is defined by $c_D(z,w)=\sup\{\rho(f(z),f(w)): f\in\mathcal{O}(D,\mathbb{D})\}$, where $\rho$ is the Poincaré distance on the unit disk $\mathbb{D}$.
- The Kobayashi pseudodistance $k_D$ is the largest pseudodistance not exceeding the Lempert function built from analytic disks in $D$.
- The Bergman pseudodistance $b_D$ is defined via the Bergman metric on $D$ (when the Bergman kernel makes this meaningful).
- $D$ is called Carathéodory (respectively Kobayashi, Bergman) complete if it is complete with respect to $c_D$ (respectively $k_D$, $b_D$).

Find a characterization, expressed purely in terms of properties of the Minkowski function $h$, of each of the following:
(i) the Carathéodory completeness of $D$;
(ii) the Bergman completeness of $D$;
(iii) the Kobayashi completeness of $D$.

(It is known that if $h$ is continuous then $D$ is Bergman complete, and that for $n\geq 3$ continuity of $h$ does not imply Kobayashi completeness of $D$.)

original_question: Find (or prove it does not exist) a complete hyperbolic manifold not biholomorphic to a convex domain where the Kobayashi and Carathéodory distances agree everywhere.
self_contained_problem:
Let $M$ be a connected complex manifold. The Kobayashi pseudodistance $k_M$ is the largest pseudodistance on $M$ for which every holomorphic map from the unit disc $\Delta \subset \mathbb{C}$ (equipped with the Poincaré distance $\omega$) to $M$ is distance-decreasing; equivalently, $k_M(p,q)$ is the infimum of $\sum_{i=1}^N \omega(z_i, w_i)$ over all chains of holomorphic discs $f_i:\Delta\to M$ with $f_1(z_1)=p$, $f_N(w_N)=q$, and $f_i(w_i)=f_{i+1}(z_{i+1})$. The Carathéodory pseudodistance is $c_M(p,q) = \sup\{\omega(f(p),f(q)) : f:M\to\Delta \text{ holomorphic}\}$. One has $c_M \le k_M$ in general. The manifold $M$ is called hyperbolic if $k_M$ is a distance, and complete hyperbolic if in addition $(M,k_M)$ is a complete metric space.

Determine whether there exists a complete hyperbolic complex manifold $M$, not biholomorphic to any convex domain in $\mathbb{C}^n$, such that $c_M(p,q) = k_M(p,q)$ for every pair of points $p,q \in M$; or prove that no such manifold exists.
status_search_result: The open symmetrized bidisc $G_2 = \{(\lambda_1+\lambda_2, \lambda_1\lambda_2) : |\lambda_1|,|\lambda_2|<1\} \subset \mathbb{C}^2$ provides such an example. Agler–Young proved that the Carathéodory and Kobayashi distances coincide on $G_2$, while Costara (and others) showed that $G_2$ is not biholomorphic to any convex domain. As a bounded taut domain it is complete hyperbolic, so the problem is solved in the affirmative.

original_question: Is every holomorphic polynomial map P:C^2 -> C^2 with everywhere nonvanishing Jacobian necessarily biholomorphic?
self_contained_problem:
Let $P:\mathbb{C}^2\to\mathbb{C}^2$ be a polynomial map, i.e. $P(z_1,z_2)=(P_1(z_1,z_2),P_2(z_1,z_2))$ where $P_1,P_2\in\mathbb{C}[z_1,z_2]$. Suppose that the Jacobian determinant
$$J_P(z_1,z_2)=\det\begin{pmatrix}\partial P_1/\partial z_1 & \partial P_1/\partial z_2\\ \partial P_2/\partial z_1 & \partial P_2/\partial z_2\end{pmatrix}$$
is a nonzero constant (equivalently, never vanishes on $\mathbb{C}^2$). Prove or disprove: $P$ is necessarily a biholomorphism of $\mathbb{C}^2$ onto itself (equivalently, $P$ admits a polynomial inverse).
status_search_result: The two-dimensional Jacobian conjecture remains a celebrated open problem. Despite many partial results and reductions (e.g., reductions to degree-bounded cases, results for low-degree maps, and Moh's bound for degrees up to 100), no proof or counterexample is known as of 2026. Numerous claimed proofs have appeared but none has been accepted by the mathematical community.

original_question: Classify Proper Holomorphic Correspondences from the unit disc to itself.
self_contained_problem:
Let $\Delta = \{z \in \mathbb{C} : |z| < 1\}$ denote the open unit disc. A proper holomorphic correspondence from $\Delta$ to $\Delta$ is an irreducible complex-analytic subvariety $V \subset \Delta \times \Delta$ of pure dimension $1$ such that both coordinate projections $\pi_1, \pi_2 : V \to \Delta$ are proper surjective holomorphic maps with finite fibers. Two such correspondences $V, V' \subset \Delta \times \Delta$ are considered equivalent if there exist automorphisms $\varphi, \psi \in \mathrm{Aut}(\Delta)$ such that $(\varphi \times \psi)(V) = V'$.

Classify, up to this equivalence, all proper holomorphic correspondences from $\Delta$ to itself.
status_search_result: A search did not return a definitive classification of proper holomorphic correspondences from the unit disc to itself. While proper holomorphic maps and automorphisms of the disc are well-understood (Möbius transformations, finite Blaschke products in the case of finite-sheeted proper maps), no authoritative source confirming a complete classification of proper holomorphic correspondences $\Delta \to \Delta$ was located, so the current status is unclear.

original_question: Do there exist wandering domains for complex Henon maps?
self_contained_problem:
A complex Hénon map is a polynomial automorphism of $\mathbb{C}^2$ of the form
$$H(x,y) = (p(x) - a y,\; x),$$
where $p \in \mathbb{C}[x]$ is a polynomial of degree at least $2$ and $a \in \mathbb{C}^*$. The Fatou set $F(H)$ of $H$ is the largest open subset of $\mathbb{C}^2$ on which the family of iterates $\{H^n\}_{n\geq 0}$ is locally equicontinuous (equivalently, a normal family). The connected components of $F(H)$ are called Fatou components. A Fatou component $U$ is called a wandering domain if $H^m(U) \cap H^n(U) = \emptyset$ for all integers $m \neq n \geq 0$ (so that $U$ is not eventually periodic).

Question: Does there exist a complex Hénon map (i.e., some choice of $p$ and $a$ as above) that possesses a wandering Fatou component?
status_search_result: The question was answered affirmatively. Berger and Biebler proved the existence of wandering Fatou components (wandering domains) for complex Hénon maps, in sharp contrast to Sullivan's no-wandering-domains theorem in one complex dimension. This is recorded in recent surveys of open problems on Hénon maps as a now-resolved problem.
