original_question: Let Fc : (z, w) → (z^2 + c − w, z), c ∈ C, be a symplectic automorphism of C^2, i.e. Fc is biholomorphic and Fc∗(dz ∧ dw) = dz ∧ dw. Can there exist c ∈ C and a periodic orbit {zi} for Fc such that z0 belongs to a Siegel domain?
self_contained_problem:
For each parameter $c\in\mathbb{C}$, consider the polynomial automorphism
$$F_c:\mathbb{C}^2\to\mathbb{C}^2,\qquad F_c(z,w)=(z^2+c-w,\;z),$$
which is biholomorphic and symplectic in the sense that $F_c^*(dz\wedge dw)=dz\wedge dw$. A periodic orbit of $F_c$ of period $n\geq 1$ is a sequence $\{p_0,p_1,\dots,p_{n-1}\}\subset\mathbb{C}^2$ with $F_c(p_i)=p_{i+1}$ (indices modulo $n$). Such a periodic point $p_0$ is called elliptic if the eigenvalues of $DF_c^n(p_0)$ lie on the unit circle; in that case $p_0$ is said to belong to a Siegel domain if there exists an $F_c^n$-invariant open neighborhood $U$ of $p_0$ on which $F_c^n$ is holomorphically conjugate to its linear part (so $F_c^n|_U$ is biholomorphically equivalent to an irrational rotation in suitable coordinates, with $U$ a maximal such linearization domain).

Question: Does there exist $c\in\mathbb{C}$ and a periodic orbit $\{p_0,\dots,p_{n-1}\}$ of $F_c$ such that $p_0$ belongs to a Siegel domain?
status_search_result: Recent surveys and works on the dynamics of complex Hénon maps discuss linearization of elliptic fixed points and existence of Siegel disks (notably for dissipative Hénon maps with golden-mean rotation number), but a list of open problems on Hénon maps does not record this specific symplectic-case question as resolved, and no source found establishes existence (or non-existence) of a periodic orbit lying in a Siegel domain for the conservative family $F_c(z,w)=(z^2+c-w,z)$. The problem appears to remain open.

original_question: Does every holomorphic map F : P^k → P^k of degree at least two have a repelling periodic point? Do meromorphic maps have periodic orbits? -sibony@anh.matups.fr
self_contained_problem:
Let $k \geq 1$ and let $\mathbb{P}^k$ denote complex projective space of dimension $k$. 

(a) Let $F : \mathbb{P}^k \to \mathbb{P}^k$ be a holomorphic map of algebraic degree $d \geq 2$. A periodic point $p$ of period $n$ (so $F^n(p)=p$) is called repelling if every eigenvalue of the derivative $DF^n(p)$ has modulus strictly greater than $1$. Must $F$ admit at least one repelling periodic point?

(b) Let $F : \mathbb{P}^k \dashrightarrow \mathbb{P}^k$ be a meromorphic (rational) self-map of $\mathbb{P}^k$. Must $F$ admit a periodic orbit, i.e., a point $p$ outside the indeterminacy set such that $F^n(p) = p$ for some $n \geq 1$?
status_search_result: Briend and Duval (Acta Math. 182, 1999) proved that for any holomorphic endomorphism of P^k of degree d ≥ 2, repelling periodic points are not only existent but are equidistributed with respect to the equilibrium measure and dense in the Julia set, fully resolving part (a). The meromorphic/rational case (b) is more subtle: positive results exist under additional assumptions (e.g., algebraically stable maps with suitable dynamical degrees, work of Diller–Jackson–Sommese, Dinh–Sibony, and others) but the general existence-of-periodic-orbits question for arbitrary meromorphic self-maps of P^k does not appear to be fully settled.

self_contained_problem: Let $p \in \mathbb{P}^k(\mathbb{C})$ and let $f$ be a holomorphic map defined either on all of the complex projective space $\mathbb{P}^k$ or merely on an open neighborhood of $p$, with $f(p) = p$. original_question: Let Hd denote the space of holomorphic maps f : P^2 → P^2 of degree d. This is a finite dimensional space parametrized by the coefficients. Does the set of f ∈ Hd with infinitely many attractive basins have measure zero?
self_contained_problem:
For an integer $d\ge 2$, let $\mathcal{H}_d$ denote the space of holomorphic self-maps $f:\mathbb{P}^2(\mathbb{C})\to\mathbb{P}^2(\mathbb{C})$ of algebraic degree $d$, viewed as a finite-dimensional complex manifold parametrized by the coefficients of the homogeneous polynomial representatives (equivalently, an open subset of a projective space of coefficient tuples). An attractive basin of $f$ is the basin of attraction of an attracting periodic cycle of $f$, i.e. a periodic orbit at which the derivative has all eigenvalues of modulus strictly less than $1$, together with all points whose forward orbit converges to that cycle. Equip $\mathcal{H}_d$ with Lebesgue measure (in any coordinate chart of the parameter space).

Question: Does the set of $f\in\mathcal{H}_d$ possessing infinitely many distinct attractive basins have Lebesgue measure zero?
status_search_result: Existence of holomorphic maps of $\mathbb{P}^2$ with infinitely many attracting basins (Newhouse-type phenomena via homoclinic tangencies) is known, but I could not find a definitive published resolution of whether the parameter set of such maps in $\mathcal{H}_d$ has Lebesgue measure zero. The question appears to remain open in this generality.

original_question: Classify critically finite maps on P3 .
self_contained_problem:
A holomorphic endomorphism $f \colon \mathbb{P}^n(\mathbb{C}) \to \mathbb{P}^n(\mathbb{C})$ of degree $d \geq 2$ is said to be critically finite (or post-critically finite) if its critical set $C_f = \{ z \in \mathbb{P}^n : \det(Df(z)) = 0 \}$ has the property that the post-critical set
$$ \mathrm{PC}(f) = \bigcup_{k \geq 1} f^k(C_f) $$
is an algebraic subvariety of $\mathbb{P}^n$, equivalently, each irreducible component of $C_f$ is preperiodic under $f$.

Problem: Give a complete classification, up to holomorphic conjugacy, of all critically finite holomorphic endomorphisms of $\mathbb{P}^3(\mathbb{C})$ of degree $d \geq 2$.
category_tag: Critically finite holomorphic maps on projective space
status_search_result: A complete classification of critically finite holomorphic endomorphisms exists only in lower dimensions and partial settings. Work by Fornaess–Sibony and subsequent authors has studied examples and structural properties (e.g., post-critical orbits, Fatou components, hyperbolicity) of post-critically finite maps on $\mathbb{P}^k$, including some constructions and rigidity results, but no full classification on $\mathbb{P}^3$ appears in the literature. The problem appears to remain open.

original_question: Let C be a smooth cubic in P^2 . Then P^2 \ C is algebraically parallellizable, but cannot be algebraically immersed in C^2 . Can it be holomorhically immersed in C^2 ? [ There are smooth cubics for which it is true . For related problems see the section called “Stein manifolds”.]
self_contained_problem:
Let $C \subset \mathbb{P}^2(\mathbb{C})$ be a smooth cubic curve, and let $X = \mathbb{P}^2(\mathbb{C}) \setminus C$ be its complement. It is known that $X$ is algebraically parallelizable (its holomorphic tangent bundle is algebraically trivial) but admits no algebraic immersion into $\mathbb{C}^2$. For certain smooth cubics $C$, $X$ is known to admit a holomorphic immersion into $\mathbb{C}^2$.

Question: Does there exist, for every smooth cubic curve $C \subset \mathbb{P}^2(\mathbb{C})$, a holomorphic immersion $\mathbb{P}^2(\mathbb{C}) \setminus C \to \mathbb{C}^2$?
status_search_result: Surveys on holomorphic embeddings and immersions of Stein manifolds (e.g., Forstnerič's 2017 survey) discuss related questions about immersing affine surfaces into $\mathbb{C}^2$, but no source located confirms a resolution for all smooth cubics. Partial results (immersions for special cubics, including cuspidal cubics, due to Nishimura and others) are known. The general question for arbitrary smooth cubics appears not to be definitively settled in the sources retrieved.

original_question: Let M be a Kähler manifold. Assume that all curvatures are between −a2 and −b2 . Construct nontrivial bounded holomorphic functions on M.
self_contained_problem:
Let $(M, g)$ be a complete Kähler manifold whose sectional curvatures $K$ satisfy
$$-a^2 \le K \le -b^2$$
everywhere, for some constants $a \ge b > 0$. Construct nontrivial bounded holomorphic functions on $M$. More precisely, exhibit a holomorphic function $f : M \to \mathbb{C}$ which is non-constant and satisfies $\sup_{p \in M} |f(p)| < \infty$, and ideally produce a family of such functions that separates points of $M$ and gives local holomorphic coordinates at every point.
category_tag: Bounded holomorphic functions on negatively curved Kähler manifolds
status_search_result: For simply-connected complete Kähler manifolds with sectional curvature pinched between two negative constants, work of Wu–Yau and subsequent results (e.g., the 2017 paper of Wu–Yau on invariant metrics on negatively pinched complete Kähler manifolds) shows that the Bergman metric is well-defined and uniformly equivalent to the background Kähler metric. This implies the existence of an abundance of bounded (indeed $L^2$) holomorphic functions separating points and giving local coordinates, thereby resolving Sibony's question affirmatively in the simply-connected case. In full generality (without simple connectivity, and only with sectional curvature bounds rather than holomorphic sectional curvature bounds), the construction of nontrivial bounded holomorphic functions is not fully settled.

original_question: Let M ⊂ P n be a compact odd dimensional CR manifold. Find conditions on M which ensure that M bounds a complex variety.(This is well understood in C^n .) -N.Sibony, sibony@anh.matups.fr
self_contained_problem:
Let $\mathbb{P}^n$ denote complex projective $n$-space, and let $M \subset \mathbb{P}^n$ be a compact, smooth, odd-dimensional CR submanifold (i.e., a real submanifold whose tangent spaces carry a CR structure: a complex subbundle $T^{1,0}M \subset T_{\mathbb{C}}M$ with $T^{1,0}M \cap \overline{T^{1,0}M} = 0$ and $[T^{1,0}M, T^{1,0}M] \subset T^{1,0}M$). We say that $M$ "bounds a complex variety" if there exists a complex analytic subvariety (or a holomorphic chain) $V \subset \mathbb{P}^n \setminus M$ of complex dimension $(\dim_{\mathbb{R}} M + 1)/2$, with finite volume, whose boundary (as a current of integration) equals $[M]$ (or an integer multiple of $[M]$).

The analogous problem in $\mathbb{C}^n$ admits a complete solution (the Harvey–Lawson moment condition for maximally complex CR submanifolds). 

Find geometric and analytic conditions on the compact odd-dimensional CR submanifold $M \subset \mathbb{P}^n$ that are necessary and sufficient for $M$ to bound a complex subvariety (holomorphic chain) of $\mathbb{P}^n$.
category_tag: CR geometry and boundaries of complex varieties
status_search_result: Substantial progress has been made: Dolbeault and Henkin ("Chaînes holomorphes de bord donné dans $\mathbb{C}P^n$", Bull. Soc. Math. France, 1997) gave conditions characterizing when a maximally complex CR cycle in $\mathbb{P}^n$ bounds a holomorphic chain, using a projective analogue of the Harvey–Lawson moment condition. Further refinements and extensions (e.g., Harvey–Lawson, and more recent works on reconstruction of Riemann surfaces with given boundary in $\mathbb{C}P^n$) continue. Thus the problem is partially solved in important cases but a fully general characterization remains an active research direction.

original_question: A diffeomorphism between two strongly pseudoconvex CR (2n + 1)-manifolds is called quasiconformal if its differential preserves the underlying contact structures and distorts the CR structures boundedly. When Hermitian metrics on the contact bundles are fixed, this distortion can be measured by checking how spheres in the contact space is mapped to ellipsoids. However, this measurement depends on the choices of the Hermitian metrics if n > 1. Fixing a quasiconformal diffeomorphism, can we choose Hermitian metrics so that the distortion is minimal? - Puqi Tang, tang@math.purdue.edu
self_contained_problem:
Let $(M_1, H_1, J_1)$ and $(M_2, H_2, J_2)$ be two strongly pseudoconvex CR manifolds of dimension $2n+1$ with $n \geq 2$, where $H_i \subset TM_i$ is the contact (Levi) distribution of rank $2n$ and $J_i : H_i \to H_i$ is the CR (almost complex) structure on the contact bundle. A diffeomorphism $f : M_1 \to M_2$ is called CR-quasiconformal if its differential maps $H_1$ onto $H_2$ and the pullback CR structure $f^*J_2$ is boundedly close to $J_1$ on $H_1$. 

Given a Hermitian metric $g_i$ on $(H_i, J_i)$, define the pointwise distortion of $f$ at $p \in M_1$ as
$$K_{g_1,g_2}(f,p) \;=\; \frac{\max_{v \in H_{1,p},\, g_1(v,v)=1} g_2(df(v), df(v))}{\min_{v \in H_{1,p},\, g_1(v,v)=1} g_2(df(v), df(v))},$$
i.e. the eccentricity of the ellipsoid which is the image under $df_p$ of the unit sphere of $g_1$ in $H_{1,p}$, measured by $g_2$. Let
$$K_{g_1,g_2}(f) \;=\; \sup_{p \in M_1} K_{g_1,g_2}(f,p).$$
For $n \geq 2$, this number depends on the choice of the Hermitian metrics $g_1, g_2$ compatible with the CR structures.

Fix a CR-quasiconformal diffeomorphism $f : M_1 \to M_2$. Determine whether one can choose Hermitian metrics $g_1$ on $(H_1, J_1)$ and $g_2$ on $(H_2, J_2)$ that minimize the distortion $K_{g_1,g_2}(f)$, and if so describe such minimizing metrics and the resulting minimal distortion.
status_search_result: A search located the dissertation of Puqi Tang on quasiconformal homeomorphisms on CR manifolds and subsequent related work, but no source directly resolves the question of whether the Hermitian metrics on the contact bundles can be chosen to minimize the distortion of a fixed CR-quasiconformal diffeomorphism when $n \geq 2$. The current status appears unverified.

original_question: Prove that if Omega is a smooth bounded pseudoconvex domain in C^n which is finite type in the sense of D’Angelo, then it is of finite type in the sense of Kohn (ideal type). Prize $50 -J. McNeal, mcneal@math.princeton.edu
self_contained_problem:
Let $\Omega \subset \mathbb{C}^n$ be a smooth bounded pseudoconvex domain with smooth defining function $r$, so that $\Omega = \{r<0\}$ and $dr \neq 0$ on $\partial\Omega$. For a point $p \in \partial\Omega$, define:

(a) The D'Angelo type $\Delta_1(\partial\Omega, p)$ as the supremum, over all germs of nonconstant holomorphic curves $\varphi:(\mathbb{C},0)\to(\mathbb{C}^n,p)$, of the ratio $v(\varphi^* r)/v(\varphi)$, where $v$ denotes the order of vanishing at $0$. The boundary point $p$ is of finite D'Angelo type if $\Delta_1(\partial\Omega, p)<\infty$.

(b) The Kohn ideal type (finite type in the sense of Kohn's subelliptic multiplier algorithm): starting with the multiplier ideal $I_0 = \sqrt{(r, \det(\partial\bar\partial r|_{T^{1,0}\partial\Omega}))}$ at $p$ (more precisely the ideal generated by $r$ together with the coefficient $\det$ of $\partial r \wedge (\partial\bar\partial r)^{n-1}$, taking real radicals at each step), and iterating Kohn's procedure of adjoining Jacobian determinants of generators and taking real radicals, $p$ is of finite Kohn type if this algorithm terminates with the unit ideal in finitely many steps.

Prove: if every boundary point $p\in\partial\Omega$ is of finite D'Angelo type, then every boundary point is of finite Kohn (ideal) type.
category_tag: finite type domains in several complex variables
status_search_result: For pseudoconvex domains with real-analytic boundary, the implication "D'Angelo finite type ⇒ Kohn finite (ideal) type" was established (Kohn 1979 via Diederich–Fornæss, with a direct proof by Brinzanescu–Nicoara). For general smooth pseudoconvex domains the implication does not appear to be settled in full generality; Siu's program on effective termination of the Kohn algorithm addresses related questions but the smooth case remains the focus of ongoing work.

context_brief: Lozenge tilings of a hexagon with one central triangular hole
original_question: Find an exact formula for the number of lozenge tilings of the hexagon with side lengths n, n+1, n, n+1, n, n+1 after deleting the central triangle.
self_contained_problem: Consider, in the plane triangular lattice, a hexagon with successive side lengths $n, n+1, n, n+1, n, n+1$ (with all interior angles equal to $120^\circ$). Dissect this hexagon into unit equilateral triangles. Because the number of upward-pointing unit triangles differs by one from the number of downward-pointing unit triangles, the hexagon itself admits no tiling by lozenges (unit rhombi with $60^\circ$ and $120^\circ$ angles, each covering exactly one upward and one downward unit triangle). Remove the single unit triangle located at the center of the hexagon; the resulting region $R_n$ has equal numbers of upward and downward unit triangles, and is tileable by lozenges. Let $T(n)$ denote the number of lozenge tilings of $R_n$. Find a closed-form (product) formula for $T(n)$ valid for all positive integers $n$.
category_tag: Lozenge tilings of hexagons with holes
status_search_result: The enumeration problem was solved independently by M. Ciucu (1998, using his Matchings Factorization / "factorial" theorem giving a product formula in terms of self-complementary plane partition counts) and by H. Helfgott and I. Gessel (1999, "Enumeration of Tilings of Diamonds and Hexagons with Defects"). Both works provide explicit product formulas for the number of lozenge tilings of the (n,n+1,n,n+1,n,n+1) hexagon with its central unit triangle removed.

context_brief: Lozenge tilings of holey regular hexagons
original_question: Determine the number of lozenge tilings of a regular hexagon after removing two innermost unit triangles, one upward-pointing and one downward-pointing. Account for the two geometrically distinct placements in which the removed triangles are opposite or adjacent.
self_contained_problem:
Consider a regular hexagon of side length $n$ drawn on the triangular lattice, so that it is naturally divided into upward- and downward-pointing unit equilateral triangles. A lozenge is the union of two unit triangles sharing an edge (one upward, one downward), and a lozenge tiling of a region is a covering by such lozenges with disjoint interiors.

The six unit triangles meeting the center of the hexagon (three upward-pointing and three downward-pointing, arranged alternately around the center) are called the innermost unit triangles. Choose one upward-pointing innermost triangle and one downward-pointing innermost triangle and delete them from the hexagon; up to symmetries of the hexagon there are exactly two geometrically distinct choices, namely:

(a) the two removed triangles are opposite (their centroids are separated by another innermost triangle), and
(b) the two removed triangles are adjacent (they share a single vertex at the center).

For each of these two cases, and for every positive integer $n$ (with $n$ chosen so that the construction makes sense, e.g., $n$ even or odd as appropriate), determine in closed form the number of lozenge tilings of the resulting region.
status_search_result: Searches indicate that Helfgott and Gessel resolved Problems 1, 2, and 10 from Propp's 1999 list of enumeration problems on tilings, but Problem 4 (the present problem) is not mentioned among those they solved. Subsequent literature on hexagons with dents, intrusions, and punctures (e.g., works of Ciucu, Krattenthaler, Lai) treats various related defect configurations, but no source found directly states a closed-form enumeration for the specific configuration of two innermost triangles (opposite or adjacent) removed. The status could not be conclusively verified from available sources.

context_brief: Meaning of the spectrum of KK* for planar bipartite graphs
original_question: For a bipartite planar graph, choose any Kasteleyn matrix K obtained from the bipartite adjacency matrix by changing signs so that all non-zero determinant contributions have the same sign. Determine the combinatorial significance of the spectrum of KK*, which is independent of the particular Kasteleyn signing.
self_contained_problem:
Let $G = (B \sqcup W, E)$ be a finite bipartite planar graph with equal-sized color classes $|B| = |W| = n$, embedded in the plane. The bipartite adjacency matrix $A$ of $G$ is the $n \times n$ matrix indexed by $B \times W$ with $A_{bw} = 1$ if $bw \in E$ and $0$ otherwise. A Kasteleyn signing of $G$ is an assignment $\varepsilon : E \to \{+1, -1\}$ such that around every bounded face with $2k$ edges, the product of the signs is $(-1)^{k+1}$; given such a signing, the associated Kasteleyn matrix $K$ is the $n \times n$ matrix with $K_{bw} = \varepsilon(bw)$ if $bw \in E$ and $0$ otherwise. With this normalization every nonzero term in the expansion of $\det K$ contributes with the same sign, so $|\det K|$ equals the number of perfect matchings of $G$.

It is known that, although $K$ depends on the choice of Kasteleyn signing, the spectrum of $K K^{*}$ (equivalently, the multiset of singular values of $K$) does not depend on this choice; it is an invariant of the planar bipartite graph $G$ itself.

Problem. Give a combinatorial interpretation of the spectrum of $K K^{*}$ for an arbitrary planar bipartite graph $G$: identify the eigenvalues (with multiplicities) of $K K^{*}$ in terms of intrinsic combinatorial or graph-theoretic data of $G$ (such as counts or generating functions involving subgraphs, matchings, cycles, faces, or related structures).
status_search_result: A web search did not turn up a definitive combinatorial interpretation of the spectrum of $KK^{*}$ for general planar bipartite graphs. Related work on dimer models, Kasteleyn theorem and spectral aspects of Kasteleyn operators exists (e.g., spectral curves for periodic bipartite graphs and Kenyon–Okounkov–Sheffield theory), but no source found explicitly resolves the general combinatorial significance of the spectrum of $KK^{*}$ for arbitrary planar bipartite graphs. The status is therefore unclear.

context_brief: Aztec rectangle with the central square removed
original_question: Find a formula for the number of domino tilings of a 2n-by-(2n+1) Aztec rectangle after deleting its central square.
self_contained_problem:
An Aztec rectangle of dimensions $a \times b$ is a region of the square lattice consisting of unit cells whose centers $(i+\tfrac12, j+\tfrac12)$ satisfy appropriate inequalities so that the region is the union of $a$ rows and $b$ columns of cells with a "staircase" boundary in the style of the Aztec diamond. Specifically, color the unit squares of the standard square lattice in a checkerboard fashion. For positive integers $a < b$ with $b = a+1$, the $a \times b$ Aztec rectangle is the region tileable in principle by horizontal and vertical $1 \times 2$ dominoes (up to a defect in the balance of colors), having $a$ rows of cells and a staircase boundary; for the case $a = 2n$, $b = 2n+1$ this region has exactly one more square of one color than of the other, and a tiling by dominoes does not exist.

Now fix a positive integer $n$ and consider the $2n \times (2n+1)$ Aztec rectangle. Remove its central unit square (the unique cell of the majority color situated at the geometric center of the region), thereby restoring the balance between the two color classes (a necessary condition for the existence of a domino tiling).

Find a closed-form formula (a product formula or other explicit expression) for the number of domino tilings of the resulting region as a function of $n$.
status_search_result: Multiple secondary sources (including Tri Lai's survey/research statements and follow-up literature) indicate that this problem was solved by Harald Helfgott, following from the main result of his 1998 Brandeis senior thesis on edge effects in the Aztec diamond. The resulting count can be expressed as a determinant evaluation; explicit product-form expressions are noted to have nontrivial (not entirely smooth) prime factorizations.

context_brief: Sum of entries of an inverse Aztec-diamond Kasteleyn matrix
original_question: Let Kn be the Kasteleyn matrix of the Aztec diamond of order n in which every other vertical domino has its sign flipped. Prove that the sum of the entries of K_n^{-1} equals (n-1)(n+3)/2 - 2^(n-1) + 2.
self_contained_problem:
Let $n \ge 1$. The Aztec diamond of order $n$ is the planar region consisting of all unit lattice squares whose centers $(x+1/2,\, y+1/2)$ satisfy $|x+1/2|+|y+1/2| \le n$. Color these unit squares as a checkerboard, and let $B$ (resp. $W$) be the set of black (resp. white) squares; one has $|B|=|W|=n(n+1)$. Form the bipartite adjacency matrix $A$ indexed by $B \times W$, where $A_{b,w}=1$ if the squares $b \in B$ and $w \in W$ share an edge and $A_{b,w}=0$ otherwise (so each domino in a tiling corresponds to such an edge).

Define the (signed) Kasteleyn matrix $K_n$ to be the matrix obtained from $A$ by flipping the sign of every other vertical edge: more precisely, fix a 2-coloring of the vertical edges of the Aztec diamond into two classes such that any two vertical edges in the same column alternate between the classes (equivalently, vertical edges in even-indexed rows get sign $+1$ and those in odd-indexed rows get sign $-1$); replace the corresponding entries of $A$ by $-1$ for one of the two classes. The matrix $K_n$ is then a square matrix with $\det K_n = \pm \, 2^{n(n+1)/2}$ (the number of domino tilings of the Aztec diamond of order $n$).

Prove that
$$\sum_{b \in B,\; w \in W} (K_n^{-1})_{w,b} \;=\; \frac{(n-1)(n+3)}{2} \;-\; 2^{\,n-1} \;+\; 2.$$

context_brief: Local substitutions for weighted perfect-matchings enumeration
original_question: In weighted graph enumeration of perfect matchings, characterize the local graph substitutions that change the weighted sum of matchings by a predictable factor or preserve it exactly.
self_contained_problem:
Let $G = (V, E, w)$ be a finite edge-weighted graph, with weight function $w: E \to R$ taking values in a commutative ring $R$. Define the matching generating polynomial (weighted perfect-matching sum) of $G$ by
$$M(G) \;=\; \sum_{\mu} \prod_{e \in \mu} w(e),$$
where the sum is over all perfect matchings $\mu$ of $G$. A local substitution rule is a pair $(H_1, H_2)$ of finite edge-weighted graphs each carrying a distinguished set of boundary vertices, together with a procedure that, given any graph $G$ containing an embedded copy of $H_1$ (matched to the boundary), produces a new graph $G'$ by removing the interior of $H_1$ and gluing in $H_2$ along the same boundary vertices. The substitution is said to have a predictable effect on weighted matchings if there exists a function $\Phi$ (depending only on $H_1, H_2$ and the boundary data, not on the rest of $G$) such that for every host graph $G$,
$$M(G') \;=\; \Phi \cdot M(G).$$
The constant case $\Phi \equiv 1$ corresponds to local substitutions that preserve the weighted sum of perfect matchings exactly. Examples of such substitutions include the "urban renewal" (spider) move and various vertex- and edge-splitting moves.

Problem: Characterize all local graph substitutions $(H_1, H_2)$ that have a predictable effect on the weighted sum of perfect matchings, i.e., that multiply $M(G)$ by a factor depending only on the local data $(H_1, H_2)$ and its boundary, independently of the ambient graph $G$. In particular, give a complete description (e.g., algebraic or combinatorial classification) of those substitutions that exactly preserve $M(G)$.
status_search_result: The problem appears as Problem 17 in Propp's survey "Enumeration of Matchings: Problems and Progress." While many specific local substitutions (urban renewal/spider move, vertex splitting, edge contractions, graphical condensation moves, and chip-removal / Pfaffian-preserving moves) have been identified and used extensively in the literature, no complete characterization of all predictable local substitutions appears to be known. Subsequent work (e.g., on the octahedron recurrence, generalized urban renewal, and graphical condensation) extends the catalogue of such moves but does not provide a full classification.

context_brief: Perfect matchings of the n-cube modulo powers of 2
original_question: Let f(n) denote the number of 1-factors (perfect matchings) of the n-dimensional cube. The paper reports a simple proof of the parity statement that f(n) has the same parity as n, and then states that similar but more complex reasoning should allow one to compute the enumerating sequence modulo any power of 2. Determine, in a self-contained explicit form, the value of f(n) modulo 2^m for arbitrary m ≥ 1.
self_contained_problem:
Let $Q_n$ denote the $n$-dimensional hypercube graph, whose vertex set is $\{0,1\}^n$ and whose edges connect pairs of vertices differing in exactly one coordinate. Let $f(n)$ be the number of 1-factors (perfect matchings) of $Q_n$. It is known that $f(n) \equiv n \pmod{2}$ for all $n \ge 1$. 

Determine, in an explicit closed form, the value of $f(n) \bmod 2^m$ for every integer $m \ge 1$ and every $n \ge 1$. That is, find an explicit description (e.g., a formula or finite-state recurrence in $n$) of the residue $f(n) \bmod 2^m$ as a function of $n$, for arbitrary $m$.
status_search_result: Searches reveal results on the parity of $f(n)$ (Lovász's argument) and lower bounds on the 2-adic valuation of the number of perfect matchings in certain graphs (e.g., channels for planar graphs), as well as exact enumeration of $f(n)$ for small $n$ (up to $n=7$). However, no source provides an explicit closed-form description of $f(n) \bmod 2^m$ for arbitrary $m \ge 1$. The status appears unresolved in the literature retrieved.

paper_title: Recent Results and Open Problems on the Hydrodynamics of Disordered Asymmetric Exclusion and Zero-Range Processes
context_brief: Finer-scale phase-transition behavior in disordered ZRP
original_question: Assume the disordered zero-range process is in the phase-transition regime with finite critical density rho^*. The known hydrodynamic theorem implies that when the initial density is everywhere above rho^*, the macroscopic profile stays fixed on the hydrodynamic scale because the flux is constant there. The open problem is to prove rigorous finer-scale results beyond this trivial hydrodynamic picture, specifically to show whether inhomogeneities form and particles concentrate on exceptionally slow sites when the density is in the high-density regime rho > rho^*.
self_contained_problem:
Consider the one-dimensional disordered zero-range process on Z defined as follows. Let {alpha_x : x in Z} be a collection of strictly positive i.i.d. random rates ("environment") with values in some interval [c,1] (c>0), and let g:N -> [0,infty) be a nondecreasing jump function with g(0)=0, g(k)>0 for k>=1, and bounded increments. A configuration eta in N^Z assigns eta(x) particles to site x; a particle leaves site x at rate alpha_x g(eta(x)) and jumps to x+1 (totally asymmetric case). 

For almost every environment, there is a one-parameter family of invariant product measures nu_phi indexed by a fugacity phi in [0, phi_c], with mean density rho(phi) increasing continuously to a (possibly finite) critical density rho^* = lim_{phi -> phi_c} rho(phi). Assume the disorder is such that rho^* < infinity (the "phase-transition regime"), and let f(rho) denote the hydrodynamic flux as a function of density; f is strictly increasing on [0, rho^*] and constant on [rho^*, infinity). 

The known hydrodynamic limit states that under Euler rescaling, the empirical density u(x,t) satisfies the conservation law u_t + f(u)_x = 0 (in the entropy sense). In particular, if the initial macroscopic profile u_0 satisfies u_0(x) >= rho^* for all x in R, then u(x,t) = u_0(x) for all t > 0.

Problem. In this high-density regime rho > rho^*, prove rigorous finer-scale (sub-hydrodynamic) results describing the microscopic behavior. Specifically, show that as t -> infinity (with appropriate space-time rescaling finer than the hydrodynamic scale), spatial inhomogeneities develop and the excess particle mass concentrates on the sites x of exceptionally small rate alpha_x, and quantify the rate and spatial distribution of this concentration phenomenon.
status_search_result: Subsequent rigorous work has established condensation on slow sites in several related disordered/inhomogeneous zero-range models (e.g., stationary measures concentrate excess mass on the site(s) of smallest rate, and hydrodynamic limits with Dirichlet conditions at macroscopic defects have been derived). However, a complete rigorous finer-scale description of the inhomogeneity formation and dynamical condensation on exceptionally slow sites for the genuinely disordered (i.i.d. environment) totally asymmetric zero-range process in the supercritical regime rho > rho^* does not appear fully resolved; partial results exist on stationary condensation and on simpler defect-site geometries.

paper_title: Recent Results and Open Problems on the Hydrodynamics of Disordered Asymmetric Exclusion and Zero-Range Processes
context_brief: Phase transition and flux shape for disordered TASEP/K-exclusion
original_question: For the disordered totally asymmetric simple exclusion process, and more generally the one-dimensional totally asymmetric K-exclusion process with site disorder where each site can hold at most K particles and the macroscopic limit has an unknown concave flux function f_K on [0,K], determine whether the model exhibits a phase transition analogous to the disordered zero-range process. A specific open question is whether the flux function f_K(rho) contains a flat segment on an interval centered around rho = K/2.
self_contained_problem:
Consider the one-dimensional totally asymmetric K-exclusion process with quenched site disorder, defined as follows. Fix an integer K ≥ 1. The state space is {0,1,…,K}^Z, where η(x) ∈ {0,…,K} denotes the number of particles at site x. To each site x ∈ Z is attached an independent random rate α(x), drawn from a common distribution supported in (0,∞) with infimum c ≥ 0 (the disorder is assumed to satisfy standard ergodicity/stationarity conditions). Given a configuration η, a particle jumps from site x to site x+1 at rate α(x) provided η(x) ≥ 1 and η(x+1) ≤ K−1 (the case K = 1 is the disordered TASEP). 

Under hyperbolic rescaling, this process admits a hydrodynamic limit governed by a scalar conservation law ∂_t ρ + ∂_x f_K(ρ) = 0, where f_K : [0,K] → [0,∞) is a concave macroscopic flux function with f_K(0) = f_K(K) = 0.

(a) Does this disordered K-exclusion process exhibit a phase transition analogous to that proved for the disordered nearest-neighbor asymmetric zero-range process — namely, the existence of a critical density above which the system fails to reach equilibrium and instead develops a condensation/plateau phenomenon?

(b) Equivalently in the macroscopic picture, does the flux function f_K(ρ) contain a flat segment on a non-degenerate interval centered around ρ = K/2?
status_search_result: For K = 1 (disordered TASEP), Bahadoran and Bodineau (Electron. J. Probab. 2018, "Quantitative estimates for the flux of TASEP with dilute site disorder") proved the existence of a flat plateau in the flux function f under a sufficiently dilute site-disorder assumption (e.g. a slow power-tail of the disorder distribution near its minimum), confirming a phase-transition signature analogous to the disordered ZRP. The full conjecture — that the plateau exists for general disorder distributions and that it is centered around ρ = 1/2 (and more generally around ρ = K/2 for the K-exclusion case with K ≥ 2) — remains open. Related work (Bahadoran–Bodineau, Braz. J. Probab. Stat. 2015) gives properties and conjectures supporting this picture.

paper_title: Open problems from the 12th International Conference on Fuzzy Set Theory and Its Applications
original_question: Let C:[0,1]^2 -> [0,1] be a 2-copula and let its dual copula be C*(x,y)=x+y-C(x,y). For a parameter lambda in [0,1], define C^(lambda) by C^(lambda)(x,y)=C(x,y)/(1+lambda-lambda C*(x,y)). Is C^(lambda) always a 2-copula? If not, characterize, for a given 2-copula C, the set of parameters lambda in [0,1] for which C^(lambda) is a 2-copula.
self_contained_problem:
A function $C:[0,1]^2\to[0,1]$ is called a 2-copula if it satisfies:
(i) $C(x,0)=C(0,x)=0$ and $C(x,1)=C(1,x)=x$ for all $x\in[0,1]$, and
(ii) $C$ is 2-increasing, i.e. $C(x_2,y_2)-C(x_2,y_1)-C(x_1,y_2)+C(x_1,y_1)\ge 0$ whenever $0\le x_1\le x_2\le 1$ and $0\le y_1\le y_2\le 1$.

Given a 2-copula $C$, define its dual by $C^*(x,y)=x+y-C(x,y)$. For each parameter $\lambda\in[0,1]$, define the function $C^{(\lambda)}:[0,1]^2\to[0,1]$ by
$$C^{(\lambda)}(x,y)=\frac{C(x,y)}{1+\lambda-\lambda\,C^*(x,y)}.$$

Question: Is $C^{(\lambda)}$ a 2-copula for every 2-copula $C$ and every $\lambda\in[0,1]$? If not, characterize, for a given 2-copula $C$, the set
$$\Lambda(C)=\{\lambda\in[0,1]:C^{(\lambda)}\text{ is a 2-copula}\}.$$
status_search_result: A targeted web search did not yield a paper that resolves the question or explicitly characterizes the admissible parameter set. Related literature on parametric copula constructions (including comprehensive families involving basic copulas) exists, but no source confirming a complete solution was found.

paper_title: Open problems from the 12th International Conference on Fuzzy Set Theory and Its Applications
original_question: Define a satisfactory notion of penalty functions and penalty-based functions on the lattice L([0,1]) of closed subintervals of [0,1], in a way that still recovers averaging aggregation operators on that lattice as penalty-based functions. The definition should handle the order structure of L([0,1]), including the partial order [a,b] <=_L [c,d] iff a<=c and b<=d, and possibly also linear admissible orders extending that partial order.
self_contained_problem:
Let $L([0,1]) = \{[a,b] : 0 \le a \le b \le 1\}$ denote the set of closed subintervals of the unit interval, equipped with the componentwise partial order $[a,b] \le_L [c,d] \iff a \le c$ and $b \le d$, which makes $(L([0,1]),\le_L)$ a complete bounded lattice with bottom $[0,0]$ and top $[1,1]$. A linear order $\preceq$ on $L([0,1])$ is called admissible if it is a total order refining $\le_L$ (i.e., $[a,b] \le_L [c,d]$ implies $[a,b] \preceq [c,d]$).

Recall that on $[0,1]$, an aggregation function $F:[0,1]^n \to [0,1]$ is averaging if $\min(x_1,\dots,x_n) \le F(x_1,\dots,x_n) \le \max(x_1,\dots,x_n)$ for all inputs, and a penalty-based function associated with a penalty $P:[0,1]^{n+1}\to[0,\infty)$ is defined by $F(\mathbf{x}) = \arg\min_{y \in [0,1]} P(\mathbf{x},y)$ (with a suitable tie-breaking rule), where $P$ satisfies: (i) $P(\mathbf{x},y) \ge 0$, (ii) $P(\mathbf{x},y) = 0$ whenever $x_1 = \cdots = x_n = y$, (iii) $P(\mathbf{x},\cdot)$ is quasi-convex in $y$ for every fixed $\mathbf{x}$. It is a classical fact that every averaging aggregation function on $[0,1]$ can be represented as a penalty-based function.

Problem: Formulate a satisfactory definition of a penalty function $P:L([0,1])^{n+1}\to[0,\infty)$ and the corresponding notion of a penalty-based function $F:L([0,1])^n \to L([0,1])$, compatible with the lattice order $\le_L$ (and, if appropriate, with admissible linear orders $\preceq$ refining $\le_L$), such that every averaging aggregation operator on $(L([0,1]),\le_L)$ — i.e., every function $F:L([0,1])^n \to L([0,1])$ satisfying $\bigwedge_i X_i \le_L F(X_1,\dots,X_n) \le_L \bigvee_i X_i$ — can be recovered as a penalty-based function in this sense.
status_search_result: Related work by Bustince, Beliakov, and collaborators has addressed standard and quasi-penalty function definitions on $[0,1]$ and penalty-based aggregation on intervals (including non-convex intervals), but no source clearly establishes a fully satisfactory penalty/penalty-based framework on the lattice $L([0,1])$ that recovers all averaging aggregation operators there. The status of this specific formulation problem is not conclusively settled by available sources.

paper_title: Open problems from the 12th International Conference on Fuzzy Set Theory and Its Applications
original_question: In quantitative logic, a formula is assigned a meta-degree by aggregating its truth degrees over all evaluations of its propositional variables, using either a normalized weighted sum on a finite truth-degree set or an integral on [0,1]. Which other kinds of aggregation operators are suitable for defining these meta-degrees, and how should the choice of aggregation operator depend on the intended applications of the logic?
self_contained_problem:
In quantitative logic one assigns to each propositional formula $\varphi(p_1,\dots,p_n)$ a so-called meta-degree, which measures the overall truth-value of $\varphi$ obtained by aggregating its truth degrees over all evaluations of the propositional variables. Two standard choices are used:

(a) If the truth-degree set is a finite chain $L=\{a_0<a_1<\dots<a_m\}\subset[0,1]$ with a probability distribution $(w_0,\dots,w_m)$ on $L$, then the meta-degree of $\varphi$ is defined as the normalized weighted sum
$$	au(\varphi)=\sum_{v\in L^n} \Bigl(\prod_{i=1}^{n} w(v(p_i))\Bigr)\,  ar v(\varphi),$$
where $ ar v(\varphi)\in L$ denotes the truth-value of $\varphi$ under the evaluation $v:\{p_1,\dots,p_n\}	o L$.

(b) If the truth-degree set is the unit interval $[0,1]$ equipped with the Lebesgue (or another) probability measure $\mu$, then the meta-degree of $\varphi$ is defined as the integral
$$	au(\varphi)=\int_{[0,1]^n}  ar v(\varphi)\,d\mu^n(v),$$
where $ ar v:[0,1]^n	o[0,1]$ is the truth-function of $\varphi$ determined by the underlying many-valued logical connectives (e.g. those of \L{}ukasiewicz, Gödel, or product logic).

Determine which other aggregation operators $A:[0,1]^{L^n}	o[0,1]$ (in case (a)) or functionals $A$ acting on measurable truth-functions on $[0,1]^n$ (in case (b)) — beyond the weighted arithmetic mean and the integral — are suitable as definitions of meta-degrees in quantitative logic. Characterize the structural properties (e.g. monotonicity, idempotence, symmetry, continuity, compatibility with logical connectives) that such an aggregation operator should satisfy, and explain how the appropriate choice of operator depends on the intended applications of the resulting quantitative logic.
status_search_result: The problem is posed as an open-ended research question about the suitability of various aggregation operators for defining meta-degrees in quantitative logic. No definitive resolution has been published; the question is broad and remains an ongoing research direction in many-valued/quantitative logic and aggregation theory.

paper_title: Open problems from the 12th International Conference on Fuzzy Set Theory and Its Applications
original_question: Generalize the quantitative-logic setup from the case where the truth-degree set is the real unit interval or a finite subset of it to the case where the truth-degree set is an arbitrary lattice. In particular, determine how formulas, truth functions, and meta-degree assignments should be formulated in that lattice-valued setting.
self_contained_problem:
Background. In quantitative logic over many-valued propositional calculi, one fixes a truth-degree set W (classically W = [0,1] or a finite chain W_n ⊂ [0,1]) together with a system of truth functions interpreting the connectives (e.g. a continuous t-norm and its residuum). For each propositional formula φ(p_1,…,p_n) one obtains an induced truth function φ̄: W^n → W. Given a probability measure (or a uniformly distributed counting measure in the finite case) on W^n, one then defines the "truth degree" τ(φ) ∈ [0,1] of φ as the expected value (integral / average) of φ̄ over all valuations, and uses these meta-degrees to define a logic pseudo-metric ρ(φ,ψ) = τ(φ ↔ ψ-complement) on the set of formulas, with which approximate reasoning, divergence degree, and consistency degree of theories are studied.

Problem. Develop an analogous quantitative-logic framework in the case where the truth-degree set is replaced by an arbitrary (bounded) lattice L (not necessarily linearly ordered, not necessarily embedded in [0,1]). Specifically:

(a) Specify a suitable class of formulas and a system of L-valued truth functions interpreting the propositional connectives over L (for instance via residuated lattice or complete lattice operations).

(b) Define an appropriate notion of "meta-degree" or truth degree τ(φ) of a formula φ in this L-valued setting, replacing the integral-with-respect-to-a-probability-measure construction available on [0,1]; in particular, identify what mathematical structure on L (measure, capacity, averaging operator, lattice-valued integral such as a Sugeno-type integral, or otherwise) plays the role of the uniform/Lebesgue measure used in the real-valued case, and what codomain (the lattice L itself, [0,1], or another structure) the meta-degree should take values in.

original_question: For the smallest semicopula-based universal integral I_S, characterize those semicopulas S for which, for every alpha in [0,1], every measurable space (X,A), every capacity m on A, and every measurable f:X->[0,1], one has I_S(m, S(alpha,f)) = S(alpha, I_S(m,f)).
self_contained_problem:
A semicopula is a function S:[0,1]^2 → [0,1] that is nondecreasing in each argument and satisfies the boundary condition S(1,x) = S(x,1) = x for all x ∈ [0,1]. Let (X, A) be a measurable space. A capacity on A is a set function m:A → [0,1] with m(∅)=0, m(X)=1, and m(B)≤m(C) whenever B ⊆ C. Denote by F(X,A) the set of A-measurable functions f:X → [0,1] and by M(X,A) the set of capacities on A.

For a semicopula S, the smallest semicopula-based universal integral is defined, for m ∈ M(X,A) and f ∈ F(X,A), by
    I_S(m, f) = sup_{t ∈ [0,1]} S( t, m({x ∈ X : f(x) ≥ t}) ).

Characterize all semicopulas S with the following property: for every α ∈ [0,1], every measurable space (X, A), every capacity m ∈ M(X,A), and every f ∈ F(X,A), one has
    I_S(m, S(α, f)) = S(α, I_S(m, f)),
where S(α, f) denotes the function x ↦ S(α, f(x)).
status_search_result: Subsequent work has provided partial characterizations and sufficient conditions (e.g., when S is associative and continuous in the second variable with appropriate monotonicity, the property holds), showing the original conjecture that only the product and minimum semicopulas qualify is false. However, a complete characterization of all such semicopulas does not appear to be established; recent papers describe their results as "another approach to" the open problem rather than its full resolution.

original_question: Determine for which classes of semicopulas S, and possibly for which classes of capacities, strict convergence in measure is equivalent to convergence in mean defined by the smallest semicopula-based universal integral I_S.
self_contained_problem:
Setup. A semicopula is a function S:[0,1]×[0,1]→[0,1] that is non-decreasing in each argument and satisfies S(1,x)=S(x,1)=x for all x∈[0,1]. Let (X,𝓐) be a measurable space. A capacity (monotone measure) on (X,𝓐) is a set function m:𝓐→[0,∞] with m(∅)=0 and m(A)≤m(B) whenever A⊆B. For a measurable function f:X→[0,∞) and a capacity m, the smallest semicopula-based universal integral is defined by
   I_S(m,f) = sup_{t>0} S( t, m({f≥t}) ).

Convergences. Let (f_n) be a sequence of 𝓐-measurable nonnegative functions and let f be such a function.
 • (f_n) converges in measure to f if for every ε>0, m({|f_n−f|≥ε}) → 0 as n→∞.
 • (f_n) converges strictly in measure to f if (f_n) converges in measure to f and, in addition, m({|f_n−f|≥ε}) = 0 for all sufficiently large n and every ε>0 outside a null set of thresholds (i.e. the stronger notion in which convergence in measure is accompanied by m({|f_n−f|≥ε})→0 uniformly in the standard "strict" sense used for semicopula-based integrals).
 • (f_n) converges in mean (with respect to I_S and m) to f if I_S(m, |f_n−f|) → 0 as n→∞.

Problem. Characterize all classes of semicopulas S (and, possibly, all classes of capacities m) for which strict convergence in measure of (f_n) to f is equivalent to convergence of (f_n) to f in mean defined by the smallest semicopula-based universal integral I_S.
status_search_result: Recent works (2023–2025) by Hutník and collaborators on almost-uniform convergence theorems and improvements on convergence in measure for semicopula-based universal integrals have produced partial answers. In particular, results show that, under natural conditions, strict convergence in measure is equivalent to convergence in measure and to convergence in mean only in degenerate cases (e.g. when the underlying monotone measure is trivial), while sufficient conditions on the semicopula (continuity, trivial zero divisors) and on the capacity (autocontinuity) yield equivalences in several settings. A complete characterization of all classes of semicopulas and capacities for which the equivalence holds does not appear to be established.

paper_title: Minimal positive realizations: a survey of recent results and open problems
original_question: For the minimality problem for positive realizations of a strictly proper rational transfer function G(z), which extra eigenvalues must sometimes be introduced in a smallest-dimensional positive realization even though they are not present in the original minimal realization? In other words, can one fully characterize the "hidden modes" that may need to be added in order to obtain a minimal positive realization?
self_contained_problem:
Let $G(z)$ be a strictly proper rational transfer function with nonnegative impulse response, i.e., the formal expansion $G(z)=\sum_{k\ge 1} g_k z^{-k}$ satisfies $g_k\ge 0$ for all $k\ge 1$. A positive realization of $G(z)$ of dimension $N$ is a triple $(A,b,c)$ with $A\in\mathbb{R}_+^{N	imes N}$, $b\in\mathbb{R}_+^{N}$, $c\in\mathbb{R}_+^{1	imes N}$ (entrywise nonnegative) such that $G(z)=c(zI-A)^{-1}b$. A positive realization is called minimal if $N$ is the smallest possible dimension, denoted $N_+(G)$. Let $n$ denote the McMillan degree of $G$ (the dimension of a minimal, not necessarily positive, realization), and let $\sigma(G)$ denote the set of poles of $G$ (counted with multiplicity).

In general $N_+(G)\ge n$, and a minimal positive realization $(A,b,c)$ of $G$ may have spectrum $\sigma(A)$ strictly larger than $\sigma(G)$; the extra eigenvalues in $\sigma(A)\setminus\sigma(G)$ are called hidden modes.

Problem. Give a complete characterization, in terms of $G(z)$ (equivalently, in terms of $\sigma(G)$ and the nonnegative sequence $\{g_k\}$), of which multisets of complex numbers can or must appear as the multiset of hidden modes $\sigma(A)\setminus\sigma(G)$ of some (equivalently, of every) minimal positive realization of $G$.
status_search_result: Recent surveys and research papers on minimal positive realizations (including a 2022 Automatica survey and works on two-pole transfer functions) indicate that a complete characterization of the hidden modes required in a minimal positive realization remains an open problem; only partial results exist for special cases such as low McMillan degree or specific pole configurations.

paper_title: Minimal positive realizations: a survey of recent results and open problems
original_question: How does the minimality problem for positive realizations extend from the single-input single-output case to the multiple-input multiple-output case? In particular, for MIMO positive systems, what are the right conditions and methods for determining the smallest state dimension of a positive realization, given that this extension is not straightforward even though the existence problem behaves more directly in the SISO setting studied in the paper?
self_contained_problem:
A discrete-time linear time-invariant system with p inputs and q outputs is described by a transfer matrix H(z), an q×p matrix of rational functions of z that are strictly proper (i.e. each entry tends to 0 as z → ∞). A positive realization of H(z) of dimension n is a quadruple (A, B, C, D) with A ∈ R^{n×n}, B ∈ R^{n×p}, C ∈ R^{q×n}, D ∈ R^{q×p} whose entries are all nonnegative, such that

  H(z) = D + C (zI − A)^{-1} B.

The dimension n is called the order of the realization. A positive realization is called minimal if no positive realization of H(z) has strictly smaller order. Denote by n_+(H) the minimal order of a positive realization of H(z), when one exists.

Problem. Develop necessary and sufficient conditions, together with constructive procedures, that determine n_+(H) for an arbitrary q×p strictly proper rational transfer matrix H(z) admitting a positive realization, in the genuinely multi-input multi-output setting (p > 1 or q > 1). In particular:

(a) Characterize n_+(H) in terms of intrinsic data of H(z) (e.g. its poles, residue structure, factorizations, or associated cone-invariance data), going beyond the known lower and upper bounds.

(b) Provide an algorithm that, given H(z) admitting a positive realization, computes a positive realization (A, B, C, D) whose order equals n_+(H).

A complete solution is known to be elusive because the MIMO minimality problem does not reduce in a direct way to the single-input single-output case (where H(z) is scalar), in contrast with the corresponding existence problem.
status_search_result: Recent surveys and research on minimal positive realizations indicate that, even in the SISO case, no general procedure is known to determine the minimum state dimension of a positive realization, and only lower/upper bounds are available. The MIMO extension is recognized as significantly harder and remains open, with ongoing work providing only partial results (e.g., bounds, special transfer-function classes, Markov-realization variants).

paper_title: Minimal positive realizations: a survey of recent results and open problems
original_question: Suppose a transfer function is described directly by system parameters such as residues and eigenvalues. How can one determine the minimum number of samples of the impulse response that must be checked in order to conclude that the entire impulse response is nonnegative, and how is that sample bound related to the minimal possible dimension of a positive realization of the system?
self_contained_problem:
Consider a discrete-time single-input single-output linear time-invariant system whose transfer function H(z) is a strictly proper rational function, given in pole-residue form

  H(z) = Σ_{i=1}^{n} r_i / (z − λ_i),

where the eigenvalues λ_1,…,λ_n ∈ ℂ are the (distinct) poles and r_1,…,r_n ∈ ℂ are the corresponding residues, with the impulse response sequence h(k) = Σ_{i=1}^{n} r_i λ_i^{k-1} for k ≥ 1.

A positive realization of H is a triple (A,b,c) with A ∈ ℝ_{+}^{N×N}, b ∈ ℝ_{+}^{N}, c ∈ ℝ_{+}^{1×N} (entrywise nonnegative) such that h(k) = c A^{k-1} b for all k ≥ 1. The minimal positive dimension N*(H) is the smallest N for which such a realization exists (it may exceed n, and may be infinite if no positive realization exists).

Problem. Provide a procedure, depending only on the data {(r_i, λ_i)}_{i=1}^{n}, that outputs an integer K = K(r_1,…,r_n, λ_1,…,λ_n) with the following property:

  if h(k) ≥ 0 for every k ∈ {1, 2, …, K}, then h(k) ≥ 0 for all k ≥ 1.

In other words, determine the minimum number K of impulse-response samples whose nonnegativity guarantees nonnegativity of the entire impulse response, expressed directly in terms of the residues and eigenvalues. Moreover, establish the precise relationship between this sample bound K and the minimal positive realization dimension N*(H).
category_tag: Positive linear systems / minimal positive realizations
status_search_result: Surveys and recent literature (including a 2022 Automatica survey and 2020/2025 follow-up works) continue to list the determination of minimal positive realization dimension, and related questions on certifying impulse-response nonnegativity from finitely many samples, as open. Only lower and upper bounds on the minimal positive dimension are currently known, and the precise sample-complexity bound for nonnegativity tied to minimality has not been settled.

paper_title: Minimal positive realizations: a survey of recent results and open problems
original_question: For the minimality problem for positive realizations, can one obtain tight lower bounds and tight upper bounds for the minimal order, meaning the smallest state dimension of a positive realization of a given transfer function?
self_contained_problem:
Let $H(z)$ be a rational transfer function with nonnegative impulse response, i.e., the formal power series expansion $H(z)=\sum_{k\ge 0} h_k z^{-k}$ satisfies $h_k\ge 0$ for all $k\ge 0$. A positive realization of $H$ is a triple $(A,b,c)$ with $A\in\mathbb{R}_{\ge 0}^{N\times N}$, $b\in\mathbb{R}_{\ge 0}^{N}$, $c\in\mathbb{R}_{\ge 0}^{1\times N}$ (all entries nonnegative), such that $H(z)=c(zI-A)^{-1}b$. The minimal positive realization order of $H$ is
$$N^*(H)=\min\{N\in\mathbb{N}: \text{there exists a positive realization }(A,b,c)\text{ of }H\text{ of dimension }N\}.$$
Note that $N^*(H)$ may strictly exceed the McMillan degree of $H$.

Problem: Find tight lower bounds and tight upper bounds for $N^*(H)$ as a function of computable invariants of $H$ (e.g., the poles, residues, and McMillan degree of $H$); that is, exhibit explicit functions $L(H)\le N^*(H)\le U(H)$ that can be achieved with equality on families of transfer functions, and ideally a procedure to compute $N^*(H)$ exactly.
status_search_result: Recent surveys and papers (including a 2022 survey in Automatica and 2025 work on positive Markov realizations) confirm that determining the minimal order of a positive realization remains open in general; only various lower and upper bounds are known, with no tight characterization for arbitrary transfer functions. Tight necessary and sufficient conditions have been obtained only in special cases (e.g., third-order systems with real poles).

paper_title: Some open problems in mutual stationarity involving inner model theory: a commentary.
context_brief: Conjectured lower bound from the stationary-set pattern in Question 3
original_question: Let A ⊆ ω be as in Question 3, and let S_A = {X ∈ [ℵ_ω]^{ω_1} | for every m > 1, cf(sup(X ∩ ω_m)) = ω when m ∈ A and cf(sup(X ∩ ω_m)) = ω_1 when m ∉ A}. If S_A is stationary for a single such A, must there exist an inner model with a strong cardinal?
self_contained_problem:
Work in ZFC. For an ordinal $\lambda$ and a cardinal $\kappa < \lambda$, let $[\lambda]^{\kappa} = \{X \subseteq \lambda : |X| = \kappa\}$. A set $\mathcal{S} \subseteq [\lambda]^{\kappa}$ is called stationary if for every function $F : [\lambda]^{<\omega} \to \lambda$ there exists $X \in \mathcal{S}$ with $X$ closed under $F$.

Fix the cardinal $\aleph_\omega$ and consider $[\aleph_\omega]^{\omega_1}$. For each subset $A \subseteq \omega$, define
$$S_A = \Big\{ X \in [\aleph_\omega]^{\omega_1} \;\Big|\; \text{for every integer } m > 1,\ \operatorname{cf}(\sup(X \cap \omega_m)) = \begin{cases} \omega & \text{if } m \in A, \\ \omega_1 & \text{if } m \notin A. \end{cases} \Big\}.$$

Assume that both $A$ and $\omega \setminus A$ are infinite (so that the cofinality pattern is genuinely "divergent" in the sense that both cofinalities $\omega$ and $\omega_1$ occur for infinitely many indices $m$).

Question: If there exists at least one such $A \subseteq \omega$ for which $S_A$ is stationary in $[\aleph_\omega]^{\omega_1}$, must there exist an inner model of ZFC containing a strong cardinal?
category_tag: mutual stationarity and inner model theory
status_search_result: The conjecture appears to remain open. paper_title: Pole solutions in the case of problems of flame front propagation and Saffman-Teylor "finger" formation without surface tension: open problems and possible ways of their solutions
context_brief: Allowed versus singular initial pole conditions
original_question: For finite-pole pole solutions of zero-surface-tension channel Laplacian growth, what are the exact necessary conditions that classify an initial pole configuration as allowed, meaning that it does not approach a finite-time singularity, rather than as an initial configuration that leads to a finite-time singularity?
self_contained_problem:
Consider two-dimensional Laplacian growth in a channel (the zero-surface-tension Saffman–Taylor problem in a Hele–Shaw cell of finite width with periodic or no-flux lateral boundary conditions). The moving interface separating the inviscid fluid (or burnt region, in the equivalent flame-front formulation) from the viscous fluid is described by a time-dependent conformal map z = f(w,t) from the exterior (or interior) of the unit disk in an auxiliary w-plane onto the physical domain occupied by the displaced fluid. The map is taken in the meromorphic "pole" ansatz

  f(w,t) = w + V(t) + Σ_{k=1}^{N} α_k(t) · log(w − w_k(t)),

where N is a fixed positive integer and {α_k(t), w_k(t)} are the (complex) strengths and locations of a finite number of logarithmic singularities ("poles"). Substituting this ansatz into the zero-surface-tension Laplacian-growth equation yields a finite-dimensional dynamical system for the parameters (α_k(t), w_k(t)).

An initial pole configuration {α_k(0), w_k(0)}_{k=1}^{N} is said to be "allowed" if the resulting solution remains conformal for all t > 0, i.e. the interface develops no finite-time singularity (no cusp formation and no pole crossing the unit circle in finite time); otherwise the configuration is called singular.

Problem. Determine the exact necessary and sufficient conditions on the initial data {α_k(0), w_k(0)}_{k=1}^{N} that characterize the set of allowed configurations (those whose evolution under the pole dynamics never reaches a finite-time singularity).
status_search_result: Available literature on pole dynamics in zero-surface-tension Laplacian growth (Mineev-Weinstein, Dawson, and collaborators) gives sufficient conditions ensuring non-singular evolution (e.g. restricting pole strengths and excluding certain pole configurations) and shows that generic non-singular initial data produce an asymptotic half-width finger, but no complete necessary-and-sufficient characterization of the set of allowed initial pole configurations appears to have been established; the problem is generally treated as open in subsequent work.

paper_title: Pole solutions in the case of problems of flame front propagation and Saffman-Teylor "finger" formation without surface tension: open problems and possible ways of their solutions
context_brief: Strict proof of half-width finger selection
original_question: Can one give a strict proof, for zero-surface-tension Saffman-Taylor channel growth in the pole-solution formulation, that the exclusion of finite-time-singular initial pole configurations together with continual introduction of new poles selects a single finger of half the channel width as the privileged or most probable asymptotic state?
self_contained_problem:
Consider the two-dimensional Saffman–Taylor problem of Hele-Shaw channel flow with zero surface tension. The channel has width 1, and a less viscous fluid displaces a more viscous fluid satisfying Darcy's law, so that the interface evolves by Laplacian growth (the normal velocity of the interface equals the normal derivative of a harmonic pressure field, with constant pressure on the interface). Using a conformal map from the exterior of the unit disk to the fluid domain, the dynamics admit a pole-decomposition formulation: the conformal map has the form of a sum of logarithmic poles whose positions in the complex plane evolve according to an autonomous system of ODEs. New poles may be continually introduced into the configuration during the evolution.

Adopt the following regularization rule (without invoking surface tension): at every time, exclude any pole configuration (whether initial or newly introduced) that would lead to a finite-time singularity (a cusp on the moving interface). With this rule in force, and allowing continual introduction of new admissible poles:

Provide a rigorous mathematical proof that the asymptotic state (as t → ∞) of this dynamics is, in the privileged or "most probable" sense (e.g., almost surely under a reasonable measure on admissible pole insertions, or as the unique attractor of the regularized dynamics), a single Saffman–Taylor finger occupying exactly one half of the channel width. Equivalently, prove that the relative finger width λ(t) converges to 1/2 under the pole-dynamics formulation with the above non-surface-tension regularization.
status_search_result: Several works (Mineev-Weinstein, PRL 1998; subsequent Laplacian Growth papers) claim that pole dynamics with regularization (no surface tension) selects a single 1/2-width finger asymptotically and present arguments toward an "exact result." However, this claim was contested by a published Comment (PRL 81, 5950), and the rigor and generality of the proof remain debated. No universally accepted strict proof appears in the literature, so the precise question of a fully rigorous proof of half-width selection in this pole formulation is best classified as unknown/partially addressed.

paper_title: Pole solutions in the case of problems of flame front propagation and Saffman-Teylor "finger" formation without surface tension: open problems and possible ways of their solutions
context_brief: Gaussian-noise saturation-point study for cylindrical flames
original_question: In numerical simulations of cylindrical flame-front propagation, does adding explicit Gaussian noise produce a flame-front velocity saturation point, and how does the position or behavior of that saturation point depend on the Gaussian-noise amplitude when extrapolated toward small numerical noise?
self_contained_problem:
Consider the Sivashinsky equation governing the dynamics of an outward-propagating (cylindrical/radial) premixed flame front in two dimensions. Let the front be described by a single-valued function whose evolution is given by the (Michelson–)Sivashinsky equation supplemented with an additive Gaussian white-noise forcing term of amplitude ε > 0:

  ∂_t Φ = (1/2)(∂_x Φ)^2 + ν ∂_x^2 Φ + I[Φ] + ε η(x,t),

where I[Φ] denotes the singular (Landau–Darrieus) linear integral operator with symbol |k|, the geometry is cylindrical (radially outward propagating front of growing radius R(t)), and η is zero-mean Gaussian white noise with unit variance.

Perform numerical simulations of this system and answer the following:

(a) Does the mean propagation velocity V(t) of the cylindrical flame front, computed in the presence of explicit Gaussian noise of amplitude ε, exhibit a finite saturation point — i.e., a time t_sat(ε) (or equivalently a radius R_sat(ε)) at which V transitions from systematic growth/acceleration to an approximately steady (saturated) behaviour?

(b) If such a saturation point exists, determine how its location t_sat(ε) (or R_sat(ε)) and the saturated velocity V_sat(ε) depend on the noise amplitude ε. In particular, characterize the scaling/behaviour of these quantities as ε → 0, and determine whether the extrapolation ε → 0 yields a well-defined limiting saturation behaviour distinct from that produced by intrinsic numerical roundoff noise alone.
status_search_result: The analogous question for planar and outward-propagating (cylindrical) Sivashinsky fronts with explicit Gaussian forcing has been investigated numerically and analytically: scaling laws for velocity/acceleration versus system size and noise amplitude have been obtained, and in radial geometry external noise is reported as crucial and capable of producing accelerated fronts via the appearance of new poles. While saturation phenomena and noise-amplitude dependence have been documented for related setups (planar, channel, and outward-propagating cases), a complete, quantitative characterization of the saturation point as a function of ε with controlled ε → 0 extrapolation in the cylindrical geometry does not appear to be fully settled.

paper_title: Open questions in quarkonium and electromagnetic probes
context_brief: Overall evidentiary status of new-physics claims
original_question: Do the experimental data available for quarkonium production and electromagnetic probes in high-energy heavy-ion collisions already provide convincing evidence, beyond reasonable doubt, for the existence of genuinely new physics in those collisions, rather than effects that can still be explained by uncertainties in baseline measurements and conventional nuclear processes?
self_contained_problem:
Consider the body of experimental measurements obtained in high-energy heavy-ion collisions concerning (i) quarkonium production yields (e.g., J/ψ, ψ(2S), Υ states and their suppression or enhancement patterns relative to proton–proton or proton–nucleus baselines), and (ii) electromagnetic probes (direct photons and dilepton invariant-mass spectra in the low, intermediate, and high mass regions). Let a "conventional baseline explanation" denote any combination of (a) measured or extrapolated proton–proton and proton–nucleus reference cross sections with their quoted uncertainties, (b) cold nuclear matter effects (nuclear parton distribution modifications, initial-state energy loss, nuclear absorption, Cronin-like broadening), and (c) standard hadronic-phase contributions (resonance decays, hadronic rescattering, in-medium hadron production) treated within accepted modeling uncertainties. Define "new physics in heavy-ion collisions" to mean phenomena that cannot be accommodated by any such conventional baseline explanation — in particular, signatures requiring deconfined partonic matter, chiral symmetry restoration, or thermal radiation from a quark-gluon plasma. 

Question: Do the currently available experimental data on quarkonium production and on electromagnetic probes in high-energy heavy-ion collisions, taken together, establish the existence of new physics in the above sense beyond reasonable doubt, in the precise sense that no conventional baseline explanation (within stated experimental and theoretical uncertainties of the references and cold/hot hadronic effects) is compatible with the observed yields, spectra, and centrality/system-size dependences?
category_tag: quarkonium and electromagnetic probes in heavy-ion collisions
status_search_result: The question of whether quarkonium suppression and electromagnetic-probe measurements definitively establish new physics (e.g., a deconfined quark-gluon plasma) beyond baseline and cold-nuclear-matter uncertainties is widely regarded as still open in the heavy-ion community. While LHC-era results (sequential Υ suppression, regeneration of charmonium, thermal photon and dilepton observations) have strengthened the QGP interpretation, recent reviews continue to emphasize baseline and CNM uncertainties as limiting factors and have not declared the matter settled beyond reasonable doubt.

paper_title: Open questions in quarkonium and electromagnetic probes
context_brief: Prompt dimuon baseline in proton-nucleus collisions
original_question: Can proton-nucleus measurements determine the non-thermal prompt dimuon baseline in the intermediate mass region well enough to distinguish genuine thermal dimuon production in heavy-ion collisions, given that low-mass Drell-Yan production is not reliably calculable and may be enhanced in proton-nucleus and nucleus-nucleus collisions by interactions involving extra partons from the colliding hadrons?
self_contained_problem:
Consider high-energy hadronic collisions producing prompt muon pairs (dimuons) in the intermediate invariant-mass region 1 GeV/c² < M_{μμ} < 2.5 GeV/c². In this region the observed prompt dimuon yield in heavy-ion (nucleus–nucleus) collisions is expected to contain:

(i) a Drell–Yan contribution (q q̄ → γ* → μ⁺μ⁻, including possible higher-order partonic corrections and contributions involving additional partons from the colliding hadrons),
(ii) correlated semileptonic decays of D D̄ pairs (open charm),
(iii) a putative "thermal" component originating from a hot, possibly partonic, medium produced in the collision.

The Drell–Yan cross section at such low dimuon masses is not reliably calculable from perturbative QCD because higher-order effects are large, and nuclear effects (e.g., extra-parton interactions in pA and AA) may enhance it relative to a pp extrapolation.

Problem. Determine whether measurements of prompt dimuon production in proton–nucleus (pA) collisions, used as a non-thermal baseline, can be made precise and theoretically controlled enough to fix the non-thermal prompt dimuon yield (Drell–Yan plus correlated open-charm decays, including possible nuclear-enhancement effects) in the intermediate-mass region 1 GeV/c² < M_{μμ} < 2.5 GeV/c² with sufficient accuracy that an excess in nucleus–nucleus collisions over this pA-based baseline constitutes unambiguous evidence for genuine thermal dimuon production.

Equivalently: Is it possible, using only pA data together with current or foreseeable theoretical inputs, to subtract the non-thermal prompt dimuon contribution in AA collisions in the intermediate-mass region to a precision that isolates a thermal signal?
category_tag: Thermal dimuon production in heavy-ion collisions
status_search_result: NA60 measurements in In–In collisions at 158 A GeV established that, after subtracting the Drell–Yan and open-charm contributions calibrated on proton–nucleus data, a prompt excess remains in the intermediate-mass region 1 < M < 2.5 GeV/c², interpreted as evidence for thermal dimuons of partonic origin. This addresses the question affirmatively at SPS energies in the regime studied, but a fully theoretically controlled pA baseline (including possible extra-parton enhancements of low-mass Drell–Yan) remains an active topic, with the proposed NA60+ experiment aiming to improve precision. Hence the question is partially resolved rather than fully settled.

paper_title: Open questions in quarkonium and electromagnetic probes
original_question: After properly accounting for the normal nuclear effects already present in proton-nucleus collisions, how much of the φ-meson enhancement observed in heavy-ion collisions remains genuinely anomalous?
self_contained_problem:
Consider the production of φ(1020) mesons in high-energy nuclear collisions. In proton–nucleus (p–A) collisions, ordinary "cold nuclear matter" effects (e.g., nuclear shadowing/anti-shadowing of parton distributions, initial-state multiple scattering, and final-state hadronic absorption) are known to modify φ-meson production relative to elementary proton–proton (p–p) baselines; in particular, the ratio σ(φ)/σ(ω) is observed to grow with the mass number A.

Define the φ nuclear modification factor in nucleus–nucleus (A–A) collisions at center-of-mass energy √s_NN as
  R_{AA}^{φ}(p_T, y; √s_NN) = (1/⟨N_coll⟩) · (d²N_{AA}^{φ}/dp_T dy) / (d²N_{pp}^{φ}/dp_T dy),
and the analogous factor R_{pA}^{φ} for p–A collisions. Let the "expected" φ yield in A–A collisions from a smooth extrapolation of p–A data be the value of R_{AA}^{φ} obtained by composing/scaling the measured R_{pA}^{φ} (e.g., via a Glauber-based folding of cold nuclear matter effects from each colliding nucleus). Define the "anomalous" φ enhancement as
  Δ^{φ}_{anom}(p_T, y; √s_NN) = R_{AA}^{φ,measured} − R_{AA}^{φ,from p-A extrapolation}.

Problem: Quantify Δ^{φ}_{anom} as a function of collision energy √s_NN, centrality (⟨N_coll⟩ or ⟨N_part⟩), transverse momentum p_T, and rapidity y. In particular, determine whether, after a complete and consistent extrapolation of p–A observations (including A-dependence of σ(φ)/σ(ω), shadowing, and absorption) to the A–A geometry, any statistically significant enhancement of φ production in A–A collisions remains, and characterize its magnitude and kinematic dependence.
category_tag: Quarkonium and dilepton production in heavy-ion collisions
status_search_result: Reviews of φ-meson production in heavy-ion collisions and dedicated p–Pb measurements (e.g., at the LHC by ALICE) have substantially clarified cold nuclear matter effects, but a definitive, quantitative subtraction of p–A baselines yielding a universally agreed residual "anomalous" φ enhancement across energies, centralities, and kinematics has not been established. The status of the question therefore appears unresolved/unknown in a precise sense.
