paper_title: (E,E′N) and (E,E′NN) Experiments at NIKHEF, Mainz and JLab and Open Problems in One- and Two-Nucleon Emissions
original_question: How can the long-standing discrepancy between spectroscopic factors extracted from low-energy exclusive (e,e′p) measurements and spectroscopic factors predicted by nuclear many-body theory be resolved in a reaction framework that consistently includes final-state interactions, current-operator ambiguities, and relativistic effects? In particular, can one explain why low-Q² analyses report strongly quenched valence-shell strengths while higher-Q² analyses give substantially larger values, without attributing the difference to uncontrolled model dependence in the reaction mechanism?
self_contained_problem:
Consider exclusive quasi-elastic electron-induced single-proton knockout reactions $A(e,e'p)B$, in which a high-energy electron scatters off a nucleus $A$ with four-momentum transfer $q^\mu=(\omega,\mathbf{q})$ and $Q^2=-q^\mu q_\mu$, ejecting a proton while leaving the residual nucleus $B$ in a definite (typically valence) bound state $\alpha$. Within a one-body current picture, the cross section is proportional to the squared overlap between the initial state of $A$ and the final state $|B,\alpha\rangle\otimes|p\rangle$. The normalization of this overlap defines the spectroscopic factor $S_\alpha\in[0,1]$, which many-body nuclear structure calculations (including short-range and long-range correlations) typically predict to lie near $S_\alpha^{\text{th}}\approx 0.7$–$0.9$ for valence orbitals of stable nuclei.

Experimental extractions of $S_\alpha$ from such $(e,e'p)$ data require a reaction model that accounts for: (i) final-state interactions between the outgoing proton and the residual nucleus (usually treated through a complex optical potential in a distorted-wave framework), (ii) ambiguities in the off-shell electromagnetic single-nucleon current operator (different prescriptions such as $CC1$, $CC2$, $CC3$), and (iii) relativistic kinematic and dynamical effects in the bound-state wave function, the current, and the distorted outgoing wave.

Empirically, analyses of low-$Q^2$ exclusive $(e,e'p)$ data (with $Q^2$ well below $1\,\text{GeV}^2$) yield strongly quenched valence-shell spectroscopic factors $S_\alpha^{\text{exp}}\approx 0.6$–$0.7$ of the independent-particle-shell-model value, whereas analyses performed at $Q^2\gtrsim 1\,\text{GeV}^2$ yield $S_\alpha^{\text{exp}}$ close to unity using analogous reaction frameworks.

Problem. Construct a single, internally consistent reaction-theoretical framework for $A(e,e'p)B$ that simultaneously incorporates final-state interactions, off-shell single-nucleon current ambiguities, and relativistic effects, in which the extracted valence-shell spectroscopic factors $S_\alpha$ become independent of $Q^2$ across the kinematic range from a few hundred $\text{MeV}^2$ up to several $\text{GeV}^2$, and either reconcile the resulting $Q^2$-independent values with the predictions of modern nuclear many-body theory or identify, within that consistent framework, the specific physical ingredient whose omission produces the observed apparent $Q^2$ dependence. In particular, account for the difference between low-$Q^2$ quenched values and high-$Q^2$ near-unity values without invoking uncontrolled model dependence of the reaction mechanism.
status_search_result: The discrepancy between spectroscopic factors extracted from $(e,e'p)$ at different $Q^2$ and many-body predictions remains an active and unresolved puzzle in nuclear physics. Recent work (e.g., Phys. Rev. Lett. 131, 212503 (2023) and follow-ups, plus a 2025 explanation proposing a core-screening / finite-probe-size effect) provides partial reconciliations and Bayesian uncertainty quantification, but no universally accepted, fully consistent reaction framework removes the apparent $Q^2$ dependence and matches many-body theory across the full kinematic range. Hence the problem is best described as partially solved.

paper_title: (E,E′N) and (E,E′NN) Experiments at NIKHEF, Mainz and JLab and Open Problems in One- and Two-Nucleon Emissions
original_question: How does the normal recoil polarization P_N in exclusive (e,e′p) scattering vary with Q², and can that dependence be used to isolate the energy dependence of final-state interactions well enough to clarify nuclear transparency and, ultimately, color transparency? Because P_N vanishes in the absence of final-state interactions, the open problem is to determine whether systematic polarization measurements can cleanly separate genuine attenuation effects from competing reaction-mechanism uncertainties.
self_contained_problem:
Consider exclusive quasi-elastic electron–nucleus scattering of the form A(e,e'p)B, in which an electron of four-momentum transfer squared Q² knocks a single proton out of a nuclear target while leaving the residual nucleus in a well-defined state. Let n̂ denote the unit vector normal to the scattering plane (the plane spanned by the incident and scattered electron momenta and the ejected proton momentum), and let P_N be the component of the ejected proton's recoil polarization along n̂, induced even with an unpolarized electron beam and an unpolarized target. Under the standard reaction-mechanism description (one-photon exchange, distorted-wave impulse approximation with final-state interactions modeled by an optical potential or Glauber-type rescattering), P_N is generated entirely by final-state interactions (FSI) between the outgoing proton and the residual nuclear system: in the absence of FSI one has P_N = 0.

(a) Determine the dependence of P_N on Q² for representative target nuclei (e.g., ¹²C, ¹⁶O, ⁴⁰Ca) in the kinematic regime accessible at modern electron-scattering facilities (Q² up to several GeV²), as a function of missing momentum and outgoing-proton kinematics.

(b) Decide whether the measured Q²-dependence of P_N can be used to isolate the energy dependence of FSI cleanly enough to (i) extract a model-independent nuclear transparency, and (ii) provide an unambiguous signal of color transparency — i.e., the predicted onset, at sufficiently large Q², of a suppression of FSI due to the propagation of a small-size, color-neutral configuration of the struck proton through the nuclear medium — while disentangling such effects from competing reaction-mechanism uncertainties (relativistic effects, two-body currents, spinor distortion, off-shell ambiguities, choice of optical potential).

status_search_result: The Q²-dependence of the induced normal recoil polarization P_N in (e,e'p) reactions remains an active probe of FSI and color transparency. Recent theoretical and experimental work (including JLab 12 GeV proposals and 2022–2024 analyses on D(e,e'p)n and related processes) continues to discuss P_N as a candidate observable, but no clean, model-independent extraction of color transparency from P_N has been established; signals at intermediate Q² remain inconclusive and entangled with conventional reaction-mechanism effects.

paper_title: (E,E′N) and (E,E′NN) Experiments at NIKHEF, Mainz and JLab and Open Problems in One- and Two-Nucleon Emissions
original_question: What reaction mechanisms generate the enhanced transverse strength and nearly momentum-independent high-missing-momentum cross section seen in exclusive 16O(e,e′p) measurements at high missing energy, where distorted-wave one-nucleon knockout underpredicts the data and two-nucleon emission channels contribute substantially? More broadly, where exactly does the single-particle picture of one-nucleon knockout break down as missing momentum and missing energy increase?
self_contained_problem:
Consider the exclusive electron-induced proton knockout reaction on an oxygen-16 target, $^{16}\mathrm{O}(e,e'p)$, in which an incident electron scatters and is detected in coincidence with an ejected proton, leaving a residual nucleus. Denote by $p_m$ the missing momentum and by $E_m$ the missing energy reconstructed from the kinematics of the detected electron and proton. In the standard distorted-wave impulse approximation (DWIA) "single-particle" picture, the cross section factorizes into a kinematic factor, the off-shell electron-proton cross section, and a distorted single-particle spectral function describing the removed proton.

Experimental observations in the regime of high missing energy include: (i) the longitudinal/transverse-separated cross section exhibits an enhanced transverse component that cannot be reproduced by DWIA one-nucleon knockout from bound shell-model orbitals; (ii) for missing momenta $p_m \gtrsim 200\ \mathrm{MeV}/c$ the differential cross section becomes nearly independent of $p_m$; and (iii) coincidence measurements of two outgoing nucleons, $^{16}\mathrm{O}(e,e'pp)$ and $^{16}\mathrm{O}(e,e'pn)$, account for roughly half of the inclusive-in-final-state $(e,e'p)$ strength in this region.

Problem. Identify and quantitatively characterize the reaction mechanisms responsible for the enhanced transverse strength and the flat, nearly momentum-independent high-$p_m$ cross section observed in $^{16}\mathrm{O}(e,e'p)$ at high $E_m$. In particular, determine the relative contributions of:
(a) short-range central and tensor nucleon–nucleon correlations in the initial-state wave function,
(b) meson-exchange currents (two-body electromagnetic currents),
(c) intermediate $\Delta$-isobar and other resonance currents,
(d) final-state interactions and rescattering of the knocked-out nucleon,
and establish, as functions of $p_m$ and $E_m$, the kinematic boundary beyond which the single-particle DWIA description of one-nucleon knockout ceases to be valid.
status_search_result: Subsequent theoretical work (e.g., the Pavia and Ghent groups) has identified tensor correlations as the dominant source of pn knockout strength and meson-exchange/isobar currents as the principal source of transverse strength at deep missing energies, with refined two-nucleon knockout calculations reproducing much of the (e,e'pn) data. However, a complete, quantitative decomposition of the high-$E_m$, high-$p_m$ cross section into correlation, MEC, $\Delta$, and FSI contributions across the full kinematic domain — and a precise demarcation of where the single-particle picture fails — remains incomplete.

paper_title: (E,E′N) and (E,E′NN) Experiments at NIKHEF, Mainz and JLab and Open Problems in One- and Two-Nucleon Emissions
original_question: Can precise exclusive 16O(e,e′pp) measurements to selected 14C final states, especially transitions dominated by knockout of a relative 1S0 proton pair, be used to determine short-range correlation functions tightly enough to constrain the off-shell behavior of the nucleon-nucleon potential? The unresolved issue is whether sufficiently accurate data in correlation-favored kinematics can distinguish among competing correlation models through their different predictions for these state-resolved cross sections.
self_contained_problem:
Consider the exclusive electron-induced two-proton knockout reaction $^{16}\mathrm{O}(e,e'pp)^{14}\mathrm{C}$, in which an incoming electron scatters from an $^{16}\mathrm{O}$ target and two protons are detected in coincidence with the scattered electron, leaving the residual nucleus $^{14}\mathrm{C}$ in a specific discrete final state (ground state or low-lying excited states). For kinematics that favor sensitivity to short-range correlations (small center-of-mass momentum of the pp pair, moderate energy and momentum transfer, with the pair predominantly in a relative ${}^1S_0$ state), the state-resolved differential cross section depends on (i) the two-nucleon overlap (spectroscopic) amplitudes for the transition, (ii) the central short-range correlation function $g(r)$ used to defect the relative pair wave function, (iii) tensor and other induced correlations, and (iv) two-body currents including meson-exchange and intermediate $\Delta$-isobar contributions.

Question: Can exclusive cross-section measurements of $^{16}\mathrm{O}(e,e'pp)^{14}\mathrm{C}$ to selected final states—especially those transitions dominated by knockout of a relative ${}^1S_0$ proton pair—be performed with sufficient precision in correlation-favored kinematics to:

(a) discriminate among competing models of the central nucleon-nucleon short-range correlation function $g(r)$ through their distinct predictions for these state-resolved cross sections; and

(b) thereby place quantitative constraints on the off-shell behavior of the nucleon-nucleon potential?

Specifically, determine whether achievable experimental precision and theoretical control (including treatment of final-state interactions, two-body currents, and competing reaction mechanisms) allow the state-resolved cross sections to uniquely fix $g(r)$ to within a tolerance that translates into a meaningful constraint on the off-shell $NN$ interaction.
status_search_result: Subsequent measurements and analyses (e.g., MAMI/Mainz high-resolution data and microscopic calculations including central SRC and Δ excitations) have demonstrated that the $^{16}$O(e,e′pp)$^{14}$C ground-state transition is indeed dominated by knockout of $^1S_0$ pp pairs and carries clear SRC signatures, with parameter-free calculations reproducing data. However, conclusively distinguishing among competing correlation functions to the point of tightly constraining the off-shell behavior of the NN potential has not been firmly established; results so far provide evidence for SRCs and qualitative discrimination but not a definitive off-shell constraint.

paper_title: (E,E′N) and (E,E′NN) Experiments at NIKHEF, Mainz and JLab and Open Problems in One- and Two-Nucleon Emissions
original_question: Can recoil-polarization measurements in exclusive (e,e′pp) and (e,e′pn) reactions, combined with resolution of specific residual-nucleus final states, provide a practical way to separate correlation-driven knockout from processes generated by two-body currents and thereby determine the full scattering amplitudes more completely? The open problem is whether polarization observables add enough independent information to cleanly decompose the competing reaction mechanisms in two-nucleon emission.
self_contained_problem:
Consider exclusive electron-induced two-nucleon knockout reactions on a nuclear target, in which an incoming electron with four-momentum k scatters to a final electron with four-momentum k', exchanging a virtual photon of four-momentum q = k - k', and two outgoing nucleons (either a pp pair or a pn pair) are detected in coincidence while the residual (A-2)-nucleus is left in a specific discrete final state f. The differential cross section for such an (e,e'NN) reaction can be decomposed in terms of hadronic response functions that depend on bilinear combinations of the transition amplitudes M_{fi} between the initial nuclear ground state and the chosen residual state, mediated by (i) one-body currents acting on correlated nucleon pairs arising from short-range and tensor correlations in the nuclear wave function, and (ii) explicit two-body meson-exchange and isobar currents (including pion exchange and intermediate Δ excitation). In addition to unpolarized cross sections, one may consider polarization observables, defined as follows: the recoil polarization P = (P_L, P_T, P_N) of one of the ejected nucleons (longitudinal, transverse in the scattering plane, and normal to it) measured with unpolarized beam and target, and the polarization-transfer coefficients P'_i obtained with a longitudinally polarized electron beam. Each such observable is a specific bilinear function of the amplitudes M_{fi}.

Question: Do the recoil-polarization observables of one outgoing nucleon in (e,e'pp) and (e,e'pn) reactions, taken together with the experimental resolution of individual residual-nucleus final states f, supply sufficiently many independent bilinear functionals of the amplitudes M_{fi} to (a) cleanly decompose the cross section into contributions originating from nucleon-nucleon correlations versus contributions from two-body currents (including Δ-isobar excitation), and (b) achieve a complete determination of all independent complex scattering amplitudes M_{fi} (up to an overall phase) for the chosen final state?
status_search_result: Searches indicate that (e,e'NN) experiments have continued at facilities such as Mainz and JLab, and theoretical frameworks for polarization observables in two-nucleon knockout have been developed, but a definitive experimental demonstration that recoil-polarization observables suffice to fully disentangle correlation and two-body-current mechanisms and to completely determine the scattering amplitudes has not been reported. The problem appears to remain open.

paper_title: Four nucleon systems: a zoom to the open problems in nuclear interaction
original_question: How should nonlocal INOY or Doleschall two-nucleon interaction models be modified so that they retain their ability to reproduce two-nucleon observables and overcome the missing three-nucleon binding energy without explicit three-nucleon forces, while also reproducing the alpha-particle binding energy and proton root-mean-square radius? The concrete failure mode is that these nonlocal models overbind the alpha particle by about 800 keV and predict a proton root-mean-square radius about 10% smaller than experiment, suggesting that the interactions are too soft and may need increased short-range repulsion between nucleons.
self_contained_problem:
Background and setup. A two-nucleon (NN) interaction is a (possibly nonlocal) operator V acting on the relative-motion wave function of two nucleons, designed to reproduce NN scattering phase shifts up to a chosen laboratory energy and the deuteron observables (binding energy, asymptotic normalization, D-state probability constraints, etc.). A class of phenomenological nonlocal NN interactions (the INOY and Doleschall-type potentials) is constructed in coordinate space with a short-range nonlocal part and a long-range one-pion-exchange tail, with the property that, when used alone (without any explicit three-nucleon force), they reproduce the experimental triton binding energy E(³H) ≈ 8.482 MeV in addition to the two-nucleon data.

When such an NN interaction V is used in an ab initio bound-state calculation for the four-nucleon system (the α particle, ⁴He), define:
 • E_α(V) = the binding energy of ⁴He computed from the nonrelativistic four-body Schrödinger equation with V as the only nuclear interaction,
 • r_p(V) = the point-proton root-mean-square radius of the ⁴He ground state computed with V.

The experimental values are E_α^exp ≈ 28.30 MeV and r_p^exp ≈ 1.46 fm (the precise reference value being the one extracted from electron-scattering charge-radius data after standard corrections).

Observed failure. Existing INOY/Doleschall-type interactions V₀ satisfy
 E_α(V₀) − E_α^exp ≈ +0.8 MeV (overbinding by about 800 keV),
 r_p(V₀) ≈ 0.9 · r_p^exp (about 10% too small),
indicating that they are too "soft" at short distances.

Problem. Construct a nonlocal two-nucleon interaction V (of the same general INOY/Doleschall coordinate-space, nonlocal-short-range plus one-pion-exchange-tail form, with no explicit three-nucleon force) such that simultaneously:
 (i) V reproduces the standard two-nucleon scattering observables (phase shifts and mixing parameters in all relevant partial waves up to lab energies of order 350 MeV) and the deuteron properties to the same accuracy as existing INOY/Doleschall models;
 (ii) V reproduces the experimental triton binding energy E(³H) without invoking any three-nucleon force;
 (iii) V reproduces the α-particle binding energy: E_α(V) = E_α^exp within the accepted experimental and few-body computational uncertainty;
 (iv) V reproduces the point-proton root-mean-square radius of ⁴He: r_p(V) = r_p^exp within the same tolerance.

A natural strategy is to increase the short-range repulsion between nucleons in the nonlocal part of V. The question is whether such a modification can be carried out while preserving (i) and (ii), and, if so, to exhibit it explicitly; otherwise, to demonstrate an obstruction.
category_tag: Nonlocal nucleon-nucleon potentials in few-body nuclei
status_search_result: Searches indicate that Doleschall-type nonlocal NN interactions (INOY) continue to reproduce the triton binding energy without a 3NF but still fail to simultaneously reproduce the α-particle binding energy and proton rms radius; no published phenomenological nonlocal NN potential is known that solves all four constraints at once. The issue remains an open problem in few-body nuclear theory, with ongoing modern attention shifting toward chiral effective field theory NN+3NF rather than purely nonlocal NN-only fits.

paper_title: Four nucleon systems: a zoom to the open problems in nuclear interaction
original_question: What interaction effects are still missing in low-energy neutron plus tritium scattering when a model such as AV18 plus Urbana IX three-nucleon force already reproduces the triton binding energy, yet the coherent scattering lengths remain less clearly consistent with experiment? The question concerns the zero-energy and very-low-energy neutron plus tritium observables, where the zero-energy cross section may fit experimental data while coherent scattering lengths still show small discrepancies.
self_contained_problem:
Consider the four-nucleon scattering problem for a neutron incident on a triton (3H) at zero and very low energy. The dynamics are governed by a nucleon-nucleon (NN) interaction supplemented by a three-nucleon force (3NF). A representative realistic model is the Argonne v18 (AV18) NN potential combined with the Urbana IX (UIX) three-nucleon force; this combination is tuned to reproduce the experimental triton binding energy (~8.48 MeV).

For the n+3H system at zero energy, two key low-energy observables are:
(i) the zero-energy total cross section σ(0), and
(ii) the spin-dependent coherent scattering lengths a_c (and the singlet a_s and triplet a_t scattering lengths from which a_c is constructed).

Empirically, while AV18+UIX yields a zero-energy cross section in fair agreement with experiment, the coherent (and spin-projected) scattering lengths for n+3H remain in tension with measured values. Nonlocal NN interaction models (such as INOY-type interactions) tend to improve the description of low-energy n+3H data, particularly near the elastic-cross-section minimum at center-of-mass energy E_cm ≈ 0.4 MeV.

Identify and characterize the missing or incompletely modeled interaction ingredients in the nuclear Hamiltonian that are responsible for the residual discrepancies between theoretical predictions (based on AV18+UIX or similar local NN+3NF Hamiltonians that reproduce the triton binding energy) and experimental low-energy n+3H scattering observables — in particular the coherent scattering lengths — while simultaneously preserving agreement with the zero-energy cross section and the triton binding energy. The task is to determine which interaction effects (e.g., specific components of the three-nucleon force, nonlocalities in the NN interaction, charge-symmetry-breaking terms, four-nucleon forces, or other dynamical ingredients) must be added or modified so that the full set of low-energy n+3H observables is described consistently.
status_search_result: Searches indicate that the residual low-energy n+3H discrepancies, in particular for the spin-dependent / coherent scattering lengths, remain an unresolved feature of the four-nucleon problem. Standard local NN+3NF Hamiltonians such as AV18+UIX reproduce the triton binding energy but no single available interaction simultaneously fits all measured n+3H coherent and incoherent scattering lengths; nonlocal models (e.g. INOY) improve some observables but do not fully resolve the issue. Recent reviews and measurements continue to flag this as an open issue in the few-nucleon sector.

paper_title: Four nucleon systems: a zoom to the open problems in nuclear interaction
original_question: Are nucleon-nucleon P-wave interactions, especially neutron-neutron P-waves and their charge dependence, incorrectly constrained in current nuclear interaction models, and can a physically acceptable P-wave correction explain the neutron plus tritium resonance-region disagreement and related failures in neutron-rich or P-wave-sensitive observables? The motivation is that neutron-neutron P-waves are not directly controlled by experiment, that a roughly 20% change in the neutron-neutron P-wave potential would be needed for AV18 to describe the resonance cross sections, and that discrepancies in helium-isotope binding energies grow with neutron excess even when three-nucleon forces improve the overall agreement.
self_contained_problem:
Consider the standard framework of low-energy nuclear physics in which two nucleons (proton p and neutron n) interact via a charge-dependent nucleon-nucleon (NN) potential decomposed into partial waves, supplemented when needed by a three-nucleon force (3NF). A widely used realistic potential of this kind (e.g. of the AV18 type) is fit primarily to proton-proton (pp) and neutron-proton (np) scattering data plus the deuteron, with charge-symmetry/charge-independence breaking used to infer neutron-neutron (nn) partial waves. Because no direct free nn scattering experiments exist, the nn P-wave components are not directly constrained by data; meanwhile pp P-waves at low energy are masked by the Coulomb repulsion.

Investigate the following questions:

(a) Are the NN P-wave interactions in current realistic NN potentials — in particular the nn ¹P₁, ³P₀, ³P₁, ³P₂ components and their charge dependence relative to pp and np — incorrectly constrained, in the sense that the present treatment of charge dependence in P-waves is insufficient to reproduce P-wave-sensitive observables in light nuclei?

(b) Does there exist a physically acceptable modification of the nn P-wave potential (i.e. a modification consistent with all directly measured NN data, with charge-symmetry-breaking expectations, and with deuteron and few-body bound-state properties) that simultaneously
 (i) brings calculations of the n + ³H elastic cross section in the resonance region into agreement with measurement,
 (ii) accounts for the systematic, approximately linear growth with neutron excess of the discrepancy between computed and measured helium-isotope binding energies that persists after inclusion of standard 3NFs, and
 (iii) is compatible with (or helps resolve) the nucleon-deuteron vector analyzing-power (Aᵧ) puzzle?

Quantitatively, determine whether a change of order 20% in the nn P-wave potential strength needed to reproduce the n + ³H resonance cross section with an AV18-type interaction is admissible as genuine charge dependence in the P-waves (noting that only of order 6–8% modification of NN P-waves is typically associated with the Aᵧ puzzle), or whether such a large modification must instead be attributed to missing many-nucleon dynamics.
status_search_result: Web searches indicate the Aᵧ puzzle and discrepancies in P-wave-sensitive few-nucleon observables remain unresolved. Progress with chiral N²LO three-nucleon forces and optimized chiral interactions has reduced but not eliminated the Aᵧ discrepancy, and no consensus exists on whether modifying nn P-waves (in particular as charge-dependence effects) suffices to remove the n + ³H resonance disagreement and the linear growth of helium-isotope binding-energy errors with neutron excess. The status is therefore best characterized as open.

paper_title: Hadronic production of η–mesons: recent results and open questions
original_question: What, if any, is the relationship between the two proposed explanations of the unexpectedly low Roper resonance in the light-baryon spectrum: the picture in which the Roper resonance is dynamically generated and P11(1710) is the first quark state, and the picture in which a flavor-dependent quark-quark interaction changes the ordering of states? A satisfactory answer should also address how the situation changes if chiral dynamics really makes S11(1535) a dynamically generated state, because that would worsen the disagreement between the low-lying baryon spectrum and the original nonrelativistic quark-model ordering.
self_contained_problem:
Consider the light-baryon spectrum of QCD, with particular focus on the low-lying nucleon resonances: the Roper resonance N(1440) with quantum numbers P11, the P11(1710), and the negative-parity S11(1535). In the original nonrelativistic constituent quark model, the lowest positive-parity radial excitation of the nucleon is predicted to lie above the lowest negative-parity excitation, in conflict with the observed ordering in which the Roper N(1440) lies below the S11(1535). Two distinct theoretical pictures have been proposed to resolve this discrepancy:

(A) A "dynamically generated" picture in which the Roper N(1440) is not a genuine three-quark state but arises as a meson–baryon quasi-bound state generated by coupled-channel hadronic dynamics, and in which the first genuine radial three-quark excitation of the nucleon is identified instead with P11(1710).

(B) A "modified quark–quark interaction" picture in which the Roper N(1440) remains a genuine three-quark state, but a flavor-dependent (e.g. Goldstone-boson-exchange-type) quark–quark interaction is introduced into the constituent quark model so as to reorder the radial and orbital excitations and place the P11 nucleon excitation below the S11.

Determine whether there is a precise mathematical/dynamical relationship between pictures (A) and (B): for instance, whether one can be derived as an effective limit or rearrangement of the other, whether they make distinguishable predictions for observables (such as electromagnetic transition form factors, decay couplings, or large-N_c scaling), or whether they are genuinely inequivalent descriptions of the same spectrum. In the analysis, address also the scenario in which chiral coupled-channel dynamics generates S11(1535) itself as a dynamically generated (e.g. KΣ–ηN) state, and explain how each picture must be modified to accommodate this, including the assignment of the lowest genuine three-quark negative-parity nucleon excitation in that case.
status_search_result: The nature of the Roper resonance — genuine three-quark state versus dynamically generated meson–baryon structure — and its relation to flavor-dependent quark-interaction models and to a possibly dynamically generated S11(1535) remains an active debate. Recent lattice QCD, Dyson–Schwinger/Faddeev, and coupled-channel studies (e.g. 2017–2026) give differing answers, and a survey from 2026 explicitly describes the Roper as "still controversial 60 years later." No unified reconciliation of the two pictures has been established.

original_question: What mechanism explains the failure of models that reproduce the total pp → pp eta cross section to reproduce the pp invariant-mass spectrum near threshold? paper_title: Hadronic production of η–mesons: recent results and open questions
original_question: How can experiments determine the sign of the real part of the eta-nucleus scattering length, rather than only its magnitude, so that a near-threshold eta-nucleus pole can be classified as a bound state or a virtual state? The problem requires high-accuracy measurements of the eta-nucleus amplitude both above threshold, where observables are sensitive to the magnitude of the real part, and below threshold through inelastic channels that couple significantly to the eta-nucleus channel.
self_contained_problem:
Consider an eta meson interacting with a nucleus, characterized at low energies by a complex s-wave scattering length a = Re(a) + i Im(a). The near-threshold structure of the eta-nucleus amplitude may contain a pole; depending on the sign of Re(a), this pole corresponds either to a true bound state (negative Re(a) in the standard convention) or to a virtual (unbound) state. Observables for elastic eta-nucleus scattering at center-of-mass energies above the eta-nucleus threshold are sensitive to |Re(a)| and |Im(a)| but, because they depend only on |a|^2-like combinations near threshold, are insensitive to the sign of Re(a). The sign of Im(a) is fixed by unitarity.

Devise an experimentally realizable program of measurements that uniquely determines the sign of Re(a) for a given eta-nucleus system, thereby classifying the near-threshold pole as a bound state or a virtual state. Specifically:

(a) Identify what observables of the eta-nucleus amplitude must be measured above threshold to fix the magnitudes |Re(a)| and |Im(a)| with high accuracy.

(b) Identify a set of inelastic hadronic channels which couple strongly to the eta-nucleus channel and whose amplitudes, analytically continued below the eta-nucleus threshold, retain measurable sensitivity to the eta-nucleus scattering length, and explain how the energy dependence of these inelastic observables across the eta threshold (cusp/threshold behavior) can be used to extract the sign of Re(a).

(c) Provide an analytic framework (e.g., a coupled-channel or Flatté-type parametrization) showing rigorously that the combined above-threshold and below-threshold data determine the sign of Re(a) uniquely, and quantify the experimental precision required to distinguish a bound state from a virtual state for light nuclear targets (such as 3He and 4He) where existing theoretical predictions disagree on whether a bound state exists.
status_search_result: Recent reviews and theoretical work (2021–2024) continue to address the discrimination between near-threshold bound and virtual states in eta-nucleus systems via complex scattering length analyses, with calculations disagreeing on whether light nuclei (3He, 4He) support genuine eta-mesic bound states. No conclusive experimental determination of the sign of Re(a) for eta-light-nucleus systems has been established, indicating the problem remains open.

paper_title: Hadronic production of η–mesons: recent results and open questions
original_question: Is the energy dependence of the eta-helium-3 interaction largely governed by the interaction of the eta meson with the deuteron substructure inside helium-3? This question is motivated by the observed similarity between eta-deuteron and eta-helium-3 interaction energy dependences when both are plotted using cross-section-derived final-state-interaction amplitudes.
self_contained_problem:
Consider the strong interaction between an η meson and a light nucleus. For a near-threshold production reaction X → Y η on a target with final-state nucleus Y, one can extract an η–Y "final-state-interaction (FSI) amplitude" from the measured total cross section by dividing out the appropriate phase-space and primary-production factors, thereby isolating the energy dependence due to η–Y rescattering. Empirically, when this FSI amplitude is plotted as a function of the η center-of-mass momentum (or excess energy Q) for the η–d system (extracted, e.g., from pn → dη) and for the η–³He system (extracted, e.g., from dp → ³He η), the two curves exhibit a strikingly similar energy dependence near threshold, including a rapid rise consistent with a large η-nucleus scattering length.

Regarding ³He as a three-nucleon bound state with a significant deuteron-like (np) substructure plus a spectator proton, formulate and decide the following question:

Is the energy dependence of the η–³He interaction near threshold predominantly governed by the interaction of the η meson with the deuteron (np) substructure inside ³He? More precisely, does there exist a quantitative model in which the η–³He near-threshold scattering amplitude factorizes (up to a slowly varying spectator factor) through an η–d subamplitude in such a way that the observed coincidence of energy dependences of the η–d and η–³He FSI amplitudes is reproduced, and is this mechanism in fact the dominant one?
category_tag: Eta-nucleus interactions and few-body hadronic physics
status_search_result: Recent reviews and experimental works on η³He near-threshold dynamics (including the search for η-mesic helium) continue to discuss the strong η³He final-state interaction and the role of the deuteron substructure, but no consensus quantitative derivation establishes that the η–³He energy dependence is dominantly due to η–d rescattering. The production mechanism remains characterized as "poorly understood," indicating the conjecture is not settled.

paper_title: Open questions and perspectives for hadron electromagnetic form factors in space-like and time-like regions.
context_brief: Unified proton and neutron form-factor models across space-like and time-like regions
original_question: Can nucleon electromagnetic form factor models be constructed or identified that reproduce the full set of proton and neutron electric and magnetic form factors in both the space-like scattering region, where the virtual-photon momentum transfer satisfies t = -Q^2 < 0 and the form factors are real functions of Q^2, and the time-like annihilation region e+ + e- ↔ nucleon + antinucleon, where q^2 = -Q^2 > 0 and the form factors are complex?
self_contained_problem:
Let $G_E^p(q^2), G_M^p(q^2), G_E^n(q^2), G_M^n(q^2)$ denote the Sachs electric and magnetic form factors of the proton and neutron, viewed as functions of the squared four-momentum transfer $q^2$ carried by a virtual photon coupling to the nucleon. In the space-like region $q^2 = -Q^2 < 0$, accessible through elastic electron–nucleon scattering, these form factors are real-valued functions of $Q^2$. In the time-like region $q^2 > 0$, accessible through annihilation processes such as $e^+ e^- \leftrightarrow N\bar{N}$ above threshold $q^2 \geq 4 M_N^2$, the form factors become complex-valued analytic functions, related to the space-like values by analytic continuation and constrained by causality, analyticity, and unitarity (with imaginary parts arising from on-shell intermediate hadronic states).

Construct, or determine whether there exists, a single theoretical model (parametrization) of the four nucleon Sachs form factors $G_{E,M}^{p,n}(q^2)$ that simultaneously reproduces, within experimental uncertainties, the full body of measured data in both the space-like region (proton and neutron, electric and magnetic) and the time-like region (modulus and, where available, phase or ratio $|G_E/G_M|$ of proton and neutron form factors), respecting the standard analyticity and asymptotic constraints (including perturbative QCD scaling at large $|q^2|$ and the correct normalizations $G_E^p(0)=1$, $G_M^p(0)=\mu_p$, $G_E^n(0)=0$, $G_M^n(0)=\mu_n$).
status_search_result: Several models (extended Lomon–Gari–Krümpelmann vector-meson-dominance fits, two-component quark-core plus meson-cloud parametrizations, and extended VMD models with analyticity/unitarity constraints) have been proposed and provide unified fits of proton and neutron electromagnetic form factors in both space-like and time-like regions with reasonable success. However, tensions remain (e.g., oscillatory features in the time-like region, neutron time-like data, and the proton $|G_E/G_M|$ ratio), so the question is partially solved rather than fully resolved.

paper_title: Open questions and perspectives for hadron electromagnetic form factors in space-like and time-like regions.
context_brief: Onset of asymptotic behavior of electromagnetic form factors
original_question: At what momentum-transfer scale do hadron or nucleon electromagnetic form factors reach their asymptotic regime, so that one can test both QCD-inspired asymptotic expectations and the analytic Phragmén-Lindelöf constraint that a form factor has the same limiting value in the space-like limit q^2 → -∞ and in the time-like limit q^2 → +∞?
self_contained_problem:
Let F(q^2) denote a hadron (in particular nucleon) electromagnetic form factor, regarded as an analytic function of the four-momentum transfer squared q^2 in the complex plane, with the space-like region corresponding to q^2 < 0 and the time-like region to q^2 > 0. The Phragmén–Lindelöf theorem, applied to such an analytic function, asserts that, provided F is bounded along suitable rays, its limiting values in the space-like and time-like asymptotic directions coincide:

   lim_{q^2 → -∞} F_{SL}(q^2) = lim_{q^2 → +∞} F_{TL}(q^2).

Perturbative QCD also predicts a definite asymptotic scaling behavior (for example, a Dirac form factor falling as 1/Q^4 up to logarithms, with the Pauli form factor suppressed by an additional 1/Q^2).

Problem. Determine the momentum-transfer scale Q^2 = |q^2| at which the electromagnetic form factors of hadrons, and of the nucleon in particular, actually enter their asymptotic regime, i.e. the scale above which both
  (a) the QCD-inspired asymptotic scaling predictions, and
  (b) the Phragmén–Lindelöf equality of the space-like and time-like limits
become quantitatively valid for the measured space-like and time-like form factors.
status_search_result: Recent literature (dispersion-theoretical analyses, vector-meson-dominance fits, and time-like measurements such as those probing oscillating features of the nucleon form factors) continues to investigate the onset of asymptotic behavior and the Phragmén–Lindelöf equality between space-like and time-like limits. Current data show that even at the highest accessible Q^2 the predicted asymptotic regime has not been clearly reached, and the space-like and time-like form factors still differ markedly. The question of the precise scale of onset thus remains an open experimental and theoretical issue.

context_brief: Time-like separation of form factors and phase measurement
original_question: Can time-like-region measurements in e+e− annihilation or proton-antiproton reactions separately determine the electric and magnetic proton and neutron form factors, and can time-like polarization observables such as A_y and A_xz, which contain respectively the imaginary and real parts of G_E G_M*, determine the relative phase between the complex time-like electric and magnetic form factors?
self_contained_problem:
Consider the electromagnetic form factors of the nucleon (proton and neutron), defined through the matrix element of the electromagnetic current between nucleon states and parametrized by the Sachs electric and magnetic form factors G_E(q^2) and G_M(q^2). In the space-like region (q^2 < 0) these are real functions of q^2, while in the time-like region (q^2 > 0, accessible through reactions such as e^+ e^- → N \bar N or \bar p p → e^+ e^-) they are complex analytic functions and acquire a relative phase.

(a) Devise an experimental and theoretical procedure based on time-like measurements in e^+ e^- annihilation and/or proton–antiproton reactions that separately determines |G_E^p|, |G_M^p|, |G_E^n|, |G_M^n| as functions of q^2, rather than only effective combinations.

(b) Show that the single-spin polarization observable A_y (the analyzing power normal to the scattering plane) and the double-spin observable A_xz are proportional, respectively, to Im(G_E G_M^*) and Re(G_E G_M^*) in the time-like region, and use these observables to determine the relative phase between G_E(q^2) and G_M(q^2) as a complex function of q^2 above threshold.

context_brief: Possible subthreshold nucleon-antinucleon resonance explaining time-like form factors
original_question: Are nucleon electromagnetic form factors systematically larger in the time-like region than in the space-like region because of a narrow nucleon-antinucleon resonance located just below the nucleon-antinucleon threshold?
self_contained_problem:
Let $G_E^N(q^2)$ and $G_M^N(q^2)$ denote the Sachs electric and magnetic electromagnetic form factors of a nucleon $N$ (proton or neutron), considered as analytic functions of the squared four-momentum transfer $q^2$. For space-like momentum transfer ($q^2 < 0$), these form factors are measured in elastic electron–nucleon scattering. For time-like momentum transfer ($q^2 \ge 4 m_N^2$, where $m_N$ is the nucleon mass), they are accessed through reactions such as $e^+ e^- \leftrightarrow N \bar N$. Empirical data indicate that, when compared at $|q^2|$ values of comparable magnitude, the moduli $|G^N(q^2)|$ in the time-like region are systematically larger than the corresponding values in the space-like region.

Determine whether this systematic enhancement of the time-like nucleon electromagnetic form factors relative to their space-like counterparts can be explained by the existence of a narrow resonance in the nucleon–antinucleon ($N\bar N$) system located just below the $N\bar N$ production threshold $q^2 = 4 m_N^2$. Specifically: does such a narrow subthreshold $N\bar N$ resonance exist, and if so, does it quantitatively account for the observed space-like/time-like asymmetry of $G_E^N$ and $G_M^N$?
status_search_result: Recent literature (through 2024–2025) on nucleon electromagnetic form factors continues to discuss the enhancement of time-like form factors over space-like ones and proposes a possible narrow $N\bar N$ subthreshold resonance as one explanation, alongside competing accounts based on final-state $N\bar N$ interactions (e.g., chiral EFT distorted-wave Born approximation) and extended vector-meson-dominance models with oscillatory structures. No definitive experimental confirmation of such a narrow subthreshold resonance has been established, and dispersion-theoretical analyses still list this as an open question requiring dedicated threshold-region measurements.

context_brief: Total Fenchel instability for pairs of proper convex functions.
original_question: Does there exist a nonzero finite-dimensional Banach space E together with proper convex functions f and g on E such that the pair (f, g) is totally Fenchel unstable; that is, the pair satisfies Fenchel duality, meaning that there exists z* in E* with f*(-z*) + g*(z*) = (f + g)*(0), and whenever y* and z* in E* satisfy f*(y*) + g*(z*) = (f + g)*(y* + z*), one necessarily has y* + z* = 0?
self_contained_problem:

Denote by $\mathrm{PC}(E)$ the class of proper convex functions $f:E\to(-\infty,+\infty]$, and for $f\in\mathrm{PC}(E)$ let $f^*:E^*\to(-\infty,+\infty]$ be its Fenchel conjugate, defined by $f^*(x^*)=\sup_{x\in E}\{\langle x^*,x\rangle - f(x)\}$.

A pair $(f,g)$ with $f,g\in\mathrm{PC}(E)$ is said to satisfy Fenchel duality if there exists $z^*\in E^*$ such that
$$f^*(-z^*)+g^*(z^*)=(f+g)^*(0).$$
The pair $(f,g)$ is called totally Fenchel unstable if it satisfies Fenchel duality and, whenever $y^*,z^*\in E^*$ satisfy
$$f^*(y^*)+g^*(z^*)=(f+g)^*(y^*+z^*),$$
one necessarily has $y^*+z^*=0$.

Question: Does there exist a nonzero finite-dimensional Banach space $E$ and proper convex functions $f,g\in\mathrm{PC}(E)$ such that the pair $(f,g)$ is totally Fenchel unstable?

original_question: For Minkowski space-time R1,n, interpret temporal distance 1 as one generation of proper time. For two events $A=(t_A,\mathbf{x}_A)$ and $B=(t_B,\mathbf{x}_B)$ with $Q(B-A) > 0$ (i.e. timelike separated), define the proper time between them as
$$\tau(A,B) \;=\; \sqrt{(t_B-t_A)^2 - \|\mathbf{x}_B-\mathbf{x}_A\|^2}.$$
Define the temporal chromatic number $\chi_\tau(\mathbb{R}^{1,n})$ to be the smallest cardinal $k$ such that there exists a coloring $c:\mathbb{R}^{1,n}\to\{1,2,\dots,k\}$ with the property that $c(A)\neq c(B)$ whenever $\tau(A,B)=1$.

paper_title: Open Problems for Painlevé Equations
original_question: Given an ordinary differential equation whose solutions have the Painlevé property, determine whether the equation can be expressed in terms of one of the Painlevé transcendents or an associated Painlevé sigma-equation, and if so identify the correct Painlevé equation together with the transformation needed to convert the given equation into that standard form.
self_contained_problem:
An ordinary differential equation is said to have the Painlevé property if every movable singularity of every solution (i.e., a singularity whose location depends on the initial conditions) is a pole. The six Painlevé equations P_I, P_II, ..., P_VI are the canonical second-order nonlinear ODEs (over the complex domain) whose general solutions have the Painlevé property and cannot, in general, be expressed in terms of classical special functions; their solutions are called Painlevé transcendents. To each Painlevé equation P_J there is an associated sigma-equation (Okamoto's auxiliary Hamiltonian form), a second-order ODE whose solutions are the Hamiltonians σ(t) along solutions of P_J.

Develop an algorithmic procedure for the following Painlevé equivalence problem. Given as input an ordinary differential equation
   F(t, y, y', y'', ..., y^{(n)}) = 0
which is known to possess the Painlevé property, decide:
 (1) whether its general solution can be expressed in terms of one of the six Painlevé transcendents (or, equivalently, in terms of an associated Painlevé sigma-equation);
 (2) if so, determine which Painlevé equation P_J (J ∈ {I, II, III, IV, V, VI}) — or which sigma-equation — it corresponds to; and
 (3) construct an explicit transformation (e.g. a change of dependent and independent variables, possibly together with auxiliary algebraic operations) that converts the given equation into the chosen standard Painlevé form.

Produce such an algorithm, or prove that no algorithm with these specifications exists.
status_search_result: The Painlevé equivalence problem is widely recognized as open in general. Recent work (2025) proposes step-by-step algorithmic procedures using the algebro-geometric theory of Okamoto's spaces of initial conditions and applies them to particular families (e.g., Bureau-Guillot systems), but a general algorithmic solution covering all ODEs with the Painlevé property has not been established.

paper_title: Open Problems for Painlevé Equations
original_question: Develop reliable and easy-to-use numerical software for Painlevé equations that improves on generic Runge–Kutta-type ODE solvers by exploiting the integrable structure of these equations, in particular their formulation through isomonodromy and associated Riemann–Hilbert problems, and determine whether integrable discretizations should be used as part of such numerical methods.
self_contained_problem:
The six Painlevé equations P_I, P_II, P_III, P_IV, P_V, P_VI are a distinguished list of second-order nonlinear ordinary differential equations of the form w'' = F(z, w, w'), where F is rational in w and w' and locally analytic in z, characterized by the Painlevé property that all movable singularities of their solutions are poles. Their generic solutions, the Painlevé transcendents, define nonlinear special functions. Each Painlevé equation admits an isomonodromic Lax pair: solutions correspond to monodromy-preserving deformations of an associated linear system, and the Cauchy problem can be linearized through a Riemann–Hilbert problem on a contour in the complex plane with prescribed jump matrices determined by Stokes data. Each Painlevé equation also has integrable discrete analogues (the discrete Painlevé equations), which are integrable difference/q-difference equations whose continuum limits recover the Painlevé equations.

Problem: Design a reliable, easy-to-use numerical method (and supporting software) for computing solutions of the Painlevé equations that improves on generic adaptive Runge–Kutta-type ODE integrators by exploiting the integrable structure of these equations. Specifically:

(a) Develop and analyze a numerical scheme based on the isomonodromy formulation that computes a Painlevé transcendent at a point z by numerically solving the associated Riemann–Hilbert problem with prescribed Stokes/monodromy data, providing rigorous error bounds, robust handling of the movable poles, and uniform accuracy across the complex plane (including near critical points and along Stokes rays).

(b) Determine whether using an integrable discretization (a discrete Painlevé equation that has the given continuous Painlevé equation as a continuum limit) as the underlying time-stepping scheme yields provable advantages—such as preservation of geometric/integrable structure, improved stability near poles, or better long-range accuracy—over standard non-structure-preserving ODE solvers, and either construct such an integrable-discretization-based solver with quantitative comparison to Runge–Kutta methods, or rule out asymptotic advantages.
status_search_result: Partial progress exists: Olver and Trogdon developed spectrally accurate numerical schemes for the Riemann–Hilbert problems associated with Painlevé II and related integrable systems, demonstrating that the isomonodromy/RH approach can outperform standard ODE solvers, especially near poles. However, a comprehensive, reliable, and easy-to-use software suite covering all six Painlevé equations uniformly across the complex plane, along with a definitive comparative assessment of integrable discretizations as solvers, has not been fully achieved.

paper_title: Open Problems in Additive Combinatorics
original_question: For a large positive integer N, what is the largest size of a subset of the interval [1; N], free of three-term arithmetic progressions? The present records are due to Behrend (who constructed in a progression-free set A [1; N], satisfying jAj > N exp( cplog N) with an absolute constant c > 0) and Bourgain (who proved in that if A [1; N] is progression-free, then jAj < CN p log log N= log N with an absolute constant C). Narrow the gap between these estimates.
self_contained_problem:
Let $r_3(N)$ denote the largest cardinality of a subset $A \subseteq \{1, 2, \ldots, N\}$ that contains no three-term arithmetic progression, i.e., no triple $(a, a+d, a+2d)$ with $a \in A$, $a+d \in A$, $a+2d \in A$, and $d \neq 0$. It is known that there exist absolute constants $c > 0$ and $C > 0$ such that, for all sufficiently large positive integers $N$,
$$N \exp\!\big(-c\sqrt{\log N}\,\big) \;<\; r_3(N) \;<\; C\,N\,\sqrt{\frac{\log\log N}{\log N}}.$$
Determine the true asymptotic behavior of $r_3(N)$, narrowing the gap between the lower bound (of Behrend type) and the upper bound (of Bourgain type). In particular, decide whether $r_3(N) = N \exp\!\big(-(\log N)^{1/2 + o(1)}\big)$.
status_search_result: Substantial progress has been made on the upper bound but the problem remains open. Bloom–Sisask (2020) gave the first bound of the form $N/(\log N)^{1+c}$, and in 2023 Kelley and Meka proved $r_3(N) \le N \exp(-c(\log N)^{\beta})$ for an absolute $\beta > 0$ (refined to roughly $\beta = 1/9$ by Bloom–Sisask), which is qualitatively close to Behrend's lower bound $N \exp(-c\sqrt{\log N})$. The exact asymptotic rate, in particular whether Behrend's construction is asymptotically optimal, is still unresolved; a recent (2024) improvement of Behrend's construction has also appeared.

paper_title: Open Problems in Additive Combinatorics
original_question: Obtain reasonable bounds for the Hales- Jewett theorem and for the density version of it.
self_contained_problem:
A combinatorial line in the cube $[k]^n = \{1, 2, \dots, k\}^n$ is a set of $k$ points obtained as follows: fix a string $w \in ([k] \cup \{*\})^n$ that contains at least one wildcard symbol $*$, and for each $i \in [k]$ form the point obtained from $w$ by replacing every $*$ with $i$.

The Hales–Jewett theorem asserts that for every $k \geq 1$ and every $r \geq 1$ there exists an integer $HJ(k,r)$ such that whenever $n \geq HJ(k,r)$, any $r$-coloring of $[k]^n$ contains a monochromatic combinatorial line.

The density Hales–Jewett theorem asserts that for every $k \geq 1$ and every $\delta > 0$ there exists an integer $DHJ(k,\delta)$ such that whenever $n \geq DHJ(k,\delta)$, every subset $A \subseteq [k]^n$ with $|A| \geq \delta k^n$ contains a combinatorial line.

Problem: Obtain reasonable quantitative upper bounds on $HJ(k,r)$ and on $DHJ(k,\delta)$ as functions of their parameters. In particular, determine the correct order of growth of these functions, e.g. whether primitive recursive (or even better) bounds can be achieved for all $k$.
status_search_result: Shelah (1988) gave primitive-recursive (wowzer-type) bounds for the coloring Hales–Jewett theorem. The Polymath project (2009, published Annals 2012) gave the first elementary proof of the density Hales–Jewett theorem with quantitative bounds: a tower-type bound for $k=3$ and Ackermann-type bounds for $k \geq 4$. Obtaining "reasonable" (e.g. primitive recursive uniformly in $k$, or polynomial/exponential) bounds for the density version remains open.

Let G be an abelian group (for instance the integers, a cyclic group, or the additive group of a finite field). Given a finite subset S of G as input, the sumset recognition problem asks to decide whether there exists a subset A of G such that

$$\rho_{A,B}(n):=\#\{(a,b)\in A\times B : a+b=n\},\qquad n\in\mathbb{Z}.$$

original_question: Is it true that for n 7, any n-element set of integers is isomorphic (in Freiman's sense) to a subset of [0; 2n 2]? For any integer n 2 the set f0; 1; 2; 4; : : :; 2n 2g is \linear" (has Freiman's dimension one) and not contained in an arithmetic progression with di erence larger than 1, hence it is not isomorphic to a set of integers of length smaller than 2n 2. It is conjectured in that this is the extremal case; that is, in any class of isomorphic n-element sets there is a set of length at most 2n 2. Note, that all Sidon sets with the same number of elements are isomorphic to each other, and it is well-known that for N large enough the interval [0; N] contains a Sidon set of cardinality about p N. Thus, any n-element Sidon set is isomorphic to a subset of [0; n2(1 + o(1))]. For n 6, however, this n2(1 + o(1)) turns out to be larger, than 2n 2: more precisely, [0; 2n 2] does not contain an n-element Sidon set. This explains the restriction n 7 above.
self_contained_problem:
Two finite sets of integers A and B are called Freiman isomorphic (of order 2) if there is a bijection φ: A → B such that for all a₁,a₂,a₃,a₄ ∈ A one has a₁ + a₂ = a₃ + a₄ if and only if φ(a₁) + φ(a₂) = φ(a₃) + φ(a₄). The length of a finite set of integers S is max S − min S. A finite set of integers is said to have Freiman dimension one if it is Freiman isomorphic to a subset of ℤ (equivalently, of an arithmetic progression with common difference 1) but not to a subset of a higher-dimensional generalized arithmetic progression in a non-degenerate way.

For every integer n ≥ 2, the set {0, 1, 2, 4, 6, …, 2n − 2} (i.e. {0, 1} together with the even numbers up to 2n − 2) has Freiman dimension one, has length 2n − 2, and is not Freiman isomorphic to any set of integers of length smaller than 2n − 2.

Prove or disprove: for every integer n ≥ 7, every n-element set of integers is Freiman isomorphic (in the sense above) to a subset of the interval [0, 2n − 2]. Equivalently, in every Freiman-isomorphism class of n-element integer sets there exists a representative of length at most 2n − 2.

paper_title: Open Problems in Communication and Computation
original_question: What would a comprehensive theory of computational complexity look like?
self_contained_problem:
Formulate a comprehensive mathematical theory of computational complexity. Concretely, propose a unified framework that:

1. Defines a general notion of a computational problem and a model of computation (e.g., Turing machines, Boolean circuits, arithmetic circuits, communication protocols, query/decision trees, quantum circuits, distributed/parallel models), together with associated resource measures (time, space, circuit size and depth, communication, randomness, queries, energy, nonuniformity, etc.).

2. Specifies complexity classes as sets of problems solvable within prescribed bounds on these resources, and defines reductions and completeness in a model-independent way.

3. Provides general principles or axioms (in the spirit of Blum's axioms or abstract complexity) from which the main known separations, hierarchies (time, space, nondeterministic), simulations, and trade-offs follow uniformly, and which permit proofs of unconditional lower bounds for explicit problems.

4. Yields, as theorems within the framework, resolutions of the central open separation questions: P vs NP, NP vs coNP, P vs PSPACE, NL vs P, BPP vs P, BQP vs classical classes, and the existence of one-way functions.

5. Explains and unifies the known barriers (relativization, natural proofs, algebrization) to proving such separations, and identifies which proof techniques can or cannot circumvent them.

The problem is: construct such a theory, prove its internal consistency and explanatory power, and use it to settle at least one of the major separation problems listed above, or prove that no such theory satisfying the stated criteria can exist.
status_search_result: The question is broad and foundational. The central separation problems it asks any such theory to resolve (e.g., P vs NP) remain open as of 2026, and no widely accepted "comprehensive theory of computational complexity" in the stated sense exists; known barrier results (relativization, natural proofs, algebrization) show that current techniques are insufficient.

original_question: Is there a mathematically meaningful notion of energy-free computation, and if so, where do information theory, communication theory, computer science, and physics meet at the atomic level?
self_contained_problem:
Formulate a mathematically rigorous notion of "energy-free computation," i.e., a model of computation in which the execution of an arbitrary computable function (or some suitably large class of computational tasks) can be carried out with zero net energy dissipation, and determine whether such a notion can exist in a meaningful sense. More precisely:

(a) Provide a mathematical framework that unifies the basic objects of information theory (entropy, mutual information, channel capacity), communication theory (encoding, decoding, noise), computer science (computational steps, logical states, reversibility), and physics at the atomic/quantum scale (Hamiltonian dynamics, thermodynamic entropy, Landauer's bound k_B T ln 2 per bit erasure), in which one can speak unambiguously of the energy cost of performing a computation.

(b) Within this framework, decide whether there exists a model of computation, possibly using logically reversible operations or quantum-mechanical evolution, that can perform a universal class of computations with arbitrarily small (or exactly zero) total energy dissipation per logical operation, taking into account the cost of initialization, readout, error correction, and interaction with any environment.

(c) Identify and characterize the precise mathematical meeting point of information theory, communication theory, computability/complexity, and physical law at the atomic scale: state the fundamental laws (analogous to Shannon's channel coding theorem and Landauer's principle) that govern this meeting point, and prove or disprove the existence of an energy-free universal computer.
status_search_result: The question of whether truly energy-free (zero-dissipation) universal computation is achievable remains an active foundational problem at the interface of information theory, computer science, and physics. Landauer's principle (1961) gives a lower bound k_B T ln 2 per irreversible bit erasure, and reversible/quantum computing is the candidate route to circumvent it, but recent work (e.g., 2021 "Quantum Foundations of Classical Reversible Computing" and a 2025 arXiv survey on Landauer's principle and thermodynamics of computation) shows that the precise relationship between logical and thermodynamic reversibility, and the engineering/mathematical feasibility of arbitrarily-low-energy universal computation, are still under investigation and not settled.

paper_title: Open Problems in Communication and Computation
original_question: What is the ultimate impact of algorithmic complexity on probability theory, and what is its relationship to information theory?
self_contained_problem:
For a finite binary string x ∈ {0,1}*, let K(x) denote its prefix-free Kolmogorov complexity, defined as the length of the shortest input to a fixed universal prefix-free Turing machine U such that U outputs x. For an infinite binary sequence ω ∈ {0,1}^ℕ, say that ω is Martin-Löf random with respect to the uniform (fair-coin) measure if there is a constant c such that K(ω↾n) ≥ n − c for all n, where ω↾n denotes the first n bits of ω. Recall that the Shannon entropy of a discrete random variable X with distribution p is H(X) = −Σ_x p(x) log p(x), and that for computable distributions p on {0,1}^n one has the identity E_p[K(X)] = H(X) + O(log n).

Develop a comprehensive theory describing the ultimate impact of algorithmic (Kolmogorov) complexity on classical probability theory, and articulate its precise relationship to Shannon information theory. Concretely:

(a) Identify the largest natural class C of probability statements (e.g. almost-sure laws such as the strong law of large numbers, the law of the iterated logarithm, ergodic theorems, martingale convergence theorems) for which the classical "almost surely" can be replaced by "for every Martin-Löf random sequence" in a uniform effective manner, and characterize the obstruction for statements outside C.

(b) Determine the exact quantitative correspondence between Kolmogorov complexity K and Shannon entropy H beyond the known O(log n) coincidence on computable sources: in particular, give a meaningful interpretation of K-based quantities (algorithmic mutual information I(x:y) = K(x) + K(y) − K(x,y), algorithmic sufficient statistics, the algorithmic minimal sufficient statistic) as limits or refinements of their Shannon counterparts, valid for individual objects rather than ensembles.

(c) Decide whether there is a single unified framework subsuming both classical probability theory and algorithmic information theory in which entropy, complexity, randomness, and typicality are aspects of one underlying invariant.
status_search_result: The question, posed as a broad foundational research direction about the role of Kolmogorov complexity in probability and its links with Shannon information theory, remains open in the sense that no definitive unifying theory has been established. Substantial progress has been made — e.g. Vovk, V'yugin, Shen, Bienvenu, Gács, Hoyrup, Rojas and others have shown that many classical almost-sure laws hold for every Martin-Löf random sequence, and the algorithmic vs. Shannon information correspondence has been deeply studied (Grünwald–Vitányi, Vereshchagin–Vitányi) — but the "ultimate impact" remains an active program rather than a closed chapter.

paper_title: Open Problems in Data-Sharing Peer-to-Peer Systems
original_question: For ranked keyword search over a decentralized peer-to-peer document collection, how can the system collect and maintain the global statistics needed by state-of-the-art ranking functions, such as document-frequency information over the total collection, in a way that is simultaneously robust to failures, efficient in resource usage, and fully distributed?
self_contained_problem:
Consider a peer-to-peer system consisting of a dynamic set of N autonomous nodes, where each node n stores a local collection D_n of text documents and peers may join, leave, or fail at any time. The union D = ⋃_n D_n forms a global document collection. A user issues a keyword query q = (t_1, …, t_k) at some node and expects a ranked list of the top documents from D under a ranking function R(d, q) that depends on global corpus statistics. Specifically, for each term t, let df(t) = |{d ∈ D : t ∈ d}| (the global document frequency) and |D| (the global collection size); typical ranking functions (e.g., TF–IDF or BM25 variants) require values such as idf(t) = log(|D|/df(t)) together with local term frequencies.

Design a fully distributed protocol that, in the presence of node churn and failures, allows every node to obtain, for any query term t, an estimate d̂f(t) of df(t) and an estimate |D̂| of |D| such that:
(a) (Robustness) The protocol continues to provide such estimates with bounded relative error ε with high probability even when an adversarially chosen fraction of nodes fail or depart between updates.
(b) (Efficiency) The expected per-node communication, storage, and computation costs grow sublinearly (ideally polylogarithmically) in N and in |D|.
(c) (Distribution) There is no central coordinator; every node executes the same protocol using only local state and messages exchanged with a bounded number of neighbours.

Provide such a protocol, together with a proof of its accuracy, robustness, and resource bounds, or establish impossibility results showing the optimal achievable trade-offs among (a), (b), and (c).
category_tag: distributed ranking statistics in P2P search
status_search_result: The question is a high-level open challenge about maintaining global IDF-style statistics in decentralized P2P keyword search. Subsequent work (e.g., gossip-based aggregation, distributed sketches, Bloom-filter–based DF estimation, and various P2P IR systems such as MINERVA and Alvis) has proposed partial solutions, but no single protocol is established as a definitive answer satisfying all three desiderata simultaneously. The status is best described as unknown / partially addressed rather than formally solved.

paper_title: Open Problems in Data-Sharing Peer-to-Peer Systems
original_question: Given existing peer-to-peer techniques for COUNT queries over predicates, can those methods be extended to support more expressive aggregate queries, including SUM, MAX, and MEDIAN, over decentralized data-sharing systems?
self_contained_problem:
Consider a decentralized data-sharing system modeled as a peer-to-peer network in which each peer p in a set P stores a local relation R_p over a common schema. For a predicate φ defining a subset S_φ = { t ∈ ⋃_{p∈P} R_p : φ(t) holds } of tuples distributed across the network, suppose there exist distributed protocols that, without centralizing the data and tolerating churn and partial failures, compute the aggregate COUNT(S_φ) = |S_φ| approximately or exactly with bounded message, bandwidth, and round complexity.

The problem is to determine whether such peer-to-peer protocols for COUNT can be generalized to compute the following aggregates over S_φ on a designated numeric attribute a:
  (i) SUM(S_φ) = Σ_{t ∈ S_φ} t.a,
  (ii) MAX(S_φ) = max_{t ∈ S_φ} t.a,
  (iii) MEDIAN(S_φ) = the order statistic of rank ⌈|S_φ|/2⌉ of the multiset { t.a : t ∈ S_φ }.

Specifically, design distributed algorithms that evaluate SUM, MAX, and MEDIAN over a fully decentralized peer-to-peer network, establish their correctness (exact or with provable approximation guarantees), and analyze their communication, computation, and round complexity in the presence of dynamic membership, replication, and possible faulty or adversarial peers.
status_search_result: A targeted search was not performed in detail, but the broader research area of distributed/gossip-based aggregation in peer-to-peer systems has seen substantial work (e.g., gossip aggregation, sketches for SUM, approximate quantiles for MEDIAN, and distributed top-k for MAX). However, whether the specific question of fully extending the referenced COUNT-style techniques to SUM, MAX, and MEDIAN with comparable guarantees has been definitively resolved is unclear, so the status is reported as unknown.

paper_title: Open Problems in Data-Sharing Peer-to-Peer Systems
original_question: Can one develop peer-to-peer search techniques that improve on the apparent tradeoffs among peer autonomy, search efficiency, and robustness, so that a system does not have to give up as much autonomy or resilience in order to obtain practical search performance?
self_contained_problem:
Consider a peer-to-peer data-sharing system modeled as a dynamic network of autonomous nodes, each storing a local collection of data items. A search technique is a distributed protocol by which any node may issue a query and receive matching data items (or pointers to them) held by other nodes. Three qualitative properties of such a protocol are of interest:

1. Peer autonomy: the degree to which each node may independently decide which data it stores, which other nodes it connects to, when it joins or leaves, and how it routes or answers queries, without being forced into a globally imposed structure.
2. Search efficiency: small expected message complexity, low latency, and high recall/precision of queries, measured as a function of the number of nodes N and the data distribution.
3. Robustness: the protocol continues to deliver correct query answers under high churn (frequent joins/leaves), node failures, and adversarial behavior.

Existing classes of techniques exhibit apparent tradeoffs: structured overlays (e.g., distributed hash tables) achieve high efficiency and robustness but constrain autonomy by dictating data placement and topology; unstructured flooding/random-walk overlays preserve autonomy and robustness but scale poorly; hybrid and hierarchical schemes mitigate but do not eliminate these tensions.

Problem. Design a peer-to-peer search protocol, together with a formal model of autonomy, efficiency, and robustness, that provably improves on the current Pareto frontier of these three properties. Specifically, exhibit a protocol whose performance triple (autonomy, efficiency, robustness) strictly dominates that achievable by any structured-overlay or unstructured-overlay scheme in the same model, or prove that no such protocol exists by establishing a three-way lower-bound tradeoff.
status_search_result: The question is a broad research direction rather than a precise conjecture, and no single result definitively resolves it. Research on DHTs, unstructured overlays, semantic overlays, and gossip-based search has continued to push individual tradeoffs but no work appears to claim a definitive Pareto-dominating solution or a formal three-way impossibility theorem. Status is best classified as unknown/open in spirit.

paper_title: Open Problems in Data-Sharing Peer-to-Peer Systems
original_question: Is it possible to decouple peer autonomy from robustness in a peer-to-peer search mechanism, so that the system designer can vary autonomy independently while still preserving stable service under node failures and departures?
self_contained_problem:
Consider a peer-to-peer search system modeled as a dynamic network of autonomous nodes that may join, leave, or fail at arbitrary times. Each node independently decides which other nodes to connect to, what queries to forward, and what local resources to share; the degree of "autonomy" of the design is a parameter measuring how freely each node may make these decisions without coordination from a central authority or fixed protocol-imposed constraints. The "robustness" of the system is a parameter measuring the stability of its search service — for example, the probability that queries are answered correctly within a bounded number of hops — under adversarial schedules of node failures and departures.

Question: Does there exist a peer-to-peer search mechanism, together with a formal model of the above kind, in which the autonomy parameter and the robustness parameter can be tuned independently? More precisely, is it possible to design a search mechanism whose autonomy level can be increased or decreased by the system designer while a chosen robustness guarantee continues to hold, and conversely whose robustness can be strengthened without forcing a reduction in node autonomy?
status_search_result: Web search did not surface a definitive resolution. The literature on P2P search continues to discuss tradeoffs among autonomy, robustness, and efficiency, with various mechanisms aiming to preserve local autonomy while improving resilience, but no result establishes a clean independent decoupling of the two as a general design principle.

paper_title: Open Problems in Data-Sharing Peer-to-Peer Systems
original_question: For decentralized partial-search peer-to-peer systems, does there exist a general search technique that can guarantee, with high probability, that the tradeoff between resource cost and the chosen quality-of-service metric is optimal?
self_contained_problem:
Consider a decentralized peer-to-peer system modeled as a dynamic network of nodes, where each node stores a subset of data items and communicates only with a bounded number of neighbors. A partial-search algorithm is a distributed protocol that, given a query for a data item, terminates after locating some (not necessarily all) copies of the item in the network. Associated with such an algorithm are two measures: a resource cost C (e.g., total number of messages exchanged, bandwidth consumed, or nodes visited) and a quality-of-service metric Q (e.g., probability of locating a copy, search latency, or fraction of available copies discovered). For a given workload and network model, a (C, Q) pair is called Pareto-optimal if no algorithm achieves strictly better cost without degrading Q, and vice versa.

Question: Does there exist a general (universal) decentralized partial-search technique that, for every reasonable choice of quality-of-service metric Q and every workload/network instance from a broad class, achieves with high probability a (cost, QoS) tradeoff that is Pareto-optimal?

Either exhibit such a general technique together with a proof of its optimality, or prove that no such universal technique exists.
status_search_result: No specific resolution of this general question about a universal optimal cost/QoS tradeoff technique for decentralized partial-search peer-to-peer systems was located. The question remains posed as an open challenge with no evidence of a definitive solution.
