paper_title: Open Problems in Data-Sharing Peer-to-Peer Systems
original_question: Can peer-to-peer protocols be designed so that they do not introduce new amplification mechanisms or back-door communication channels that attackers can exploit to scale and coordinate denial-of-service attacks?
self_contained_problem:
Consider a peer-to-peer (P2P) overlay network: a distributed system in which autonomous nodes (peers) communicate directly with one another over an underlying packet-switched network (such as the Internet) to share data, route lookups, and forward messages, without relying on a fixed centralized server. A P2P protocol specifies (i) how peers join and leave the overlay, (ii) how they discover and maintain connections to other peers, (iii) how queries, requests, and responses are forwarded, and (iv) how data is published, located, and retrieved.

For such a protocol, define the following adversarial notions:

1. An amplification mechanism is any protocol feature that allows an attacker who sends a request of size s (in bytes, or in number of packets) and consumes effort e (CPU, bandwidth, or state) to cause one or more honest peers, or the protocol as a whole, to generate aggregate traffic of size S ≫ s or effort E ≫ e directed at a target chosen by the attacker. The amplification factor is the ratio S/s (or E/e). A protocol is said to introduce a new amplification mechanism (relative to the bare underlying network) if there exists an attacker strategy whose amplification factor, when measured against a chosen victim (which may be a peer, a non-participant host, or a network link), is strictly larger than what the same attacker could achieve by direct use of the underlying network.

2. A back-door communication channel is any protocol-induced capability that enables an attacker to relay, indirect, or coordinate messages among compromised or colluding nodes (or to reach a victim) in a way that is not available, or is significantly harder to achieve, using the underlying network alone. This includes using overlay routing, caches, or forwarding rules to obscure the origin of attack traffic, to synchronize distributed attackers, or to bypass network-level filtering.

A denial-of-service (DoS) attack against a target T is any attacker strategy that renders T (a peer, a host outside the overlay, or a network resource) unable to provide its normal service to legitimate users for a sustained period.

Problem. Design a P2P protocol Π satisfying the following properties simultaneously, or prove that no such protocol exists:

(a) Functionality: Π supports the standard primitives of a data-sharing P2P system, namely peer join/leave, peer discovery, key-based lookup, and data publication/retrieval, with performance (latency, lookup cost, maintenance overhead) within a constant factor of known efficient overlays.

(b) No new amplification: There exists a constant c ≥ 1 such that for every polynomial-time adversary controlling any constant fraction of peers and any chosen victim T, the amplification factor obtainable via Π (in bandwidth and in computational effort) is at most c. In particular, Π must not enable amplification factors that grow with the size of the overlay.

(c) No back-door channels: For every polynomial-time adversary, any covert relaying, indirection, or coordination capability obtainable through Π can be simulated, up to polynomial overhead, by an adversary with only direct access to the underlying network; equivalently, Π provides no protocol-level capability that materially assists an attacker in scaling or coordinating a DoS attack beyond what is possible at the network layer.

(d) Robustness: Properties (b) and (c) must hold under realistic adversarial conditions, including Sybil identities, churn, and partial compromise of peers.

Either exhibit a concrete protocol Π meeting (a)–(d) together with a rigorous proof of (b)–(d), or establish an impossibility result showing that any protocol satisfying (a) must violate (b), (c), or (d).
status_search_result: The question of designing P2P protocols that avoid introducing amplification vectors and covert relaying/coordination channels usable for DoS remains an active and unresolved research direction. Surveys on P2P DoS/DDoS and amplification (e.g., DNS, Memcached, BitTorrent DHT, and structured overlay amplification studies) continue to report new amplification vectors in deployed overlays, and no general protocol or impossibility result is known that settles the question in the form posed. Hence the problem appears to remain open.

paper_title: Open Problems in Data-Sharing Peer-to-Peer Systems
original_question: Can techniques inspired by fail-stop or Byzantine-failure handling be adapted so that they become acceptable for peer-to-peer systems from both the performance and security standpoints, despite high message overhead, complexity, and the lack of secure complete pairwise connectivity?
self_contained_problem:
Consider a peer-to-peer (P2P) distributed system consisting of a large, dynamic set of autonomous nodes that join and leave the network without central coordination. Nodes communicate by message passing over an overlay network in which secure, complete pairwise connectivity among all participants is not available, individual nodes may exhibit fail-stop behavior (halting unexpectedly) or Byzantine behavior (deviating arbitrarily and possibly maliciously from the prescribed protocol), and message overhead and protocol complexity directly impact system performance.

Classical fault-tolerance techniques developed for fail-stop and Byzantine-failure models in tightly coupled distributed systems (such as state-machine replication via Byzantine agreement, quorum-based replication, and cryptographic group protocols) typically assume reliable channels, bounded participant sets, and authenticated all-to-all communication, and they incur high message and computational overhead.

Problem: Design protocols, or prove impossibility results, for adapting fail-stop and Byzantine-failure fault-tolerance techniques to the P2P setting described above so that the resulting mechanisms are simultaneously:
(i) acceptable in performance, i.e., the message complexity, latency, and computational cost scale to large dynamic populations of peers; and
(ii) acceptable in security, i.e., they tolerate a non-trivial fraction of Byzantine peers in the absence of secure complete pairwise connectivity.

Specifically, exhibit a Byzantine-tolerant P2P protocol that provides guarantees analogous to classical Byzantine agreement or replicated state machines while meeting (i) and (ii), or establish lower bounds showing such guarantees are unattainable in the P2P model.
category_tag: Byzantine fault tolerance in peer-to-peer systems
status_search_result: The question is a broad open research direction rather than a single precise conjecture. Substantial progress has been made on Byzantine fault tolerance in P2P/overlay networks (e.g., Castro–Liskov BFT, secure overlay routing by Castro et al., S-Chord, sybil-resilient DHTs, and more recent BFT protocols underlying blockchain systems), but no single result resolves the general goal of fully performant and secure adaptation. Status is best characterized as unknown / ongoing research.

paper_title: Open Problems in Data-Sharing Peer-to-Peer Systems
original_question: Given a user query and a set of returned documents in a peer-to-peer system, how can the system determine which returned documents are the authentic matches to that query, that is, what the authentic signature or set of authentic signatures should be for the documents satisfying the query?
self_contained_problem:
Consider a peer-to-peer file-sharing system modeled as follows. Let $\mathcal{D}$ be a (possibly very large, distributed) collection of documents held by participating peers, and let $\mathcal{Q}$ be a space of admissible queries. For each query $q \in \mathcal{Q}$, define the set $A(q) \subseteq \mathcal{D}$ of documents that are the genuine, intended matches for $q$ (the "authentic" answer set). Each document $d \in \mathcal{D}$ has an associated cryptographic-style signature $\sigma(d)$ drawn from a signature space $\Sigma$, but peers may return spurious, corrupted, mislabeled, or adversarially substituted documents in response to $q$.

When a user issues query $q$ and receives a multiset $R(q) \subseteq \mathcal{D}$ of returned documents from the network, design and analyze a mechanism that determines which elements of $R(q)$ belong to $A(q)$. Equivalently, specify (a) what the authentic signature, or authentic set of signatures, $S^*(q) \subseteq \Sigma$ should be for documents satisfying $q$, and (b) a verification procedure $V \colon \mathcal{Q} \times \mathcal{D} \to \{0,1\}$ such that $V(q,d) = 1$ if and only if $d \in A(q)$, without requiring a trusted central authority and while tolerating malicious peers. Prove correctness and analyze the resource (communication, storage, computation, trust) requirements of any proposed scheme, or alternatively prove impossibility results delineating which query classes $\mathcal{Q}$ and adversary models admit such an authenticity mechanism.
status_search_result: File authenticity in decentralized peer-to-peer systems remains an active research area, addressed with partial solutions such as content-addressable hashing, Merkle DAGs (IPFS), reputation systems, and blockchain-based provenance, but no general solution exists that handles arbitrary semantic queries with adversarial peers and no trusted authority. The problem as posed (binding authentic signatures to query semantics rather than to bitwise identity) is generally regarded as open.

paper_title: Open Problems in Data-Sharing Peer-to-Peer Systems
original_question: Can a peer-to-peer data-sharing system provide meaningful anonymity guarantees while also maintaining efficiency, decentralization, and the ability of peers to discover one another and locate content?
self_contained_problem:
Consider a peer-to-peer data-sharing system modeled as a dynamic distributed network in which a set of autonomous peers store data objects and respond to queries from other peers. Each peer may act as a publisher, a requester, or a forwarder. Define the following desiderata for such a system:

(1) Anonymity: there exists a precise indistinguishability-style guarantee (for example, publisher anonymity, requester anonymity, and/or unlinkability between requesters and the content they retrieve) that holds against a global passive adversary, or at least against an adversary that controls a constant fraction of peers and observes all network traffic adjacent to those peers.

(2) Efficiency: queries are resolved using poly-logarithmic (in the number of peers and objects) communication, latency, and per-peer storage and bandwidth overhead.

(3) Decentralization: no peer or fixed set of peers is required to participate in every query or to hold global state; all operations are symmetric across peers up to local resources.

(4) Peer discovery and content location: any peer can, starting from limited local knowledge, discover other participating peers and successfully locate any content that is published in the system, with high probability.

Question: Does there exist a protocol for such a peer-to-peer data-sharing system that simultaneously satisfies properties (1), (2), (3), and (4), or is there an inherent trade-off (provable lower bound) showing that some pair among anonymity, efficiency, decentralization, and discoverability cannot be jointly achieved?
status_search_result: Combining strong anonymity with efficiency, decentralization, and peer/content discovery in P2P systems remains an active open research challenge. Anonymous P2P designs (Freenet, Tarzan, Tor-based overlays, Dissent, Riposte, etc.) continue to trade off latency, scalability, or anonymity strength, and no protocol is known to simultaneously achieve all four properties with provable guarantees, nor has a definitive impossibility result been established.

paper_title: Open Problems in Data-Sharing Peer-to-Peer Systems
original_question: How do anonymity protocols for peer-to-peer systems degrade under active attack, especially when intermediate proxy nodes may collude, and what protocol designs can better preserve anonymity in those adversarial settings?
self_contained_problem:
Consider a peer-to-peer network modeled as a graph G=(V,E) whose nodes are participants and whose edges represent communication links. An anonymity protocol on G is a randomized routing scheme in which a message originating at a source s in V is forwarded to a destination d in V through a sequence of intermediate proxy nodes, with the goal that no observer can determine the identity of the sender (sender anonymity), the receiver (receiver anonymity), or the linkage between them (relationship anonymity). Formalize an adversary model in which a subset C of the proxy nodes is actively malicious and colluding: the adversary controls the nodes in C, can observe all traffic passing through them, can drop, delay, replay, or inject messages, and can share all observations among the nodes in C. Quantify anonymity by a measure such as the entropy of the posterior distribution that the adversary assigns to the identity of the sender (or to the sender–receiver pair) given its observations, or by the probability that the adversary correctly identifies the sender.

(a) Give tight upper and lower bounds, as a function of |C|/|V|, of the network topology, and of the protocol parameters (e.g., path length, mixing strategy, cover-traffic rate), on the anonymity provided by representative anonymity protocols for peer-to-peer systems (such as Crowds-style probabilistic forwarding, onion-routing/Tor-like layered encryption, and DC-net-based broadcast schemes) under the above active colluding-proxy adversary.

(b) Determine whether there exists a protocol that, under such active colluding adversaries controlling a constant fraction of proxy nodes, preserves a non-trivial level of sender, receiver, and relationship anonymity (e.g., adversary success probability bounded away from 1 by a constant, or anonymity-set size growing with |V|), and exhibit such a protocol or prove its impossibility.

paper_title: Open Problems in Data-Sharing Peer-to-Peer Systems
original_question: What is the feasibility of equipping peer-to-peer systems with technical mechanisms for intellectual-property management and digital-rights management, and which concrete protocol or system designs could make such management workable in decentralized data-sharing applications?
self_contained_problem:
Consider a decentralized peer-to-peer data-sharing system, modeled as a dynamic network of autonomous nodes that can publish, replicate, and retrieve digital objects without relying on a central trusted authority. Assume each digital object carries a set of usage policies (e.g., restrictions on copying, redistribution, modification, time-limited access, and payment obligations) specified by its rights holder. Design and analyze a concrete protocol (or family of protocols) that equips such a peer-to-peer system with mechanisms for intellectual-property management and digital-rights management, satisfying at least the following requirements:

1. Policy binding: every replicated copy of an object remains cryptographically bound to its usage policy.
2. Enforcement: participating peers can verify and enforce the declared policies before granting access, with provable security guarantees against a defined adversary model (e.g., a constant fraction of colluding malicious peers).
3. Decentralization: no single trusted third party is required for routine policy verification, key distribution, or access control.
4. Accountability: violations (unauthorized copying or redistribution) can be detected and attributed with non-trivial probability.
5. Scalability: protocol overhead (communication, storage, cryptographic operations per access) grows at most polylogarithmically in the number of peers and objects.

Determine whether a protocol meeting all five requirements simultaneously is feasible. If feasible, exhibit such a protocol and prove its correctness, security, and scalability bounds; if not, prove an impossibility result identifying which subset of the requirements can and cannot be jointly satisfied in the stated model.
status_search_result: The question is a broad systems/protocol design challenge concerning DRM in peer-to-peer networks. While numerous partial schemes (e.g., watermarking-based tracing, license-server-assisted DRM, blockchain-based rights management) have been proposed, no single protocol is widely recognized as simultaneously satisfying decentralization, enforcement, accountability, and scalability with provable guarantees in a fully open P2P model. The general feasibility problem remains an open research direction.

paper_title: Open Problems in Distributed Communities
original_question: For wireless distributed communities, how should a shared context protocol be designed so that mobile devices and services can interact through well-understood context dimensions across a near-ubiquitous scope, rather than limiting context handling to local transport or service-discovery layers? In particular, what architecture lets context permeate device software and the surrounding service infrastructure instead of remaining a narrowly local mechanism?
self_contained_problem:
Design a shared context protocol for wireless distributed communities of mobile devices and services with the following requirements:

1. (Scope) The protocol must operate with near-ubiquitous scope, rather than being confined to a single local transport mechanism or a service-discovery layer (such as Bluetooth's service discovery).

2. (Dimensions) The protocol must expose a fixed, well-understood collection of context dimensions (e.g., identity, location, capability, availability, trust, time, environment) through which mobile devices and fixed or mobile services can mutually interpret one another's state and intent.

3. (Permeation) The architecture must allow context information to permeate every layer of both device software and the surrounding service infrastructure, so that context is not encapsulated as a narrowly local mechanism but is accessible and consistent at all layers of implementation.

4. (Interaction model) Specify how mobile devices and services interact through these context dimensions: the messages exchanged, the consistency guarantees on shared context across heterogeneous wireless transports, and the way services discover, negotiate, and adapt to context.

The problem is to give an architecture and protocol specification meeting (1)–(4), together with a justification that it generalizes existing local context handling (such as service-discovery-layer approaches) while preserving interoperability across wireless transports and service infrastructures.
status_search_result: No specific resolution of this open design question for a near-ubiquitous wireless shared-context protocol was located. Related work exists in pervasive/ubiquitous computing context-awareness frameworks, but no single architecture is established as the accepted answer to the posed question.

paper_title: Open Problems in Distributed Communities
original_question: What infrastructure should a distributed community use so that interactions among communities, sub-communities, individual members, and people outside the community can be integrated into the shared context while remaining transparent to each participant despite differences in devices, device capabilities, location, and information structure?
self_contained_problem:
Consider a distributed community modeled as a collection of participants partitioned into (possibly nested) sub-communities, together with a set of external individuals who do not belong to any sub-community. Interactions may occur (i) between two communities or sub-communities, (ii) within a community as a whole, (iii) between two individual members of a community, or (iv) between a member and an external individual. Interactions may serve collaborative, informational, or social purposes, and each participant accesses them through a device with possibly differing capabilities, from possibly differing physical locations, and possibly differing local representations of the shared information.

Design a unifying communication infrastructure for such a distributed community that satisfies the following requirements simultaneously:
1. Every interaction of types (i)–(iv), whether mediated by the shared context or initiated outside it, can be incorporated into a single coherent shared context maintained by the community.
2. From the standpoint of any individual participant, the infrastructure is transparent: the participant need not be aware of the particular device or device capabilities used by other participants, of the geographic location of any participant or resource, or of the underlying structural representation of the information being exchanged.
3. The infrastructure supports different communication styles appropriate to the purpose of each interaction (collaborative, informational, or social).

Specify the components, abstractions, and guarantees of such an infrastructure, and justify that the three requirements above hold.
status_search_result: The question is a high-level open design problem about infrastructure for distributed communities, not a precisely formulated mathematical conjecture. No specific definitive solution appears in the literature; related work on groupware, federated systems, and ubiquitous computing addresses pieces of the problem but no comprehensive accepted answer is documented.

paper_title: Open Problems in Distributed Communities
original_question: How should a shared context for distributed communities separate and support the distinct problems of basic security, privacy, and trust? More concretely, what mechanisms keep information private, what policies determine which data may be shared according to user wishes, and what system properties make participants believe both that their preferences are being respected and that the context information they receive is correct?
self_contained_problem:
Consider a distributed community of computational participants that maintains a shared "context" — a body of information (e.g., location, preferences, sensor data, presence, identity attributes) collected from and distributed among the participants. Design a formal framework for such a shared context that cleanly separates and simultaneously supports the following three concerns, and prove that the framework satisfies precise guarantees in each:

1. Basic security: specify the cryptographic mechanisms and protocols (encryption schemes, authentication, key management) that keep context information confidential against an adversary with a stated capability (e.g., a Dolev–Yao or computationally bounded eavesdropper), and prove standard confidentiality/integrity guarantees.

2. Privacy: specify a policy language and enforcement mechanism that determines, for each item of context information and each potential recipient, whether sharing is permitted according to the originating user's stated preferences; prove that any release of information by the system is consistent with these policies (a noninterference- or policy-compliance-style theorem).

3. Trust: specify system properties and supporting protocols (e.g., attestation, provenance, reputation, verifiable computation) that allow a user to justifiably believe (a) that their stated privacy preferences are being honored by other participants and the infrastructure, and (b) that the context information they receive from others is correct; formalize this as a soundness/accuracy guarantee under a stated adversary model.

The problem asks: produce such a framework in which the three concerns are treated as independent, composable layers, give precise definitions of the security, privacy-compliance, and trust/correctness properties, and exhibit concrete mechanisms together with theorems establishing each property within a single distributed-community model.
category_tag: security, privacy, and trust in distributed systems
status_search_result: The question is a broad foundational design challenge for shared-context distributed communities. No single accepted solution exists; while each of basic security, privacy policy enforcement, and trust/attestation has substantial individual literature, a unified framework that cleanly separates and provably supports all three in a distributed-community context remains an active research agenda rather than a resolved problem.

paper_title: Open Problems in Distributed Communities
original_question: As a distributed community changes over time, how should its shared context evolve with it? In particular, how should systems support changes that originate outside the current context and must be drawn back into it, and how should they handle context changes that arise from individual actions, from particular interactions that characterize the community's evolution, or from self-adaptations derived from sequences of interactions?
self_contained_problem:
Consider a distributed community modeled as a tuple (A, I, C_t) where A is a set of autonomous agents (individuals), I is a set of permissible interactions among subsets of A, and C_t is a shared context at time t — formalized as a structured collection of facts, norms, protocols, and resources that all agents in A reference when interacting. The context evolves over discrete time steps as a sequence (C_t)_{t \ge 0}. Three classes of update events are distinguished:

(i) External updates: changes that originate outside C_t (for example, from the environment or from agent behavior that is not currently expressible within C_t) and that must be reflected back into C_{t+1}.
(ii) Individual updates: changes to C_t initiated by a single agent a ∈ A.
(iii) Interaction-driven updates: changes to C_t that arise either from a single interaction i ∈ I, or as a self-adaptation derived from an observed sequence of interactions (i_1, i_2, …, i_k).

Design a formal framework, together with update operators U_ext, U_ind, U_int, and U_seq acting on the space of contexts, that:

(a) specifies how external changes are detected and "drawn back" into the context (i.e., gives a procedure C_{t+1} = U_ext(C_t, e) for an external event e that guarantees consistency of C_{t+1} with both the prior context and the observed event);
(b) specifies how individual and interaction-level updates compose with one another while preserving a chosen notion of community-level consistency;
(c) specifies how self-adaptations derived from sequences of interactions are integrated, with provable convergence or stability properties as t → ∞.

State and justify what properties (consistency, monotonicity, convergence, fairness across agents) such a framework should satisfy, and exhibit a concrete instantiation that realizes them.
status_search_result: The question is posed as an open conceptual/design problem about how shared contexts in distributed communities should evolve over time. No specific solution or formal resolution has been identified; the problem remains an open research direction within the distributed-communities/context-aware computing literature.

original_question: For the Gaussian fluid queue above, assume that the variance function σ_X^2(t) is regularly varying at infinity with index α_∞ in [1,2). Determine whether the correlation function ρ(t)=Corr(Q(t),Q(0)) has the following asymptotic behavior as t→∞: if α_∞=1, then log ρ(t)/t converges to −γ_1 for some constant γ_1 in (0,∞); if α_∞ is in (1,2), then ρ(t) divided by σ_X^2(t)/t^2 converges to γ_{α_∞} for some constant γ_{α_∞} in (0,∞).

(ii) If $\alpha_\infty\in(1,2)$, then there exists a constant $\gamma_{\alpha_\infty}\in(0,\infty)$ such that
$$\lim_{t\to\infty}\frac{\rho(t)}{\sigma_X^2(t)/t^2}=\gamma_{\alpha_\infty}.$$

original_question: For fractional Brownian motion B_H with Hurst parameter H, is the associated classical Pickands constant equal to 1/Γ(1/(2H))? That is, does the identity H_{B_H} = 1/Γ(1/(2H)) hold for the full range of H under consideration?
self_contained_problem:
Let $B_H = (B_H(t))_{t \ge 0}$ be a fractional Brownian motion with Hurst parameter $H \in [1/2, 1)$, i.e., the centered Gaussian process with stationary increments, almost surely continuous sample paths, $B_H(0) = 0$, and covariance
$$\mathrm{Cov}(B_H(s), B_H(t)) = \tfrac{1}{2}\bigl(|s|^{2H} + |t|^{2H} - |t-s|^{2H}\bigr).$$
The classical Pickands constant associated with $B_H$ is defined by
$$\mathcal{H}_{B_H} \;=\; \lim_{T \to \infty} \frac{1}{T}\, \mathbb{E}\!\left[\exp\!\left(\sup_{t \in [0,T]} \bigl(\sqrt{2}\, B_H(t) - t^{2H}\bigr)\right)\right],$$
the limit being known to exist and to lie in $(0, \infty)$.

Decide whether the identity
$$\mathcal{H}_{B_H} \;=\; \frac{1}{\Gamma\!\bigl(1/(2H)\bigr)}$$
holds for every $H \in [1/2, 1)$.
category_tag: Pickands constants for fractional Brownian motion
status_search_result: The folklore identity $\mathcal{H}_\alpha = 1/\Gamma(1/\alpha)$ (with $\alpha = 2H$) was disproved by A. J. Harper (Bernoulli, 2017; arXiv:1404.5505) for all sufficiently small $\alpha$, where he showed $\mathcal{H}_\alpha \ge (1.1527)^{1/\alpha}/\Gamma(1/\alpha)$. This corresponds to $H$ close to $0$, outside the range $H \in [1/2,1)$ for standard fractional Brownian motion. For the actual Hurst range $H \in [1/2,1)$ (equivalently $\alpha \in [1,2)$) the conjecture has not been confirmed nor refuted; simulation evidence is often cited as suggesting it is not exact, but no rigorous resolution in this range appears in the literature.

paper_title: Open Problems in Geometric Methods for Instance-Based Learning
original_question: For the k-nearest-neighbor decision rule, how fast does the probability of error Pe[k-NN] converge to the Bayes error Pe as the training-set size n tends to infinity?
self_contained_problem:
Let $(X,Y)$ be a random pair taking values in $\mathbb{R}^d \times \{1,2,\dots,M\}$ with joint distribution $P$, where $X$ is the feature vector and $Y$ is the class label. Given an i.i.d. training sample $\mathcal{D}_n = \{(X_1,Y_1),\dots,(X_n,Y_n)\}$ drawn from $P$, and an integer $k \ge 1$, the $k$-nearest-neighbor (k-NN) decision rule classifies a query point $x \in \mathbb{R}^d$ by majority vote among the labels $Y_{(1)}(x),\dots,Y_{(k)}(x)$ of the $k$ training points whose features $X_i$ are closest to $x$ under the Euclidean metric (ties broken in a fixed way). Let
$$P_e[\text{k-NN}](n) \;=\; \Pr\!\big(g_{n,k}(X) \neq Y\big)$$
denote the probability of error of the k-NN rule (where $g_{n,k}$ is the classifier built from $\mathcal{D}_n$), and let
$$P_e^* \;=\; \inf_{g} \Pr(g(X) \neq Y)$$
denote the Bayes error (the infimum over all measurable classifiers $g:\mathbb{R}^d \to \{1,\dots,M\}$).

(a) Determine the rate at which $P_e[\text{k-NN}](n) - P_e^*$ tends to $0$ as $n \to \infty$ (with $k=k(n)$ chosen suitably, e.g.\ $k(n)\to\infty$ and $k(n)/n \to 0$), in terms of natural assumptions on the underlying distribution $P$ (smoothness/Lipschitz conditions on the regression function $\eta(x) = \Pr(Y=1\mid X=x)$, margin conditions, and dimension $d$).

(b) Provide non-asymptotic (finite-sample) bounds on $P_e[\text{k-NN}](n) - P_e^*$ as a function of $n$, $k$, and the distributional parameters.
status_search_result: Substantial progress has been made on this classical question. Under margin (Tsybakov-type) and smoothness assumptions on the regression function, both asymptotic rates such as $O(k^{-(1+\alpha)/2}) + O((k/n)^{(\alpha+1)/d})$ and finite-sample/minimax-optimal bounds (e.g.\ $O(n^{-4/(d+4)})$ with local choice of $k$) have been established by Chaudhuri–Dasgupta, Samworth, Gadat–Klein–Marteau, Döring–Györfi–Walk and others. General consistency ($P_e[\text{k-NN}]\to P_e^*$ when $k\to\infty,\ k/n\to 0$) is classical (Stone, 1977). Sharp rates without distributional assumptions or under minimal assumptions remain an active research area, so the question is partially solved.

paper_title: Open Problems in Geometric Methods for Instance-Based Learning
original_question: How can the storage required for the training set in an instance-based learning system be reduced without degrading the performance of the resulting decision rule?
self_contained_problem:
Let $(X,d)$ be a metric space and let $T=\{(x_1,y_1),\dots,(x_n,y_n)\}\subset X\times\mathcal{Y}$ be a finite labeled training set, where $\mathcal{Y}$ is a finite set of class labels. For a subset $S\subseteq T$, define the associated nearest-neighbor decision rule $h_S:X\to\mathcal{Y}$ by $h_S(x)=y_{i^*}$, where $(x_{i^*},y_{i^*})\in S$ minimizes $d(x,x_{i^*})$ (ties broken by a fixed rule). Given a probability distribution $\mathcal{D}$ on $X\times\mathcal{Y}$ from which $T$ is drawn i.i.d., let the error of a rule $h$ be $\mathrm{err}_\mathcal{D}(h)=\Pr_{(x,y)\sim\mathcal{D}}[h(x)\neq y]$.

Develop a general procedure (and accompanying guarantees) for selecting, given any input $T$, a subset $S\subseteq T$ with $|S|\ll |T|$ such that the resulting decision rule $h_S$ satisfies $\mathrm{err}_\mathcal{D}(h_S)\le \mathrm{err}_\mathcal{D}(h_T)+\varepsilon$ for prescribed $\varepsilon\ge 0$. Characterize the smallest achievable $|S|$ as a function of $T$, of the underlying geometry of $(X,d)$, and of $\varepsilon$, and identify conditions under which storage can be reduced without any degradation of the decision rule's performance.
status_search_result: The question of reducing training-set storage for nearest-neighbor / instance-based learning (training-set condensation, editing, prototype selection) has been studied extensively since Hart's Condensed Nearest Neighbor rule (1968) and continues to generate active research on coresets and approximation guarantees; no single optimal general-purpose solution is known, and the question as posed remains an open research direction rather than a settled theorem.

original_question: How large should the neighborhood size k be in the k-nearest-neighbor rule, and how should that value of k be chosen from the data?
self_contained_problem:
Let $(X_1,Y_1),\dots,(X_n,Y_n)$ be an i.i.d. sample drawn from an unknown joint distribution on $\mathbb{R}^d\times\{1,\dots,M\}$, and let a metric $\rho$ on $\mathbb{R}^d$ be fixed. For a query point $x\in\mathbb{R}^d$ and an integer $k\in\{1,\dots,n\}$, the $k$-nearest-neighbor classifier $\hat g_{n,k}$ assigns to $x$ the plurality class label among the $k$ training points $X_i$ closest to $x$ under $\rho$ (with some fixed tie-breaking rule). Let $L_n(k)=\mathbb{P}\{\hat g_{n,k}(X)\ne Y\}$ denote the expected misclassification probability, where $(X,Y)$ is independent of the sample and has the same distribution.

(a) Determine, as a function of the sample size $n$, the dimension $d$, and properties of the underlying distribution, how the neighborhood size $k=k_n$ should grow in order to make $L_n(k_n)$ as small as possible (in particular, to attain the optimal rate of convergence of $L_n(k_n)$ to the Bayes risk).

(b) Construct a fully data-driven rule $\hat k=\hat k(X_1,Y_1,\dots,X_n,Y_n)$ for choosing $k$ from the sample alone, and analyze its theoretical performance (consistency, rate of convergence, and behavior of $L_n(\hat k)$ relative to $\inf_k L_n(k)$).
status_search_result: The question of how to choose the neighborhood size $k$ in $k$-NN classification optimally and in a fully data-driven way remains an active research area. Cross-validation is standard practice but is known to suffer from multiple minimizers of the estimated misclassification rate, and the theoretically optimal $k$ depends on unknown quantities (dimension, smoothness, class-conditional densities, sample proportions). Various proposals (Bayesian, smoothed CV, adaptive $k$) exist, but no universally accepted optimal data-driven rule has been established.

paper_title: Open Problems in Geometric Methods for Instance-Based Learning
original_question: Should all measured features or attributes be weighted equally in an instance-based learning rule, and if not, how should the feature weights be selected?
self_contained_problem:
Consider an instance-based (lazy) learning rule that classifies a query point x ∈ ℝ^n by comparing it to a stored set of labeled training instances {(x_i, y_i)}_{i=1}^N using a parameterized distance of the form

   d_w(x, x') = ( Σ_{j=1}^n w_j · ρ(x_j, x'_j) )^{1/2},

where w = (w_1, …, w_n) is a vector of nonnegative feature weights and ρ is a per-feature dissimilarity (e.g. squared difference for numeric features, 0/1 mismatch for symbolic features). The prediction at x is obtained from the labels of the nearest stored instances under d_w (e.g. by k-nearest-neighbor voting).

Address the following:

(a) Determine whether the uniform choice w_1 = w_2 = … = w_n (equal weighting of all measured features/attributes) is, in general, an appropriate choice for such a learning rule, in the sense of minimizing expected generalization error over arbitrary learning problems.

(b) If equal weighting is not appropriate, provide a principled, general method for selecting the weight vector w from the training data (and any available prior information about feature relevance), and justify the choice by characterizing the class of problems on which the method yields provably good predictive performance.
status_search_result: Surveys and reviews of feature weighting methods for lazy/instance-based learning algorithms (k-NN and its variants) continue to be published, and recent literature explicitly states that determining a generally optimal weighting scheme remains an unsolved challenge. Numerous filter, wrapper, supervised/unsupervised, and global/local weighting techniques have been developed, but no universal solution exists, so the question remains open.

paper_title: Open Problems in Geometric Methods for Instance-Based Learning
original_question: How can a nearest-neighbor decision rule be made robust when the training data contain overlapping classes or noise?
self_contained_problem:
Let $\mathcal{X} \subseteq \mathbb{R}^d$ be a feature space and let $\mathcal{Y} = \{1, 2, \ldots, c\}$ be a finite set of class labels. Suppose we are given a training sample $S = \{(x_i, y_i)\}_{i=1}^n$ drawn from an unknown joint distribution $P$ on $\mathcal{X} \times \mathcal{Y}$, where the distribution $P$ may exhibit:

(a) class overlap, meaning that there exist regions $R \subseteq \mathcal{X}$ with $P(Y = j \mid X \in R) > 0$ for more than one class $j$; and

(b) label noise, meaning that each observed label $y_i$ may differ from the true latent class $\tilde y_i$ with some unknown probability.

The standard nearest-neighbor decision rule classifies a query $x \in \mathcal{X}$ by assigning it the label of its nearest training point under a chosen metric $\rho$ on $\mathcal{X}$, namely $\hat{y}(x) = y_{i^*}$ where $i^* \in \arg\min_i \rho(x, x_i)$.

Design a modification of the nearest-neighbor decision rule (allowing, for example, weighting schemes, editing or condensing of $S$, locally adaptive metrics, $k$-NN extensions, reject options, or other geometric devices) that is provably robust to class overlap and label noise in the following sense: as $n \to \infty$, the expected misclassification probability of the modified rule converges to (or stays close to) the Bayes-optimal risk of $P$, even when a positive fraction of labels in $S$ are corrupted and the class-conditional supports overlap. Specify the rule, identify the assumptions on $P$, the noise model, and the metric under which the robustness guarantee holds, and quantify the convergence rate.
status_search_result: Numerous partial solutions exist (edited/condensed NN rules, weighted k-NN, mutual k-NN, locally adaptive metrics, prototype selection, and noise-filtering methods), each providing robustness under specific assumptions. However, a unified geometric nearest-neighbor decision rule that is provably robust to arbitrary class overlap and label noise with strong finite-sample guarantees remains an active research problem; published surveys note that performance on combined overlap-plus-noise scenarios is not yet satisfactory.

paper_title: Open Problems in Geometric Methods for Instance-Based Learning
original_question: How can the nearest neighbors of a new query point be computed efficiently?
self_contained_problem:
Let $(X, d)$ be a metric space and let $P = \{p_1, \ldots, p_n\} \subset X$ be a finite set of $n$ points, given in advance and available for preprocessing. For a positive integer $k$, the $k$-nearest-neighbor problem asks, given a query point $q \in X$, to return a subset $N_k(q) \subseteq P$ of size $k$ such that for every $p \in N_k(q)$ and every $p' \in P \setminus N_k(q)$, $d(q,p) \le d(q,p')$.

Design a data structure that, after preprocessing $P$, answers $k$-nearest-neighbor queries efficiently. Specifically, identify schemes that achieve sublinear query time (ideally polylogarithmic in $n$) using only polynomial space and preprocessing, while remaining effective in high-dimensional Euclidean spaces $X = \mathbb{R}^d$ as well as in general metric spaces. Characterize the best achievable trade-offs among space, preprocessing time, and query time for both exact and $(1+\varepsilon)$-approximate nearest-neighbor search, and determine whether the "curse of dimensionality" — the apparent impossibility of obtaining query time sublinear in $n$ with space polynomial in $n$ and $d$ for exact nearest neighbors when $d$ is large — can be overcome.
status_search_result: Nearest-neighbor search is a classical problem with substantial progress: kd-trees, ball trees, cover trees, and metric trees give efficient algorithms in low dimensions; locality-sensitive hashing (Indyk–Motwani, Andoni–Indyk) and data-dependent LSH (Andoni–Razenshteyn 2015) give near-optimal approximate solutions in high dimensions. However, exact nearest-neighbor search in high dimensions still suffers from the curse of dimensionality, and tight bounds on the space/time trade-off remain open. The problem is therefore partially solved.

paper_title: Open Problems in Geometric Methods for Instance-Based Learning
original_question: Let {X, Y} be a training set of n labeled patterns in d dimensions, and let C be the condensed training-set-consistent subset produced by Hart's condensed nearest neighbor rule. A naive brute-force algorithm computes C in O(dn^3) time. By how much can the complexity of computing this condensed subset be reduced?
self_contained_problem:
Let $\{X, Y\} = \{(x_i, y_i) : 1 \le i \le n\}$ be a training set of $n$ labeled patterns, where each $x_i \in \mathbb{R}^d$ and each $y_i$ is a class label drawn from a finite set. For a subset $S \subseteq \{X, Y\}$, define the 1-nearest-neighbor classifier $\mathrm{NN}_S$ which assigns to a query point $q \in \mathbb{R}^d$ the label of the closest point in $S$ under the Euclidean metric (ties broken by some fixed rule). A subset $C \subseteq \{X, Y\}$ is said to be training-set-consistent if $\mathrm{NN}_C(x_i) = y_i$ for every $i = 1, \ldots, n$.

Hart's Condensed Nearest Neighbor (CNN) rule produces such a consistent subset $C$ by the following procedure: initialize $C$ with one arbitrary labeled pattern; then repeatedly scan the remaining points of $\{X, Y\}$, and for each point $(x_i, y_i)$ for which $\mathrm{NN}_C(x_i) \neq y_i$, add $(x_i, y_i)$ to $C$. Repeat the scanning process until an entire pass through the training set produces no additions to $C$. The output $C$ depends on the order of scanning, but in all cases the naive brute-force implementation of this rule runs in time $O(d n^3)$.

Determine the best possible worst-case time complexity, as a function of $n$ and $d$, for computing a subset $C$ produced by Hart's CNN rule. In particular, by how much can the $O(d n^3)$ bound of the brute-force algorithm be improved?
status_search_result: The Fast Condensed Nearest Neighbor (FCNN) rule by Angiulli (ICML 2005) achieves a subquadratic worst-case time complexity for computing a training-set-consistent subset, improving substantially on the cubic brute-force bound. However, FCNN does not reproduce Hart's specific output, and the precise optimal complexity of computing a Hart CNN-condensed subset is not known to be fully settled.

paper_title: Open Problems in Geometric Methods for Instance-Based Learning
original_question: The selective nearest neighbor rule SNN is reported empirically to have average running time O(dn^3). Can one prove theoretical results giving average-case running-time bounds of this kind for SNN?
self_contained_problem:
Setup. Let $S = \{(x_1, y_1), \ldots, (x_n, y_n)\} \subset \mathbb{R}^d \times \mathcal{C}$ be a labeled training set, where $\mathcal{C}$ is a finite set of class labels. For a query point $x \in \mathbb{R}^d$ and a subset $T \subseteq S$, the nearest neighbor classifier $\mathrm{NN}_T(x)$ assigns to $x$ the label of the point in $T$ whose feature vector is closest (in Euclidean distance) to $x$.

A subset $T \subseteq S$ is called consistent with $S$ if $\mathrm{NN}_T(x_i) = y_i$ for every $(x_i, y_i) \in S$. The selective nearest neighbor (SNN) rule produces a minimum-cardinality subset $T^* \subseteq S$ such that, for every $(x_i, y_i) \in S$, the nearest point of $T^*$ to $x_i$ has label $y_i$ and is at least as close to $x_i$ as the nearest neighbor of $x_i$ in $S \setminus \{x_i\}$ (so that selecting $T^*$ preserves the original $1$-NN classification on every training point).

Assume the points $x_1, \ldots, x_n$ are drawn i.i.d. from some reasonable probability distribution on $\mathbb{R}^d$ (e.g., absolutely continuous with respect to Lebesgue measure on a bounded region, with the labels generated by some measurable rule).

Problem. Prove (or disprove) a rigorous average-case complexity bound of the form
$$\mathbb{E}[\,t_{\mathrm{SNN}}(S)\,] \;=\; O(d\,n^{3}),$$
where $t_{\mathrm{SNN}}(S)$ denotes the running time of a specified algorithm that computes the SNN subset $T^*$ from $S$, and the expectation is taken over the random draw of $S$. More generally, establish theoretical average-case running-time bounds for algorithms implementing the SNN rule.
category_tag: Average-case complexity of nearest neighbor instance selection
status_search_result: Web searches turn up only empirical claims of an O(dn^3) average running time for the selective nearest neighbor rule (attributed to Wilson and Martinez) and complexity results for related but distinct algorithms (e.g., FCNN, shared-NN). No rigorous average-case analysis of the SNN rule appears to be available, so the question appears to still be open.

paper_title: Open Problems in Geometric Methods for Instance-Based Learning
original_question: In high-dimensional data, can one design worst-case algorithms for computing the Gabriel graph or the rectangular-influence graph of a training set {X, Y} in o(dn^3) time?
self_contained_problem:
Let $S = \{x_1, \ldots, x_n\} \subset \mathbb{R}^d$ be a finite set of $n$ points in $d$-dimensional Euclidean space (think of $d$ as large, possibly comparable to $n$). Define the following two proximity graphs on the vertex set $S$:

1. The Gabriel graph $G(S)$: an unordered pair $\{x_i, x_j\}$ is an edge if and only if the closed Euclidean ball whose diameter is the segment $\overline{x_i x_j}$ (i.e. the ball of radius $\|x_i - x_j\|/2$ centered at the midpoint $(x_i+x_j)/2$) contains no other point of $S$ in its interior. Equivalently, $\{x_i, x_j\}$ is an edge iff for every $x_k \in S \setminus \{x_i, x_j\}$,
$$\|x_i - x_j\|^2 \le \|x_i - x_k\|^2 + \|x_j - x_k\|^2.$$

2. The rectangular-influence graph $R(S)$: an unordered pair $\{x_i, x_j\}$ is an edge if and only if the open axis-aligned hyperrectangle (in the coordinate system in which $x_i$ and $x_j$ are taken as a pair of opposite corners) determined by $x_i$ and $x_j$ contains no other point of $S$. Equivalently, $\{x_i, x_j\}$ is an edge iff there is no $x_k \in S\setminus\{x_i,x_j\}$ with each coordinate of $x_k$ strictly between the corresponding coordinates of $x_i$ and $x_j$.

A straightforward brute-force algorithm computes either graph in $O(d\,n^3)$ worst-case time by checking, for each of the $\binom{n}{2}$ candidate edges, the defining condition against all remaining $n-2$ points (each check costing $O(d)$ time).

Question: Does there exist a deterministic algorithm that, given any input $S \subset \mathbb{R}^d$ of $n$ points, computes the Gabriel graph $G(S)$ in worst-case time $o(d\,n^3)$? Likewise, does there exist such an algorithm computing the rectangular-influence graph $R(S)$ in worst-case time $o(d\,n^3)$?
status_search_result: A web search returned standard results on planar Gabriel graph construction (e.g. $O(n\log n)$ via Delaunay triangulation in 2D) and brute-force $O(n^3)$ approaches, but no algorithm or hardness result was located that beats $O(d\,n^3)$ worst-case time for either the Gabriel graph or the rectangular-influence graph in arbitrary high dimension. The question therefore appears to remain unresolved in the literature accessible via search.

paper_title: Open Problems in Geometric Methods for Instance-Based Learning
original_question: Can the graph neighbors of a query point be computed approximately rather than exactly, while guaranteeing that the resulting approximation does not adversely affect classification error?
self_contained_problem:
Let $(X,d)$ be a metric space and let $S=\{(x_1,y_1),\dots,(x_n,y_n)\}\subset X\times\{1,\dots,c\}$ be a labeled training set. Fix an integer $k\ge 1$ and define the $k$-nearest-neighbor graph $G_k(S)$ on $S$ in which each $x_i$ is connected to its $k$ nearest neighbors in $S\setminus\{x_i\}$ under $d$. For a query point $q\in X$, let $N_k(q)\subseteq S$ denote the set of exact $k$ graph neighbors of $q$ (the $k$ points of $S$ closest to $q$), and let $\hat h_k(q)$ be the classifier that assigns to $q$ the plurality label among $N_k(q)$. Let $\mathcal D$ be an unknown distribution on $X\times\{1,\dots,c\}$ from which $S$ and test points are drawn i.i.d., and let $\mathrm{err}(\hat h_k)=\Pr_{(q,y)\sim\mathcal D}[\hat h_k(q)\ne y]$ denote its classification error.

Question: Does there exist an algorithm $\mathcal A$ which, given $S$, $k$ and a query point $q$, returns a set $\widetilde N_k(q)\subseteq S$ of size $k$ (a possibly approximate set of graph neighbors) using strictly sub-linear time in $n$ per query, and induces a classifier $\tilde h_k$ via plurality vote on $\widetilde N_k(q)$, such that for every distribution $\mathcal D$ and every $n$,
$$\mathrm{err}(\tilde h_k)\le \mathrm{err}(\hat h_k)+\varepsilon(n),$$
with $\varepsilon(n)\to 0$ as $n\to\infty$ (or, more strongly, $\varepsilon(n)=0$)? Characterize the conditions on $(X,d)$, on $\mathcal D$, and on the approximation rule used by $\mathcal A$ under which the approximate neighbor computation provably does not adversely affect classification error.
status_search_result: Approximate nearest-neighbor search with classification-error guarantees has been studied extensively; recent work (e.g., on instance-based approximation guarantees for graph-based ANNS) provides per-instance distance-ratio guarantees but does not fully resolve the question of when approximate neighbor retrieval preserves the Bayes/empirical classification error in all settings. The general problem as posed appears not to have a definitive, settled answer in the literature.

paper_title: Open Problems in Geometric Methods for Instance-Based Learning
original_question: Is there a condensing algorithm for instance-based learning that works well both when the data distributions are homogeneous and when they are not, rather than performing well in only one of those situations?
self_contained_problem:
Setting. In instance-based (nearest-neighbor type) classification, a training set $T = \{(x_i, y_i)\}_{i=1}^n \subset \mathcal{X} \times \mathcal{Y}$ is used directly at prediction time: a query $x \in \mathcal{X}$ is classified using the labels of its nearest neighbors in $T$ under a metric $d$ on $\mathcal{X}$. A condensing algorithm is a procedure $\mathcal{A}$ that outputs a subset (or, more generally, a set of prototypes) $S = \mathcal{A}(T)$ with $|S| \ll |T|$, intended to be used in place of $T$ for nearest-neighbor classification.

Call a labeled training set homogeneous if the class-conditional distributions are well separated and class regions form compact connected clusters with low overlap; call it non-homogeneous otherwise (e.g., classes with overlapping supports, multimodal class regions, varying local density, or high boundary complexity).

For a condensing algorithm $\mathcal{A}$ and a data distribution $\mathcal{D}$ on $\mathcal{X} \times \mathcal{Y}$, define its performance to consist of (i) the reduction ratio $|S|/|T|$ and (ii) the generalization accuracy of the nearest-neighbor classifier built on $S = \mathcal{A}(T)$, measured against $\mathcal{D}$.

Problem. Does there exist a single condensing algorithm $\mathcal{A}$ that simultaneously achieves high reduction ratio and high generalization accuracy in both the homogeneous and the non-homogeneous regimes, rather than performing well only in one of the two regimes? Equivalently, exhibit such an algorithm together with theoretical or empirical guarantees over both regimes, or prove that no condensing algorithm can be uniformly competitive across both regimes.
status_search_result: Research on prototype selection and generation (e.g., RHC, RSP3, and multi-label extensions like MLRHC) continues actively, with different algorithms favoring either homogeneous or heterogeneous class structures. No authoritative source confirms the existence of a single condensing algorithm that uniformly dominates across both regimes, nor a proof of impossibility, so the status remains unverified.

paper_title: Open Problems in Number Theory
original_question: In the same setting, with N a large prime and H_2^+(N) the weight-2 newforms of level Γ_0(N) with even functional equation, can one prove a stronger lower-bound statement: that more than 50% of the central values L(f,1) are at least (log N)^(-A) for some fixed positive constant A?
self_contained_problem:
Let $N$ be a (large) prime number, and let $H_2^+(N)$ denote the set of normalized weight-$2$ Hecke newforms $f$ on $\Gamma_0(N)$ whose completed $L$-function $\Lambda(f,s)$ satisfies a functional equation $\Lambda(f,s) = +\Lambda(f,2-s)$ (i.e., the sign of the functional equation is $+1$, so the central value $L(f,1)$ is not forced to vanish for parity reasons).

For $f \in H_2^+(N)$, let $L(f,s)$ denote the associated automorphic $L$-function, with central point $s=1$.

Prove or disprove: there exists an absolute constant $A>0$ such that, as $N \to \infty$ through primes,
$$\#\{f \in H_2^+(N) : L(f,1) \ge (\log N)^{-A}\} > \left(\tfrac{1}{2} + \delta\right)\, \#H_2^+(N)$$
for some fixed $\delta>0$ (independently of $N$).

That is, show that strictly more than $50\%$ of the central values $L(f,1)$, as $f$ ranges over $H_2^+(N)$, are bounded below by $(\log N)^{-A}$.
status_search_result: The best known unconditional results give that at least 50% of such central L-values are nonzero. Going strictly beyond 50% with a quantitative lower bound of the form (log N)^{-A} is known to be intimately tied to ruling out Landau–Siegel zeros for real Dirichlet L-functions (work of Iwaniec–Sarnak and subsequent authors), and remains open.

paper_title: Open problems in queueing theory inspired by datacenter computing
original_question: Consider the multiserver job queueing model with n servers, First-Come-First-Served scheduling, and classes of jobs where a class-i job simultaneously requests n_i servers and holds them for a service duration S_i. self_contained_problem:
Consider a multiserver job queueing system with a fixed number n of identical servers and First-Come-First-Served (FCFS) scheduling. Jobs arrive according to a Poisson process and are partitioned into finitely many classes indexed by i = 1, 2, …, K. A class-i job arrives with probability p_i (independently of the past), simultaneously requires exactly n_i of the n servers (1 ≤ n_i ≤ n), and, once it begins service, holds those n_i servers for a service duration S_i. Under FCFS, the head-of-line job waits until n_i servers are simultaneously available, at which point it occupies n_i servers for its entire service duration; jobs behind it in the queue cannot leapfrog ahead. Assume the system is stable. The response time T of a job is the elapsed time from its arrival until its service completion.

Specialize to the case in which every job, regardless of class, has the same service-time distribution S_i = S ~ Exp(μ) (independent across jobs). The problem is consistently described as open in the recent literature.

paper_title: Open problems in queueing theory inspired by datacenter computing
original_question: Assume all jobs follow the same speedup function, but their inherent sizes are known when they are scheduled. What allocation policy minimizes mean response time in this known-size parallel scheduling setting?
self_contained_problem:
Consider a parallel scheduling system with $k$ identical servers (cores) and a stream of jobs arriving over time. Each job $j$ has an inherent size $x_j > 0$, which is fully known to the scheduler at the moment of its arrival. All jobs share a common speedup function $s : [0,k] \to \mathbb{R}_{\ge 0}$, which is nondecreasing, concave, satisfies $s(0)=0$, and specifies the instantaneous service rate of a job when $a \in [0,k]$ servers are allocated to it. At each time $t$, a scheduler must choose a (possibly time-varying) allocation $(a_j(t))_j$ of the $k$ servers among the jobs currently in the system, where $a_j(t) \ge 0$ and $\sum_j a_j(t) \le k$. A job $j$ that arrives at time $r_j$ departs at the first time $c_j$ such that $\int_{r_j}^{c_j} s(a_j(t))\, \mathrm{d}t = x_j$, and its response time is $T_j = c_j - r_j$.

Determine the allocation policy (possibly preemptive, with full knowledge of remaining sizes and elapsed system state) that minimizes the long-run mean response time $\mathbb{E}[T]$ for jobs arriving according to a Poisson process with arbitrary size distribution, under a common concave speedup function $s$. Specifically, characterize the optimal policy and prove its optimality.
status_search_result: The general problem (Poisson arrivals, arbitrary size distribution, general concave speedup) appears largely open. Partial results are known: heSRPT (Berg, Dorsman, Harchol-Balter) gives an optimal allocation minimizing mean slowdown/response time in the all-jobs-present-at-time-0 setting under a common speedup curve, and EQUI is optimal under common speedup with exponential sizes. Recent work (2025) characterizes optimal policies under general concave speedup via a Consistent Derivative Ratio rule, but optimal scheduling for general size distributions with arrivals remains incompletely resolved.

original_question: When jobs with partially parallelizable speedup functions arrive over time, even for simple speedup models such as threshold-based speedup, what online allocation policy is optimal?
self_contained_problem:
Consider a single-server-pool system with $k$ identical servers (or processors). Jobs arrive over time according to a Poisson process of rate $\lambda$, and each arriving job $j$ has an i.i.d. size (work requirement) $X_j$ drawn from a known distribution. Each job has a threshold-based speedup function: there is a parameter $s_j \in \{1, 2, \dots, k\}$ such that if $a$ servers are allocated to job $j$ at some instant, the instantaneous service rate of job $j$ is $\min(a, s_j)$ (i.e., the job experiences linear speedup up to $s_j$ servers and no additional speedup beyond that). At every instant, a scheduler must decide how to partition the $k$ servers among the jobs currently in the system (servers may be allocated fractionally or in integer amounts, and reallocation may occur at any time without switching cost); jobs that are not allocated any server make no progress, and a job departs upon completing its work. 

Determine an online allocation/scheduling policy that minimizes the long-run mean response time (sojourn time) of jobs, where the policy may use only causal information (arrival times, current ages/remaining sizes, and the speedup thresholds of jobs already present), and not future arrivals. For the general dynamic arrival setting with threshold-based speedup, no exactly optimal online allocation policy is known; the problem remains open, with only asymptotic or heuristic results available.

paper_title: Open problems in queueing theory inspired by datacenter computing
original_question: When there are many job types, each with its own speedup function and its own distribution of inherent size, how should servers be allocated across jobs over time?
self_contained_problem:
Consider a queueing system with $k$ servers and $J$ distinct job types arriving over time according to independent stochastic arrival processes. Each job type $j \in \{1,\dots,J\}$ is characterized by:

(i) an inherent size distribution $S_j$ (the amount of inherent work a job of type $j$ requires when run on a single server), and

(ii) a speedup function $s_j : \{1,2,\dots,k\} \to \mathbb{R}_{\geq 0}$, where $s_j(a)$ is the instantaneous service rate received by a type-$j$ job when allocated $a$ servers (typically $s_j$ is non-decreasing and sublinear, i.e., concave with $s_j(1)=1$).

A scheduling policy dynamically allocates, at every time $t$, the $k$ servers among the jobs currently in the system, with the constraint that the total number of servers allocated does not exceed $k$ and each job receives an integer number of servers. A job of type $j$ assigned $a$ servers completes service after receiving cumulative work equal to its inherent size at rate $s_j(a)$.

Problem: Determine an allocation policy that minimizes the long-run mean response time (mean sojourn time) of jobs in this system, valid for general $J$, general inherent-size distributions $\{S_j\}$, and general (concave) speedup functions $\{s_j\}$. Either characterize an optimal policy explicitly or establish provable approximation/asymptotic optimality guarantees in terms of $(k, J, \{S_j\}, \{s_j\})$ and the arrival rates.
status_search_result: The general problem of allocating servers across many job types with heterogeneous speedup functions and size distributions remains open. Recent work has obtained partial results: asymptotically optimal policies have been derived for multiple classes of parallelizable jobs in heavy-traffic and light-traffic scaling regimes (e.g., Least-Parallelizable-First in light load, SERPT-type prioritization in heavy load), and analyses exist for moldable jobs with concave speedups. However, a fully general optimal allocation for arbitrary speedup functions and size distributions has not been established.

original_question: For DAG-job scheduling policies in which jobs arrive over time and each job is complete only when all tasks in its DAG are complete, how can one analyze the mean job response time of a given allocation policy?
self_contained_problem:
Consider a queueing model in which jobs arrive over time according to a stochastic arrival process (for example, a Poisson process with rate λ) and are served by a system of identical servers (say k ≥ 2 servers, each of unit speed). Each arriving job J is described by a directed acyclic graph (DAG) G_J = (V_J, E_J), where each vertex v ∈ V_J represents a task with an associated random service requirement S_v drawn from a known distribution, and each directed edge (u, v) ∈ E_J expresses a precedence constraint: task v may not begin execution until task u has been completed. Tasks of the same job may be executed in parallel on distinct servers, subject to the precedence constraints. A job is regarded as complete only when all of its tasks have completed.

Fix an allocation (scheduling) policy π that, at every decision epoch, assigns ready tasks (those whose predecessors are all done) to available servers based only on the current system state, the DAG structures of jobs in the system, and information about task service distributions. Let T_J denote the response time of job J under policy π, i.e., the time elapsed between J's arrival and the completion of its last task. Define the mean job response time of policy π as
   E[T^π] = lim_{n→∞} (1/n) Σ_{J=1}^{n} E[T_J],
assuming the system is stable under π.

Problem: Develop a method to compute or characterize E[T^π] as a function of the arrival rate, the distribution over job DAG structures, the task service time distributions, the number of servers k, and the policy π. In particular, derive a closed-form expression, tight bounds, or an asymptotically exact analysis (e.g., heavy-traffic or large-k limits) for E[T^π] for natural families of allocation policies acting on DAG-structured jobs.
status_search_result: Mean response time analysis for DAG-structured jobs under general allocation policies in multiserver queueing systems is widely acknowledged to be an open and difficult problem. Even for much simpler models (e.g., M/G/k with k ≥ 2 under non-trivial scheduling), exact response-time analysis has long resisted solution, and recent surveys on datacenter-motivated scheduling continue to list DAG-job response time analysis as an open challenge. No general solution appears in the literature.

original_question: In the limited fork-join model, what is the mean job response time when each arriving job dispatches its k tasks to the k shortest queues, or to the k queues with the least work, rather than to random queues?
self_contained_problem:
Consider the following limited fork–join queueing model. There are N identical first-come-first-served servers, each with its own infinite-capacity queue and unit service rate. Jobs arrive according to a Poisson process of rate λN (so that the per-server arrival rate is λ < 1). Each arriving job consists of exactly k ≤ N tasks. The task service times are i.i.d. exponential with mean 1 (or, in a second variant, i.i.d. from a general distribution G with finite mean). A job is considered complete only when all k of its tasks have finished service; its response time is the time from arrival until the last of its k tasks completes.

In the standard limited fork–join model the k tasks of each arriving job are dispatched to k servers chosen uniformly at random (without replacement) from the N servers. Consider instead the following two dispatch policies:

(a) Join-the-k-Shortest-Queues (JSQ-k): upon arrival, the job sends its k tasks to the k servers whose queues currently contain the fewest tasks (ties broken arbitrarily).

(b) Join-the-k-Least-Work (JLW-k): upon arrival, the job sends its k tasks to the k servers with the smallest remaining workload (sum of remaining service requirements of all tasks currently at that server).

Determine, in closed form or via a tractable analytical expression, the mean job response time E[T] in steady state under each of policies (a) and (b), as a function of N, k, λ, and the service-time distribution.

The problem appears to remain open.

paper_title: Open problems in queueing theory inspired by datacenter computing
original_question: In the single-server M/G/1 setting with unknown job sizes, can the known factor-5 guarantee for a simple policy relative to the optimal Gittins policy be improved, or can other simple policies be found that achieve comparably near-optimal mean response time?
self_contained_problem:
Consider an M/G/1 queue: jobs arrive according to a Poisson process of rate $\lambda$ to a single server, and each job has an i.i.d. size drawn from a distribution $S$ with finite mean, so that the load is $\rho = \lambda \mathbb{E}[S] < 1$. The scheduler may preempt jobs at any time but does not know the exact remaining size of a job; instead, for a job that has so far received service (age) $a$, the scheduler knows the conditional distribution of its remaining size given that it has been served for $a$ time units. A scheduling policy is a rule, based only on each job's age, deciding which job to serve at each instant. Let $\mathbb{E}[T^\pi]$ denote the steady-state mean response time (sojourn time) under policy $\pi$, and let $\mathrm{Gittins}$ denote the Gittins index policy, which is known to minimize $\mathbb{E}[T^\pi]$ in this setting.

Define the policy M-SERPT (monotonic shortest expected remaining processing time), which assigns to each job of age $a$ the rank
$$r(a) = \sup_{b \ge a} \, \mathbb{E}[S - a \mid S > a, \text{ remaining work after age } a \text{ is observed up to age } b],$$
or more simply a monotonized version of the expected-remaining-size function, and at all times serves the job of smallest rank. It is known that
$$\mathbb{E}[T^{\text{M-SERPT}}] \le 5 \, \mathbb{E}[T^{\text{Gittins}}]$$
for every job size distribution $S$ and every load $\rho < 1$.

(a) Can the constant $5$ in the above inequality be replaced by a smaller universal constant (and what is the optimal constant)?

(b) Does there exist another scheduling policy $\pi$, whose rank function is "simple" in the sense of being substantially less complex to compute than the Gittins index, such that $\mathbb{E}[T^\pi] \le C \, \mathbb{E}[T^{\text{Gittins}}]$ holds for a universal constant $C$, ideally with $C$ smaller than $5$?
status_search_result: The factor-5 bound was established by Scully, Harchol-Balter, and Scheller-Wolf (2019/2020) for M-SERPT versus Gittins. Subsequent work, including Scully's 2022 thesis and related papers, has refined the analysis (showing the ratio is at most 3 for load ρ ≤ 8/9) and noted that the worst observed ratio in examples is only about 2, but no published result improves the universal constant below 5 nor exhibits a different simple policy with a better universal approximation guarantee. The problem appears to remain open.

original_question: Suppose every arriving job has a hard deadline of 400 ms and the objective is to minimize the fraction of jobs whose response time exceeds that deadline. What scheduling policy minimizes P{Response time > 400 ms}?
self_contained_problem:

The response time $T$ of a job is the time from its arrival until its completion.

Fix a deadline $d = 400$ ms (in the units of service time). Among all work-conserving scheduling policies that may use full knowledge of job sizes and arrival times, determine the policy $\pi^\star$ that minimizes the steady-state probability
$$\mathbb{P}\{T > d\}$$
that a job's response time exceeds the deadline $d$. Equivalently, find the scheduling discipline that minimizes the fraction of jobs whose response time exceeds $400$ ms, and characterize the optimal value.
status_search_result: The problem of finding a scheduling policy that minimizes the tail probability P{Response time > d} for a fixed deadline d in an M/G/1-type queue is listed as an open problem in the queueing-theory open-problems survey on datacenter computing. While SRPT is known to minimize mean response time in M/G/1 (Schrage 1968), no policy is known to minimize the deadline-miss probability for a fixed finite deadline, and the relevant literature continues to treat this as unresolved.

paper_title: Open problems in queueing theory inspired by datacenter computing
original_question: For the Drop-The-Larger-Hopeless policy in deadline-based scheduling, what is the probability that an arriving job is dropped?
self_contained_problem:
Consider a single-server queue with the following setup. Jobs arrive according to a Poisson process of rate $\lambda$. Each arriving job $i$ has an i.i.d. service-time requirement $S_i$ drawn from a known distribution and an i.i.d. relative deadline $D_i$ drawn from a known distribution; the job must complete service by time $A_i + D_i$, where $A_i$ is its arrival time. At any time $t$, a job currently in the system is called "hopeless" if, given its remaining service requirement and the current system state, it cannot possibly meet its deadline (for instance, under any non-preemptive or preemptive work-conserving schedule its deadline will be missed with certainty).

The Drop-The-Larger-Hopeless (DTLH) admission/scheduling policy is defined as follows. Upon each arrival, and whenever the set of hopeless jobs in the system changes, the policy identifies all hopeless jobs currently present (including possibly the new arrival). If the set of hopeless jobs is nonempty, the policy drops the hopeless job with the largest (remaining) service requirement. The server otherwise serves jobs according to a deadline-aware discipline (e.g., earliest-deadline-first among non-hopeless jobs).

Determine, in closed form or as a tractable expression, the steady-state probability $p_{\mathrm{drop}}$ that an arbitrary arriving job is eventually dropped under the DTLH policy, as a function of $\lambda$ and the distributions of $S$ and $D$.

paper_title: Open problems in queueing theory inspired by datacenter computing
original_question: For the M/M/k queue with setup times, where idle servers shut down and must incur setup delay before serving jobs again, can one derive a simple approximation as a function of k that captures how the response-time effect of setup diminishes in larger systems?
self_contained_problem:
Consider the M/M/k queueing system with server setup times, defined as follows. Jobs arrive according to a Poisson process of rate λ to a system with k identical servers, each of which serves jobs at exponential rate μ; let ρ = λ/(kμ) < 1 denote the load. Each server can be in one of three states: BUSY (currently serving a job), OFF, or SETUP. A server in the OFF state cannot serve jobs; when a job needs a server and an OFF server is available, that server enters the SETUP state, during which it incurs an Exp(α) setup delay before it can begin serving. Whenever a server completes a job and no jobs are waiting, it immediately transitions to OFF. Jobs waiting in a FCFS queue are assigned to servers as soon as any server becomes BUSY-ready.

Let E[T(k)] denote the mean response time (sojourn time) of a job in this system, and let E[T_{M/M/k}] denote the corresponding mean response time in the standard M/M/k system (no setup) with the same λ, μ, k.

status_search_result: Recent work (Williams, Harchol-Balter and collaborators, 2023–2024 PhD thesis and SIGMETRICS/ACM publications, plus a 2025 arXiv preprint) has produced closed-form multiplicatively-tight lower and upper bounds and a highly accurate approximation for mean waiting time in many-server systems with setup times (mainly deterministic setup, and with offered load R = kρ assumed reasonably large). paper_title: Open problems in renewal, coupling and Palm theory
original_question: Let S_n = S_0 + X_1 + ··· + X_n be a renewal process with nonnegative delay S_0 and i.i.d. strictly positive recurrence times X_1, X_2, … independent of S_0. For t ≥ 0 let N_t = inf{n ≥ 0 : S_n > t}, let A_t = t - S_{N_t-1} be the age at time t, let B_t = S_{N_t} - t be the residual life, let D_t = X_{N_t} = A_t + B_t be the total life, and let U_t = A_t / D_t be the relative age. Assume the renewal process is null recurrent, meaning E[X_1] = ∞. Does U_t converge in distribution to a Uniform[0,1] random variable as t → ∞?
self_contained_problem:
Let $S_0 \ge 0$ be a nonnegative random variable, and let $X_1, X_2, \ldots$ be i.i.d. strictly positive random variables, independent of $S_0$. Define the renewal process $S_n = S_0 + X_1 + \cdots + X_n$ for $n \ge 0$. For each $t \ge 0$, let
\[ N_t = \inf\{n \ge 0 : S_n > t\}, \qquad A_t = t - S_{N_t - 1}, \qquad B_t = S_{N_t} - t, \]
\[ D_t = X_{N_t} = A_t + B_t, \qquad U_t = A_t / D_t, \]
called respectively the age, residual life, total life and relative age at time $t$. Assume the renewal process is null recurrent in the sense that $\mathbb{E}[X_1] = \infty$.

Question: Does $U_t$ converge in distribution to a Uniform$[0,1]$ random variable as $t \to \infty$?
status_search_result: The question has been resolved negatively in general. Work on the ratio of current age to total life for null recurrent renewal processes shows that when the inter-arrival distribution is regularly varying with index $\alpha \in (0,1)$, $A_t/D_t$ converges in distribution to a nondegenerate limit (a generalized arcsine / Beta-type law, e.g. $U^{1/\alpha}$ with $U$ Uniform$[0,1]$ in one parameterization) rather than to Uniform$[0,1]$. Hence the Uniform$[0,1]$ limit characteristic of the positive-recurrent case does not extend to the null-recurrent case.

original_question: Assume again that S_n = S_0 + X_1 + ··· + X_n is a null-recurrent renewal process, that U_t = A_t / D_t is the relative age, and that the preceding two questions have positive answers, so that D_t / φ(t) converges in distribution to some random variable D_φ and U_t converges in distribution to a Uniform[0,1] random variable U. Must the pair (D_t / φ(t), U_t) then converge in distribution, as t → ∞, to (D_φ, U) with D_φ and U independent?

Let $S_0, X_1, X_2, \dots$ be independent random variables with $X_1, X_2, \dots$ i.i.d. and strictly positive, and set $S_n = S_0 + X_1 + \cdots + X_n$ for $n \ge 0$. Assume the renewal process $\{S_n\}_{n\ge 0}$ is null-recurrent, i.e., $\mathbb{E}[X_1] = \infty$. For $t \ge 0$, let
\[
N_t = \inf\{n \ge 0 : S_n > t\}, \qquad A_t = t - S_{N_t - 1}, \qquad B_t = S_{N_t} - t, \qquad D_t = A_t + B_t = X_{N_t},
\]
denote, respectively, the age, the residual lifetime, and the total length of the current renewal interval at time $t$. Define the relative age
\[
U_t = \frac{A_t}{D_t} \in [0,1].
\]
Suppose there exists a positive measurable function $\varphi:(0,\infty)\to(0,\infty)$ and a random variable $D_\varphi$ such that
\[
\frac{D_t}{\varphi(t)} \xrightarrow{d} D_\varphi \quad\text{and}\quad U_t \xrightarrow{d} U \quad\text{as } t \to \infty,
\]
where $U$ is uniformly distributed on $[0,1]$.
