paper_title: Open Problems on Search Games
original_question: Can two lions catch a man in finite time in a bounded planar region containing rectifiable lakes, when all players have equal maximum speeds and capture requires the lion and the man to coincide?
self_contained_problem:
Consider a bounded region R in the Euclidean plane whose complement (within some bounding box) consists of finitely many "lakes," each lake being an open set whose boundary is a rectifiable Jordan curve. Three players — two "lions" L_1, L_2 and one "man" M — are modeled as points moving inside the closure of R. All three move along continuous trajectories and have the same maximum speed (normalized to 1); that is, each trajectory is 1-Lipschitz with respect to time. The lions choose their strategy knowing the position of the man at every time, and the man likewise knows the positions of the lions. The lions "capture" the man if at some finite time t ≥ 0 the position of at least one lion coincides with the position of the man.

Question: Do the two lions always have a strategy that guarantees capture of the man in finite time, regardless of the shape of R (subject to the rectifiable-lakes condition) and regardless of the man's strategy?
status_search_result: The question (originally posed by Littlewood) has been resolved in the negative: there exists a bounded planar region with finitely many rectifiable lakes in which the man has a strategy to evade two lions forever. The same line of work shows that three lions always suffice to capture the man under these conditions, so two lions are not enough in general.

paper_title: Open Problems on Search Games
original_question: For the princess and monster game on a tree, does there exist an optimal princess strategy with the confluency property that whenever two princess trajectories meet at some time t0, they coincide for all earlier times up to t0?
self_contained_problem:
Consider the princess-and-monster search game played on a finite tree $T$ (a connected graph without cycles, viewed as a metric space with unit-length edges). Two players, the princess (hider) and the monster (searcher), move continuously along $T$ with speeds bounded by $1$. Neither player can see the other; capture occurs at the first time $t \ge 0$ at which the two players occupy the same point of $T$. The princess wishes to maximize, and the monster wishes to minimize, the expected capture time.

A (mixed) strategy for the princess is a probability distribution over Lipschitz trajectories $p:[0,\infty) \to T$ with $|p'| \le 1$ almost everywhere. Let $\mathcal{P}$ denote the support of such a strategy. The strategy is said to have the confluency property if for every pair of trajectories $p_1, p_2 \in \mathcal{P}$ and every time $t_0 \ge 0$ such that $p_1(t_0) = p_2(t_0)$, one has $p_1(t) = p_2(t)$ for all $t \in [0, t_0]$ (i.e., trajectories that meet at some time must have coincided at every earlier time).

Question: For the princess-and-monster game on an arbitrary finite tree, does there exist an optimal strategy for the princess that satisfies the confluency property?
status_search_result: The princess-and-monster game on general networks (beyond the circle) remains largely unsolved, and no published resolution of the tree confluency conjecture was found. Searches return general background on the game with no result establishing existence of an optimal confluent princess strategy on trees.

paper_title: Open Problems on Search Games
context_brief: Continuous guessing game: mixed vs pure searcher
original_question: In the continuous high-low guessing game where Blue chooses h in [0,1], Red repeatedly guesses, is told whether each guess is too high or too low, and Blue's payoff is the infinite sum of the absolute errors Σ|g_n-h|, Steve Alpern found a pure minimax strategy for the searcher. Does there exist any mixed searcher strategy with strictly better performance than that known pure minimax strategy?
self_contained_problem:
Consider the following two-player zero-sum continuous high–low guessing game. Player Blue (the hider) chooses a number h ∈ [0,1]. Player Red (the searcher) makes an infinite sequence of guesses g_1, g_2, … ∈ [0,1]. After each guess g_n, Red is told whether g_n > h or g_n < h (the event g_n = h has probability zero and is ignored). Red's strategy may be adaptive: each g_n may depend on the responses to g_1,…,g_{n-1}. Blue's payoff (which Red wishes to minimize and Blue wishes to maximize) is
   P(h, (g_n)) = Σ_{n=1}^∞ |g_n − h|.
A pure searcher strategy is a deterministic rule producing g_n from the history of responses; a mixed searcher strategy is a probability distribution over pure searcher strategies, with payoff taken in expectation. It is known that there exists a pure searcher strategy achieving the minimax value V* = sup_h P(h, ·) among pure strategies.

Question: Does there exist a mixed searcher strategy σ such that
   sup_{h ∈ [0,1]} E_{σ}[ Σ_n |g_n − h| ] < V* ?
That is, can randomization strictly improve the searcher's worst-case expected total error below the best pure-strategy guarantee?
status_search_result: The problem is stated as an open question in the search-games open-problems literature, and no subsequent paper appears to have resolved whether a mixed searcher strategy can outperform the known pure minimax strategy in this continuous high–low guessing game. A web search returned only general references on search games and the Alpern–Gal mixed-strategy minimax framework, with no record of a resolution.

paper_title: Open Problems on Search Games
original_question: Modify the continuous guessing game by allowing the hider to move from one secret number h_n to the next h_{n+1} between consecutive guesses, and score the hider by Σ|g_n-h_∞|, where h_∞ is the limiting value of the hider's secret numbers. The source states that Alpern's pure minimax strategy still works for this payoff. Can one prove that this pure minimax strategy is actually optimal for the moving-hider version of the game?
self_contained_problem:
Consider the following two-player zero-sum continuous guessing game between a Hider and a Guesser. At each step n = 1, 2, 3, ..., the Hider selects a real number h_n ∈ ℝ (which may differ from h_{n-1}), and the Guesser, without observing h_n, announces a guess g_n ∈ ℝ. After each guess, the Hider truthfully reveals whether g_n < h_n, g_n = h_n, or g_n > h_n. The sequence (h_n) is assumed to converge to a limit h_∞ ∈ ℝ. The Hider's strategy space therefore allows the secret to move between consecutive guesses, subject only to the comparison responses already given and to the existence of the limit h_∞. The payoff (paid by the Guesser to the Hider) is
    P = Σ_{n=1}^{∞} |g_n - h_∞|.
The Guesser seeks to minimize P and the Hider seeks to maximize it.

In the classical static version of this game (where h_n = h is fixed), Alpern's pure minimax strategy for the Guesser is known to be optimal. The same pure minimax strategy is still well-defined when the Hider is allowed to move, and it yields a finite value against any admissible Hider strategy with payoff Σ |g_n - h_∞|.

Prove that Alpern's pure minimax Guesser strategy is optimal (i.e. achieves the value of the game) in this moving-hider variant with payoff Σ |g_n - h_∞|.
status_search_result: A web search did not surface any published proof that Alpern's pure minimax strategy is optimal in the moving-hider variant of the continuous guessing game with payoff Σ|g_n - h_∞|. The question is listed among open problems in search games, and no later resolution was found in available sources.

paper_title: Open Problems on Search Games
original_question: In Dresher's guessing game on the set {1,2,...,n}, where Blue chooses a secret number and Red repeatedly guesses with too-high/too-low feedback, is Johnson's conjecture true that for n>4 the probability Blue assigns to the number 1 equals the total probability Blue assigns to the set {2,3}?
self_contained_problem:
Fix an integer n ≥ 1 and consider the following two-player zero-sum game (Dresher's guessing game). Player Blue (the Hider) chooses a number h ∈ {1, 2, …, n} according to some probability distribution p = (p_1, …, p_n). Player Red (the Searcher) does not see h and repeatedly guesses integers from {1, 2, …, n}; after each guess g, Red is told whether g < h, g > h, or g = h, and continues guessing until g = h. Red may adapt his strategy based on the history of responses. The payoff that Blue receives (equivalently, the cost to Red) is the total number of guesses Red makes until guessing h correctly. Both players play optimally: Blue chooses p to maximize the expected number of guesses, while Red chooses an adaptive guessing strategy (possibly randomized) to minimize it. Let p* = (p*_1, …, p*_n) denote an optimal mixed strategy for Blue at equilibrium.

Prove or disprove the following conjecture (Johnson): for every integer n > 4, every optimal Blue strategy p* satisfies
   p*_1 = p*_2 + p*_3.
status_search_result: The conjecture is described as having remained unsolved for nearly 50 years and is characterized as possibly the longest-standing open problem in search games. No published resolution was located.

paper_title: Open problems, questions and challenges in finite-dimensional integrable systems
original_question: Do local symplectic invariants exist for diffeomorphic dege nerate singularities? How many and of what kind are they? This question makes sense even in the simplest case of one-degree- of-freedom systems. As we know from concrete examples of integrable systems, many de generate singularities are stable in the sense that they cannot be destroyed by a small perturbatio n of the system [25, 85, 124]. The problem of description of stable degenerate singularities is very impo rtant on its own right, but for many degrees of freedom, it is quite complicated. However, in the ca se of two degrees of freedom (perhaps depending on a parameter), there is a number of well-kno wn examples of stable bifurcations (e.g., integrable period-doubling [25] and Hamiltonian Hopf bifurcation [70]). It would be interesting to clarify the situation with asymptotic behaviour of angle variables a t least for them. V. Kalashnikov [124] has described all stable singularities of rank 1 fo r Hamiltonian systems of two degrees of freedom.
self_contained_problem:
Let $(M,\omega)$ be a smooth symplectic manifold and let $F=(f_1,\dots,f_n)\colon M\to\mathbb{R}^n$ be the momentum map of a completely integrable Hamiltonian system, i.e. the functions $f_1,\dots,f_n$ are smooth, functionally independent on an open dense subset, and pairwise Poisson-commuting with respect to $\omega$. A point $p\in M$ is a singular point of $F$ if $\mathrm{rank}\,dF(p)<n$, and it is called degenerate if the linearization of the system at $p$ does not satisfy the Williamson non-degeneracy condition (so that Eliasson's symplectic linearization theorem does not apply). Two singularities $(F,p)$ and $(F',p')$ are diffeomorphic (or fibrewise topologically equivalent) if there is a local diffeomorphism of neighbourhoods sending the level sets of $F$ to those of $F'$ and $p$ to $p'$; they are symplectically equivalent if this diffeomorphism can be chosen to be a symplectomorphism that intertwines the foliations defined by $F$ and $F'$.

(a) Do there exist local symplectic invariants distinguishing diffeomorphic but symplectically inequivalent degenerate singularities of integrable Hamiltonian systems? In other words, can two degenerate singularities be topologically (fibrewise) equivalent yet fail to be symplectically equivalent?

(b) If such invariants exist, describe their nature, classify them, and determine how many independent invariants are needed in the case of one degree of freedom ($n=1$), and in the case of two degrees of freedom ($n=2$), including families depending on a parameter and the stable bifurcation types such as the integrable period-doubling bifurcation and the Hamiltonian Hopf bifurcation. In particular, clarify the asymptotic behaviour of the action–angle variables near such stable degenerate singularities.
status_search_result: The general question remains open, but partial progress has been made. Bolsinov, Guglielmi and Kudryavtseva (2018) and follow-up work (e.g. arXiv:2110.13758, 2023) have constructed local symplectic invariants for parabolic orbits and cusp singularities of integrable systems with two degrees of freedom; a 2025 Regular and Chaotic Dynamics paper gives a symplectic classification for universal unfoldings of $A_n$ singularities. Kalashnikov's classification of stable rank-1 singularities for two-degree-of-freedom systems is known, but a general classification of symplectic invariants for arbitrary degenerate singularities (and the asymptotics of angle variables near them) is not yet established.

paper_title: Open problems, questions and challenges in finite-dimensional integrable systems
original_question: Describe all the topological types of singularities that ma y appear in algebraically inte- grable systems with a small (≤ 3) degree of freedom. Next, describe the symplectic invariant s of such singularities. We expect that solving local and semi-global problems mentioned abo ve will simplify the passage to global results. Some open problems related to classification of integ rable systems in global setting are stated below. Recall that an integrable system F = (J, H) is called semitoric if all of its singularities are nondegen- erate and of either elliptic or focus types (hyperbolic singularties ar e forbidden) and, in addition, J is proper and generates a Hamiltonian S1-action on the manifold. 6
self_contained_problem:
Let $F=(f_1,\dots,f_n):M^{2n}\to\mathbb{R}^n$ be an algebraically integrable Hamiltonian system on a real symplectic manifold of dimension $2n$, with $n\le 3$. Here "integrable" means that $f_1,\dots,f_n$ are Poisson-commuting functionally independent functions, and "algebraically integrable" means that the system extends to a complex algebraic completely integrable system, i.e. the generic complex fibers are open subsets of abelian varieties and $f_1,\dots,f_n$ are polynomial (or algebraic) in suitable coordinates.

A singular point of $F$ is a point $p\in M$ where $df_1\wedge\cdots\wedge df_n$ vanishes. Two singular points (or their germs/saturated neighborhoods) are called topologically equivalent if there exists a homeomorphism of neighborhoods sending leaves of the singular Lagrangian foliation defined by $F$ to leaves, and symplectically equivalent if there is a symplectomorphism realizing this equivalence.

Problem:
(a) Describe (classify) all topological types of singular points and singular fibers of $F$ that may occur in algebraically integrable systems with $n\in\{1,2,3\}$ degrees of freedom, locally and semi-locally (in a saturated neighborhood of the singular fiber).
(b) For each topological type appearing in (a), determine a complete set of symplectic invariants classifying such singularities up to symplectic equivalence.
status_search_result: The classification of topological and symplectic types of singularities in (algebraically) integrable systems with up to three degrees of freedom remains an active research area. Partial results exist: nondegenerate singularities are well understood in two degrees of freedom (Eliasson, Vũ Ngọc, Zung), and recent work (e.g., 2023 arXiv preprint on saddle-focus singularities) gives semi-local topological classifications for specific singularity types in three degrees of freedom. Symplectic invariants have been obtained for certain unfoldings of $A_n$-singularities. A general classification covering all topological types and symplectic invariants in the algebraically integrable case for $n\le 3$ is not available, and the question remains open.

paper_title: Open problems, questions and challenges in finite-dimensional integrable systems
original_question: Consider a compact connected 2n-dimensional symplectic manifold M, endowed with a Hamiltonian (S1)n- 1-action; these are called complexity one spaces. Consider an integrable system f1,..., fn on M where (f1,..., fn- 1): M → Rn- 1 is the momentum map of the Hamiltonian (S1)n- 1-action. Suppose that the singularities of the integrable s ystem are non-degenerate and also they do not contain hyperbolic blocks. Study how the invariants of the complexity one space are related to the invariants of the semitoric system. For recent progress in the case 2 n = 4 see Hohloch et al [116]. Recently there have been many works on integrable systems which c an be obtained by the method of toric degenerations. In particular, many well-known integrable sys tems can be constructed this way, including the bending flow of 3D polygons Foth et al [77] and the Gelfand-Cetlin 1 system Nishinou et al [174]. See also [113, 130, 175]. A common feature of integrable syste ms coming from toric degenerations is that their base space (the space of fibers of the momentum map) is a convex polytope, which implies that the singular fibers are quite special.
self_contained_problem:
Let $(M,\omega)$ be a compact connected symplectic manifold of dimension $2n$, equipped with an effective Hamiltonian $(S^1)^{n-1}$-action with momentum map $\mu=(f_1,\dots,f_{n-1}):M\to\mathbb{R}^{n-1}$. Such a triple $(M,\omega,\mu)$ is called a complexity one space. Suppose that $f_n:M\to\mathbb{R}$ is a smooth function such that $F=(f_1,\dots,f_n):M\to\mathbb{R}^n$ defines a completely integrable system (the components Poisson-commute and are functionally independent on a dense open set). Assume further that every singular point of $F$ is non-degenerate in the Williamson sense and that the local symplectic normal form at each singularity contains no hyperbolic block (so only elliptic and focus–focus blocks occur); call such an $F$ a (higher-dimensional) semitoric system on the complexity one space.

Determine an explicit correspondence between the symplectic invariants of $(M,\omega,\mu)$ as a complexity one space (its Karshon-type combinatorial/graph invariants and equivariant data) and the symplectic invariants of the semitoric system $F$ (such as the number of focus–focus singular fibers, the polygon invariant, the height invariant, the Taylor series invariant at each focus–focus fiber, and the twisting index invariant). In particular, describe how the invariants of $(M,\omega,\mu)$ determine, and are determined by, those of $F$, generalizing the known case $2n=4$.

paper_title: Open problems, questions and challenges in finite-dimensional integrable systems
original_question: Give a clear description of these special singular fibers.
self_contained_problem:
Setup. Let $(M^{2n},\omega)$ be a smooth symplectic manifold and let $F=(f_1,\dots,f_n):M\to\mathbb{R}^n$ be a smooth integrable system, i.e. the functions $f_1,\dots,f_n$ are Poisson-commuting with respect to $\omega$ and are functionally independent on an open dense subset of $M$. The fibers of $F$ that contain critical points are called singular fibers; nondegenerate singular points are locally of elliptic, hyperbolic, or focus-focus type in the sense of Eliasson and Vey.

In the geometric context motivated by special Lagrangian fibrations on Calabi--Yau manifolds (in particular in real dimension $2n\ge 6$), there typically appear codimension-two strata of focus-focus type singularities forming one-parameter families, together with a finite collection of additional singular fibers that lie at the intersections/limits of these focus-focus families. Call these latter fibers the special singular fibers.

Problem. Give a clear topological and symplectic description of these special singular fibers: describe
(i) the local structure of the integrable system near such a fiber (a normal form, including the types of degeneracies of the critical points that occur on it),
(ii) the topology of the fiber itself and of a saturated neighborhood, including the monodromy of $F$ around it, and
(iii) classifying invariants (analogous to the Vũ Ngọc invariants for focus-focus fibers) that determine such a fiber up to a suitable notion of symplectic equivalence.
status_search_result: The problem of describing these special singular fibers (at intersections of focus-focus families, relevant to SYZ Lagrangian fibrations on Calabi-Yau manifolds) is listed in the 2018 survey of open problems in finite-dimensional integrable systems and does not appear to have been resolved in general. Subsequent works (e.g., on Gelfand-Cetlin systems and on smooth invariants of focus-focus singularities) treat specific examples or related singularities, but no general clear description of the special fibers has been established.

original_question: If a natural Hamiltonian system with a nonconstant potentia l on T 2 admits an integral that is polynomial of odd degree in momenta, then it admits a linear integral. If it admits a nontrivial integral of even degree, then it admits a nontriv ial quadratic integral. Resent results in this conjecture include [55]. Even the case when th e integral has degrees 3 and 4 is not solved! Yet an easier version is the following conjecture:
self_contained_problem:
Let $T^2 = \mathbb{R}^2/2\pi\mathbb{Z}^2$ be the two-dimensional torus with standard coordinates $(q_1,q_2)$ and conjugate momenta $(p_1,p_2)$. Consider a natural Hamiltonian system on $T^*T^2$ with Hamiltonian
$$H(q,p) = \tfrac{1}{2}(p_1^2+p_2^2) + U(q_1,q_2),$$
where the potential $U:T^2\to\mathbb{R}$ is smooth and nonconstant. A function $F:T^*T^2\to\mathbb{R}$ is called a polynomial integral of degree $n$ in momenta if $\{H,F\}=0$ and $F(q,p)=\sum_{i+j\le n} a_{ij}(q)\,p_1^i p_2^j$ with the homogeneous part of degree $n$ not identically zero. The integral is called nontrivial if it is functionally independent of $H$. Prove or disprove the following:

(a) If the system admits a nontrivial polynomial integral of odd degree in the momenta, then it admits a nontrivial integral that is linear in the momenta.

(b) If the system admits a nontrivial polynomial integral of even degree in the momenta, then it admits a nontrivial integral that is quadratic in the momenta.

In particular, settle the cases of polynomial integrals of degree $3$ and degree $4$.
status_search_result: The conjecture remains open in general. Partial results are known: the nonexistence of irreducible polynomial integrals of degrees 3 and 4 was established under additional assumptions (e.g., when the potential is a trigonometric polynomial, by Denisova–Kozlov, and in further special cases by Bialy, Mironov, and others). Recent work has extended estimates to degrees 5 and 7 under restrictions on the spectrum of the potential, but the full conjecture (including degrees 3 and 4 in general) is still unresolved.

original_question: Construct a natural Hamiltonian system with a nonconstant p otential on S2 that admits a nontrivial polynomial integral of degree 5 and does not admit any nontrivial integrals of smaller degrees. 10 Additional interesting generalisations of the above questions appe ar if we consider a slightly more general class of Hamiltonian systems on T ∗M, namely such that H:= K + L + U, where K and U are as in (3.1), and L is a linear in momenta function (sometimes referred to as magnetic terms); the solutions of this Hamiltonian system describe t rajectories of charged particles in a magnetic field. In this case, only few explicit examples are known (e.g., those coming from Kovalevskaya, Clebsh, and Steklov integrable cases in rigid body dyn amics, and also from Veselova system and Chaplygin ball from non-holonomic integrable systems), so any new example would be an interesting result. Notice that even an explicit local description of s uch systems in the simplest case of quadratic integrals in dimension two remains an open problem (we re fer to [157] by V. Marikhin et al and [193] by G. Pucacco et al for the latest progress in the area). Note that in this case one can consider integrability on the whole cota ngent bundle, as it was done, for example, in [157], or on one energy level as, for example, in [32, §3]; both types of integrability are interesting. We also would like to draw attention to two recent papers containing o pen problems on integrable natural Hamiltonian systems on two-dimensional manifolds: Burns et al [45], see §10.2 there, and Butler [46], see §§3.3-3.5 there. 3.1.2 Polynomial in momenta integrals in higher dimensions. In most known examples, the integrals of natural systems are eith er related to Hamiltonian reduction leading to integrable systems on Lie algebras (which may possess non trivial polynomial integrals of arbitrary degree, see e.g. [26]), or the integrals are quadratic in mo menta and the quadratic terms are simultaneously diagonalisable. There are also examples with polynomial integrals of higher degrees coming from physical models, such as the Toda lattice and Calogero- Moser systems. Generally, one simply needs more examples, which either are interesting to mathema tical physics or "live" on closed manifolds.
self_contained_problem:
Let $S^2$ denote the standard two-dimensional sphere equipped with a Riemannian metric $g$, and let $T^*S^2$ be its cotangent bundle with the canonical symplectic structure. A natural Hamiltonian system on $T^*S^2$ is one whose Hamiltonian has the form
$$H(q,p) = \tfrac{1}{2} g^{ij}(q) p_i p_j + U(q),$$
where $U \colon S^2 \to \mathbb{R}$ is a smooth function called the potential. A function $F \colon T^*S^2 \to \mathbb{R}$ that is polynomial in the momenta $p$ is called a polynomial integral of degree $d$ if $\{H,F\} = 0$ (where $\{\cdot,\cdot\}$ is the canonical Poisson bracket) and the highest-degree homogeneous component of $F$ in $p$ is of degree $d$ and does not vanish identically. An integral $F$ is called nontrivial if it is functionally independent from $H$. 

Construct an explicit example of a Riemannian metric $g$ on $S^2$ and a nonconstant smooth potential $U \colon S^2 \to \mathbb{R}$ such that the associated natural Hamiltonian system $H = \tfrac{1}{2}g^{ij}p_i p_j + U$ on $T^*S^2$:
\begin{enumerate}
\item admits a nontrivial polynomial-in-momenta first integral of degree exactly $5$, and
\item admits no nontrivial polynomial-in-momenta first integrals of degree less than $5$ (i.e., no nontrivial linear, quadratic, cubic, or quartic integrals).
\end{enumerate}

original_question: Construct stationary axially symmetric 4-dimensional Ein stein metrics admitting Killing tensors of higher order. The condition "stationary axially symmetric" simply means the existen ce of two commuting vector fields, one of which is space-like and the other time-like. 11 Let us also touch upon two problems related to the homogeneous ca se. Recall that a scalar invariant of order k of a Riemannian manifold ( M, g) is a function on M, constructed from covariant derivatives of order k or less of the curvature tensor R or, equivalently, an algebraic expression in the components of covariant derivatives of R (of order ≤ k) which transforms as a function under coordinate changes. We say that ( M, g) is k-homogeneous, if all its scalar invariants up to order k are constants. It is known that, for a sufficiently big k, any k-homogeneous manifold is automatically locally homoge- neous, i.e., admits a locally transitive isometry group. As it follows from Singer [201], k = n(n+1)/2+1, where n is the dimension of the manifold, is sufficiently big in this sense; later bet ter estimations were found in [192, 54].
self_contained_problem:
A 4-dimensional pseudo-Riemannian manifold $(M,g)$ is called stationary and axially symmetric if it admits two commuting Killing vector fields, one time-like and one space-like. The metric $g$ is called Einstein if its Ricci tensor satisfies $\mathrm{Ric}(g)=\Lambda g$ for some constant $\Lambda\in\mathbb{R}$. A symmetric $(0,k)$-tensor field $K$ on $(M,g)$ is called a Killing tensor of order $k$ if $\nabla_{(i_0}K_{i_1\dots i_k)}=0$, where $\nabla$ is the Levi-Civita connection of $g$ and parentheses denote symmetrization. A Killing tensor is said to be trivial (reducible) if it is a polynomial expression with constant coefficients in the metric and in symmetrized products of Killing vector fields.

Problem: Construct an explicit example of a 4-dimensional stationary axially symmetric Einstein metric $g$ on a manifold $M$ that admits a non-trivial Killing tensor of order $k\geq 3$, or prove that no such metric exists.
status_search_result: Recent work (e.g., Vollmer 2017, arXiv:1602.08968) establishes nonexistence of nontrivial higher-valence Killing tensors for several specific stationary axisymmetric spacetimes (Tomimatsu-Sato up to valence 7, C-metric up to valence 9, Zipoy-Voorhees up to valence 11), and methodological frameworks (2024) use ansatz-based Killing tensors to recover known solutions like Kerr (which has a valence-2 Killing tensor). No explicit construction of a stationary axially symmetric 4D Einstein metric admitting a genuinely higher-order (k≥3) irreducible Killing tensor appears in the literature; the problem is widely regarded as open.

original_question: In a symmetric space, is every Killing tensor a sum of symmetr ic products of Killing vectors? Equivalently, is it true that the algebra of all pol ynomial integrals of the geodesic flow in a symmetric space is generated by linear integrals? Note that for general metrics the answer is clearly negative: ther e exist metrics admitting nontrivial Killing tensors and no Killing vectors. For constant curvature space s, the answer is positive [212]. 3.2 Superintegrable systems Recall that a natural Hamiltonian system is superintegrable, if it admits more functionally independent integrals (of some special form) than the dimension of the manifold ( in addition, one usually assumes that common level surfaces of these integrals are isotropic subma nifolds in T ∗ M ). A system is called maximally superintegrable, if the number of functionally independent integrals is 2 n - 1, which is the maximal number for an n-dimensional manifold. An interesting and well-studied class of superintegrable natural Ha miltonian systems consists of geodesic flows of Zoll metrics. Recall that a Riemannian metric (on a closed man ifold) is called a Zoll metric if all its geodesics are closed, see e.g. [11]. In this case, the Hamiltonian flow can be viewed as a symplec- tic action of S1, the orbit space is an orbifold, and any function defined on this orbif old is an integral. Notice that locally, near almost every point, each natural Hamiltonia n system is superintegrable. It is therefore standard to consider superintegrability in the class of in tegrals of a special form, typically, polynomial in momenta. Then, superintegrability is a nontrivial condit ion on the system, even locally. In dimension two, superintegrable systems with quadratic integrals were locally essentially described in [57]. Superintegrable systems with one linear and one cubic integral were described in [162]; the 12 methods can be generalised for the case when one integral is linear a nd the second of arbitrary degree, see e.g. [218].
self_contained_problem:
Let $(M,g)$ be a Riemannian symmetric space. A Killing vector field on $M$ is a vector field whose flow consists of isometries; equivalently, a vector field $X$ with $\mathcal{L}_X g = 0$. A symmetric Killing tensor of degree $k$ on $M$ is a symmetric $(0,k)$-tensor field $K$ satisfying the Killing equation $\operatorname{Sym}(\nabla K)=0$ (equivalently, the function $(x,p)\mapsto K_x(p,\dots,p)$ on $T^*M$ is a polynomial integral, of degree $k$ in the momenta, of the geodesic flow of $g$). The symmetric product of two symmetric Killing tensors is again a symmetric Killing tensor, so the space of all symmetric Killing tensors carries the structure of a graded commutative algebra.

Question: For every Riemannian symmetric space $(M,g)$, is every symmetric Killing tensor on $M$ expressible as a finite sum of symmetric products of Killing vector fields? Equivalently, is the algebra of polynomial-in-momenta integrals of the geodesic flow on $M$ generated by the linear integrals (those arising from Killing vector fields)?
status_search_result: The question is answered in the negative for general Riemannian symmetric spaces. While decomposability of Killing tensors into symmetric products of Killing vectors holds on spaces of constant curvature (and on complex projective spaces), recent work exhibits explicit quadratic Killing tensors on the quaternionic projective spaces and on the Cayley projective plane that are not polynomials in Killing vector fields. This completes the classification of quadratic Killing tensor fields on rank-one Riemannian symmetric spaces and refutes the general decomposability conjecture.

original_question: Does there exist a non-conformally flat metric on the sphere Sn, n > 2, whose geodesic flow is maximally superintegrable (in the class of integrals which are polynomial in momenta)?
self_contained_problem:
Let $n>2$ and consider the $n$-sphere $S^n$ equipped with a smooth Riemannian metric $g$. The geodesic flow of $g$ is the Hamiltonian flow on $T^*S^n$ generated by the Hamiltonian $H(x,p)=\tfrac12 g^{ij}(x)p_ip_j$. A function $F\colon T^*S^n\to\mathbb{R}$ that is polynomial in the fiber variables $p$ is called a polynomial-in-momenta integral if $\{F,H\}=0$, where $\{\cdot,\cdot\}$ is the canonical Poisson bracket. The geodesic flow is called maximally superintegrable (in the class of polynomial-in-momenta integrals) if there exist $2n-1$ functions $F_1=H,F_2,\dots,F_{2n-1}$ on $T^*S^n$, each polynomial in the momenta, that Poisson-commute with $H$ and are functionally independent on an open dense subset of $T^*S^n$.

A Riemannian metric $g$ on $S^n$ is said to be conformally flat if every point has a neighborhood on which $g$ is conformal to the Euclidean metric.

Question: Does there exist a non-conformally-flat Riemannian metric on $S^n$ (for some $n>2$) whose geodesic flow is maximally superintegrable in the class of integrals polynomial in the momenta?
status_search_result: Recent literature on superintegrable geodesic flows on spheres focuses on the 2-dimensional case (e.g., constructions of nonconstant-curvature superintegrable metrics on S^2 with higher-degree polynomial integrals, and resolutions of related Bolsinov–Kozlov–Fomenko conjectures in dimension 2). Examples of maximally superintegrable systems on n-dimensional spaces of nonconstant curvature exist for open domains, but no construction of a non-conformally-flat maximally superintegrable metric on S^n with n>2 has been reported. The question appears to remain open.

original_question: Assume that the exterior of an outer billiard table is foliat ed by invariant curves. Prove that the table is an ellipse. The integral-geometric methods used by Bialy in his proofs fail due to non-compactness of the phase space. The following is a generalization of Birkhoff's conjecture.
self_contained_problem:
Let $\gamma \subset \mathbb{R}^2$ be a smooth strictly convex closed curve (the boundary of an outer billiard table) bounding a convex domain $D$. The outer (dual) billiard map $T$ is defined on the exterior $\mathbb{R}^2 \setminus \overline{D}$ as follows: for a point $p$ outside $D$, draw the right tangent line from $p$ to $\gamma$ touching $\gamma$ at a point $q$; then $T(p)$ is the reflection of $p$ through $q$, i.e. $T(p) = 2q - p$. A curve $\Gamma$ in the exterior is called invariant under $T$ if $T(\Gamma) = \Gamma$.

Suppose that the exterior of $\gamma$ is foliated by continuous closed curves, each of which is invariant under the outer billiard map $T$. Prove that $\gamma$ must be an ellipse.
status_search_result: Recent work (M. Bialy, "Integrable outer billiards and rigidity", Journal of Modern Dynamics, 2024) proves the conjecture under the additional smoothness/positive-curvature hypothesis: if the exterior of a smooth convex curve of positive curvature is foliated by continuous invariant curves of the outer billiard map, then the curve is an ellipse. The proof uses a new generating function and weighted integral-geometric methods reducing to the Blaschke–Santaló inequality. The fully general version (without smoothness/positive-curvature assumptions) does not appear to be settled, and the result is the outer analog of the still-open Birkhoff–Poritsky conjecture for ordinary billiards.

original_question: Is it possible to choose the domain so that the dynamics of the corresponding billiard map are locally (near the 2-periodic orbit) conjugated to th e dynamics of the rigid rotation through some angle α? V. Schastnyy and D. Treschev [199] provide numerical evidence th at this is possible if α/π is a Dio- phantine number. 4.2.2 Geometry of caustics, invariant surfaces, and commut ing billiard maps A p/q-rational caustic corresponds to an invariant circle of the billiard ma p that consists of periodic points with the rotation number p/q. For example, a curve of constant width has a 1 /2 caustic, the envelop of the 2-periodic, back and forth, billiard orbits. A Birkhoff in tegrable billiard has a family 16 of p/q-rational caustics for all sufficiently small values of p/q - this follows from the Arnold-Liouville theorem. An ellipse possesses p/q-rational caustics for all p/q < 1/2. Kaloshin and K. Zhang [128] proved that, in an appropriate topology, the set of Birkhoff billiards that possess a rational caustic is dense in the space of Birkhoff billiards. Baryshnikov and Zharnitsky [7] and Landsberg [145] used methods of exterior differential systems to construct infinite-dimensional families of billiards having a p/q-rational caustic for a fixed value of p/q; see [84] for outer billiards.
self_contained_problem:
Let $\Omega \subset \mathbb{R}^2$ be a smooth strictly convex planar domain, and let $T:\partial\Omega \times (0,\pi) \to \partial\Omega \times (0,\pi)$ be the associated Birkhoff billiard map (sending an inward-pointing unit vector based at a boundary point to the next such vector after elastic reflection at the boundary). A 2-periodic orbit of $T$ is a back-and-forth trajectory along a chord that meets $\partial\Omega$ orthogonally at both endpoints.

Fix $\alpha\in(0,\pi)$. The question is: does there exist a smooth strictly convex domain $\Omega$ possessing a 2-periodic billiard orbit $p$ such that, in some neighborhood of $p$ in phase space, the billiard map $T$ is (smoothly, or analytically) conjugate to the rigid rotation $R_\alpha$ of a disk by angle $\alpha$?

In particular, can such a smooth (or analytic) conjugacy be realized whenever $\alpha/\pi$ is Diophantine (i.e., there exist $C,\tau>0$ such that $|\alpha/\pi - p/q| \ge C q^{-\tau}$ for all integers $p,q$ with $q\ge 1$)?
status_search_result: The problem is classical (Treschev). Formal power series solutions exist when α/π is irrational, and numerical evidence supports convergence for Diophantine α. Wang–Zhang (arXiv:2211.03182) proved Gevrey regularity of the Treschev formal solution under a Diophantine condition, but actual convergence (existence of a genuine smooth/analytic domain with the desired local conjugacy) remains open as of recent literature.

original_question: (V. Kaloshin) A q0-rationally integrable billiard is elliptic. The next conjecture is motivated by a theorem of N. Innami's: if the re is a sequence of convex caustics with rotation numbers tending to 1 /2, then the billiard table is an ellipse [120] (see [3] for a simpler proof). An invariant circle of the billiard map is called rotational if it consists of periodic points.
self_contained_problem:
Let $\Omega \subset \mathbb{R}^2$ be a smooth strictly convex bounded domain, and consider the associated billiard map $T$ on the cylinder of unit inward tangent vectors at boundary points (equivalently, on pairs (boundary point, chord direction)). A smooth convex curve $\Gamma \subset \Omega$ is called a caustic of the billiard in $\Omega$ if any trajectory that is tangent to $\Gamma$ remains tangent to $\Gamma$ after each reflection from $\partial \Omega$. An invariant curve of $T$ is called rotational if it is homotopically non-trivial in the phase cylinder; such an invariant curve has a well-defined rotation number $\rho \in (0,1/2]$. For an integer $q_0 \geq 2$, say that the billiard in $\Omega$ is $q_0$-rationally integrable if, for every rational number $p/q \in (0, 1/q_0]$ with $\gcd(p,q)=1$, the billiard map admits a rotational invariant curve of rotation number $p/q$ consisting entirely of periodic points (equivalently, the billiard admits a rational caustic of rotation number $p/q$ for every such $p/q$).

original_question: Suppose that a billiard table has a sequence of convex causti cs with rotation numbers converging to some number omega ∈ (0, 1/2). Does it imply that the table is an ellipse? The previously discussed rotation numbers, 0 and 1 /2, are clearly special. One may generalize the notion of caustic for higher-dimensional billiar ds as a hypersurface such that if a segment of the billiard trajectory is tangent to it, then the refle cted segment is again tangent to this hypersurface. However, this notion is very restrictive: if the dimension of the Euclidean space is at least three, the only convex billiard table that possess caustics a re ellipsoids [10, 98].
self_contained_problem:
Let $\Omega \subset \mathbb{R}^2$ be a strictly convex planar domain with smooth boundary $\Gamma = \partial \Omega$, and consider the associated Birkhoff billiard: a point particle moves inside $\Omega$ along straight lines and reflects off $\Gamma$ according to the law of equal angles. A smooth convex curve $\gamma \subset \Omega$ is called a (convex) caustic of the billiard in $\Omega$ if every billiard trajectory tangent to $\gamma$ remains tangent to $\gamma$ after each reflection. To each convex caustic $\gamma$ one associates a rotation number $\rho(\gamma) \in (0, 1/2)$, defined as the limiting average fraction of the perimeter of $\Gamma$ traversed per reflection by any trajectory tangent to $\gamma$.

Question: Suppose that the billiard table $\Omega$ admits a sequence of convex caustics $\{\gamma_n\}_{n \ge 1}$ whose rotation numbers $\rho(\gamma_n)$ converge to some number $\omega \in (0, 1/2)$. Must $\Gamma$ then be an ellipse?
status_search_result: The question is a generalization of the classical Birkhoff–Poritsky conjecture. Partial results are known: if the sequence of rotation numbers tends to 1/2, the table must be an ellipse (a result by Avila–De Simoi–Kaloshin and related work), and for centrally symmetric tables with a foliation of caustics with rotation numbers in (0,1/4] the conclusion holds (Bialy–Mironov, Annals 2022). For a general accumulation value ω ∈ (0,1/2) the problem appears to remain open.

original_question: (V. Retakh) Establish complete integrability of the noncommutative version of the leapfrog map. Define noncommutative versions of the pentagram m ap and its higher-dimensional analogs and establish their complete integrability. Let us add that a version of the pentagram map was defined and stu died for polygons in Grassmannians [75]. It is a further challenge to define a noncommutative version of t hese maps and to investigate their integrability.
self_contained_problem:
Background. The pentagram map is a discrete dynamical system acting on projective equivalence classes of polygons in the projective plane: given a polygon P, one forms the new polygon T(P) whose vertices are the intersection points of consecutive shortest diagonals of P. Its 1‑dimensional analogue is the leapfrog map, a discrete map on configurations of points on the projective line defined using cross-ratios. The classical pentagram map and its higher-dimensional generalizations (acting on polygons in RP^d) are known to be completely integrable in the Liouville sense, with invariants constructed from a Lax representation and an underlying cluster/Poisson structure. A version of the pentagram map has also been defined for polygons in Grassmannians.

Problem. 
(a) Formulate a noncommutative analogue of the leapfrog map, in which the underlying scalar coordinates are replaced by elements of a noncommutative associative algebra (for example using a noncommutative cross-ratio), and establish its complete integrability in an appropriate noncommutative sense (e.g. existence of a sufficient family of commuting invariants with respect to a noncommutative Poisson/double-bracket structure, or a noncommutative Lax representation with a suitable spectral curve).

(b) Define noncommutative analogues of the pentagram map on polygons in the projective plane, of its higher-dimensional generalizations acting on polygons in higher projective spaces, and of the Grassmannian pentagram map (acting on polygons whose vertices lie in a Grassmannian). For each of these noncommutative maps, establish complete integrability in an appropriate noncommutative sense.
status_search_result: Significant progress has been made. The Grassmann pentagram map has been given a noncommutative interpretation (via Van den Bergh double brackets) and shown to be noncommutatively integrable (Izosimov, Adv. Math. 2020). A noncommutative leapfrog map was constructed and its integrability structure (Lax/zero-curvature representation, Poisson structure via noncommutative networks, and connection to noncommutative Laurent bi-orthogonal polynomials) was developed by Wang and collaborators (arXiv:2310.01993, J. London Math. Soc. 2025). However, a fully general noncommutative pentagram map in arbitrary dimensions with a complete proof of Liouville-type integrability is not yet established in full generality.

A "non-linear analog" of the existence of bi-Lagrangian subspaces would be the existence of complete subalgebras F ⊂ C∞ (M ) consisting of functions in involution with respect to all the bracket s from a given Poisson pencil. By completeness in this case we mean that the s ubspace generated by the differentials of functions f ∈ F in the cotangent space T ∗ x M is maximal isotropic. It is natural to refer to such a subalgebra (or to a collection of its generators) as a bi-integrable system. In the case of Kronecker pencils, such a subalgebra F is generated by the (local) Casimir functions of the brackets in the pencil. It is well known that F so obtained is complete and commutative with respect to all the brackets in the pencil ([20, 83]). Similar results in t he symplectic case are due to P. Olver [176] and H. Turiel [216]. In the mixed case (when the Jord an-Kronecker decomposition of a pencil includes both Kronecker and Jordan blocks), bi-integra ble systems do exist locally in a neighbourhood of a generic point. However, to the best of our kno wledge, this result has never been published. In view of the above discussion on the partition of LG( V, J ) into different orbits, it would be natural to distinguish bi-integrable systems of different algebraic types. Mo re precisely, let f1,..., fk be a complete set of functions in bi-involution. We restrict our considera tions to a small neighbourhood U of a generic point x ∈ M such that for each y ∈ U the Jordan-Kronecker type of the pencil defined on T ∗ y M by a pair of compatible Poisson brackets is the same. If we think of T ∗ y M as a bi-Poisson vector space, then the subspace Ly = span{d f1(y),..., d fk(y)} ⊂ T ∗ y M is bi-Lagrangian and therefore can be characterised by its algebraic type (i.e., by the type of the orbits of the automorphism group action in the bi-Lagrangian Grassmannian to which L belongs). If this type remains the same for all points y ∈ U, we refer to it as the algebraic type of the bi-integrable system f1,..., fk.

Let $V$ be a finite-dimensional vector space over $\mathbb{R}$ or $\mathbb{C}$, and let $J = \{\omega_\lambda = \omega_0 + \lambda \omega_\infty\}_{\lambda \in \mathbb{P}^1}$ be a pencil of skew-symmetric bilinear forms on $V$ (so $(V,J)$ is a bi-Poisson vector space). A subspace $L \subset V$ is called bi-Lagrangian if it is maximal isotropic with respect to every form in the pencil $J$. Denote by $LG(V,J)$ the bi-Lagrangian Grassmannian, i.e. the set of all bi-Lagrangian subspaces, viewed as an algebraic subvariety of an appropriate Lagrangian Grassmannian. (a) Find necessary and sufficient conditions, in terms of the Jordan–Kronecker invariants of the pencil $J$, for the bi-Lagrangian Grassmannian $LG(V,J)$ to be a smooth algebraic variety.

(b) Describe the partition of $LG(V,J)$ into orbits of the natural action of $\mathrm{Aut}(V,J)$.

A family $F$ of polynomials on $\mathfrak{g}^*$ in bi-involution is called complete if at a generic point $x\in\mathfrak{g}^*$ the differentials of elements of $F$ span an isotropic subspace of $T_x^*\mathfrak{g}^*$ (with respect to the symplectic leaf through $x$) of maximal possible dimension, equal to $\tfrac{1}{2}(\dim\mathfrak{g}+\mathrm{ind}\,\mathfrak{g})$, where $\mathrm{ind}\,\mathfrak{g}$ is the index of $\mathfrak{g}$.

original_question: Are there any restrictions on the algebraic type of the penci ls Ax+λa? Which algebraic types can be realised by means of an appropriately chosen Lie algebra? A recent observation by I. Kozlov (see details in [38]) shows that som e restrictions do exist. Roughly speaking, Kozlov has obtained the answer for Lie algebras of pure J ordan and pure Kronecker type. The mixed case remains open because of possible non-trivial interac tion between Kronecker and Jordan blocks. To further develop these ideas, it would be interesting to study Pois son pencils generated by one quadratic and one linear brackets. Compatible brackets of this kind appear, in particular, in the theory of Poisson-Lie groups.
self_contained_problem:
Let g be a finite-dimensional Lie algebra over C with Lie bracket [·,·], and let g* denote its dual space. For each x ∈ g*, define the skew-symmetric bilinear form A_x on g by A_x(ξ, η) = ⟨x, [ξ, η]⟩. For a fixed regular covector a ∈ g*, consider the one-parameter pencil of skew-symmetric bilinear forms

    P_{x,a}(λ) := A_x + λ A_a,   x ∈ g*, λ ∈ C.

By the Jordan–Kronecker theorem, for generic x the pencil P_{x,a} admits a canonical decomposition into Kronecker blocks (of certain odd sizes) and Jordan blocks (associated with eigenvalues λ_i, of certain sizes); the collection of these block sizes and eigenvalue data is called the algebraic type of the pencil. A Lie algebra g is said to be of pure Kronecker type if all blocks of the generic pencil are Kronecker, of pure Jordan type if all blocks are Jordan, and of mixed type otherwise.

(a) Determine the precise restrictions (if any) on the algebraic types of pencils A_x + λ A_a that can arise from a finite-dimensional Lie algebra. Equivalently, characterize which collections of Kronecker block sizes and Jordan block data (sizes plus eigenvalues) are realizable as the Jordan–Kronecker invariant of some finite-dimensional Lie algebra g (with a appropriately chosen).

(b) In particular, resolve the mixed case in which the pencil contains both Kronecker and Jordan blocks, including all possible non-trivial interactions between them.

(c) Develop the analogous theory for compatible Poisson pencils on a vector space generated by one quadratic Poisson bracket and one linear Poisson bracket (such as those arising on Poisson–Lie groups): describe the possible algebraic types of such pencils and which can be realized.

However, no complete classification of realizable algebraic types in the mixed Kronecker+Jordan case has appeared, and the quadratic-plus-linear (Poisson–Lie) variant remains largely unexplored. The problem is therefore still open.

original_question: Is it true that for any quadratic Poisson bracket (defined on a vector space), there exists a polynomial integrable system? 5.3 Nijenhuis operators: singular points and global proper ties Let L = ( Li j(x) ) be a (1, 1)-tensor field (field of endomorphisms) on a smooth manifold M. We say that L is a Nijenhuis operator if its Nijenhuis torsion NL identically vanishes on M, i.e., NL(v, w) = L2[v, w] + [Lv, Lw] - L[Lv, w] - L[v, Lw] = 0, for arbitrary vector fields v, w on M. It is known that Nijenhuis operators are closely related to compatib le Poisson brackets and therefore naturally appear in the theory of finite dimensional integrable syste ms, see e.g. Magri et al [140, 154]. Indeed, if a Poisson structure given by the tensor P ij is compatible with the Poisson structure given by the symplectic form omega, then Li j:= P isomegasj is a Nijenhuis operator. Nijenhuis tensors appear also in other topics in the theory of integrable systems, see e.g. [24, 119 ], in differential geometry, see e.g. 27 [6, 29, 33], so investigation of Nijenhuis tensors is expected to be ge nerally important for the theory of integrable systems and other branches of mathematics; in this sec tion we collect open problems about it. Let L = L(x) be a (1, 1)-tensor field. Then at each point x ∈ M, we can characterize L(x) by its algebraic type (Segre characteristic), that is, the type of its Jor dan normal form (eigenvalues with multiplicities + sizes of Jordan blocks for each eigenvalue). The algebr aic type of L depends on x and may vary from point to point. We will say that x ∈ M if generic, if the algebraic type of L is locally constant at x (i.e., is the same for all points from a certain neighbourhood U (x)). Otherwise, x is called singular. One can show that generic points form an open dense subset of M. Almost all results known in the literature concern local properties o f Nijenhuis operators at generic points, e.g. for semisimple Nijenhuis operators a local description is d ue to Haantjes [109]. However, Nijenhuis operators also occur in problems which require a global tre atment and analysis of singular points. Indeed, in the theory of bi-Hamiltonian systems, the Nijenh uis operators appear as recursion operators R (see [154, 140]). The first integrals (for an important class of integ rable systems) are the coefficients of the characteristic polynomial of R. This means, in particular, that the structure of singularities of the corresponding Liouville foliations is determined by t he local structure of singular points of R. Analysing them, we may find topological obstruction to bi-Hamiltonis ation, which would be an interesting result. Philosophically, we want to say that the sing ularities of bi-integrable systems are determined by the singularities of the underlying structure (in o ur case, this is just the recursion operator). We also notice that integrability of finite-dimensional Ha miltonian systems is essentially a global phenomenon, so that it might be important to understand g lobal properties of recursion operators. Similarly, in differential geometry, Nijenhuis operators play an import ant role in the theory of pro- jectively equivalent (pseudo-)Riemannian metrics, where underst anding of singular points of related Nijenhuis tensors led to the proof of the projective Lichnerowicz c onjecture in the Riemannian and Lorentzian signature [161, 35]. In view of the above discussion, we find the following directions of res earch very important: • Studying global properties of Nijenhuis operators and topological obstructions to the existence of Nienhuis operators (of a certain type) on compact manifolds. • Studying local behaviour of Nijenhuis operators at singular points. Speaking of topological obstructions to the existence of Nijenhuis opertors on compact manifolds, we should take into account two simple but important observations: (i) The operators of the form f (x) ·Id are Nijenhuis for any smooth function f: M → R. Such operators exist on any manifold but this example is too trivial. (ii) In Rn, there exist C∞ -smooth Nijenhuis operators with compact support and such that, in a certain domain, they take the standard diagonal form L(x) = diag( λ1(x1), λ2(x2),..., λn(xn)) 28 with distinct non-constant real eigenvalues λi(xi). Since the support of such an operator is contained in a certain ball, we can construct a Nijenhuis operator wit h similar properties on any (compact) manifold. This leads to the following natural questions. We will say that a linear operator L: V → V is algebraically regular if the dimension of the orbit of L under the canonical GL(V )-action on the space of operators is maximal (equivalently, the dim ension of the centraliser of L is minimal, i.e., equals n = dim V ). In particular, diagonalisable operators with simple spectrum are regular. For non-diagonalisable operators, the algebraic regularity condition means that geometric multiplicity of each eigenvalue of L is one.

original_question: Let us fix a certain algebraic type of a linear operator, i.e., its Segre characteristic (see above). Does there exist a Nijenhuis operator L in Rn with the following two properties: 1. L has compact support; 2. in a certain domain U ⊂ Rn, the algebraic type of L does not change and coincides with the given one? More generally, find necessary and sufficient conditions, in t erms of the Segre characteristic, for the existence of a Nijenhuis operator in Rn with the above properties. Notice that for semisimple operators L with real eigenvalues, the answer to the above question is positive. However, if some of the eigenvalues of L are complex, then L cannot have compact support. Also, one can easily construct an example of a Nijenhuis operator L with compact support which has the form of a Jordan block, e.g., L = ( y x 0 y ), on a certain disc. However, even for single Jordan blocks of size ≥ 3 the answer is unknown.
self_contained_problem:
Background and definitions.

(a) A (1,1)-tensor field on $\mathbb{R}^n$ is a smooth field $L$ of linear operators $L(x):T_x\mathbb{R}^n\to T_x\mathbb{R}^n$. Its Nijenhuis torsion is the (1,2)-tensor
$$\mathcal{N}_L(X,Y) := L^2[X,Y] - L[LX,Y] - L[X,LY] + [LX,LY],$$
where $X,Y$ are smooth vector fields and $[\,,\,]$ denotes the Lie bracket. The tensor $L$ is called a Nijenhuis operator if $\mathcal{N}_L \equiv 0$.

(b) The Segre characteristic of a linear operator $A$ on a complex vector space is the unordered tuple of sizes of its Jordan blocks, with blocks corresponding to the same eigenvalue grouped together; it encodes the conjugacy class of $A$ up to the values of the eigenvalues. We say a (1,1)-tensor $L$ on a domain $U\subset \mathbb{R}^n$ has constant algebraic type with Segre characteristic $\sigma$ if at every $x\in U$ the operator $L(x)$ (viewed over $\mathbb{C}$) has Segre characteristic $\sigma$.

(c) The support of $L$ is the closure of $\{x\in\mathbb{R}^n : L(x)\ne 0\}$. We say $L$ has compact support if this set is compact.

Problem. Fix an integer $n\ge 1$ and a Segre characteristic $\sigma$ of an $n\times n$ operator.

(1) Does there exist a Nijenhuis operator $L$ on $\mathbb{R}^n$ such that:
    (i) $L$ has compact support, and
    (ii) there exists an open set $U\subset\mathbb{R}^n$ on which $L$ has constant algebraic type equal to $\sigma$?

(2) More generally, give necessary and sufficient conditions, expressed purely in terms of $\sigma$, for such a Nijenhuis operator to exist.

Known partial information: if $\sigma$ corresponds to a semisimple operator with only real eigenvalues, the answer to (1) is positive; if $\sigma$ involves any non-real (complex) eigenvalue, no such compactly supported Nijenhuis operator can exist. For a single $2\times 2$ Jordan block (e.g. $L=\begin{pmatrix} y & x\\ 0 & y\end{pmatrix}$ on a disc) the answer is positive. The case of a single Jordan block of size $\ge 3$ is what is principally in question.
status_search_result: Recent literature on Nijenhuis geometry (e.g. work on gl-regular Nijenhuis operators and Nijenhuis operators with a unity, 2020–2024) develops local normal forms and studies algebraically generic points, but does not announce a solution to the global existence question of compactly supported Nijenhuis operators with prescribed Segre type, in particular for single Jordan blocks of size ≥ 3. No source found resolving the problem; it appears to remain open.

original_question: Describe/classify the collections of algebraically indep endent homogeneous polynomials σ1,..., σn, deg σk = k, in n variables x1,..., xn with the required property. Finally, one question revealing the relationship between singularities o f bi-Hamiltonian systems and singular points of Nijenhuis operators. In a recent paper [31], it was shown that the structure of singularities of bi-Hamiltonian systems related to Poisson pencils of Kr onecker type is determined by the singularities of the pencil. We expect that a similar principle works f or Poisson pencils of sympletic type, i.e., when one of two compatible Poisson brackets is non-degen erate. In this case, we have a well-defined recursion operator R (which is automatically a Nijenhuis operator) and the commuting 31 functions we are interested in are just the coefficients σ1,..., σn of the characteristic polynomial of R. We assume that they are independent almost everywhere on M and want to study singular points of the mapping Phi = ( σ1,..., σn): M → Rn playing the role of the momentum mapping for our bi-Hamiltonian system.
self_contained_problem:
Let $M$ be a smooth $2n$-dimensional manifold endowed with two compatible Poisson brackets $\{\cdot,\cdot\}_0$ and $\{\cdot,\cdot\}_1$ (i.e., every linear combination $\{\cdot,\cdot\}_0+\lambda\{\cdot,\cdot\}_1$ is again a Poisson bracket) such that $\{\cdot,\cdot\}_0$ is non-degenerate. The corresponding recursion operator $R:TM\to TM$, defined by $\{f,g\}_1=\{f,R\,dg\}_0$ (equivalently $R=P_1 P_0^{-1}$ where $P_i$ are the Poisson tensors), is then a Nijenhuis operator. Let $\sigma_1,\dots,\sigma_n$ denote the coefficients of the characteristic polynomial of $R$ (so $\det(tI-R)=(t^n-\sigma_1 t^{n-1}+\sigma_2 t^{n-2}-\dots)^2$ after taking the square root in the symplectic case, with $\sigma_k$ a smooth function on $M$). Assume these functions are functionally independent almost everywhere and pairwise Poisson-commute, so that $\Phi=(\sigma_1,\dots,\sigma_n):M\to\mathbb{R}^n$ serves as the momentum map of the resulting bi-Hamiltonian integrable system.

Consider the linearization of this setup at a singular point: at such a point one obtains, after a suitable choice of coordinates $x_1,\dots,x_n$, a collection of algebraically independent homogeneous polynomials $\sigma_1,\dots,\sigma_n\in\mathbb{R}[x_1,\dots,x_n]$ with $\deg\sigma_k=k$ that pairwise commute with respect to a constant Poisson structure and arise as the coefficients of the characteristic polynomial of a linear Nijenhuis operator.

Problem. Describe and classify all such collections $(\sigma_1,\dots,\sigma_n)$ of algebraically independent homogeneous polynomials with $\deg\sigma_k=k$ in $n$ variables having this property, and use the classification to describe the singular points of the momentum map $\Phi=(\sigma_1,\dots,\sigma_n):M\to\mathbb{R}^n$ of a bi-Hamiltonian system of symplectic (i.e., non-degenerate) type in terms of the singularities of the underlying Poisson pencil / Nijenhuis operator.

original_question: Extend the action-angle theorem in a neighbourhood of a Liou ville torus at singular points of the Poisson structure. The first adversity in doing so is that, contrary to the expectation s, in general, an integrable system is not a product of two integrable systems (one on the symplectic leaf and the other one in the transverse part). So there is no simultaneous splitting theorem for the Poisson structure and the integrable system. Counterexamples to this decomposability can be found in [14 3]. When this happens, we say the system is splittable. So the problem above can be refined as follow s:
self_contained_problem:
Let $(M,\Pi)$ be a smooth Poisson manifold and let $F=(f_1,\dots,f_n):M\to\mathbb{R}^n$ be an integrable system on $(M,\Pi)$, meaning that the functions $f_i$ pairwise Poisson-commute, $\{f_i,f_j\}_\Pi=0$, and are functionally independent on a dense open subset, with the number of independent commuting functions matching the rank conditions of an integrable system on a Poisson manifold. Suppose $p\in M$ is a point at which the Poisson tensor $\Pi$ is singular (its rank drops), and suppose that the connected component of the fiber $F^{-1}(F(p))$ containing $p$ is a compact regular Liouville torus $\mathbb{T}^r$ of the symplectic foliation. Call the integrable system splittable near $p$ if there exist a neighbourhood $U$ of $p$ and a Poisson isomorphism of $U$ with a product $(S,\omega_S)\times(N,\Pi_N)$ of a symplectic manifold and a transverse Poisson manifold, such that $F$ decomposes as the sum of an integrable system on $S$ and an integrable system on $N$.

Problem: For splittable integrable systems on Poisson manifolds, establish an action–angle theorem in a neighbourhood of a Liouville torus that lies over a singular point of the Poisson structure. Explicitly, construct coordinates $(\theta_1,\dots,\theta_r,p_1,\dots,p_r,z_1,\dots,z_{s})$ on a saturated neighbourhood of the torus, where the $\theta_i$ are angle coordinates on $\mathbb{T}^r$, the $p_i$ are action coordinates conjugate to them on the symplectic leaf, and the $z_j$ are transverse coordinates, in which the Poisson bracket and the integrable system $F$ take a normal form generalising the classical Liouville–Mineur–Arnold theorem.

However, the general action-angle theorem near a Liouville torus sitting over a singular point of the Poisson structure for splittable systems does not appear to have been established in full generality; the problem is repeatedly listed as open in surveys of finite-dimensional integrable systems.

paper_title: Open problems, questions and challenges in finite-dimensional integrable systems
original_question: Determine obstructions to the global existence of action-a ngle coordinates on regular Poisson manifolds. Realisation problem is also important:
self_contained_problem:
Let $(M,\pi)$ be a regular Poisson manifold, i.e. a smooth manifold $M$ equipped with a Poisson bivector $\pi \in \Gamma(\wedge^2 TM)$ whose induced symplectic foliation has leaves of locally constant dimension. A (non-commutative) integrable system on $(M,\pi)$ is, roughly, a map $F=(f_1,\dots,f_n):M\to\mathbb{R}^n$ whose components Poisson-commute appropriately and whose joint level sets, when compact and connected, are diffeomorphic to tori. Around each such torus, the Liouville–Mineur–Arnold theorem on Poisson manifolds gives local action-angle coordinates.

Problem: Identify and describe the obstructions (cohomological, topological, geometric, or otherwise) to the existence of globally defined action-angle coordinates for such integrable systems on a regular Poisson manifold $(M,\pi)$. In particular, determine a complete set of invariants whose vanishing is necessary and sufficient for the local action-angle coordinates to be patched into global ones, and address the associated realisation problem of which abstract data (action bundles, lattice bundles, transverse structures) can arise from genuine integrable systems on regular Poisson manifolds.
status_search_result: The problem has been actively studied with partial results. Laurent-Gengoux, Miranda, and Vanhaecke proved an action-angle theorem on Poisson manifolds with local coordinates. Global obstructions for non-commutative integrable systems on Poisson manifolds (using action bundles, lattice bundles, and three transverse foliations) have been investigated, generalizing Duistermaat and Dazord–Delzant. Concrete examples illustrating additional obstructions beyond the symplectic case have been constructed. However, a complete classification of obstructions and a full solution to the realisation problem in the regular Poisson setting do not appear to be definitively established.

original_question: Consider a Poisson manifold M of even dimension such that it is symplectic on a dense set U ⊂ M. Assume that M is endowed with a toric action which is Hamiltonian on U. Is there an analog of Delzant theorem for the image of the moment map? 34 Furthermore, in view of [168] where the Moser homotopy method is p resented also for foliated mani- folds, can Delzant theorem be generalised for regular Poisson manif olds? We conclude this section with a problem related to the symplectic case. However, its solution might require some Poisson techniques. There are two obstructions to g lobalizing action-angle coordinates, as described by Duistermaat [68]: the Hamiltonian monodromy and the Chern (or Duistermaat-Chern) class. Contrary to the former, the latter has been very little inves tigated. There are, clearly, at least two reasons for this: • The Chern class always vanishes for two degrees of freedom syste ms; • There are no known physically meaningful examples with non-trivial C hern class in three degrees of freedom. Although it is easy to manually construct any Chern class, see [8], hav ing a natural example from classical mechanics would provide better motivation for further st udy (see also Problem 7.4).

Let $M$ be a Poisson manifold of even dimension, and let $U \subset M$ be a dense open subset on which the Poisson structure is nondegenerate (so $(U,\omega)$ is symplectic). Suppose an $n$-torus $T^n$ (with $\dim M = 2n$) acts effectively on $M$, and that the restricted action on $U$ is Hamiltonian with moment map $\mu : U \to \mathfrak{t}^*$ which extends continuously to $M$.

(a) Formulate and prove an analogue of the Delzant classification theorem in this setting: determine to what extent the image $\mu(M) \subset \mathfrak{t}^*$ (together with appropriate combinatorial data on its boundary, reflecting the locus where the Poisson structure degenerates) is a complete invariant of $(M,\pi,T^n\text{-action})$ up to equivariant Poisson isomorphism, and characterize which subsets of $\mathfrak{t}^*$ arise as such moment-map images.

(b) More generally, let $(M,\pi)$ be a regular Poisson manifold (the symplectic foliation has constant rank) endowed with an effective Hamiltonian torus action of dimension equal to half the leaf dimension. Generalize the Delzant classification theorem to this regular Poisson setting, classifying such Hamiltonian toric regular Poisson manifolds by suitable polytopal/combinatorial data on the leaf space.

paper_title: Open problems, questions and challenges in finite-dimensional integrable systems
original_question: Assume that a classical integrable system (p1,..., pn) is given on M. Does there exist a quantum integrable system (P1,..., Pn) such that pj = σ(Pj )? See Charles et al [49] for a solution in the compact toric case. More specific versions o f this general question are discussed in Section 7.3. The difficulty is to construct operators Pj with the exact commutation property [ Pj, Pk] = 0. Us- ing microlocal analysis and, in particular, Fourier integral operator s [66], one should be able to obtain [ Pj, Pk] = O(hbar∞ ). In many classical examples, an exact quantisation is known, see f or in- stance [215, 114]. Symmetry considerations should help greatly. Th is is a typical local-to-global obstruction problem, and one expects a corresponding cohomolog y complex. In the case of polynomial symbols in Cn, the complex was constructed in [78].
self_contained_problem:
Let $M$ be a smooth symplectic manifold of dimension $2n$, and let $(p_1,\dots,p_n)$ be a classical integrable system on $M$; that is, $p_1,\dots,p_n\in C^\infty(M)$ are smooth functions whose differentials are almost everywhere linearly independent and which pairwise Poisson-commute, $\{p_i,p_j\}=0$ for all $i,j$.

Fix a semiclassical quantization scheme on $M$ with principal symbol map $\sigma$ sending $\hbar$-pseudodifferential (or Berezin–Toeplitz, in the compact Kähler setting) operators on an appropriate Hilbert space to smooth functions on $M$.

Question: Does there always exist a quantum integrable system $(P_1,\dots,P_n)$ — i.e., self-adjoint $\hbar$-(pseudo)differential operators satisfying the exact commutation relations
$$[P_i,P_j]=0 \quad \text{for all } i,j$$
— such that the principal symbols satisfy
$$\sigma(P_j)=p_j \quad \text{for } j=1,\dots,n?$$

Equivalently, characterize the local-to-global obstructions (presumably organized by a cohomology complex) to upgrading a classical Liouville-integrable system on $M$ to a quantum integrable system with exactly commuting quantizations of its commuting Hamiltonians, going beyond the asymptotic statement $[P_i,P_j]=O(\hbar^\infty)$ achievable by microlocal/Fourier-integral-operator methods.
status_search_result: The general existence problem for an exact quantization of a classical integrable system with strict (not merely asymptotic) operator commutation appears to remain open. Quantization is known in special cases — compact toric manifolds (Charles et al.), Hitchin systems, and various classical examples — and microlocal/Fourier-integral-operator techniques yield commutation only up to $O(\hbar^\infty)$. The literature consistently treats this as an unresolved local-to-global obstruction problem, with no general theorem currently available.

paper_title: Open problems, questions and challenges in finite-dimensional integrable systems
original_question: Write Bohr-Sommerfeld rules for focus-focus singularities in Berezin-Toeplitz quantisation.
self_contained_problem:
Let $(M,\omega,J)$ be a prequantizable compact Kähler manifold with prequantum line bundle $(L,h)\to M$ whose Chern curvature equals $-i\omega$. For each positive integer $k$, let $\mathcal{H}_k=H^0(M,L^{\otimes k})$ be the space of holomorphic sections, equipped with the $L^2$-inner product induced by $h$ and the Liouville volume, and let $\Pi_k:L^2(M,L^{\otimes k})\to\mathcal{H}_k$ be the Szegő (Bergman) projector. For a smooth real-valued function $f\in C^\infty(M)$, the Berezin–Toeplitz operator at semiclassical parameter $\hbar=1/k$ is 
$$T_k(f)=\Pi_k\,M_f\,\Pi_k:\mathcal{H}_k\to\mathcal{H}_k,$$
where $M_f$ denotes multiplication by $f$.

Consider an integrable system of $n$ Poisson-commuting Hamiltonians $f_1,\dots,f_n\in C^\infty(M)$ generating a momentum map $F=(f_1,\dots,f_n):M\to\mathbb{R}^n$, and assume that $m\in M$ is a non-degenerate critical point of focus-focus type, i.e., $n=2$ and there exist local symplectic coordinates $(x_1,y_1,x_2,y_2)$ around $m$ in which the Hessians of $f_1,f_2$ at $m$ span the focus-focus subalgebra generated by $q_1=x_1 y_1+x_2 y_2$ and $q_2=x_1 y_2-x_2 y_1$. The quantum integrable system is the commuting tuple $(T_k(f_1),T_k(f_2))$, and its joint spectrum is
$$\mathrm{JointSpec}(T_k(f_1),T_k(f_2))=\{(\lambda_1,\lambda_2)\in\mathbb{R}^2: \exists\,v\neq 0,\ T_k(f_j)v=\lambda_j v\}.$$

Derive Bohr–Sommerfeld quantization conditions describing, as $k\to\infty$ (equivalently $\hbar\to 0$), the joint eigenvalues of $(T_k(f_1),T_k(f_2))$ lying in any sufficiently small neighborhood of the critical value $F(m)\in\mathbb{R}^2$. original_question: A semitoric system F = ( J, H) is determined, up to symplectic equivalence, by its semicla ssical joint spectrum (i.e., the collection of points (λ, ν) ∈ R2, where λ is a eigenvalue of ˆJhbar and ν is an eigenvalue of ˆHhbar, restricted to the λ-eigenspace of ˆJ, as hbar → 0). Moreover, from any such semiclassical spectrum, one can e xplicitly construct the associated semitoric system. This conjecture is now a theorem for the special cases of quantum toric integrable systems on compact 37 manifolds [49], and for semitoric integrable systems of Jaynes-Cumm ings type [149]. The problem is that it is unclear whether one of the most subtle (perhaps the most subtle) invariants of integrable systems, known as the twisting index, can be detected in the semicla ssical spectral asymptotics. If this is the case (which is very likely), then the Pelayo-V u Ngo. c inverse spectral conjecture ([187]) above will hold. An important part of the problem is to recover the Taylor series inva riant that classifies semi-global neighbourhood s of focus-focus fibers [225]. A positive solution was given in [189, 149], but the procedure was not constructive: one had to first let hbar → 0 for a regular value c near the focus-focus value c0, and then take the limit c → c0, which doesn't help computing the Taylor series in an explicit way from the spectrum.
self_contained_problem:
Setup. A semitoric integrable system on a connected symplectic 4-manifold $(M,\omega)$ is a pair $F=(J,H)$ of Poisson-commuting smooth functions $\{J,H\}=0$ such that:
(i) $J$ generates an effective Hamiltonian $S^1$-action and is proper;
(ii) the map $F=(J,H):M\to\mathbb{R}^2$ has only non-degenerate singularities (in the Williamson sense) with no hyperbolic blocks.

Two semitoric systems $F=(J,H)$ on $(M,\omega)$ and $F'=(J',H')$ on $(M',\omega')$ are symplectically equivalent if there exists a symplectomorphism $\varphi:M\to M'$ with $\varphi^*J' = J$ and $\varphi^*H' = f(J,H)$ for a smooth function $f$ with $\partial f/\partial H>0$.

Quantization. Assume $F$ is quantized by a pair of commuting self-adjoint semiclassical (pseudo)differential operators $(\hat J_\hbar,\hat H_\hbar)$ with principal symbols $(J,H)$. The semiclassical joint spectrum of $F$ is the collection
$$\Sigma(\hbar) := \{(\lambda,\nu)\in\mathbb{R}^2 \mid \lambda\in\operatorname{Spec}(\hat J_\hbar),\ \nu\in\operatorname{Spec}(\hat H_\hbar\!\upharpoonright_{\ker(\hat J_\hbar-\lambda)})\},$$
considered as $\hbar\to 0$.

Problem. Prove the following two statements:
(a) (Uniqueness/inverse spectral.) If two semitoric systems $F$ and $F'$ have the same semiclassical joint spectrum (in an appropriate asymptotic sense as $\hbar\to 0$), then $F$ and $F'$ are symplectically equivalent.
(b) (Constructive recovery.) Give an explicit constructive procedure that, from the semiclassical joint spectrum, produces a representative of the symplectic equivalence class of $F$, including the explicit recovery of all symplectic invariants. In particular, recover the twisting index, and provide an explicit reconstruction of the Taylor series invariant classifying a semi-global neighborhood of each focus-focus fiber — directly from the spectral data, not merely as an iterated limit (first $\hbar\to 0$ at a regular value $c$ near a focus-focus value $c_0$, then $c\to c_0$).
category_tag: semitoric integrable systems / inverse spectral theory
status_search_result: Recent work has substantially resolved the conjecture: Le Floch–Pelayo–Vũ Ngọc (arXiv:2104.06704) showed one can recover the first four symplectic invariants of simple semitoric systems from the joint spectrum, and Le Floch–Vũ Ngọc (arXiv:2309.16614) showed the twisting index can also be heard, completing the qualitative inverse-spectral statement for simple semitoric systems. The fully explicit/constructive recovery of the Taylor series invariant from the spectrum (without the iterated-limit procedure) does not appear to be fully achieved in the literature, so the constructive part of the problem remains partially open.
