paper_title: Open problems for tractability of multivariate integration
original_question: For integration of infinitely differentiable real functions on [0,1]^d whose partial derivatives are all bounded by one, is the number of function values needed for relative error epsilon not bounded by any polynomial in d and epsilon^{-1}?
self_contained_problem:
Let $d\ge 1$ and consider the class
$$F_{d,\infty}=\{f\in C^{\infty}([0,1]^d):\ \|D^{\alpha}f\|_{\infty}\le 1\ \text{for every multi-index }\alpha\in\mathbb{N}_0^d\},$$
i.e. real-valued infinitely differentiable functions on the unit cube all of whose partial derivatives (of every order) are bounded in absolute value by $1$. For $f\in F_{d,\infty}$ consider the integration problem $I_d(f)=\int_{[0,1]^d} f(x)\,dx$, approximated by deterministic algorithms that use $n$ function values
$$A_{n,d}(f)=\phi_n\bigl(f(x_1),\dots,f(x_n)\bigr),$$
with adaptively chosen sample points $x_i\in[0,1]^d$ and arbitrary (measurable) mapping $\phi_n$. Define the $n$-th minimal worst-case error
$$e(n,d)=\inf_{A_{n,d}}\ \sup_{f\in F_{d,\infty}}\ |I_d(f)-A_{n,d}(f)|,$$
noting that $e(0,d)\le 1$. For $\varepsilon\in(0,1)$, let the information complexity for relative error $\varepsilon$ be
$$n(\varepsilon,d)=\min\{n\ge 0:\ e(n,d)\le \varepsilon\,e(0,d)\}.$$
The class $F_{d,\infty}$ is said to be polynomially tractable for integration if there exist constants $C,p,q\ge 0$ such that
$$n(\varepsilon,d)\le C\,d^{q}\,\varepsilon^{-p}\qquad\text{for all }d\in\mathbb{N},\ \varepsilon\in(0,1).$$
Decide whether $F_{d,\infty}$ is intractable in this sense; equivalently, prove or disprove that no such constants $C,p,q$ exist (i.e. $n(\varepsilon,d)$ cannot be bounded by any polynomial in $d$ and $\varepsilon^{-1}$).
status_search_result: Subsequent work by Hinrichs, Novak, Ullrich, and Woźniakowski (2014) established the curse of dimensionality for integration over classes of $C^\infty$ functions when the bounds on successive derivatives are sufficiently large, and weak tractability is known under bounded directional derivatives. However, the specific case where all partial derivatives are bounded by one (the class $F_{d,\infty}$) remains unresolved: even weak tractability is reported as an open problem, so polynomial tractability/intractability in this class is not settled in the literature retrieved.

paper_title: Open problems for tractability of multivariate integration
original_question: For integration in the weighted Sobolev Hilbert space on [0,1]^d with kernel product_{j=1}^d (1 + gamma_j min(x_j,t_j)) and summable positive nonincreasing weights gamma_j, is the strong-tractability exponent p* equal to 1 if and only if sum gamma_j^{1/2} is finite?
self_contained_problem:
Let $d\ge 1$ and consider the weighted Sobolev Hilbert space $H_d$ of functions on $[0,1]^d$ defined as the reproducing-kernel Hilbert space with product kernel
$$K_d(x,t)=\prod_{j=1}^{d}\bigl(1+\gamma_j\,\min(x_j,t_j)\bigr),\qquad x,t\in[0,1]^d,$$
where $(\gamma_j)_{j\ge 1}$ is a fixed nonincreasing sequence of positive real numbers with $\sum_{j=1}^{\infty}\gamma_j<\infty$. For the multivariate integration problem $\mathrm{INT}_d(f)=\int_{[0,1]^d}f(x)\,dx$, let $n(\varepsilon,d)$ be the minimal number of function evaluations needed by any (deterministic, linear) algorithm to achieve worst-case error at most $\varepsilon$ relative to the initial error, over the unit ball of $H_d$. The integration problem is called strongly tractable if there exist constants $C,p>0$ such that
$$n(\varepsilon,d)\le C\,\varepsilon^{-p}\qquad\text{for all }d\ge 1,\ \varepsilon\in(0,1),$$
and the strong-tractability exponent is $p^*=\inf\{p>0:\text{such a bound holds}\}$. It is known that under the standing assumption $\sum_j\gamma_j<\infty$ one has $p^*\in[1,2]$.

Question: Is it true that $p^*=1$ if and only if $\sum_{j=1}^{\infty}\gamma_j^{1/2}<\infty$?
status_search_result: Available sources confirm that Sloan and Woźniakowski's framework only pins $p^*$ to the interval $[1,2]$ under $\sum\gamma_j<\infty$, and that the optimal value $p^*=1$ has been achieved constructively under stronger assumptions (such as $\sum\gamma_j^{1/2}<\infty$), but a full "if and only if" characterization of $p^*=1$ in terms of $\sum\gamma_j^{1/2}<\infty$ does not appear to have been established in the literature. The question therefore appears to remain open.

paper_title: Open problems for tractability of multivariate integration
original_question: For randomized integration in the weighted Sobolev Hilbert space on [0,1]^d with kernel product_{j=1}^d (1 + gamma_j min(x_j,t_j)) and positive nonincreasing weights gamma_j, is limsup_{d->infinity} (sum_{j=1}^d gamma_j^2)/ln d finite a necessary condition for tractability?
self_contained_problem:
Let $d\ge 1$ and let $\gamma=(\gamma_j)_{j\ge 1}$ be a sequence of positive nonincreasing weights. For each $d$ define the weighted Sobolev reproducing kernel Hilbert space $H_{d,\gamma}$ on $[0,1]^d$ as the tensor product Hilbert space with reproducing kernel
$$K_{d,\gamma}(x,t)=\prod_{j=1}^d\bigl(1+\gamma_j\min(x_j,t_j)\bigr),\qquad x,t\in[0,1]^d.$$
For $f\in H_{d,\gamma}$ consider the integration problem $I_d(f)=\int_{[0,1]^d} f(x)\,dx$. A randomized algorithm using $n$ function values is a measurable mapping $\omega\mapsto A_{n,\omega}$ where each $A_{n,\omega}(f)$ depends on $n$ values of $f$ at randomly chosen points and the random choice is independent of $f$. The randomized error is
$$e^{\mathrm{ran}}(n,d):=\inf_{A_n}\sup_{\|f\|_{H_{d,\gamma}}\le 1}\Bigl(\mathbb{E}\bigl|I_d(f)-A_n(f)\bigr|^2\Bigr)^{1/2},$$
and the randomized information complexity is $n^{\mathrm{ran}}(\varepsilon,d):=\min\{n: e^{\mathrm{ran}}(n,d)\le\varepsilon\}$. The integration problem is called tractable in the randomized setting if there exist constants $C,p,q\ge 0$ such that
$$n^{\mathrm{ran}}(\varepsilon,d)\le C\,\varepsilon^{-p}\,d^{q}\qquad\text{for all }\varepsilon\in(0,1),\ d\ge 1.$$

Question: Is the condition
$$\limsup_{d\to\infty}\frac{\sum_{j=1}^d \gamma_j^{\,2}}{\ln d}<\infty$$
necessary for tractability of randomized multivariate integration in the spaces $H_{d,\gamma}$?

The problem appears to remain open.

paper_title: Billiard Dynamics: A Survey with the Emphasis on Open Problems
original_question: Construct a planar billiard table with positive entropy in either of the following regularity classes: (a) a strictly convex table whose boundary is C1-smooth, or (b) a convex table whose boundary is C2-smooth.
self_contained_problem:
Consider a planar billiard table, that is, a compact connected planar domain Ω ⊂ ℝ² with non-empty interior whose boundary ∂Ω is a piecewise smooth simple closed curve. The billiard flow describes a point particle moving in straight lines inside Ω at unit speed and reflecting elastically (angle of incidence equals angle of reflection) upon hitting ∂Ω. This flow preserves the Liouville measure on the unit tangent bundle of Ω; define the (metric) entropy of the billiard to be the Kolmogorov–Sinai entropy of the billiard flow with respect to this Liouville measure.

Solve either of the following:

(a) Construct a strictly convex planar billiard table Ω whose boundary ∂Ω is a C¹-smooth simple closed curve and whose billiard has positive metric entropy.

paper_title: Billiard Dynamics: A Survey with the Emphasis on Open Problems
original_question: Does there exist an irrational polygon, meaning a polygon whose side angles are not all rational multiples of π, whose billiard dynamics is nonergodic?
self_contained_problem:
A polygon $P \subset \mathbb{R}^2$ is called rational if every interior angle between adjacent sides is a rational multiple of $\pi$; otherwise $P$ is called irrational. The billiard flow on $P$ is the geodesic flow on the unit tangent bundle of $P$ where trajectories travel in straight lines inside $P$ and reflect from the boundary according to the law of equal angles (with trajectories hitting corners left undefined). This flow preserves the Liouville (Lebesgue) measure on the unit tangent bundle, and is said to be ergodic if every flow-invariant measurable set has either full or zero measure.

Problem: Exhibit an explicit example of an irrational polygon $P$ whose billiard flow is not ergodic with respect to Liouville measure, or prove that no such polygon exists.
status_search_result: The question of whether an irrational nonergodic polygon exists is a well-known open problem in the dynamics of polygonal billiards. Surveys and expositions (Masur–Tabachnikov handbook chapter, Schwartz's ICM survey, Matheus's blog post, and Misiurewicz's list of open problems) all describe the ergodicity behavior of billiards in irrational polygons as essentially unknown; it is known that a generic (in a Baire sense) polygon is ergodic (Kerckhoff–Masur–Smillie), but no irrational nonergodic example is known.

original_question: Does every polygonal billiard table have at least one periodic billiard orbit?
self_contained_problem:
Let $P \subset \mathbb{R}^2$ be a polygon (a compact connected planar region bounded by finitely many straight line segments). The billiard flow on $P$ is the dynamical system that describes a point particle moving in straight lines inside $P$ with unit speed and reflecting elastically (angle of incidence equals angle of reflection) upon hitting the interior of an edge; trajectories that hit a vertex are left undefined. A billiard orbit is called periodic if, after finitely many reflections, the particle returns to its initial position with its initial velocity.

Consider the billiard flow on $P$ (a point particle moving at unit speed in a straight line in the interior, reflecting elastically off the sides). A periodic billiard trajectory in $P$ belongs to a maximal parallel family of periodic trajectories of the same length, called a "periodic band" (or cylinder); its length is the common length of the trajectories in the family. It is known that there exist constants $0<c_*(P)\le c^*(P)<\infty$ such that
$$c_*(P)\,\ell^2 \;\le\; f_P(\ell)\;\le\; c^*(P)\,\ell^2$$
for all sufficiently large $\ell$.

paper_title: Some Open Problems in Topological Algebra
original_question: Does every topological group arise as a quotient group of a zero-dimensional topological group of the same weight, and under what conditions is an almost metrizable topological group a quotient of a zero-dimensional group of the same weight? paper_title: Some Open Problems in Topological Algebra
original_question: Let X be a compact space and let H be a distal subgroup of S(X) that acts transitively on X. Must H be left bounded? Here S(X) is the semigroup of continuous self-maps of X, and a subgroup H is distal if for any distinct points x1, x2 in X and any point x in X there exists a neighborhood U of x such that {h(x1), h(x2)} is not contained in U for every h in H.
self_contained_problem:
Let $X$ be a compact Hausdorff space, and let $S(X)$ denote the semigroup of continuous self-maps of $X$ under composition. A subgroup $H \subseteq S(X)$ is called *distal* if for any two distinct points $x_1, x_2 \in X$ and any point $x \in X$, there exists an open neighborhood $U$ of $x$ such that $\{h(x_1), h(x_2)\} \not\subseteq U$ for every $h \in H$. The subgroup $H$ is said to act *transitively* on $X$ if for every pair $x, y \in X$ there exists $h \in H$ with $h(x) = y$. Finally, $H$ is called *left bounded* if for every neighborhood $V$ of the diagonal in $X \times X$ there exists a finite set $F \subseteq H$ such that for each $h \in H$ one has $(h(x), f(x)) \in V$ for some $f \in F$ and all $x \in X$ (equivalently, the orbit of $H$ under left translation in the appropriate uniform structure is totally bounded).

Question: Must every distal subgroup $H$ of $S(X)$ that acts transitively on $X$ be left bounded?
status_search_result: A web search did not locate any published resolution of this question, which was posed by Protasov as an open problem in topological algebra. The converse direction (left bounded transitive subgroups are distal) is known, but the question of whether distality together with transitivity implies left boundedness appears to remain unresolved in the available literature.

paper_title: Some Open Problems in Topological Algebra
original_question: Does every zero-dimensional compact homogeneous space admit the structure of a left topological group, and in particular, if K is a first-countable zero-dimensional compact space, does its countable power K^ω admit the structure of a left topological group? paper_title: Some Open Problems in Topological Algebra
original_question: Is there a metrizable o-bounded topological group G such that player I has a winning strategy in the game OF(G)? Here a subset A of a topological group G is o-bounded if for every sequence (U_n) of neighborhoods of the origin there exists a sequence of finite sets (F_n) such that A is contained in the union of F_n U_n, and in the game OF(A), player I chooses neighborhoods U_n while player II chooses finite sets F_n, with player II winning when A is contained in the union of F_n U_n.
self_contained_problem:
Let $G$ be a topological group with identity (origin) $e$. A subset $A \subseteq G$ is called o-bounded if for every sequence $(U_n)_{n\in\omega}$ of neighborhoods of $e$ in $G$ there exists a sequence $(F_n)_{n\in\omega}$ of finite subsets of $G$ such that
$$A \subseteq \bigcup_{n\in\omega} F_n U_n.$$
Given a subset $A \subseteq G$, define the two-player game $\mathrm{OF}(A)$ (Open–Finite) as follows. At each step $n \in \omega$, player I chooses a neighborhood $U_n \subseteq G$ of $e$, and then player II chooses a finite subset $F_n \subseteq G$. Player II wins the play if $A \subseteq \bigcup_{n\in\omega} F_n U_n$; otherwise player I wins.

Question: Does there exist a metrizable o-bounded topological group $G$ such that player I has a winning strategy in the game $\mathrm{OF}(G)$?

self_contained_problem:
Let $P_n$ be a finite set of $n$ points in the Euclidean plane. For a pair of points $p, q \in P_n$, define $f(p,q)$ to be the minimum, over all circles $C$ in the plane passing through or containing both $p$ and $q$ (i.e., with $p$ and $q$ in the closed disk bounded by $C$), of the number of points of $P_n$ contained in (the closed disk bounded by) $C$. 

Question: Does there exist an absolute constant $c$ such that for every finite set $P_n$ of $n$ points in the plane, one can find a pair of points $p, q \in P_n$ with
$$f(p,q) \;\ge\; \frac{n}{4} - c\,?$$
Equivalently, prove or disprove that every $n$-point planar set contains two points such that every circle containing both of them encloses at least $n/4 \pm c$ points of the set.

original_question: For every family F of n pairwise disjoint closed line segments in the plane, must there exist a simple alternating path using at least on the order of log n input segments, where a simple alternating path is a nonintersecting polygonal chain that alternates between input segments from F and connecting segments, and the connecting segments are not allowed to intersect any other segment of F?
self_contained_problem:
Let F = {l_1, ..., l_n} be a family of n pairwise disjoint closed line segments in the Euclidean plane. A simple alternating path of F is a non-self-intersecting polygonal chain whose edges alternate between (i) "input edges," each of which is a segment of F, and (ii) "connecting edges," each of which has its two endpoints on segments of F and does not intersect any segment of F other than at those two endpoints. The length of such a path is the number of input edges (elements of F) it uses.

Prove or disprove: there exists an absolute constant c > 0 such that for every n and every family F of n pairwise disjoint closed line segments in the plane, F admits a simple alternating path that uses at least c · log n elements of F.
status_search_result: Hoffmann and Tóth proved that the segment endpoint visibility graph of any set of n pairwise disjoint line segments in the plane admits a non-crossing alternating path of length Ω(log n), confirming the conjecture; matching upper-bound constructions show the log n order is tight. Subsequent work ("Long Alternating Paths Exist," SoCG 2020) further extends results in this area.

paper_title: Some Open Problems
original_question: For every family F of n pairwise disjoint closed convex sets in the plane, is there an element C in F and a straight line l such that l separates C from at least floor(n/3) up to an additive constant c other elements of F, where separating two convex sets means they lie in opposite open half-planes determined by l?
self_contained_problem:
Let n be a positive integer and let F = {C_1, ..., C_n} be a family of n pairwise disjoint closed convex sets in the Euclidean plane R^2. Say that a straight line l separates two convex sets A, B ⊂ R^2 if A and B lie in the two distinct open half-planes determined by l (so neither set meets l). 

Prove or disprove the following: there exists an absolute constant c ≥ 0 such that for every such family F there exist an element C ∈ F and a straight line l with the property that l separates C from at least ⌊n/3⌋ − c of the remaining elements of F.
category_tag: Discrete and combinatorial geometry — separation of convex sets
status_search_result: The conjecture (that for n pairwise disjoint planar convex sets some element can be separated by a single line from ≈ n/3 of the others) appears to remain open in full generality. Partial results are known: for disks, a separation of about (n−7)/4 elements is achievable; for line segments that can be extended to pairwise disjoint half-lines, a bound of ⌈n/3⌉+1 has been established. No proof or counterexample for arbitrary convex sets achieving the n/3 bound has been found in the search.

paper_title: Some Open Problems
original_question: What is the tight worst-case number of vertex pi-floodlights needed to illuminate every simple polygon with n vertices under the same one-floodlight-per-vertex model; specifically, is the correct bound 5(n-1)/8 up to an additive constant c?
self_contained_problem:
Consider the following illumination model for simple polygons. A vertex π-floodlight placed at a vertex v of a simple polygon P is a light source whose illuminated region is the intersection of P with a closed half-plane whose bounding line passes through v; equivalently, it is a floodlight of aperture π placed at v with a freely chosen orientation. At most one π-floodlight may be placed at each vertex of P. A set of vertex π-floodlights is said to illuminate P if the union of their illuminated regions equals P.

Let f(n) denote the smallest integer such that every simple polygon with n vertices can be illuminated by at most f(n) vertex π-floodlights under this one-floodlight-per-vertex model.

Determine the exact asymptotic value of f(n). In particular, decide whether
f(n) = 5(n−1)/8 + O(1),
i.e. whether there exists a constant c such that |f(n) − 5(n−1)/8| ≤ c for all sufficiently large n.
status_search_result: The vertex π-floodlight illumination problem remains open. Known bounds place the worst-case fraction of vertices needed between 5/8 (lower bound by Urrutia, 2002, via examples requiring 5(k+1)/(8k+9) floodlights) and 2/3 (upper bound, with refinements such as ⌊(2n−c)/3⌋ by Speckmann and Tóth where c counts convex vertices). The conjectured tight value 5(n−1)/8 ± O(1) has not been proven.

paper_title: Some Open Problems
original_question: Does there exist a threshold n0 such that every polygon P with n >= n0 vertices has a subset of at most floor(n/4) edges whose visibility covers all points of P, meaning every point of P is visible from at least one selected edge?
self_contained_problem:
Let P be a simple polygon in the plane with n vertices, regarded as a closed region bounded by its edges. For an edge e of P, say that a point x ∈ P is visible from e if there exists a point y ∈ e such that the closed segment xy lies entirely in P. A set E of edges of P is said to illuminate (or cover) P if every point of P is visible from at least one edge in E; the elements of E are called edge guards.

Determine whether there exists a positive integer n₀ with the following property: for every simple polygon P having n ≥ n₀ vertices, one can choose a set E of at most ⌊n/4⌋ edges of P such that every point of P is visible from some edge in E.
status_search_result: Toussaint's edge-guard conjecture (that ⌊n/4⌋ edge guards suffice to cover any simple polygon with sufficiently many vertices) remains a long-standing open problem in computational geometry. Subsequent work has established weaker upper bounds and studied variants (open edge guards, mobile guards, curvilinear galleries), but the original ⌊n/4⌋ conjecture has not been proved or disproved.

paper_title: Spectral analysis for a class of integral-difference operators: known facts, new results, and open problems
original_question: Consider the Gaussian equilibrium distribution case in which the truncated restricted operator K_phi^a acts on functions on [-a,a] by (K_phi^a u)(x) = integral from -a to a of (u(x) phi(s) - u(s) phi(x)) / |x - s| ds, with phi(x) = C exp(-x^2), and is equivalently rescaled to an operator K_a on [-1,1] with phi_a(x) = C_a exp(-a^2 x^2). Suppose the established asymptotic result is that, for every M > 0, the dimension of the spectral subspace E_a[-M,M] H_a tends to infinity as a tends to infinity, so zero is a spectral concentration point for the limit operator. Do the discrete spectra of these truncated operators condense into continuous spectrum as a tends to infinity, and what are the other spectral properties of the limit operator?
self_contained_problem:
For each a > 0, let H_a = L^2([-a, a]) and consider the integral-difference operator K_φ^a acting on suitable functions u on [-a, a] by
  (K_φ^a u)(x) = ∫_{-a}^{a} (u(x) φ(s) − u(s) φ(x)) / |x − s| ds,
where φ(x) = C e^{−x^2} and C > 0 is a fixed normalization constant (e.g. so that ∫_{-∞}^{∞} φ = 1). By the rescaling x = a y, this operator is unitarily equivalent to an operator K_a on L^2([-1, 1]) defined by
  (K_a u)(x) = ∫_{-1}^{1} (u(x) φ_a(s) − u(s) φ_a(x)) / |x − s| ds,
with φ_a(x) = C_a e^{−a^2 x^2} (C_a chosen analogously). Each K_a is self-adjoint and nonnegative; let E_a(·) denote its spectral projection. It is known that for every M > 0,
  dim E_a([−M, M]) H_a → ∞ as a → ∞,
so that 0 is a point of spectral concentration in the large-a limit.

Question: As a → ∞, does the discrete spectrum of the family {K_a} condense into continuous spectrum of a limiting operator? More generally, determine the spectral properties (nature of the spectrum: pure point, absolutely continuous, singular continuous; multiplicity; spectral measure) of the limit operator obtained from K_a as a → ∞.
status_search_result: A search for the spectral analysis of this family of integral-difference operators with Gaussian equilibrium turns up the related work on spectral analysis of integral-difference collision operators (e.g. by Melnikov and collaborators), but no source establishes the condensation of the discrete spectrum into a continuous one for the Gaussian truncation, nor a complete description of the limit operator's spectral properties. The question is explicitly stated as not yet resolved in the available literature.

paper_title: Open Problems in Affine Algebraic Geometry: Problems for Problem Session
context_brief: Roots of the affine Cremona group
original_question: Let k be an algebraically closed field of characteristic 0, let n be an integer greater than 1, and let k[n] = k[x1, ..., xn] be the polynomial algebra in n variables. Let Aut*_k k[n] be the subgroup of polynomial k-automorphisms sigma of k[n] whose Jacobian determinant det(D_i(sigma(x_j))) is 1, where D_i = partial/partial x_i. Let T be the diagonal torus of volume-preserving automorphisms sigma = diag(t1, ..., tn) such that sigma(x_i) = t_i x_i and t1 ... tn = 1. A nonzero locally nilpotent derivation D of k[n] is a root vector of Aut*_k k[n] with respect to T when there is a nontrivial character chi: T -> G_m such that sigma o D o sigma^(-1) = chi(sigma)D for every sigma in T; chi is the corresponding root. What are all roots and all root vectors of Aut*_k k[n] with respect to T?
self_contained_problem:
Let $k$ be an algebraically closed field of characteristic $0$, let $n>1$ be an integer, and let $k^{[n]}=k[x_1,\dots,x_n]$ be the polynomial algebra in $n$ variables over $k$. Define
$$\mathrm{Aut}^*_k k^{[n]} := \{\sigma\in \mathrm{Aut}_k k^{[n]}\mid \det(D_i(\sigma(x_j)))_{1\le i,j\le n}=1\},$$
where $D_i=\partial/\partial x_i$. Let $T$ be the diagonal torus
$$T:=\{\sigma=\mathrm{diag}(t_1,\dots,t_n)\in \mathrm{Aut}^*_k k^{[n]}\mid \sigma(x_i)=t_i x_i,\; t_i\in k^*,\; t_1\cdots t_n=1\}.$$
A nonzero locally nilpotent derivation $D$ of $k^{[n]}$ is called a root vector of $\mathrm{Aut}^*_k k^{[n]}$ with respect to $T$ if there exists a nontrivial character $\chi:T\to \mathbb{G}_m$ such that $\sigma\circ D\circ \sigma^{-1}=\chi(\sigma)D$ for every $\sigma\in T$; the character $\chi$ is then called the corresponding root.

Determine all roots and all root vectors of $\mathrm{Aut}^*_k k^{[n]}$ with respect to $T$.
category_tag: Affine Cremona group / locally nilpotent derivations
status_search_result: The problem (a question of Popov on roots of the affine Cremona group with respect to the diagonal torus) was solved by A. Liendo (arXiv:1010.4034, 2010; published in Transformation Groups, 2011). The root vectors are exactly the locally nilpotent derivations of the form $x^\alpha\,\partial/\partial x_i$, where $x^\alpha$ is a monomial not depending on $x_i$; the corresponding roots are the associated characters of $T$.

paper_title: Open Problems in Affine Algebraic Geometry: Problems for Problem Session
original_question: Let k be an algebraically closed field of characteristic 0, let n > 1, and let Aut*_k k[n] be the group of volume-preserving polynomial k-automorphisms of affine n-space, meaning automorphisms of k[x1, ..., xn] with Jacobian determinant 1. Is every algebraic torus action on affine n-space that lies in Aut*_k k[n] linearizable? Equivalently, does Aut*_k k[n] have no maximal algebraic tori of dimension less than n - 1?
self_contained_problem:
Let $k$ be an algebraically closed field of characteristic $0$ and let $n>1$. Let $\mathrm{Aut}_k k[n]$ denote the group of polynomial $k$-automorphisms of the polynomial ring $k[x_1,\dots,x_n]$, identified with the group of regular automorphisms of affine $n$-space $\mathbb{A}^n_k$. Let
$$\mathrm{Aut}^*_k k[n] := \{\varphi \in \mathrm{Aut}_k k[n] : \det(\mathrm{Jac}(\varphi)) = 1\}$$
be the subgroup of volume-preserving (Jacobian determinant $1$) automorphisms. An algebraic torus action on $\mathbb{A}^n_k$ is a morphism of algebraic groups $T \to \mathrm{Aut}_k k[n]$, where $T \cong (k^*)^r$ for some $r\ge 1$; the action is called linearizable if there exist coordinates on $\mathbb{A}^n_k$ in which $T$ acts by diagonal linear transformations. Call the action volume-preserving if its image lies in $\mathrm{Aut}^*_k k[n]$.

Question: Is every volume-preserving algebraic torus action on $\mathbb{A}^n_k$ linearizable? Equivalently, is it true that $\mathrm{Aut}^*_k k[n]$ contains no maximal (with respect to inclusion) algebraic tori of dimension less than $n-1$? In particular, resolve the first nontrivial case $n=3$.
category_tag: Linearization of torus actions on affine space
status_search_result: The general linearization conjecture for torus actions on affine n-space is known in low complexity (Białynicki-Birula for codimension one; Koras-Russell and Kraft-Schwarz when fixed-point locus is positive-dimensional), but remains open in higher complexity, including the volume-preserving variant. Recent work (e.g. arXiv:2411.14645, 2024) classifies candidates for counterexamples in the codimension/complexity-two case, indicating the problem is still open, with n=3 being the first nontrivial case.

paper_title: Open Problems in Affine Algebraic Geometry: Problems for Problem Session
original_question: Let k be an algebraically closed field of characteristic 0, let n > 1, and let k[n] = k[x1, ..., xn]. Given two locally nilpotent derivations P and Q of k[n], when is the smallest closed subgroup of Aut_k k[n] that contains the one-parameter subgroups {exp(tP) | t in k} and {exp(tQ) | t in k} finite-dimensional?
self_contained_problem:
Let $k$ be an algebraically closed field of characteristic $0$, let $n > 1$ be an integer, and let $k^{[n]} = k[x_1, \dots, x_n]$ denote the polynomial ring in $n$ variables over $k$. A $k$-derivation $D$ of $k^{[n]}$ is called locally nilpotent if for every $f \in k^{[n]}$ there exists $m \geq 1$ such that $D^m(f) = 0$. For such a $D$, the exponential
$$\exp(tD) = \sum_{i \geq 0} \frac{t^i}{i!} D^i, \qquad t \in k,$$
is a well-defined $k$-algebra automorphism of $k^{[n]}$, and $\{\exp(tD) \mid t \in k\}$ is a one-parameter subgroup of $\operatorname{Aut}_k k^{[n]}$ isomorphic to the additive group $\mathbb{G}_a$. Equip $\operatorname{Aut}_k k^{[n]}$ with its standard ind-group structure, so that one can speak of closed subgroups and their dimension.

Given two locally nilpotent $k$-derivations $P$ and $Q$ of $k^{[n]}$, let $G(P,Q)$ denote the smallest closed subgroup of $\operatorname{Aut}_k k^{[n]}$ that contains both one-parameter subgroups $\{\exp(tP) \mid t \in k\}$ and $\{\exp(tQ) \mid t \in k\}$.

Determine necessary and sufficient conditions on the pair $(P, Q)$ under which $G(P, Q)$ is finite-dimensional.
status_search_result: The question is posed as an open problem in a problem session on affine algebraic geometry. No published solution or general criterion characterizing pairs of locally nilpotent derivations whose generated closed subgroup of automorphisms is finite-dimensional was located. Standard references on locally nilpotent derivations and ind-group structures on polynomial automorphism groups discuss related notions but do not resolve this question.

paper_title: Space and Time Complexity of Exact Algorithms: Some Open Problems
original_question: For Table-6-SUM, where the input is a 6 by m table of integers together with a goal sum S and the task is to choose exactly one entry from each row so that the six chosen entries sum to S, is there an algorithm running in O(m^3 log m) time while using only O(m) space?
self_contained_problem:
Define the Table-6-SUM problem as follows. The input consists of a 6 × m matrix A of integers (six rows, m columns) and a target integer S. The task is to decide whether one can select exactly one entry from each of the six rows so that the six chosen entries sum to S; equivalently, decide whether there exist column indices j_1, j_2, j_3, j_4, j_5, j_6 ∈ {1, …, m} (not required to be distinct) such that A[1, j_1] + A[2, j_2] + A[3, j_3] + A[4, j_4] + A[5, j_5] + A[6, j_6] = S. Assume the standard word-RAM model in which arithmetic on integers of size polynomial in the input fits in O(1) words and space is counted in words.

Question: Does there exist a deterministic algorithm that solves Table-6-SUM in O(m^3 log m) time while using only O(m) words of working space?
status_search_result: A web search did not turn up a published resolution of this specific Table-6-SUM time–space tradeoff question (O(m^3 log m) time with O(m) space). Related work on space-efficient k-SUM algorithms (e.g., Bansal–Garg–Korten–Nederlof–Vyas and subsequent low-space subset-sum/k-SUM results) gives space-efficient algorithms for k-SUM variants, and randomized algorithms achieving O(n^{k-0.5} polylog n) time with O(log n) space for random k-SUM instances are known, but none of these appear to settle the deterministic worst-case Table-6-SUM bound asked for. Status appears unresolved based on available sources.

paper_title: Space and Time Complexity of Exact Algorithms: Some Open Problems
original_question: For the k-SUM problem, where k is fixed, the input consists of m integers and a goal sum S, and the task is to decide whether some k of the integers add up to S, prove any non-trivial lower bound in either the algebraic decision tree model or the algebraic computation tree model.
self_contained_problem:
Fix an integer k ≥ 2. In the k-SUM problem, the input consists of m integers a_1, ..., a_m together with a target integer S, and one must decide whether there exist indices 1 ≤ i_1 < i_2 < ... < i_k ≤ m such that a_{i_1} + a_{i_2} + ... + a_{i_k} = S.

Recall the following two models of computation on inputs viewed as points in R^m:

(a) Algebraic decision tree model. A computation is a rooted ternary tree whose internal nodes are labeled by polynomials p(x_1, ..., x_m) of bounded degree; the branch taken at a node depends on the sign (negative, zero, positive) of p evaluated on the input. Leaves are labeled "yes" or "no". The complexity is the depth (worst-case number of polynomial tests).

(b) Algebraic computation tree model. A computation tree in which each internal node either performs an arithmetic operation (+, −, ×, ÷, √) on previously computed values or the input variables, or branches on the sign of a previously computed value. The complexity is again the depth.

Problem: Establish any non-trivial (i.e., super-linear, or more generally super-(m log m)) lower bound on the depth required to solve the k-SUM problem in either the algebraic decision tree model or the algebraic computation tree model, for some fixed k ≥ 3.
category_tag: k-SUM lower bounds in algebraic decision trees
status_search_result: Only Ω(m log m) bounds (matching element distinctness, due to Ben-Or / Steele–Yao topological methods) are known for k-SUM in the general algebraic decision tree and algebraic computation tree models. Stronger lower bounds (e.g., Erickson's Ω(m^⌈k/2⌉)) are known only in restricted models such as k-linear decision trees. Recent results (Cardinale Tardos–type and Kane–Lovett–Moran near-linear linear decision trees) actually give surprisingly shallow trees, making non-trivial lower bounds in the algebraic model appear out of reach; the problem remains open.

paper_title: Space and Time Complexity of Exact Algorithms: Some Open Problems
original_question: For SUBSET-SUM, where the input is n positive integers b_1, ..., b_n and a goal sum B and the task is to decide whether some subset of the integers sums to B, construct an exact algorithm running in O*(1.99^n) time and using only polynomial space, where O* suppresses polynomial factors.
self_contained_problem: The SUBSET-SUM problem is defined as follows: given n positive integers b_1, b_2, ..., b_n and a target integer B, decide whether there exists a subset S ⊆ {1, 2, ..., n} such that ∑_{i ∈ S} b_i = B. Using the O*(·) notation to suppress factors polynomial in the input size, design a (deterministic) exact algorithm that solves SUBSET-SUM in time O*(1.99^n) while using only space polynomial in n and in the bit-length of the inputs.
status_search_result: A randomized polynomial-space algorithm for SUBSET-SUM running in O*(2^{0.86n}) time was given by Bansal, Garg, Nederlof, and Vyas (2017), and further improvements (e.g., Jin–Vyas) achieve faster polynomial-space randomized running times. These results resolve the bound 1.99^n in the randomized setting (assuming random read-only access to random bits), but a deterministic polynomial-space algorithm running in time O*(c^n) for any constant c < 2 remains open.

paper_title: Space and Time Complexity of Exact Algorithms: Some Open Problems
original_question: For EQUAL-SUBSET-SUM, where the input is n positive integers b_1, ..., b_n and the task is to decide whether there exist two disjoint non-empty subsets with the same sum, can one design exact algorithms faster than the known O*(2^n) approach obtained by translating the instance to Table-4-SUM, and can one clarify how fast algorithms for EQUAL-SUBSET-SUM relate to fast algorithms for SUBSET-SUM?
self_contained_problem:
EQUAL-SUBSET-SUM is the following decision problem: given n positive integers b_1, ..., b_n, decide whether there exist two disjoint non-empty subsets A, B ⊆ {1, ..., n} such that Σ_{i∈A} b_i = Σ_{i∈B} b_i. A baseline exact algorithm runs in O*(2^n) time (where O* hides factors polynomial in n) via reduction to a 4-SUM-style tabulation. SUBSET-SUM is the related problem of, given positive integers b_1, ..., b_n and a target t, deciding whether some subset sums to t; it admits an O*(2^{n/2}) meet-in-the-middle algorithm.

(a) Design an exact algorithm for EQUAL-SUBSET-SUM whose worst-case running time is strictly better than O*(2^n) (and ideally better than the meet-in-the-middle bound O*(3^{n/2}) ≈ O*(1.7321^n)).

(b) Clarify the relationship between the time complexities of exact algorithms for SUBSET-SUM and for EQUAL-SUBSET-SUM: in particular, determine whether a faster-than-2^{n/2} algorithm for SUBSET-SUM yields a correspondingly faster algorithm for EQUAL-SUBSET-SUM, and conversely.
status_search_result: Part (a) has been partially resolved: Mucha, Nederlof, Pawlewicz, and Węgrzycki (ESA 2019) gave a Monte Carlo algorithm running in O*(1.7088^n) time, beating the meet-in-the-middle bound of O*(3^{n/2}) and hence the trivial O*(2^n). They also obtained an O*(2.6817^n) polynomial-space algorithm. The precise relationship between the complexities of SUBSET-SUM and EQUAL-SUBSET-SUM (part b) does not appear to be fully settled.

paper_title: Space and Time Complexity of Exact Algorithms: Some Open Problems
original_question: For 10-CLIQUE, where the input is an undirected simple loopless p-vertex graph G and the task is to decide whether G contains a clique on 10 vertices, is there an algorithm running in O(p^7.5) time?
self_contained_problem:
Let G = (V, E) be an undirected simple loopless graph on p = |V| vertices (no self-loops, no multiple edges). A clique on 10 vertices in G is a subset S ⊆ V with |S| = 10 such that every pair of distinct vertices in S is joined by an edge of G. The 10-CLIQUE decision problem asks, given such a graph G as input, to decide whether G contains a clique on 10 vertices.

Question: Does there exist an algorithm that solves the 10-CLIQUE decision problem in time O(p^{7.5}) on the standard word-RAM model (uniformly in G), where p denotes the number of vertices of the input graph?
status_search_result: The fastest known k-clique algorithms use the Nešetřil–Poljak reduction to (rectangular) matrix multiplication, giving running time O(n^{ωk/3}) when 3 | k, and improvements due to Eisenbrand–Grandoni when k ≢ 0 (mod 3). For k = 10, the current best published bounds rely on the matrix multiplication exponent ω ≈ 2.371, yielding running times above n^{7.9}, well above n^{7.5}. No published algorithm achieves O(p^{7.5}) for 10-CLIQUE, and the question of attaining such a bound appears to remain open.

paper_title: Space and Time Complexity of Exact Algorithms: Some Open Problems
original_question: For MAX-CUT, where the input is an n-vertex graph G = (V, E) and the task is to find a subset X of V that maximizes the number of edges between X and V - X, design a faster exact algorithm than the O*(2^(omega n/3))-time approach based on reducing to 3-clique in an auxiliary graph, where omega is the matrix multiplication exponent and O* suppresses polynomial factors.
self_contained_problem:
Let $\omega$ denote the exponent of square matrix multiplication, i.e., the infimum of real numbers $c$ such that two $n \times n$ matrices over a ring can be multiplied using $O(n^c)$ ring operations. Use $O^*(\cdot)$ to suppress factors polynomial in the input size.

The MAX-CUT problem is defined as follows: given an undirected graph $G = (V, E)$ on $n = |V|$ vertices, find a subset $X \subseteq V$ that maximizes the number of edges with exactly one endpoint in $X$, i.e., the size of the cut $|\{\{u,v\} \in E : |\{u,v\} \cap X| = 1\}|$.

A known exact algorithm solves MAX-CUT in time $O^*(2^{\omega n/3})$ by reducing the problem to finding a maximum-weight triangle in an auxiliary graph of $2^{n/3}$ vertices and then applying fast matrix multiplication.

Problem: Design an exact algorithm for MAX-CUT on general $n$-vertex graphs whose worst-case running time is asymptotically faster than $O^*(2^{\omega n/3})$.
status_search_result: The $O^*(2^{\omega n/3})$ bound due to Williams (via reduction to max-weight triangle) remains the best known worst-case running time for exact MAX-CUT on general $n$-vertex graphs. Subsequent work has focused on sparse graphs, special graph classes (e.g., split graphs), counting versions, or polynomial-space variants, but no improvement on the general-graph exponent has been reported. The problem appears to still be open.

paper_title: Space and Time Complexity of Exact Algorithms: Some Open Problems
original_question: For BISECTION, where the input is an n-vertex graph G = (V, E) and the task is to find a subset X of V with |X| = n/2 minimizing the number of edges between X and V - X, can one improve on the O*(2^(omega n/3))-time approach, where omega is the matrix multiplication exponent and O* suppresses polynomial factors?
self_contained_problem:
Let G = (V, E) be an undirected graph on n vertices, where n is even. A bisection of G is a subset X ⊆ V with |X| = n/2; its cut size is the number of edges of G with exactly one endpoint in X. The BISECTION problem asks for a bisection X minimizing this cut size. Let ω denote the exponent of square matrix multiplication, i.e., the infimum of real numbers t such that two n × n matrices can be multiplied in O(n^t) arithmetic operations, and let O*(·) suppress factors polynomial in n.

There is a known exact algorithm solving BISECTION in time O*(2^(ωn/3)). Design an exact algorithm for BISECTION running in time O*(c^n) for some constant c < 2^(ω/3), or prove that no such improvement is possible.
category_tag: Exact exponential algorithms for graph partitioning
status_search_result: Web searches did not surface a published exact algorithm for BISECTION on general graphs that improves on the O*(2^(ωn/3)) bound. Related work focuses on FPT algorithms parameterized by cut size (e.g., 2^O(k^3) n^3 log^3 n by Cygan et al.) and on practical branch-and-bound combinatorial algorithms, neither of which directly addresses the worst-case exponential exponent in n. The status appears to remain unresolved based on available sources.

paper_title: Space and Time Complexity of Exact Algorithms: Some Open Problems
original_question: For the n-city travelling salesman path problem with cities 1 through n, a start at city 1, an end at city n, distances d(i, j), and the goal of visiting cities 2 through n-1 in some order while minimizing total path length, construct an exact algorithm running in O*(2^n) time while using only polynomial space, where O* suppresses polynomial factors.
self_contained_problem:
Let n ≥ 2 be an integer and let d : {1,…,n} × {1,…,n} → ℝ≥0 be a distance function. The (Hamiltonian path) travelling salesman problem asks for a permutation π of {2,…,n−1} that minimizes
  d(1, π(2)) + Σ_{i=2}^{n−2} d(π(i), π(i+1)) + d(π(n−1), n),
i.e. a minimum-length Hamiltonian path from city 1 to city n visiting every other city exactly once.

Design a deterministic exact algorithm that, on every such instance, computes the optimal value (and a corresponding optimal permutation) in time O*(2^n) while using only polynomial (in n) working space, where O*(·) suppresses factors polynomial in n and in the bit-length of the input distances. Equivalently: does there exist a 2^n · poly(n)-time, poly(n)-space exact algorithm for TSP?
status_search_result: Achieving an O*(2^n)-time polynomial-space exact algorithm for the general TSP is widely regarded as open. The classical Held–Karp algorithm achieves O*(2^n) time but uses exponential space, while known polynomial-space algorithms (e.g., Gurevich–Shelah, Bjorklund-type approaches) have worse running times such as O*(4^n · n^{log n}) or similar. Polynomial-space O*(2^n) algorithms are known only in restricted settings (bounded-degree graphs, many-visits TSP, etc.).

paper_title: Space and Time Complexity of Exact Algorithms: Some Open Problems
original_question: For an n-vertex graph G, construct an exact counting algorithm running in O*(1.99^n) time that counts the total number of cycles in G, where O* suppresses polynomial factors.
self_contained_problem:
Let $G$ be a simple undirected graph on $n$ vertices. A cycle in $G$ is a subgraph isomorphic to $C_k$ for some $k \geq 3$ (i.e., a simple cycle on $k$ distinct vertices). Let $c(G)$ denote the total number of simple cycles in $G$ (of all lengths from $3$ to $n$).

Design an exact algorithm that, given $G$, computes $c(G)$ and runs in time $O^*(1.99^n)$, where the $O^*$ notation suppresses factors polynomial in $n$. Equivalently, exhibit a constant $c < 2$ and an algorithm computing $c(G)$ in time $O^*(c^n)$, or prove that no such algorithm exists.
status_search_result: The problem of counting all simple cycles in a general n-vertex graph in time O*(c^n) for some c<2 appears to remain open. Surveys and texts on exact exponential algorithms (e.g., Fomin–Kratsch) list cycle counting among problems lacking a known sub-2^n algorithm; subexponential results are known only for restricted classes such as planar graphs. No general-graph algorithm achieving O*(1.99^n) was found in the search.

paper_title: Space and Time Complexity of Exact Algorithms: Some Open Problems
original_question: For an n-vertex graph G and a specified length l, construct an exact counting algorithm running in O*(1.99^n) time that counts the number of cycles of length l in G, where O* suppresses polynomial factors.
self_contained_problem:
Let $G=(V,E)$ be a simple undirected graph on $n$ vertices, and let $\ell$ be a positive integer with $3\le \ell\le n$. A cycle of length $\ell$ in $G$ is a sequence of distinct vertices $v_1,v_2,\dots,v_\ell\in V$ (considered up to cyclic rotation and reflection) such that $\{v_i,v_{i+1}\}\in E$ for all $1\le i<\ell$ and $\{v_\ell,v_1\}\in E$.

Design a deterministic exact algorithm that, given $G$ and $\ell$ as input, outputs the exact number of cycles of length $\ell$ in $G$, and whose worst-case running time is $O^{*}(1.99^{n})$, where the $O^{*}$ notation suppresses factors that are polynomial in $n$. Equivalently, exhibit a constant $c<2$ and an algorithm running in time $O^{*}(c^{n})$ that solves this counting problem, or prove that no such algorithm exists.
category_tag: Exact exponential algorithms for cycle counting
status_search_result: A web search did not reveal a published exact algorithm counting cycles of arbitrary specified length $\ell$ in an $n$-vertex graph in time $O^*(c^n)$ for any constant $c<2$. Existing work (e.g., the general-purpose algorithm of Giscard–Kriege–Wilson, and surveys on faster/space-efficient exact exponential algorithms) addresses related cycle-counting tasks but does not appear to settle the $O^*(1.99^n)$ bound for counting $\ell$-cycles. The status therefore appears unresolved based on available evidence.

paper_title: Complete intersection liaison and Gorenstein liaison: new results and open problems
context_brief: ACM schemes and Gorenstein liaison classes
original_question: Let k be an algebraically closed field of characteristic 0, and consider arithmetically Cohen-Macaulay subschemes X of projective space P^n of fixed codimension c. Two equidimensional schemes without embedded components are in the same Gorenstein liaison class when they can be connected by a sequence of direct Gorenstein links through arithmetically Gorenstein schemes; a scheme is glicci when it lies in the Gorenstein liaison class of a complete intersection. Is there only one Gorenstein liaison class containing all arithmetically Cohen-Macaulay subschemes of P^n of codimension c, equivalently are all such subschemes glicci?
self_contained_problem:
Let $k$ be an algebraically closed field of characteristic $0$, and let $\mathbb{P}^n = \mathbb{P}^n_k$ be projective $n$-space. A closed subscheme $X \subset \mathbb{P}^n$ is called arithmetically Cohen–Macaulay (ACM) if its homogeneous coordinate ring $k[x_0,\dots,x_n]/I_X$ is a Cohen–Macaulay ring. A subscheme is called arithmetically Gorenstein if its homogeneous coordinate ring is Gorenstein. 

Given two equidimensional closed subschemes $V_1, V_2 \subset \mathbb{P}^n$ without embedded components and of the same codimension $c$, one says that $V_1$ and $V_2$ are directly Gorenstein linked if there exists an arithmetically Gorenstein subscheme $G \subset \mathbb{P}^n$ containing both, with $I_G : I_{V_1} = I_{V_2}$ and $I_G : I_{V_2} = I_{V_1}$. The Gorenstein liaison equivalence relation is the equivalence relation generated by direct Gorenstein links. A subscheme $X \subset \mathbb{P}^n$ is called glicci if it lies in the same Gorenstein liaison class as some complete intersection in $\mathbb{P}^n$ of the same codimension.

Fix an integer $c \ge 1$. Is it true that every arithmetically Cohen–Macaulay closed subscheme $X \subset \mathbb{P}^n$ of codimension $c$ is glicci, equivalently, that there is exactly one Gorenstein liaison class containing all codimension-$c$ ACM subschemes of $\mathbb{P}^n$?
status_search_result: The question of whether every arithmetically Cohen–Macaulay subscheme of projective space is glicci is widely cited as a central open problem in Gorenstein liaison theory. It is known to hold in codimension 2 (where glicci is equivalent to having an N-type resolution) and for various special classes (e.g., certain monomial ideals, standard determinantal schemes), but the general case—even for zero-dimensional schemes in $\mathbb{P}^3$—remains open as of recent literature.

paper_title: Complete intersection liaison and Gorenstein liaison: new results and open problems
context_brief: Determinantal schemes from r by r minors
original_question: Let X_{p,q,r} be a subscheme of P^n defined by the r by r minors of a p by q homogeneous matrix, where r <= min(p,q). Assume X_{p,q,r} has the expected codimension codim(X_{p,q,r}) = (p-r+1)(q-r+1), and is arithmetically Cohen-Macaulay. Is X_{p,q,r} in the Gorenstein liaison class of a complete intersection, i.e. is X_{p,q,r} glicci?
self_contained_problem:
Let $k$ be an algebraically closed field, and let $\mathbb{P}^n = \mathbb{P}^n_k$ denote projective $n$-space. Fix positive integers $p, q, r$ with $r \le \min(p,q)$, and let $M = (f_{ij})$ be a $p \times q$ matrix whose entries $f_{ij}$ are homogeneous polynomials in the coordinate ring $R = k[x_0, \dots, x_n]$, with the degrees of $f_{ij}$ chosen so that the $r \times r$ minors of $M$ are homogeneous. Let $I_r(M) \subset R$ be the ideal generated by the $r \times r$ minors of $M$, and let $X_{p,q,r} \subset \mathbb{P}^n$ be the closed subscheme defined by $I_r(M)$.

Assume that $X_{p,q,r}$ has the expected codimension
$$\mathrm{codim}\,X_{p,q,r} = (p-r+1)(q-r+1),$$
and that $X_{p,q,r}$ is arithmetically Cohen–Macaulay (i.e., $R/I_r(M)$ is a Cohen–Macaulay ring).

A subscheme $Y \subset \mathbb{P}^n$ is said to be glicci if it lies in the Gorenstein liaison class of a complete intersection, that is, if there is a finite sequence of Gorenstein links connecting $Y$ to a complete intersection subscheme of $\mathbb{P}^n$.

Question: Is every such $X_{p,q,r}$ glicci?
status_search_result: The case of maximal (i.e., $r = \min(p,q)$) standard determinantal schemes is known to be glicci by results going back to Gaeta and extended in the work on Gorenstein liaison (e.g., Kleppe–Migliore–Miró-Roig–Nagel–Peterson). Various subclasses—mixed ladder determinantal varieties, symmetric and skew-symmetric cases, and schemes arising from geometric vertex decomposition—have also been shown to be glicci. However, the general question for non-maximal $r \times r$ minors of an arbitrary $p \times q$ homogeneous matrix (with expected codimension and arithmetically Cohen–Macaulay) does not appear to have been settled in full generality, and remains a guiding open question in the area, of which the broader conjecture "every arithmetically Cohen–Macaulay subscheme of $\mathbb{P}^n$ is glicci" is the well-known umbrella problem.

paper_title: Periods of Integrals on Algebraic Manifolds: Summary of Main Results and Discussion of Open Problems
original_question: Find methods for proving or disproving local Torelli theorems for algebraic varieties, where the local Torelli problem asks whether the Hodge structure on the cohomology of a fiber separates points in its local moduli (Kuranishi) space. In particular, determine whether the local Torelli theorem is true or false for simply connected canonical surfaces, meaning surfaces with ample canonical bundle.
self_contained_problem:
Let X be a smooth complex projective variety, and let {X_s : s ∈ S} → S be the Kuranishi (local versal) deformation of X, where S is a germ of the local moduli space at the point 0 corresponding to X. For each s ∈ S the complex cohomology H^k(X_s, C) carries a pure Hodge structure of weight k, given by the Hodge filtration F^p H^k(X_s, C). The local period map sends s ∈ S to the point in the appropriate flag variety (period domain) parametrising this Hodge filtration on the fixed underlying vector space H^k(X, C) (identified via the Gauss–Manin connection).

The local Torelli problem asks whether this local period map is injective (equivalently, whether the Hodge structures on the cohomology of the fibers separate points of S near 0).

(a) Develop general methods, applicable to broad classes of smooth projective varieties, by which the local Torelli theorem can be either established or refuted.

(b) Determine whether the local Torelli theorem holds for every simply connected smooth complex projective surface X with ample canonical bundle K_X (i.e. a simply connected canonical surface of general type): that is, decide whether for every such X the local period map on its Kuranishi space is injective at 0, or exhibit a counterexample.
category_tag: Local Torelli for surfaces of general type
status_search_result: The problem is partially resolved. Kynev (1977) constructed a simply connected surface of general type (a "Kunev surface", with p_g = 1, K^2 = 1) for which the local/infinitesimal Torelli theorem fails; this gives a negative answer for general simply connected canonical surfaces. Catanese and Todorov subsequently produced families with K ample violating global Torelli. The broader question of finding general methods/criteria for local Torelli, and of classifying exactly which canonical surfaces satisfy local Torelli, remains an active area of research.

paper_title: Periods of Integrals on Algebraic Manifolds: Summary of Main Results and Discussion of Open Problems
original_question: Does the global Torelli theorem hold for nonsingular cubic threefolds, meaning that the polarized Hodge structure or total period matrix of a nonsingular cubic threefold uniquely determines its polarized algebraic structure?
self_contained_problem:
Let $X \subset \mathbb{P}^4_{\mathbb{C}}$ be a smooth (nonsingular) cubic hypersurface (a smooth cubic threefold). The third integral cohomology $H^3(X,\mathbb{Z})$ carries a Hodge structure of weight 1 with Hodge decomposition $H^3(X,\mathbb{C}) = H^{2,1}(X) \oplus H^{1,2}(X)$ and a unimodular intersection form, giving rise to the intermediate Jacobian $J(X) = H^{1,2}(X)/H^3(X,\mathbb{Z})$, which is a principally polarized abelian variety of dimension 5; equivalently, $X$ determines a polarized Hodge structure on $H^3(X,\mathbb{Z})$.

Question: Does the global Torelli theorem hold for smooth cubic threefolds? That is, if $X_1, X_2 \subset \mathbb{P}^4_{\mathbb{C}}$ are two smooth cubic threefolds such that their principally polarized intermediate Jacobians $(J(X_1),\Theta_1)$ and $(J(X_2),\Theta_2)$ are isomorphic as principally polarized abelian varieties (equivalently, the polarized Hodge structures on $H^3(X_1,\mathbb{Z})$ and $H^3(X_2,\mathbb{Z})$ are isomorphic), must $X_1$ and $X_2$ be isomorphic as projective varieties?
status_search_result: The global Torelli theorem for smooth cubic threefolds was established by Clemens and Griffiths in "The intermediate Jacobian of the cubic threefold," Annals of Mathematics 95 (1972), 281–356, where they proved that a smooth cubic threefold over $\mathbb{C}$ is uniquely determined up to isomorphism by its principally polarized intermediate Jacobian. Subsequent works (e.g., Beauville, Mumford) gave alternative proofs.

paper_title: Periods of Integrals on Algebraic Manifolds: Summary of Main Results and Discussion of Open Problems
context_brief: Finite order monodromy for isolated hypersurface singularities
original_question: For an isolated hypersurface singularity given locally by f(z1,...,z_{n+1})=s, with nonsingular Milnor fibers M_s over s in the punctured disc and Picard-Lefschetz transformation T acting on H^n(M_s0,Q), is T of finite order?
self_contained_problem:
Let $U \subset \mathbb{C}^{n+1}$ be an open neighborhood of the origin and let $f : U \to \mathbb{C}$ be a holomorphic function with $f(0) = 0$ such that $0$ is an isolated critical point of $f$. For sufficiently small $\varepsilon > 0$ and $0 < \eta \ll \varepsilon$, set $B = \{z \in \mathbb{C}^{n+1} : \|z\| \le \varepsilon\}$ and let $D^* = \{s \in \mathbb{C} : 0 < |s| < \eta\}$. For $s \in D^*$ define the Milnor fiber
$$M_s = \{z \in B : f(z) = s\},$$
which is a smooth compact manifold with boundary, homotopy equivalent to a bouquet of $n$-spheres. Fix a base point $s_0 \in D^*$ and let $T : H^n(M_{s_0}, \mathbb{Q}) \to H^n(M_{s_0}, \mathbb{Q})$ be the Picard–Lefschetz monodromy transformation obtained by parallel-transporting cohomology classes once around the origin along the loop $s_0 e^{2\pi i t}$, $t \in [0,1]$.

Question: Is $T$ necessarily of finite order, i.e. does there exist a positive integer $N$ such that $T^N = \mathrm{id}$ on $H^n(M_{s_0}, \mathbb{Q})$?
status_search_result: The question is resolved by the monodromy theorem (Brieskorn, "Die Monodromie der isolierten Singularitäten von Hyperflächen", 1970; also Landman, Clemens, Deligne, Grothendieck): for any isolated hypersurface singularity the Picard–Lefschetz monodromy $T$ acting on $H^n(M_{s_0}, \mathbb{Q})$ is quasi-unipotent — its eigenvalues are roots of unity and $(T^N - I)^{n+1} = 0$ for some positive integer $N$. Consequently $T$ is of finite order if and only if it is semisimple (equivalently, if and only if a resolution graph contains no cycles in the surface case); in general nontrivial Jordan blocks occur, so $T$ need not be of finite order. Thus the question is answered: $T$ is always quasi-unipotent but not always of finite order.

paper_title: Periods of Integrals on Algebraic Manifolds: Summary of Main Results and Discussion of Open Problems
context_brief: Topological partial compactification of period quotients
original_question: For a period matrix domain D with arithmetic group T, does there exist a separated, locally compact partial compactification {D/T}* that contains D/T as an open dense subset, is set-theoretically obtained by adjoining quotients of rational boundary components F_j/T_j, gives each boundary quotient its natural topology, and admits continuous extensions of every horizontal holomorphic period mapping S->D/T from a smooth algebraic family?
self_contained_problem:
Let D be a period matrix domain (a classifying space for polarized Hodge structures of a fixed type, realized as an open orbit G(ℝ)/V in its compact dual, where G is a ℚ-algebraic group of Hodge type and V is the compact isotropy of a reference Hodge structure). Let Γ ⊂ G(ℚ) be an arithmetic subgroup acting properly discontinuously on D, and form the analytic quotient D/Γ. For each rational boundary component F_j of D (in the sense of Hodge-theoretic boundary components stabilized by ℚ-parabolic subgroups), let Γ_j be the arithmetic subgroup of the stabilizer acting on F_j, and equip F_j/Γ_j with its natural topology.

Question: Does there exist a separated, locally compact topological space (D/Γ)* with all of the following properties?
(i) (D/Γ)* contains D/Γ as an open dense subset.
(ii) Set-theoretically, (D/Γ)* = (D/Γ) ⊔ ⨆_j (F_j/Γ_j), the union running over a chosen collection of rational boundary components, each F_j/Γ_j carrying its natural topology as a subspace of (D/Γ)*.
(iii) For every smooth algebraic family X → S of polarized algebraic manifolds whose associated period mapping Φ : S → D/Γ is horizontal and holomorphic, Φ extends continuously to a map Φ* : S* → (D/Γ)*, where S* is a suitable (e.g. smooth projective) completion of S.
status_search_result: The problem, posed by Griffiths in the late 1960s, has been the subject of extensive work. Kato–Usui constructed partial compactifications Γ\D_Σ of period domain quotients using fans of nilpotent cones, achieving the desired extension property in classical (Hermitian symmetric) cases and conditionally in general (subject to existence of a "complete fan"). Watanabe gave a counterexample to the existence of a complete fan in non-classical cases, so a fully general Kato–Usui-type compactification with continuous extension for arbitrary horizontal period maps is not known. More recent work (Bakker–Brunebarbe–Tsimerman, Green–Griffiths–Laza–Robles, et al.) has constructed Hodge-theoretic and toroidal-type completions of period maps in various settings (e.g., every two-parameter horizontal period map admits a log-manifold completion), giving partial answers. The general question remains open.

paper_title: Periods of Integrals on Algebraic Manifolds: Summary of Main Results and Discussion of Open Problems
context_brief: Deligne limit mixed Hodge structure conjecture
original_question: For a one-parameter degeneration whose Picard-Lefschetz transformation T on E=H^q(V_s,C) is unipotent, does the Picard-Lefschetz filtration W induced by log T, together with the limiting Hodge filtration, define graded Hodge structures of the appropriate weights on W^k/W^{k-1}, polarized on the primitive pieces by the bilinear forms built from Q and log T, with the filtrations varying holomorphically over the punctured disc and extending across the central point so that log T maps the limiting filtration as required?
status_search_result: Deligne's conjecture on the limit mixed Hodge structure for a one-parameter degeneration with unipotent monodromy was proved by W. Schmid in his 1973 work "Variation of Hodge structure: The singularities of the period mapping" (Invent. Math. 22), via the Nilpotent Orbit Theorem and SL_2-Orbit Theorem. The existence and holomorphic extension of the limiting Hodge filtration, the purity of the induced Hodge structures on the graded pieces of the monodromy weight filtration, and the polarization of the primitive parts by Q(·, N^k ·) are all established there. Generalizations to several variables (Cattani–Kaplan–Schmid) and to admissible variations of mixed Hodge structure (Steenbrink–Zucker, Kashiwara) further confirm and extend the result.

paper_title: Periods of Integrals on Algebraic Manifolds: Summary of Main Results and Discussion of Open Problems
context_brief: Existence of automorphic forms for period images
original_question: For a horizontal holomorphic period mapping Phi:S->D/T from an algebraic variety S to a quotient of a general period matrix domain, is the image S_Phi an algebraic variety such that Phi:S->S_Phi is an algebraic morphism and the canonical bundle on S_Phi is ample, thereby providing automorphic forms or algebraic projective embeddings analogous to the bounded symmetric domain case?
self_contained_problem:
Let $D$ be a period domain parametrizing polarized Hodge structures of a fixed weight and Hodge numbers on a polarized lattice, and let $\check D$ be its compact dual. Let $\Gamma \subset \mathrm{Aut}(D)$ be a discrete arithmetic monodromy group acting properly discontinuously on $D$, and form the analytic quotient $D/\Gamma$. Let $S$ be a smooth quasi-projective complex algebraic variety, and let \[ \Phi : S \longrightarrow D/\Gamma \] be a horizontal, locally liftable holomorphic period mapping (i.e., the local lifts to $D$ satisfy Griffiths transversality). Denote by $S_\Phi := \Phi(S) \subseteq D/\Gamma$ the image.

Prove or disprove the following:

(a) The image $S_\Phi$ carries the structure of a (quasi-projective) algebraic variety such that the induced map $\Phi : S \to S_\Phi$ is a morphism of algebraic varieties.

(b) On $S_\Phi$ there is a naturally defined canonical line bundle $K_{S_\Phi}$ (the descent of the Griffiths/Hodge-theoretic canonical bundle on $D$ to the quotient) that is ample, so that sufficiently high powers of its sections furnish a projective embedding of (a suitable compactification of) $S_\Phi$ — providing an analogue, for general period domains, of the automorphic forms and projective embeddings constructed for arithmetic quotients of bounded symmetric domains via the Baily–Borel theory.
status_search_result: Part (a), the algebraicity of period images and of the map $\Phi: S \to S_\Phi$, was established by Bakker, Brunebarbe and Tsimerman ("o-minimal GAGA and a conjecture of Griffiths", Invent. Math. 2023), settling Griffiths' algebraicity conjecture. Part (b) is partially resolved: Bakker, Brunebarbe and Tsimerman (2024/2025, "Baily–Borel compactifications of period images and the b-semiampleness conjecture", arXiv:2508.19215) construct a functorial projective compactification of $S_\Phi$ and prove that the Griffiths/Hodge bundle extends to a semiample line bundle, yielding an analogue of the Baily–Borel compactification. Full ampleness (rather than semiampleness) on the image and the complete construction of automorphic forms in the generality conjectured remain open in general.

paper_title: Periods of Integrals on Algebraic Manifolds: Summary of Main Results and Discussion of Open Problems
original_question: How is the automorphic cohomology H^{q0}(D/T,O(K^mu)) of a period matrix domain quotient related to horizontal holomorphic maps S->D/T that arise from variations of Hodge structure, and can such automorphic cohomology be used to construct the automorphic forms needed to algebrize period images?
self_contained_problem:
Let $D = G_{\mathbb{R}}/T$ be a period matrix domain, i.e. the classifying space for polarized Hodge structures on a fixed real vector space with given Hodge numbers, where $G_{\mathbb{R}}$ is the real isometry group of the polarization and $T$ is the compact isotropy subgroup fixing a reference Hodge filtration. Let $\Gamma \subset G_{\mathbb{R}}$ be an arithmetic subgroup acting properly discontinuously on $D$, and write $X = \Gamma\backslash D$. For a dominant character $\mu$ of $T$, let $K^\mu \to D$ denote the associated $G_{\mathbb{R}}$-homogeneous holomorphic line bundle (a tensor power of the canonical bundle determined by $\mu$), descending to a line bundle on $X$ also denoted $\mathcal{O}(K^\mu)$. Let $q_0$ be the dimension of a maximal compact subvariety of $D$ (so that, in the non-classical case where $D$ is not Hermitian symmetric, the relevant cohomology occurs in middle degree $q_0 > 0$).

A horizontal holomorphic map $\Phi : S \to X$, from a quasi-projective complex manifold $S$, is one whose differential takes values in the horizontal tangent subbundle of $D$ (equivalently, $\Phi$ arises as the period map of a polarized variation of Hodge structure over $S$).

(a) Describe the relationship between the automorphic cohomology group $H^{q_0}(X, \mathcal{O}(K^\mu))$ and horizontal holomorphic maps $\Phi: S \to X$ arising from variations of Hodge structure: specifically, exhibit a natural pullback / pairing construction that produces, from classes in $H^{q_0}(X,\mathcal{O}(K^\mu))$, holomorphic invariants of such period maps.

(b) Determine whether $H^{q_0}(X,\mathcal{O}(K^\mu))$ can be used to construct sufficiently many automorphic forms on $D$ (i.e., $\Gamma$-invariant holomorphic sections of suitable line bundles over images of period maps) to algebrize the images of period maps, in the sense of realizing closures of period images as quasi-projective algebraic varieties.
status_search_result: Substantial progress has been made on this circle of questions through work of Griffiths, Green, Kerr, Carayol and others (e.g., "Hodge Domains and Automorphic Cohomology", "Special Values of Automorphic Cohomology Classes", and Kerr's work on cup products in automorphic cohomology for Sp(4)). These works develop Penrose-type transforms relating $H^{q_0}(\Gamma\backslash D,\mathcal{O}(K^\mu))$ to holomorphic data on cycle spaces and to horizontal period maps, and treat low-rank cases (e.g., $SU(2,1)$, $Sp_4$). However, a complete general theory using automorphic cohomology to algebrize images of non-classical period maps remains open.

paper_title: Periods of Integrals on Algebraic Manifolds: Summary of Main Results and Discussion of Open Problems
context_brief: Universal covers of good algebraic neighborhoods
original_question: For a smooth algebraic variety W, a point w in W, and an affine good Zariski neighborhood U of w whose universal cover U_tilde is a Stein manifold topologically equivalent to a cell, what is the complex-analytic structure of U_tilde? Is U_tilde a domain in C^n, where n=dim_C W, and can every point w have such a good neighborhood whose universal cover is a bounded domain?
self_contained_problem:
Let $W$ be a smooth complex algebraic variety of complex dimension $n$. For a point $w \in W$, define a good Zariski neighborhood of $w$ to be an affine Zariski-open subset $U \subset W$ containing $w$ such that the universal covering $\widetilde{U}$ of $U$ is a Stein manifold that is topologically equivalent to (homeomorphic to) a cell, i.e. to $\mathbb{R}^{2n}$.

Address the following:

(a) Describe the complex-analytic structure of $\widetilde{U}$. In particular, determine whether $\widetilde{U}$ is necessarily biholomorphic to a domain in $\mathbb{C}^n$.

(b) Show whether every point $w \in W$ admits a good Zariski neighborhood $U$ in the above sense whose universal cover $\widetilde{U}$ is biholomorphic to a bounded domain in $\mathbb{C}^n$.
status_search_result: Griffiths proved that any smooth projective variety has a Zariski-open subset whose universal cover is a bounded domain of holomorphy in C^n, which gives a positive answer in the projective case for the existence of good neighborhoods with bounded universal covers. The full local question—whether every point of an arbitrary smooth algebraic variety admits such a good Zariski neighborhood, and the precise complex-analytic classification of these universal covers—does not appear to be fully resolved in the literature reviewed.

paper_title: Periods of Integrals on Algebraic Manifolds: Summary of Main Results and Discussion of Open Problems
original_question: For a horizontal holomorphic map Phi:H->D from the upper half-plane to a period matrix domain, satisfying Phi(z+1)=Phi(z)T for an infinite-order integral element T of G, let Omega_0 be the limiting boundary point of Phi(z) as Im(z)->infinity and let B(Omega_0) be its parabolic stabilizer in G. Is some positive power T^N contained in the unipotent radical R_u(B(Omega_0))?
self_contained_problem:
Let G be a real semisimple Lie group acting on a period (classifying) domain D for polarized Hodge structures of fixed type, realized as an open G-orbit in the compact dual flag variety, and let H denote the complex upper half-plane. A holomorphic map Φ : H → D is called horizontal if its differential at every point takes values in the horizontal tangent subbundle of D (the subbundle imposed by Griffiths transversality).

Suppose Φ : H → D is a horizontal holomorphic map satisfying the equivariance relation
   Φ(z + 1) = Φ(z) · T  for all z ∈ H,
where T ∈ G is an element of infinite order which preserves an integral lattice (so that T is an "integral" element of G).

Assume that as Im(z) → ∞, the image Φ(z) converges to a boundary point Ω₀ lying on the boundary of D in the compact dual. Let B(Ω₀) ⊂ G denote the parabolic subgroup of G stabilizing Ω₀, and let R_u(B(Ω₀)) denote its unipotent radical.

Prove or disprove: there exists a positive integer N such that T^N ∈ R_u(B(Ω₀)).
status_search_result: The statement is essentially the local monodromy theorem for variations of Hodge structure: monodromy around a puncture is quasi-unipotent, and a power lies in the unipotent radical of the parabolic stabilizer of the limiting Hodge filtration. Quasi-unipotency was proved by Borel and Landman, and the full statement (a power of T lies in the unipotent radical of the parabolic stabilizing the limit point) is a consequence of Schmid's Nilpotent Orbit Theorem and SL₂-orbit theorem (Schmid, Invent. Math. 1973). The conjecture is therefore considered solved.

paper_title: Perspectivas sobre a Estatística de Extremos. Resultados básicos e problemas em aberto
original_question: For bivariate extreme-value modeling, consider independent random pairs with reduced exponential margins and limiting survival function S(x,y)=exp{-(x+y)A(x/(x+y))} for x,y greater than 0, where A is a dependence function with A(0)=A(1)=1, endpoint derivative constraints 0 <= -A'(0) and A'(1) < 1, and convexity. Equivalently, under the transformation from reduced Gumbel maxima to reduced exponential minima, A corresponds to the dependence function k(w). Existing intrinsic or nonparametric estimators, such as the cited Pickands and Tiago de Oliveira estimators, yield dependence functions that are not twice differentiable, so the induced bivariate extreme-value survival or distribution models do not have a planar density. How can one estimate A(u), or equivalently k(w), by an intrinsic or nonparametric estimator that remains a valid dependence function and is twice differentiable, so that the resulting bivariate extreme-value model has a planar density and better analytic manageability?
status_search_result: Several smooth nonparametric estimators of the Pickands dependence function that respect the shape constraints have been proposed since the question was posed, including constrained Bernstein-polynomial estimators (Marcon, Padoan, Naveau and coauthors, 2014–2017), constrained B-spline smoothing estimators (Cormier, Genest, Nešlehová and others), and recent works on twice-differentiable approximation of A and its derivatives (Extremes, 2024). These give estimators that are smooth and satisfy the dependence-function constraints, so the problem is at least partially solved; questions of optimality, asymptotic distribution under minimal assumptions, and full higher-dimensional analogues remain active.

paper_title: Homogenization in mechanics. A survey of solved and open problems
original_question: For thermoelastic composite bodies, how should homogenization describe local stress and strain fields, local material properties, and nonlinear effects such as plasticity, fracture, or irreversible damage when thermal loading can create nonzero local stress even if the macroscopic boundary is free and the temperature is later returned to zero?
self_contained_problem:
Consider a thermoelastic composite body occupying a bounded domain $\Omega \subset \mathbb{R}^3$, composed of two or more constituents arranged on a microscale of characteristic length $\varepsilon$ that is much smaller than the macroscopic dimensions of $\Omega$. Each constituent is assumed to obey a local constitutive law that combines linear thermoelasticity with possible nonlinear effects, namely:
(i) elasto-plastic response with a yield criterion and hardening law,
(ii) progressive damage characterized by an internal scalar or tensorial damage variable, and
(iii) brittle fracture along internal interfaces.
The body is subjected to a prescribed temperature field $T(x,t)$ which varies in time and returns to its reference value $T \equiv 0$ at the final time; the macroscopic boundary $\partial \Omega$ is left traction-free, and no external body forces are applied. Owing to mismatch of thermal expansion coefficients between constituents, the microscopic stress and strain fields may remain nonzero (residual stresses, residual plastic strains, and accumulated damage) even after the temperature has been restored.

Develop a rigorous homogenization theory that, in the limit $\varepsilon \to 0$, produces:
(a) effective (macroscopic) constitutive relations linking macroscopic stress, strain, temperature, and internal variables for the composite, accounting for the three nonlinear mechanisms above;
(b) a reconstruction (localization) procedure that recovers, from the macroscopic fields, the local stress and strain fields together with the local material state (plastic strain, damage, crack distribution) inside a representative volume element; and
(c) a characterization of the residual local stress/strain state that persists after a thermal loading-unloading cycle returning the temperature to zero, including conditions on microstructure and constituent properties that guarantee existence, uniqueness, and stability of the homogenized evolution.
category_tag: homogenization of thermoelastic composites with nonlinear dissipation
status_search_result: The literature contains many partial results: computational and mean-field homogenization schemes for thermo-elastoplastic composites, reduced-order models for temperature-dependent thermoelasticity, finite-volume micromechanics for ratcheting with thermal residual stresses, and nonlinear viscoelastic/viscoplastic constitutive frameworks with damage. However, a unified rigorous homogenization theory that simultaneously handles thermoelasticity, plasticity, damage, and fracture with full local field reconstruction and residual-stress characterization after thermal cycling remains an active area with no complete solution; the topic continues to be treated as an open problem in surveys of homogenization in mechanics.
