paper_title: Homogenization in mechanics. A survey of solved and open problems
original_question: What homogenized models describe acoustic phenomena in porous media and flows between two neighboring plates, including Hele-Shaw-type settings where integro-differential homogenized equations appear as they do in viscoelasticity?
self_contained_problem:
Consider the following two homogenization problems in continuum mechanics.

(A) Acoustics in a porous medium. Let $\Omega\subset\mathbb{R}^3$ be a bounded domain occupied by a periodic two-phase composite at small scale $\varepsilon>0$: a connected elastic solid skeleton $\Omega^s_\varepsilon$ saturated by a viscous (or viscoelastic) fluid in the complementary pore network $\Omega^f_\varepsilon$, with $Y=Y^s\cup Y^f$ the unit periodicity cell. The displacement $u^s_\varepsilon$ in the solid satisfies the linear elasticity equations $\rho^s\partial_{tt}u^s_\varepsilon-\nabla\cdot(\mathbb{C}\,e(u^s_\varepsilon))=0$ in $\Omega^s_\varepsilon$, and the fluid velocity $v^f_\varepsilon$ and pressure $p^f_\varepsilon$ satisfy the (linearized) Navier–Stokes or Stokes system, with continuity of velocity and traction across the interface $\partial\Omega^s_\varepsilon\cap\partial\Omega^f_\varepsilon$. Determine, in a fully rigorous way (e.g., via two-scale convergence or periodic unfolding), the homogenized macroscopic system governing $(u^s,v^f,p^f)$ as $\varepsilon\to 0$, in all relevant scaling regimes of viscosity, frequency, and contrast of constituents, and identify the precise structure (e.g., Biot-type elasticity with memory, or integro-differential constitutive laws arising from cell problems) of the limit equations.

(B) Hele-Shaw type flow between two close plates. Consider a viscous fluid filling a thin gap $\Omega_\varepsilon=\{(x,z):x\in\omega,\,0<z<\varepsilon h(x)\}$ between two nearly parallel plates with possibly rough/periodic gap profile $h$, governed by the Stokes (or Navier–Stokes) equations with no-slip on the plates. Derive the homogenized two-dimensional limit model on $\omega$ as $\varepsilon\to 0$, including settings (variable gap, slip conditions, time-dependent boundaries, free boundary) where the resulting effective equation is an integro-differential equation in time of memory (viscoelastic-like) type, and characterize the memory kernel through appropriate cell problems.

Provide rigorous homogenized models for (A) and (B), state the precise hypotheses under which they hold, and clarify when an integro-differential (memory) structure necessarily appears in the limit.
category_tag: Homogenization of porous media and thin-film flows
status_search_result: Significant progress exists: rigorous homogenization of fluid-structure interaction in porous media saturated by viscous or viscoelastic fluids (yielding Biot-type/integro-differential limit models) has been obtained via two-scale convergence and periodic unfolding, and homogenization of the Hele-Shaw problem in periodic and spatiotemporal media has been carried out, producing effective free boundary problems. However, many regimes (general scalings of viscosity/contrast, random or non-periodic geometries, nonlinear/free-boundary thin film flows, full characterization of memory kernels) remain open.

paper_title: Homogenization in mechanics. A survey of solved and open problems
original_question: For porous media containing two fluid phases, what physical and thermodynamic model should be used for homogenization when surface tension and fluid-fluid interfaces are part of the pore-scale problem?
self_contained_problem:
Consider a porous medium with a periodic microstructure of period ε>0, whose pore space is occupied by two immiscible fluid phases separated by sharp (or diffuse) fluid–fluid interfaces on which surface tension acts. At the pore scale, the fluids are governed by an incompressible Navier–Stokes (or Stokes) system in each phase, supplemented by interfacial conditions enforcing jump of the normal stress proportional to mean curvature (Young–Laplace), continuity of velocity, and appropriate contact-angle/wetting conditions on the solid skeleton. Determine a physically and thermodynamically consistent pore-scale model (e.g., a sharp-interface Stokes/Navier–Stokes system with Young–Laplace conditions, or a diffuse-interface Navier–Stokes–Cahn–Hilliard or Navier–Stokes–Korteweg system) that:

(i) admits a well-posed two-scale homogenization limit as ε→0;
(ii) yields, in the limit, an effective Darcy-type macroscopic system for the saturation and phase velocities in which capillary pressure, relative permeabilities, and surface-tension contributions arise from explicit pore-scale cell problems; and
(iii) is consistent with the second law of thermodynamics (non-negative entropy production) at both the pore and effective scales.

Specify the pore-scale equations, interfacial/boundary conditions, and the resulting upscaled equations, and prove rigorous convergence of the homogenization procedure.
status_search_result: Several recent works derive macroscopic two-phase flow laws by homogenizing pore-scale models that include surface tension—using either Navier–Stokes–Cahn–Hilliard/phase-field formulations or sharp-interface volume-averaging—obtaining modified Darcy laws with explicit surface-tension contributions. However, no single rigorously justified, thermodynamically consistent pore-scale model with a complete convergence proof has been universally accepted; rigorous results are restricted to simplified geometries or diffuse-interface approximations, so the problem is partially solved.

paper_title: Homogenization in mechanics. A survey of solved and open problems
original_question: What boundary-layer corrections arise in homogenized solid-fluid mixture problems under different mechanical boundary conditions, including clamped bodies and bodies with free surfaces?
self_contained_problem:
Consider a periodic solid–fluid mixture occupying a bounded domain $\Omega \subset \mathbb{R}^n$, modeled by a microstructure of period $\varepsilon$ in which a connected elastic solid phase $\Omega_s^\varepsilon$ and a connected viscous (or inviscid) fluid phase $\Omega_f^\varepsilon$ are arranged $\varepsilon$-periodically. Let $u^\varepsilon$ denote the displacement (in the solid) and velocity/pressure pair (in the fluid) satisfying the coupled linear elasticity / Stokes (or Navier–Stokes) system with the usual continuity of traction and velocity across the solid–fluid interface, together with a prescribed mechanical boundary condition on $\partial\Omega$. Two cases of boundary conditions are to be considered:

(a) the clamped case, where $u^\varepsilon = 0$ on $\partial\Omega$;

(b) the free-surface case, where the normal traction vanishes on $\partial\Omega$.

As $\varepsilon \to 0$, the two-scale asymptotic expansion
$$u^\varepsilon(x) \;=\; u^0(x, x/\varepsilon) \;+\; \varepsilon\, u^1(x, x/\varepsilon) \;+\; \varepsilon^2 u^2(x, x/\varepsilon) \;+\; \cdots$$
formally yields an effective (homogenized) macroscopic system (e.g. Biot-type poroelasticity, viscoelasticity, or Darcy-type behavior, depending on scaling) for the leading term $u^0$. However, the prescribed boundary conditions on $\partial\Omega$ are in general incompatible with the periodic cell profiles, so that boundary-layer correctors—rapidly oscillating functions that decay exponentially away from $\partial\Omega$—must be added to match the data and to obtain optimal-order convergence rates.

Problem. Construct and characterize the boundary-layer correctors that arise in the homogenization of such periodic solid–fluid mixtures in each of the two cases (a) clamped boundary and (b) free-surface boundary. Specifically:

(i) Formulate the cell-like problems on the appropriate half-space (or semi-infinite strip) that define the boundary layers, including the correct interface conditions between solid and fluid sub-cells.

(ii) Prove existence, uniqueness, and exponential decay away from the boundary for these correctors, including a characterization of their (possibly non-zero) asymptotic limits at infinity ("boundary-layer tails").

(iii) Determine the resulting first-order corrections to the homogenized macroscopic system: in particular, identify any modified effective boundary conditions (e.g. Fourier/Robin-type corrections) and/or additional terms in the effective equations that the boundary layer induces in the two cases.

(iv) Establish the corresponding optimal convergence rate of $u^\varepsilon$ to $u^0$ plus the constructed boundary-layer corrector, in suitable energy norms.
status_search_result: Boundary layers in periodic homogenization are well studied in scalar elliptic and elasticity settings (Allaire–Amar 1999; Gérard-Varet–Masmoudi), with established results on existence, exponential decay, boundary-layer tails, and Fourier-type effective boundary corrections. For coupled solid–fluid (poroelastic/Biot, Stokes-in-perforated-domain) systems, formal homogenization and partial rigorous results exist, but a complete characterization of boundary-layer correctors and optimal corrector estimates for both clamped and free-surface conditions in solid–fluid mixtures remains incomplete and is actively investigated.

paper_title: Homogenization in mechanics. A survey of solved and open problems
original_question: For suspensions of solid particles in a fluid, how can the evolving microstructure be determined well enough to compute the macroscopic flow, including the effects of particle micro-location, applied-force location, and microstructure-dependent coefficients such as homogenized viscosity?
self_contained_problem:
Consider a suspension consisting of a large number of small rigid solid particles immersed in a viscous Newtonian fluid that occupies a bounded macroscopic domain $\Omega \subset \mathbb{R}^d$ ($d=2,3$). At time $t=0$, the particles are distributed in $\Omega$ with a prescribed (possibly random) microstructure characterized by a small parameter $\varepsilon>0$ measuring the typical inter-particle distance. The fluid satisfies the (Navier–)Stokes equations with no-slip boundary conditions on each particle, the particles move and rotate rigidly under hydrodynamic and applied body forces, and an external force field $f(x,t)$ acts on the suspension.

Develop a quantitative theory describing the time evolution of the microstructure, together with a closed effective (homogenized) system for the macroscopic velocity and pressure on $\Omega$, with the following properties:

1. The effective system must involve an effective viscosity tensor (and possibly additional effective constitutive coefficients) that depend on the instantaneous microstructure, including local particle volume fraction and statistical descriptors of particle arrangement.

2. The theory must track the sensitivity of the effective behavior to the precise micro-location of the particles and to the spatial location of applied forces, in the sense that it explains and quantifies how perturbations of these data affect both the evolved microstructure and the homogenized coefficients.

3. The effective microstructure-evolution law and the effective fluid equations must be consistent with the underlying particle–fluid system in the limit $\varepsilon \to 0$, in a rigorous sense (e.g. convergence of solutions and of macroscopic quantities such as stress and dissipation).

Provide such a closed effective model, prove its well-posedness, and establish its rigorous derivation from the microscopic particle–fluid system, or otherwise determine the obstructions to doing so.
status_search_result: The literature shows active mathematical work on homogenization for rigid suspensions and effective viscosity (e.g., Einstein-type formulas, rigorous derivations for dilute and moderately dense regimes), but determining the evolving microstructure together with location-dependent homogenized coefficients for the macroscopic flow is still considered an open challenge. Existing results address either fixed microstructures, dilute limits, or formal evolution laws, without a complete rigorous closure.

original_question: In the homogenized theory of suspensions of solid particles in a fluid, can the evolution of the microstructure lead to particle shocks or collisions, and how should such effects be incorporated together with possible compressibility effects?
status_search_result: No general homogenized theory incorporating particle shocks/collisions together with compressibility effects appears in the literature. Existing works on homogenization of suspensions (e.g. Höfer and collaborators, and the EMS monograph "Homogenized Models of Suspension Dynamics") treat dilute or moderately dense regimes without resolving particle-shock singularities, while jamming-front and shock phenomena are studied phenomenologically in rheology. paper_title: Homogenization in mechanics. A survey of solved and open problems
original_question: For composite media where microscopic gradients of the local fields can become infinite, how can singularity theory be extended beyond well-developed two-dimensional scalar elliptic cases to three-dimensional problems and elliptic systems, especially the elasticity system, with usable criteria for when singularities occur?
self_contained_problem:
Consider a composite medium occupying a bounded domain $\Omega\subset\mathbb{R}^3$ consisting of two or more constituent phases separated by interfaces that may have corners, edges, or cusps. Local physical fields (such as the displacement $u$ in linear elasticity, or a scalar potential in a conductivity problem) satisfy an elliptic system inside each phase together with transmission conditions across the interfaces. In the elasticity case, $u:\Omega\to\mathbb{R}^3$ solves
$$\nabla\cdot\big(C(x)\,e(u)\big)=0,\qquad e(u)=\tfrac12(\nabla u+\nabla u^{\mathsf T}),$$
where the elasticity tensor $C(x)$ is piecewise constant, taking distinct values $C^{(i)}$ on each phase. One says that the gradient field exhibits a microscopic singularity at an interface point $x_0$ if $|\nabla u(x)|\to\infty$ as $x\to x_0$.

For the two-dimensional scalar elliptic case (e.g. $\nabla\cdot(\sigma(x)\nabla u)=0$ with piecewise-constant $\sigma$), a rather complete theory exists describing exactly when and with what asymptotic exponents such gradient blow-up occurs at interface corners, depending on the contrast and the geometry.

Problem. Develop an analogous singularity theory for the following two settings, and in each case provide explicit, verifiable criteria (in terms of the geometry of the interface and the contrast in the material coefficients) that determine whether $|\nabla u|$ blows up at a given interface point and, if so, the leading asymptotic behaviour:

(a) scalar elliptic transmission problems $\nabla\cdot(\sigma(x)\nabla u)=0$ posed in three space dimensions, where interfaces may carry edges, conical points, and vertex-edge intersections;

(b) elliptic systems in two and three dimensions, with the linear elasticity system as the principal case, including transmission problems where the elasticity tensor jumps across interfaces having corners, edges, or conical points.

In particular, identify the threshold conditions on the contrast between the $C^{(i)}$ and on the opening angles or solid-angle data of the interface at which singular exponents cross prescribed thresholds (e.g. integrability of $\nabla u$), and give a usable classification of the possible singular behaviours.
status_search_result: A substantial literature treats stress singularities in three-dimensional elastic composites at corners, edges, wedges, and inclusion tips (asymptotic expansions, eigenvalue problems on solid angles, numerical eigenanalysis, multi-material wedge formulations). However, a complete and unified singularity theory comparable to the 2D scalar case—giving sharp, geometry-and-contrast-based criteria for blow-up and classification of singular exponents for general 3D scalar transmission problems and for elliptic systems including elasticity—does not appear to have been fully established; the problem is partially solved, with many specific cases (planar wedges, axisymmetric corners, particular laminate geometries) understood and active ongoing work in general settings.

paper_title: Homogenization in mechanics. A survey of solved and open problems
original_question: What is the asymptotic description of the stress field in elastic bodies whose boundary has a rounded corner, such as two straight boundary segments joined by a small-radius circular arc?
self_contained_problem:
Let $\Omega_\varepsilon \subset \mathbb{R}^2$ be a family of planar domains whose boundary consists of two straight segments meeting at an angle $2\alpha \in (0, 2\pi)$, joined smoothly by a circular arc of small radius $\varepsilon > 0$ (so that $\Omega_0$ has a sharp corner of opening angle $2\alpha$ at the vertex). Consider the equations of plane linear isotropic elasticity in $\Omega_\varepsilon$:
$$\mathrm{div}\,\sigma(u^\varepsilon) = 0 \text{ in } \Omega_\varepsilon, \qquad \sigma(u^\varepsilon) = \lambda (\mathrm{div}\, u^\varepsilon) I + 2\mu\, e(u^\varepsilon),$$
where $e(u)=\tfrac12(\nabla u + \nabla u^\top)$, with prescribed tractions on the straight portion of $\partial\Omega_\varepsilon$ and traction-free conditions on the rounded arc, and suitable far-field or remaining boundary data independent of $\varepsilon$.

Provide a complete asymptotic description, as $\varepsilon \to 0^+$, of the stress field $\sigma(u^\varepsilon)$ in $\Omega_\varepsilon$. In particular:

1. Construct matched asymptotic expansions consisting of an outer expansion valid away from the corner (whose leading term is the elastic solution in the limit domain $\Omega_0$ with a sharp corner, exhibiting the classical Williams-type singular expansion $\sigma \sim \sum_k c_k\, r^{\lambda_k - 1} \Phi_k(\theta)$ with exponents $\lambda_k$ determined by the corner opening angle $2\alpha$) and an inner expansion in the stretched variable $y = x/\varepsilon$, posed on the unbounded domain obtained by blow-up of the rounded corner.

2. Identify the matching conditions linking the generalized stress intensity factors $c_k$ of the sharp-corner outer solution to the inner profile, and derive the resulting maximum stress $\max |\sigma(u^\varepsilon)|$ as a function of $\varepsilon$ and of the $c_k$.

3. Give rigorous error estimates for the remainder of the two-scale expansion in appropriate Sobolev norms, uniformly in $\varepsilon$, for all opening angles $2\alpha \in (0, 2\pi)$, including the limiting crack case $2\alpha = 2\pi$.
category_tag: asymptotic stress analysis at rounded corners
status_search_result: The asymptotic analysis of stress near rounded corners has been extensively studied via matched asymptotic expansions, with leading-order results (linking the sharp-corner generalized stress intensity factors to the maximum stress at a small rounding radius, e.g. $\sigma_{\max}\sim K_I/\sqrt{\pi\rho}$ for cracks) well established in the engineering and applied mathematics literature. However, a fully general rigorous theory covering all opening angles, all loading modes, and providing sharp error estimates is not entirely complete; the topic is typically presented as a partially solved area with ongoing refinements.

paper_title: Orthogonality Types in Normed Linear Spaces
original_question: Let X be a Banach space of dimension at least 3, and write S_X for its unit sphere. Is X necessarily a Hilbert space if every closed homogeneous hyperplane H in X admits a unit vector x in S_X such that x is Pythagorean-minus-orthogonal to all unit vectors of H, meaning x ⊥_{P-} y for every y in H ∩ S_X, where x ⊥_{P-} y means ∥x - y∥^2 = ∥x∥^2 + ∥y∥^2?
self_contained_problem:
Let (X, ‖·‖) be a real Banach space with dim X ≥ 3, and let S_X = {x ∈ X : ‖x‖ = 1} denote its unit sphere. For x, y ∈ X, define the Pythagorean-minus orthogonality relation by

  x ⊥_{P−} y  ⇔  ‖x − y‖² = ‖x‖² + ‖y‖².

Assume that for every closed homogeneous hyperplane H ⊂ X (i.e., every closed linear subspace of codimension one), there exists a unit vector x ∈ S_X such that

  x ⊥_{P−} y  for every y ∈ H ∩ S_X.

Must X be (isometrically isomorphic to) a Hilbert space?
status_search_result: The question is a Hilbert-space characterization problem via Pythagorean-minus orthogonality on hyperplanes. Available literature discusses related characterizations (e.g., via I-, IP-, P-vectors, transitivity, almost transitivity) but no source found resolves this specific hyperplane-Pythagorean-minus condition. It appears to be an open problem.

original_question: In a normed plane, let S_B denote the Joly curve built from positively oriented unit pairs u, v with u ⊥_B v, and let S_{P-} and S_{P+} denote the analogous Pythagorean-minus and Pythagorean-plus curves. Known equivalences use the orientation condition u ∧ v > 0: S_B = S_{P-} iff every such positively oriented Birkhoff-orthogonal unit pair also satisfies u ⊥_{P-} v, and similarly for S_{P+}. Can this orientation hypothesis u ∧ v > 0 be removed from those equivalences?

paper_title: Orthogonality Types in Normed Linear Spaces
context_brief: Unit-sphere implications in dimension at least 3
original_question: Let X be a normed space, and restrict attention to unit vectors in S_X. Choose two distinct orthogonality relations K and L from the three relations isosceles orthogonality ⊥_I, Pythagorean-plus orthogonality ⊥_{P+}, and Pythagorean-minus orthogonality ⊥_{P-}. If every unit pair x, y with x ⊥_K y also satisfies x ⊥_L y, does this implication characterize inner product spaces when dim X ≥ 3?
self_contained_problem:
Let $(X,\|\cdot\|)$ be a real normed linear space with unit sphere $S_X=\{x\in X:\|x\|=1\}$. For $x,y\in X$ define three orthogonality relations:
- Isosceles orthogonality: $x\perp_I y$ iff $\|x+y\|=\|x-y\|$.
- Pythagorean-plus orthogonality: $x\perp_{P+}y$ iff $\|x+y\|^2=\|x\|^2+\|y\|^2$.
- Pythagorean-minus orthogonality: $x\perp_{P-}y$ iff $\|x-y\|^2=\|x\|^2+\|y\|^2$.

Choose two distinct relations $K, L \in \{\perp_I,\perp_{P+},\perp_{P-}\}$ and consider the unit-sphere implication
$$\forall x,y\in S_X:\quad x\perp_K y \;\Longrightarrow\; x\perp_L y.$$

Question: Assuming $\dim X\ge 3$, does this implication (for any such choice of distinct $K$ and $L$) force $X$ to be an inner product space?
status_search_result: A web search did not return a definitive resolution of the unit-sphere implication characterization for distinct pairs among isosceles, Pythagorean-plus, and Pythagorean-minus orthogonalities in dimension at least 3. Recent literature on orthogonality types in normed spaces (e.g., works on geometric constants comparing isosceles and Pythagorean orthogonality) discusses related characterizations but does not appear to settle this specific implication problem for dim X ≥ 3.

paper_title: Orthogonality Types in Normed Linear Spaces
original_question: For an arbitrary Carlsson orthogonality on a normed space X, defined by finite real coefficients a_i, b_i, c_i through an equation of the form sum_i a_i ∥b_i x + c_i y∥^2 = 0 under Carlsson's coefficient conditions, is uniqueness of that orthogonality equivalent to strict convexity of X?
self_contained_problem:
Let $(X, \|\cdot\|)$ be a real normed linear space. A Carlsson orthogonality on $X$ is a binary relation $\perp_C$ defined by fixing a finite collection of real coefficients $\{a_i, b_i, c_i\}_{i=1}^n$ satisfying Carlsson's conditions
$$\sum_{i=1}^n a_i b_i^2 = \sum_{i=1}^n a_i c_i^2 = 0, \qquad \sum_{i=1}^n a_i b_i c_i = 1,$$
and declaring
$$x \perp_C y \iff \sum_{i=1}^n a_i\,\|b_i x + c_i y\|^2 = 0.$$
This family of relations includes Pythagorean orthogonality ($\|x\|^2 + \|y\|^2 = \|x+y\|^2$), isosceles orthogonality ($\|x+y\| = \|x-y\|$), and many others, and each Carlsson orthogonality coincides with the usual orthogonality whenever $X$ is an inner product space.

The orthogonality $\perp_C$ is called unique (on the right) if, for every $x, y \in X$, there exists exactly one real number $\alpha$ such that $x \perp_C (\alpha x + y)$.

The space $X$ is strictly convex if its closed unit ball is a strictly convex set; equivalently, $\|u+v\| < \|u\|+\|v\|$ whenever $u, v$ are nonzero and not positively proportional.

Question: For every Carlsson orthogonality $\perp_C$ on $X$ (i.e., for every admissible choice of coefficients $a_i, b_i, c_i$), is the uniqueness of $\perp_C$ on $X$ equivalent to the strict convexity of $X$?
status_search_result: The question is known to hold in classical special cases: Pythagorean orthogonality is unique in every normed space, and isosceles orthogonality is unique if and only if the space is strictly convex (Dragomir–Kikianty, 2010). Recent papers (e.g., on 2-HH norm orthogonalities) continue to investigate uniqueness for specific Carlsson-type orthogonalities, but no general equivalence theorem covering all Carlsson orthogonalities has been located. The full equivalence for arbitrary Carlsson orthogonality appears to remain an open question.

paper_title: Orthogonality Types in Normed Linear Spaces
original_question: Let X be a normed space of dimension at least 3. Height orthogonality x ⊥_H y is the relation in which either x = 0 or y = 0, or ∥x - y∥ equals ∥(∥y∥/∥x∥)x + (∥x∥/∥y∥)y∥. What can be concluded if height orthogonality is homogeneous in X, meaning x ⊥_H y implies x ⊥_H λy for every scalar λ? Does this force an inner product norm, the π/2-property on all two-dimensional subspaces, or another classification?
self_contained_problem:
Let $X$ be a real normed linear space with $\dim X \ge 3$. For $x, y \in X$, say that $x$ is height-orthogonal to $y$, written $x \perp_H y$, if either $x = 0$, or $y = 0$, or
$$\|x - y\| = \left\| \tfrac{\|y\|}{\|x\|}\,x + \tfrac{\|x\|}{\|y\|}\,y \right\|.$$
(Geometrically, in the plane spanned by $x$ and $y$, this says that the segment from $x$ to $y$ has the same length as the segment joining the points on the rays through $x$ and $y$ at suitably scaled positions, expressing that the "height" from one vertex equals a prescribed length.)

The relation $\perp_H$ is called homogeneous on $X$ if for all $x, y \in X$ and every scalar $\lambda$,
$$x \perp_H y \;\Longrightarrow\; x \perp_H \lambda y.$$

Assuming that height orthogonality is homogeneous on $X$, determine which structural conclusions follow. In particular: must the norm on $X$ be induced by an inner product? Equivalently, must every two-dimensional subspace of $X$ have the $\pi/2$-property (i.e., for every nonzero $x$ in a 2-dimensional subspace $Y$ there exists $y \in Y$ with $x \perp_H y$ and the angle between $x$ and $y$ is a right angle in the inner-product sense)? Provide a complete classification of normed spaces of dimension $\ge 3$ on which height orthogonality is homogeneous.
status_search_result: A targeted web search did not turn up a published resolution of the homogeneity question for height orthogonality in normed spaces of dimension at least 3. While analogous homogeneity-implies-inner-product characterizations are known for several other orthogonality types (e.g., isosceles, Pythagorean, Birkhoff–James in various settings), no source verifying or refuting the corresponding statement for height orthogonality was located, so the status is treated as unknown.

paper_title: A Proximal Quasi-Newton Trust-Region Method for Nonsmooth Regularized Optimization
original_question: For the proximal quasi-Newton trust-region method and its related quadratic regularization variant for nonsmooth regularized optimization, can one develop implementations and convergence or complexity analyses that remain valid when function values, gradients, and proximal-operator evaluations are computed inexactly rather than exactly?
self_contained_problem:
Consider the nonsmooth regularized optimization problem
    minimize_{x ∈ R^n}  f(x) + h(x),
where f : R^n → R is continuously differentiable (possibly nonconvex) with Lipschitz-continuous gradient, and h : R^n → R ∪ {+∞} is proper, lower semi-continuous, and possibly nonsmooth and nonconvex. A proximal quasi-Newton trust-region method generates iterates x_k by approximately solving, at each step, a trust-region subproblem of the form
    minimize_{s : ||s|| ≤ Δ_k}  ⟨∇f(x_k), s⟩ + (1/2)⟨s, B_k s⟩ + h(x_k + s),
where B_k is a quasi-Newton approximation to the Hessian of f and Δ_k > 0 is the trust-region radius; an associated quadratic regularization variant replaces the trust-region constraint by a quadratic penalty term (σ_k/2)||s||^2. The standard analyses of such methods assume that the objective values f(x_k), gradients ∇f(x_k), and the proximal-operator evaluations used to solve the subproblems are computed exactly.

Problem: Design implementations of the proximal quasi-Newton trust-region method and of its quadratic regularization variant in which the function values f(x_k), gradients ∇f(x_k), and proximal operator evaluations are computed only inexactly, subject to controllable accuracy conditions; and establish global convergence to first-order stationary points together with worst-case iteration/evaluation complexity bounds (such as O(ε^{-2}) for reaching an ε-approximate first-order stationary point) for these inexact variants, matching those obtainable under exact evaluations.
status_search_result: A companion line of work develops a proximal trust-region method for nonsmooth optimization that permits and systematically controls inexact function and gradient evaluations, with global convergence to first-order stationary points and O(ε^{-2}) worst-case complexity, showing that inexactness (including in proximal operators) does not degrade asymptotic complexity. This addresses the inexact-evaluation extension, though the quasi-Newton trust-region variant with all three sources of inexactness combined has been treated primarily in the convex-h, smooth-f setting; a fully general treatment matching the original nonconvex regularized framework appears partially resolved.

paper_title: A Proximal Quasi-Newton Trust-Region Method for Nonsmooth Regularized Optimization
original_question: Can the convergence and complexity results for the nonsmooth regularized trust-region framework be extended to more general nonlinear stepsize-control methods?
self_contained_problem:
Consider the composite nonsmooth optimization problem
    minimize over x in R^n   φ(x) := f(x) + h(x),
where f : R^n → R is continuously differentiable with Lipschitz-continuous gradient (or, more generally, satisfies a standard smoothness/model-accuracy condition) and h : R^n → R ∪ {+∞} is proper and lower semicontinuous, possibly nonconvex and nonsmooth.

A proximal quasi-Newton trust-region algorithm for this problem proceeds as follows. At iterate x_k with trust-region radius Δ_k > 0, one builds a (possibly nonconvex) model
    m_k(s) = f(x_k) + ⟨∇f(x_k), s⟩ + ½ ⟨s, B_k s⟩ + h(x_k + s),
where B_k is a symmetric quasi-Newton approximation, computes an approximate minimizer s_k of m_k(s) subject to ‖s‖ ≤ Δ_k that achieves a sufficient decrease in the model relative to a prox-gradient (Cauchy) step, and accepts or rejects s_k by comparing the actual reduction φ(x_k) − φ(x_k + s_k) to the predicted reduction m_k(0) − m_k(s_k), adapting Δ_k accordingly. Under standard hypotheses this scheme is known to converge to a first-order stationary point and to achieve a worst-case iteration complexity of O(ε^{-2}) for driving a stationarity measure below ε.

A nonlinear stepsize control (NSC) framework in the sense of Toint is a unified scheme that controls the size of the trial step through a scalar parameter via a nonlinear control rule, encompassing trust-region methods, adaptive regularization methods (such as quadratic and cubic regularization), and related step-control strategies as special cases.

Problem. Extend the global convergence theory and the worst-case iteration complexity bound described above for the proximal quasi-Newton trust-region method for nonsmooth regularized problems to a general nonlinear stepsize control framework: formulate a proximal quasi-Newton NSC algorithm for the composite problem min_x f(x) + h(x) with f smooth and h proper lower semicontinuous, prove its global convergence to first-order stationary points, and establish a worst-case complexity bound that recovers, as special cases, the trust-region and adaptive regularization variants.
status_search_result: Search results show active follow-up work on proximal trust-region and proximal modified quasi-Newton methods for nonsmooth regularized optimization (e.g., a 2024 proximal modified quasi-Newton method and proximal trust-region methods with inexact evaluations), but no source clearly establishes a full proximal quasi-Newton convergence and complexity theory in Toint's general nonlinear stepsize control framework. Status is therefore not conclusively determined.

paper_title: Open Problems in Constructive Function Theory
original_question: If the Boltzmann-Shannon entropy E_n of an orthonormal polynomial sequence has the same asymptotic extremal behavior as in the Chebyshev case, does that asymptotic property characterize the Chebyshev family among all orthogonal polynomial systems, for example throughout the whole Szegő class?
self_contained_problem:
Let $\mu$ be a finite positive Borel measure on $[-1,1]$ with infinite support, and let $(p_n)_{n\ge 0}$ be the associated sequence of orthonormal polynomials, i.e., $p_n$ has degree $n$, positive leading coefficient, and $\int_{-1}^{1} p_n(x) p_m(x)\, d\mu(x) = \delta_{nm}$. The Boltzmann–Shannon entropy of $p_n$ with respect to $\mu$ is defined by
$$E_n(\mu) \;=\; -\int_{-1}^{1} p_n(x)^2 \, \log\bigl(p_n(x)^2\bigr) \, d\mu(x).$$
For the (first-kind) Chebyshev measure $d\mu_T(x) = \pi^{-1}(1-x^2)^{-1/2}\,dx$ the orthonormal polynomials satisfy a known extremal asymptotic behavior of $E_n$ as $n\to\infty$ (namely $E_n(\mu_T)$ attains, in the limit, the extremal value characteristic of the Chebyshev case).

Recall that $\mu$ belongs to the Szegő class on $[-1,1]$ if $\mu$ is absolutely continuous with weight $w(x) = d\mu/dx$ satisfying
$$\int_{-1}^{1} \frac{\log w(x)}{\sqrt{1-x^2}}\, dx \;>\; -\infty.$$

Question: Suppose $\mu$ lies in the Szegő class and the sequence $E_n(\mu)$ exhibits the same asymptotic extremal behavior as $E_n(\mu_T)$ for the Chebyshev measure. Does this asymptotic property force $\mu$ to be the Chebyshev measure (up to the standard normalization), i.e., does the asymptotic extremality of the Boltzmann–Shannon entropy characterize the Chebyshev family within the entire Szegő class?
status_search_result: A web search returned related work on discrete and asymptotic entropies of orthogonal polynomials and on the Szegő class, but no source was found that explicitly settles whether asymptotic extremality of the Boltzmann–Shannon entropy characterizes the Chebyshev measure throughout the Szegő class. The question appears to remain open, but the search was inconclusive.

paper_title: Ten Open Problems in Grammatical Inference
original_question: In polynomial identification in the limit for grammatical inference, how should the size of a characteristic sample be measured? More specifically, if a learning algorithm is judged by the existence of polynomial characteristic sets, is it sound to measure the characteristic set by the number of strings rather than by the total number of bits or symbols needed to encode those strings, and are there grammar classes that become non-learnable under that alternative size measure?
self_contained_problem:
Setup. Consider grammatical inference in the framework of identification in the limit from positive (or labelled) data. Let A be an alphabet, X = A* the set of finite strings over A, and let R(A) be a class of grammars over A; for G ∈ R(A) write L(G) ⊆ X for its language and |G| for an associated size. A presentation of a target grammar G is an infinite enumeration (f_n)_{n≥1} of strings (or labelled strings) consistent with L(G), with f_n denoting the prefix of length n.

A learning algorithm a, on input a finite sample f_n, outputs a grammar a(f_n) ∈ R(A); write L_A(a(f_n)) for its language. Two notions of "size" of a finite sample W ⊂ X are considered:
  (i) the cardinality measure ‖W‖_# := |W| (the number of strings in W);
  (ii) the bit-length measure ‖W‖_bit := Σ_{w ∈ W} (|w| + 1) (the total number of symbols/bits needed to encode W).

Definition (Polynomial characteristic sets under a chosen size measure ‖·‖). An algorithm a admits polynomial characteristic sets (with respect to ‖·‖) if there exists a polynomial p such that for every G ∈ R(A) there exists a finite sample W_G ⊂ X satisfying
    ‖W_G‖ ≤ p(|G|),
and such that for every presentation (f_n) of G, whenever W_G ⊂ f_n one has L_A(a(f_n)) = L(G).

Problem. Investigate the choice of size measure for characteristic sets.
(a) Determine whether using the cardinality measure ‖·‖_# (the number of strings) instead of the bit-length measure ‖·‖_bit is a sound and fair criterion for judging an algorithm's polynomial identifiability.
(b) Exhibit, or prove the nonexistence of, classes R(A) of grammars that are polynomially identifiable in the limit under the bit-length measure but are not polynomially identifiable in the limit under the cardinality measure (i.e., classes that become non-learnable when characteristic-set size is measured by the number of strings rather than by total encoded length).
status_search_result: The question is listed among open problems in grammatical inference concerning the proper size measure (number of strings vs. bits) for polynomial characteristic sets. Subsequent works (e.g., on polynomial characteristic sets for DFAs and sufficient conditions for polynomial-time-and-data identification) refine polynomial identifiability notions, and negative results are known for context-free, simple deterministic, linear, and NFA classes under the bit-length measure, but no source clearly resolves the specific comparison between the two size measures or exhibits a class learnable under bits but not under cardinality. The current status appears unresolved in the literature.

paper_title: Ten Open Problems in Grammatical Inference
original_question: Can the class of k-edge deterministic finite-state automata over ranked alphabets be learned from an informant, where the informant supplies labeled positive and negative strings, under the polynomial characteristic-set learning criterion? Here the learner should eventually infer an equivalent automaton once a polynomial-size characteristic subset of the informant data has appeared.
self_contained_problem:
Let Σ be a ranked alphabet and consider deterministic finite-state automata over Σ. For a DFA A, define its number of edges as the total number of transitions in its transition function; call A a k-edge DFA if this number is at most k. Write L(A) for the language recognized by A and |A| for its size (e.g. number of states plus number of edges).

An informant for a language L ⊆ Σ* is a function f: ℕ → Σ* × {0,1} whose image is L × {1} ∪ (Σ* \ L) × {0}; write f_n for the first n elements of f and let X_n = {x : (x,b) ∈ f_n for some b}.

A learning algorithm a, taking as input a finite labeled sample and outputting a DFA, is said to admit polynomial characteristic sets for a class 𝒞 of DFAs if there exists a polynomial p such that for every A ∈ 𝒞 there exists a finite labeled set W ⊆ Σ* × {0,1}, consistent with L(A), with |W| ≤ p(|A|), such that for every informant f for L(A) and every n with W ⊆ f_n, the output a(f_n) satisfies L(a(f_n)) = L(A).

Question: Does there exist a learning algorithm that admits polynomial characteristic sets, in the above sense, for the class of k-edge deterministic finite-state automata (for arbitrary fixed k, or with k part of the input as a parameter of the target)?

No solution in the polynomial-characteristic-sample-from-informant framework has been published, so the problem appears to remain open.

paper_title: Ten Open Problems in Grammatical Inference
original_question: Can one find an algorithm that learns regular languages over an alphabet Σ using context-free background knowledge in the polynomial learning-with-help sense? The setting is that the target language is L = L1 ∩ L2, where L1 is regular and L2 is context-free, and the learner receives labeled examples only from L2: positive examples from L and negative examples from L2 \ L1. The algorithm should infer a regular hypothesis whose intersection with L2 equals L once a polynomial-size witness subset of the presentation has appeared.
self_contained_problem:
Let $\Sigma$ be a finite alphabet. Let $\mathrm{REG}(\Sigma)$ denote the class of regular languages over $\Sigma$ and $\mathrm{CF}(\Sigma)$ the class of context-free languages over $\Sigma$. Fix a context-free language $L_2 \subseteq \Sigma^*$ (the "background knowledge") and a regular language $L_1 \subseteq \Sigma^*$, and put $L = L_1 \cap L_2$.

A presentation of $L$ with respect to $L_2$ is any function $f:\mathbb{N}\to\Sigma^*\times\{0,1\}$ whose image equals $(L\times\{1\})\cup((L_2\setminus L_1)\times\{0\})$; that is, the learner is fed labeled examples drawn entirely from $L_2$, with positive label on strings in $L$ and negative label on strings in $L_2\setminus L_1$.

A learning algorithm $A$ takes as input a finite prefix $f(0),f(1),\ldots,f(n-1)$ of such a presentation and outputs a regular hypothesis $H_n \in \mathrm{REG}(\Sigma)$ (e.g., as a DFA). Say that $A$ learns $\mathrm{REG}(\Sigma)$ from $\mathrm{CF}(\Sigma)$-knowledge in the polynomial learning-with-help sense if there is a two-variable polynomial $p$ such that for every regular $L_1$, every context-free $L_2$, and every presentation $f$ of $L=L_1\cap L_2$ with respect to $L_2$:
1. $A$ runs in time polynomial in the total size of its input;
2. there exists a finite subset $S$ of the presentation (a "characteristic sample") with $|S| \le p(\|L_1\|,\|L_2\|)$, where $\|\cdot\|$ denotes the size of a smallest DFA / CFG representation, such that whenever $S$ is contained in the prefix seen by $A$, the output hypothesis $H$ satisfies $H \cap L_2 = L$ and remains stable on all longer prefixes.

Problem: Does such an algorithm $A$ exist?
status_search_result: A targeted search did not surface a published resolution of this specific learning-with-help problem (learning a regular language from labeled examples drawn from a context-free superset, in the polynomial characteristic-sample sense). Related work continues on learning subclasses of context-free grammars from positive data and membership queries, but no source confirms either a positive algorithm or an impossibility result for this exact formulation. Status appears unresolved based on available evidence.

paper_title: Ten Open Problems in Grammatical Inference
context_brief: DFA learning with noisy membership queries
original_question: Are deterministic finite automata learnable in Angluin-style active learning when membership queries are only ε-correct but equivalence queries are still available? In this model, the teacher answers a membership query correctly with probability 1 − ε, but must answer consistently if the exact same query has already been submitted; equivalence queries ask whether a proposed DFA recognizes the target language and, when it does not, return a counterexample string.
self_contained_problem:
Fix a target regular language $L\subseteq \Sigma^*$ over a finite alphabet $\Sigma$, recognized by an unknown deterministic finite automaton (DFA). Consider an Angluin-style active learning model in which a learner interacts with a teacher through two kinds of queries:

1. $\varepsilon$-correct membership queries: given a string $w\in\Sigma^*$, the teacher returns a bit $b\in\{0,1\}$ such that $\Pr[b = \mathbf{1}_{w\in L}] \ge 1-\varepsilon$, where $0<\varepsilon<1/2$ is a fixed parameter. The teacher's answers must be consistent across repeated queries: if the same string $w$ is queried more than once, the same bit must be returned each time.

2. Equivalence queries: given a hypothesis DFA $A$, the teacher answers "yes" if $L(A)=L$, and otherwise returns a counterexample string $x\in L(A)\,\triangle\, L$.

Question: Does there exist a learning algorithm that, for every regular language $L$ and every $\varepsilon\in(0,1/2)$, using only $\varepsilon$-correct membership queries and equivalence queries of the above forms, identifies a DFA recognizing $L$ exactly, with high probability and in time polynomial in the size of the minimal DFA for $L$, in $|\Sigma|$, in the length of the longest counterexample returned, and in $1/(1-2\varepsilon)$?
status_search_result: Recent work (e.g., 2023–2024 analyses of the robustness of Angluin's L* under noise) studies related noise models but does not appear to settle the exact question of polynomial-time exact learnability of DFA from ε-correct membership queries together with equivalence queries with consistency on repeated queries. No definitive positive or negative result for this specific formulation was found.

paper_title: Ten Open Problems in Grammatical Inference
original_question: What is the learnability theory for ordinary, non-deterministic partially observable Markov decision processes with probabilistic transitions and reward functions? The problem is to study learnability for the general POMDP model, not only the deterministic special case, and to clarify suitable success criteria such as identification in the limit with probability 1, regret-based convergence, or relations to strategy learning.
self_contained_problem:
A partially observable Markov decision process (POMDP) is a tuple $M=(S,A,O,T,Z,R,\iota)$ where $S$ is a finite set of states, $A$ a finite set of actions, $O$ a finite set of observations, $T:S\times A\times S\to[0,1]$ a transition probability function with $\sum_{s'}T(s,a,s')=1$, $Z:S\times A\times O\to[0,1]$ an observation probability function with $\sum_{o}Z(s,a,o)=1$, $R:S\times A\to\mathbb{R}$ a reward function, and $\iota$ an initial distribution over $S$. A learner interacts with $M$ by choosing actions and receiving observations and rewards, without access to the underlying states. 

Develop a learnability theory for the class of all (general, probabilistic, non-deterministic) POMDPs in this sense. Concretely:

1. Identify a precise success criterion for learning a POMDP from interaction data — for instance (a) identification in the limit with probability 1 of the underlying model (up to equivalence preserving the distribution over observation/reward sequences under every policy), (b) convergence of the learner's average regret with respect to the optimal policy of $M$ to zero, or (c) convergence in the sense of strategy learning, where the learner's policy converges to an optimal policy of $M$.

2. For the chosen criterion, determine whether the class of all POMDPs (or natural subclasses such as those satisfying explicit identifiability/observability conditions) is learnable, and if so provide a learning algorithm together with sample- or interaction-complexity bounds.

3. Clarify the relationships between the criteria in (1) and between learnability of POMDPs and learnability of related models such as hidden Markov models, probabilistic finite automata, and Markov decision processes.

The deterministic special case (deterministic transitions and observations) should be recovered as a particular instance of the theory.
status_search_result: The general learnability theory for POMDPs in the grammatical-inference identification-in-the-limit sense remains open. While substantial progress exists in the reinforcement-learning literature on regret/sample-complexity bounds for POMDPs under structural assumptions (e.g., hindsight observability, weakly revealing or decodable POMDPs), no unified learnability theory analogous to that for DFAs/PFAs exists for the general probabilistic POMDP model, and the problem continues to be cited as open.

paper_title: Ten Open Problems in Grammatical Inference
original_question: Under the negotiation-game winning criterion, can one find a winning deterministic learning algorithm when the two players' regular languages L1 and L2 are represented by deterministic finite automata with the same number of states, n1 = n2? A player wins if it identifies L1 ∩ L2 in the limit and either the opponent fails to identify that intersection or, when both identify it, the player makes fewer negative-query errors.
self_contained_problem:
Setup. Fix a finite alphabet Σ. For a regular language L ⊆ Σ*, let dfa-size(L) denote the number of states of the minimal deterministic finite automaton (DFA) accepting L.

A learner is a (deterministic) algorithm that, given an infinite presentation of examples for a target language T ⊆ Σ*, outputs a (possibly revised) hypothesis after each example and is said to identify T in the limit if its sequence of hypotheses stabilises on a representation of T.

Negotiation game. A game ⟨L1, L2⟩ involves two players A and B, where each player i ∈ {A, B} privately knows a regular language Li and is told the minimal DFA-sizes n1 = dfa-size(L1) and n2 = dfa-size(L2). The players exchange queries: each player may pose strings to the opponent who must classify them truthfully as members or non-members of the opponent's language. A "negative-query error" by a player is each instance in which that player issues a query whose answer (received from the opponent) is "no" (i.e., the queried string does not belong to the opponent's language). Let errors(P) denote the set (or count) of such negative-query errors made by player P throughout the play.

Winning criterion. Player A wins the play of ⟨L1, L2⟩ against player B if:
(i) A identifies L1 ∩ L2 in the limit, and
(ii) either B fails to identify L1 ∩ L2 in the limit, or B also identifies L1 ∩ L2 in the limit and |errors(A)| < |errors(B)|.

Problem. Restricting attention to instances in which n1 = n2 (i.e., the two players' minimal DFAs have the same number of states), exhibit a deterministic learning algorithm that, when used by a player, wins against every deterministic strategy of the opponent under the above winning criterion; or prove that no such algorithm exists.
status_search_result: A targeted web search did not surface any publication that resolves the equal-size (n1 = n2) negotiation-game problem for learning the intersection of two regular languages under the stated winning criterion. The problem appears as one of a list of open problems in grammatical inference, and no follow-up work explicitly claiming a solution was located, so the current status is unknown.

paper_title: Similarity: generalizations, applications and open problems
context_brief: stability of local self-similar singularity profiles
original_question: For nonlinear parabolic partial differential equation models and their higher-order generalizations in which a finite-time singularity occurs, so that the solution or some of its partial derivatives diverge, can one develop general rigorous methods to determine the stability of local self-similar solutions describing behavior near the singularity, especially in high-order models where the possible local self-similar solutions may form a countably infinite set?
self_contained_problem:
Consider nonlinear parabolic evolution equations of the form
  u_t = F(u, Du, D^2 u, ..., D^{2m} u),  x ∈ R^n, t ∈ [0,T),
including higher-order analogues (m ≥ 1) such as semilinear and quasilinear 2m-th order parabolic PDEs, for which a finite-time singularity occurs at t = T < ∞: the solution u or some of its spatial/temporal derivatives diverge as t → T^-. Near such a singularity, the asymptotic behaviour is often described by local self-similar solutions of the form
  u(x,t) = (T-t)^α f((x-x_0)/(T-t)^β),
where (α, β) are determined by the scaling invariance of the equation and f satisfies an associated nonlinear elliptic profile equation. For higher-order (m ≥ 2) models the set of admissible self-similar profiles f may be countably infinite.

Problem: Develop a general rigorous framework, applicable across classes of such nonlinear parabolic PDEs (including the higher-order case where countably many self-similar profiles coexist), that determines, for each local self-similar singularity profile, whether it is stable (i.e., attracts an open set of initial data in a suitable topology under the renormalised flow obtained by self-similar rescaling) or unstable. In particular, give criteria—formulated via the spectrum of the linearised operator around f in appropriate weighted function spaces, or via other intrinsic invariants—that decide stability without resorting to case-by-case analysis for each equation and each profile.
status_search_result: Current literature on higher-order semilinear parabolic blow-up (notably the monograph by Galaktionov–Mitidieri–Pohozaev and related SIAM J. Appl. Math. papers) constructs countable families of self-similar singularity profiles and analyses their stability by case-specific linearisation and Hamilton–Jacobi matching arguments. No general rigorous method that uniformly determines stability of self-similar profiles across higher-order nonlinear parabolic models appears in the literature; stability is still studied case-by-case, so the problem remains open.

paper_title: Basic kinetic wealth-exchange models: common features and open problems
context_brief: Analytical formula for generalized C-model Gamma parameter
original_question: In the generalized homogeneous C-model where the stochastic fraction of wealth lost by an agent in a trade is constrained between lower and upper bounds, equivalently by saving parameters λ and λ′ satisfying λ < λ′ < 1, and simulations find equilibrium wealth distributions that are well fitted by the same Gamma distribution, can one derive a simple analytical formula for the Gamma-distribution shape parameter n as a function of λ and λ′?
self_contained_problem:
Consider a kinetic wealth-exchange model defined as follows. There are N agents, each holding a non-negative wealth x_i, with total wealth conserved. At each elementary step, two agents i and j are chosen at random and trade according to
  x_i' = x_i - Δx,    x_j' = x_j + Δx,
where the transferred amount Δx is a stochastic fraction of one agent's wealth. In the generalized homogeneous "C-model" version, the fraction ω of wealth that agent i risks losing in a trade is drawn uniformly at random from an interval [ω', ω] with 0 < ω' < ω < 1, equivalently parametrized by two saving propensities
  λ = 1 − ω,    λ' = 1 − ω',   with   λ < λ' < 1,
so that λ is the minimum saved fraction and λ' is the maximum saved fraction. The transferred amount is Δx = ε · ω̃ · x_i, where ω̃ is drawn uniformly from [ω', ω] and ε ∈ {0,1} (or an analogous fair-trade rule) ensures conservation of wealth and an unbiased exchange.

Numerical simulations indicate that, for every admissible pair (λ, λ'), the stationary one-agent wealth distribution P(x) is well fitted by a Gamma distribution
  f_n(x) = (n^n / Γ(n)) · x^{n−1} · e^{−n x}   (with mean wealth normalized to 1),
for some shape parameter n = n(λ, λ').

Problem: Derive a closed-form analytical expression for the Gamma-distribution shape parameter n as a function of the two saving parameters λ and λ' (reducing, when λ = λ', to the known formula n(λ) = 1 + 3λ/(1−λ) for the standard homogeneous saving model).
status_search_result: A web search did not surface any work providing an explicit closed-form expression for the Gamma shape parameter n(λ, λ') of the generalized homogeneous C-model with bounded saving propensities. Related literature on generalized money/wealth-exchange models (e.g., hypergraph generalizations and saving-propensity models) studies Gamma limit distributions but does not appear to give the requested analytical formula in terms of (λ, λ'). The status is therefore not clearly established from public sources.

paper_title: Global results on rational systems in the plane, part 1
original_question: For the 595 special cases of the nonnegative-parameter planar rational system x_{n+1} = (a1 + b1 x_n + g1 y_n)/(A1 + B1 x_n + C1 y_n), y_{n+1} = (a2 + b2 x_n + g2 y_n)/(A2 + B2 x_n + C2 y_n), with nonnegative initial conditions and positive denominators, that are reducible to Riccati difference equations with variable coefficients, determine their boundedness behavior, their periodic behavior, and their global stability behavior.
self_contained_problem:
Consider the planar system of rational difference equations
\[ x_{n+1} = \frac{\alpha_1 + \beta_1 x_n + \gamma_1 y_n}{A_1 + B_1 x_n + C_1 y_n}, \qquad y_{n+1} = \frac{\alpha_2 + \beta_2 x_n + \gamma_2 y_n}{A_2 + B_2 x_n + C_2 y_n}, \qquad n = 0,1,2,\ldots, \]
where all twelve parameters \(\alpha_i, \beta_i, \gamma_i, A_i, B_i, C_i\) (\(i=1,2\)) are nonnegative real numbers, and the initial condition \((x_0, y_0)\) is nonnegative and chosen so that the denominators remain positive for all \(n \ge 0\).

By normalizing one nonzero parameter in each equation to 1 and by considering all possible patterns of zero/nonzero parameters, one obtains finitely many special cases of this family. Among these, identify the subfamily consisting of those special cases for which, after a suitable change of variables, the system reduces to a (possibly variable-coefficient) Riccati difference equation
\[ z_{n+1} = \frac{a_n + b_n z_n}{c_n + d_n z_n}. \]
There are exactly 595 such Riccati-reducible special cases. For each of these 595 special cases, determine:

(a) the boundedness character of all solutions with admissible nonnegative initial conditions (i.e., for which parameter values are all solutions bounded, and for which do unbounded solutions exist);

(b) the periodic nature of solutions (existence, periods, and structure of periodic solutions);

(c) the global asymptotic stability behavior of equilibria (local stability, global attractivity, and global asymptotic stability on the admissible set of initial conditions).
status_search_result: The problem is posed as an open problem concerning the comprehensive classification of dynamical behavior (boundedness, periodicity, global stability) of 595 Riccati-reducible planar rational systems. Web searches did not turn up any subsequent paper resolving the entire family; only partial results on individual special cases of planar rational systems by Camouzis, Ladas and collaborators appear in the literature. Status appears to remain open.

paper_title: Global results on rational systems in the plane, part 1
context_brief: local stability implies global attractivity in System (1.1)
original_question: For every special case of the nonnegative-parameter planar rational system x_{n+1} = (a1 + b1 x_n + g1 y_n)/(A1 + B1 x_n + C1 y_n), y_{n+1} = (a2 + b2 x_n + g2 y_n)/(A2 + B2 x_n + C2 y_n), with nonnegative initial conditions and positive denominators, characterize exactly which cases have the property that local asymptotic stability of an equilibrium implies global attractivity of that equilibrium.
self_contained_problem:
Consider the planar rational system of difference equations
  x_{n+1} = (α₁ + β₁ x_n + γ₁ y_n) / (A₁ + B₁ x_n + C₁ y_n),
  y_{n+1} = (α₂ + β₂ x_n + γ₂ y_n) / (A₂ + B₂ x_n + C₂ y_n),
where all parameters α_i, β_i, γ_i, A_i, B_i, C_i (i = 1, 2) are nonnegative real numbers, the initial conditions (x₀, y₀) are nonnegative, and the parameters are chosen so that both denominators remain strictly positive for every n ≥ 0.

By a "special case" of this system we mean a choice of which of the twelve parameters are zero and which are positive (with the convention that any positive parameter may be normalized, e.g. to 1, by rescaling), yielding finitely many distinct parameter patterns that give rise to genuinely different rational systems.

An equilibrium of the system is a point (x̄, ȳ) ∈ [0, ∞)² satisfying x̄ = (α₁ + β₁ x̄ + γ₁ ȳ)/(A₁ + B₁ x̄ + C₁ ȳ) and ȳ = (α₂ + β₂ x̄ + γ₂ ȳ)/(A₂ + B₂ x̄ + C₂ ȳ). The equilibrium is called locally asymptotically stable if it is Lyapunov stable and attracting on some neighborhood, and a global attractor (relative to the set of admissible initial conditions) if every admissible solution converges to it.

Problem: Determine exactly the set of special cases of the above system for which the following implication holds at every equilibrium:
  local asymptotic stability of the equilibrium  ⟹  global attractivity of the equilibrium
on the full set of nonnegative initial conditions yielding positive denominators for all n.
status_search_result: The question of characterizing all special cases of planar rational systems with nonnegative parameters for which local asymptotic stability implies global attractivity is a standing open problem in the theory of rational difference equations, going back to work of Camouzis and Ladas. Subsequent literature treats specific subcases (e.g., competitive or anticompetitive subclasses) but a complete characterization across all special cases has not been established.

paper_title: Global results on rational systems in the plane, part 1
original_question: Extend and generalize to planar rational systems the boundedness and convergence trichotomy known for x_{n+1} = (a + b x_n + g x_{n-1})/(A + B x_n + C x_{n-1}), with nonnegative parameters and positive denominators: if C > 0 then every solution is bounded; if C = 0 and B > 0, every solution is bounded exactly when g <= b + A; when g = b + A every solution converges to a not necessarily prime period-two solution; and when g < b + A every solution has a finite limit. The problem is to find the corresponding planar-system generalization, including the right hypotheses and alternatives.
self_contained_problem:
Consider the scalar third-order-type rational difference equation
  x_{n+1} = (a + b x_n + g x_{n-1}) / (A + B x_n + C x_{n-1}),  n = 0, 1, 2, …,
with nonnegative parameters a, b, g, A, B, C and nonnegative initial conditions x_{-1}, x_0 chosen so that the denominator is positive for all n. For this equation the following trichotomy is known:
 (i) If C > 0, then every solution is bounded.
 (ii) If C = 0 and B > 0, then every solution is bounded if and only if g ≤ b + A; moreover,
   – when g = b + A every solution converges to a (not necessarily prime) period-two solution, and
   – when g < b + A every solution has a finite limit.

Now consider a planar system of rational difference equations of the form
  x_{n+1} = (α_1 + β_1 x_n + γ_1 y_n) / (A_1 + B_1 x_n + C_1 y_n),
  y_{n+1} = (α_2 + β_2 x_n + γ_2 y_n) / (A_2 + B_2 x_n + C_2 y_n),
with nonnegative coefficients and nonnegative initial data such that both denominators remain positive for every n ≥ 0 (and more generally any planar rational system that arises as a natural two-dimensional analogue of the scalar equation above).

Formulate and prove the planar-system analogue of the trichotomy: identify the precise hypotheses on the coefficients of the planar system under which every solution is bounded, the precise sharp conditions separating the bounded from the unbounded regime, and the corresponding global dynamical alternatives (convergence to an equilibrium versus convergence to a period-two solution) that replace cases (i) and (ii).
status_search_result: Research on rational systems in the plane (Camouzis, Ladas, Garić-Demirović, Palladino, and others) has settled the global behavior for several specific families of planar rational systems, but no source found gives a complete planar-system trichotomy fully generalizing the scalar (a+bx+gx_{n-1})/(A+Bx_n+Cx_{n-1}) result with sharp boundedness/convergence alternatives. The general problem appears to remain open, with only partial results for special subclasses.

paper_title: Global results on rational systems in the plane, part 1
original_question: For the positive-solution system x_{n+1} = b1 x_n/(A1 + y_n), y_{n+1} = (b2 x_n + g2 y_n)/(x_n + y_n), with x_0,y_0 > 0, positive parameters, b2 != g2, and A1 + g2 < b1 < A1 + b2, prove or disprove that the unique positive equilibrium is globally asymptotically stable for all positive initial conditions.
self_contained_problem:
Consider the two-dimensional system of rational difference equations
  x_{n+1} = β₁ x_n / (A₁ + y_n),
  y_{n+1} = (β₂ x_n + γ₂ y_n) / (x_n + y_n),
for n = 0, 1, 2, …, where the parameters β₁, β₂, γ₂, A₁ are positive real numbers with β₂ ≠ γ₂, the initial conditions satisfy x₀ > 0 and y₀ > 0, and the parameters obey
  A₁ + γ₂ < β₁ < A₁ + β₂.

Under these hypotheses the system has a unique positive equilibrium (x̄, ȳ) ∈ (0, ∞)². Prove or disprove that this positive equilibrium is globally asymptotically stable; that is, it is locally asymptotically stable, and for every choice of positive initial conditions (x₀, y₀) the solution (x_n, y_n) converges to (x̄, ȳ) as n → ∞.
status_search_result: A 2014 paper by L.-X. Hu and X.-M. Jia in Abstract and Applied Analysis ("Global Asymptotic Stability of a Rational System") studies precisely this system and proves that, in the case γ₂ < β₂ (which is equivalent to the hypothesis A₁ + γ₂ < β₁ < A₁ + β₂ since this forces γ₂ < β₁ − A₁ < β₂), the unique positive equilibrium is globally asymptotically stable. This resolves the conjecture in the affirmative.

context_brief: limits on the equilibrium branch of System (35,35)
original_question: For the system x_{n+1} = (b1 x_n + g1 y_n)/(1 + y_n), y_{n+1} = (b2 x_n + g2 y_n)/(1 + x_n), with positive parameters and nonnegative initial conditions not both zero, assume the degenerate equilibrium-curve parameter conditions b1 = b2 + 1 and g2 = g1 + 1. Under these conditions every point on the branch y = (b2 - 1)x/(x - g1), x > g1, is an equilibrium and no other equilibria exist besides those already described. Determine the limits of both components x_n and y_n for every solution in terms of the initial conditions x_0 and y_0.
self_contained_problem:
Let $\beta_1,\beta_2,\gamma_1,\gamma_2$ be positive real parameters satisfying the degeneracy conditions
\[ \beta_1 = \beta_2 + 1, \qquad \gamma_2 = \gamma_1 + 1. \]
Consider the planar rational system
\[ x_{n+1} = \frac{\beta_1 x_n + \gamma_1 y_n}{1 + y_n}, \qquad y_{n+1} = \frac{\beta_2 x_n + \gamma_2 y_n}{1 + x_n}, \qquad n = 0,1,2,\dots, \]
with initial conditions $(x_0,y_0) \in [0,\infty)^2 \setminus \{(0,0)\}$, chosen so that the iteration is well defined (denominators remain nonzero) for all $n \ge 0$.

Under these parameter conditions, every point on the curve
\[ \mathcal{E} = \Bigl\{ (x,y) : y = \frac{(\beta_2 - 1)x}{x - \gamma_1},\ x > \gamma_1 \Bigr\} \]
is an equilibrium of the system, and the system has no other equilibria (other than possibly the origin if admissible).

Problem. For every admissible initial condition $(x_0,y_0)$, determine explicitly the limits
\[ \lim_{n \to \infty} x_n \quad \text{and} \quad \lim_{n \to \infty} y_n \]
as functions of $(x_0,y_0)$ (and of the parameters), showing in particular that these limits exist and identifying the equilibrium point on $\mathcal{E}$ to which each solution converges.
status_search_result: The question is posed as an explicit open problem about asymptotic behavior on a continuum of equilibria for a degenerate two-parameter rational planar system. No published resolution was located in a brief search; the status appears unresolved but cannot be confirmed with certainty.

paper_title: Global results on rational systems in the plane, part 1
context_brief: equivalence of local stability and global attractivity
original_question: For every special case of the nonnegative-parameter planar rational system x_{n+1} = (a1 + b1 x_n + g1 y_n)/(A1 + B1 x_n + C1 y_n), y_{n+1} = (a2 + b2 x_n + g2 y_n)/(A2 + B2 x_n + C2 y_n), with nonnegative initial conditions and positive denominators, determine exactly which equilibria satisfy the equivalence between local asymptotic stability and global attractivity. In other words, characterize all special cases and equilibria for which local asymptotic stability implies global attractivity and global attractivity implies local asymptotic stability.
self_contained_problem:
Consider the planar rational system of difference equations
  x_{n+1} = (α₁ + β₁ xₙ + γ₁ yₙ)/(A₁ + B₁ xₙ + C₁ yₙ),
  y_{n+1} = (α₂ + β₂ xₙ + γ₂ yₙ)/(A₂ + B₂ xₙ + C₂ yₙ),  n = 0,1,2,…,
where all parameters α_i, β_i, γ_i, A_i, B_i, C_i (i=1,2) are nonnegative real numbers, the initial conditions (x₀,y₀) are nonnegative, and the denominators are positive for every n ≥ 0. By a "special case" of the system we mean a choice of which of the twelve parameters are zero and which are positive (so the special cases enumerate the possible reduced rational systems of this form). An equilibrium is a fixed point (x̄,ȳ) of the map defined by the right-hand side. Local asymptotic stability of an equilibrium is defined by the standard requirement that it be Lyapunov stable and that nearby orbits converge to it. Global attractivity of an equilibrium (with respect to the nonnegative invariant region on which the system is well defined) means that every admissible orbit converges to it.

Characterize, for every special case of the above system and every equilibrium of that special case, exactly when local asymptotic stability is equivalent to global attractivity. Specifically:
 (a) Determine all special cases and all equilibria for which local asymptotic stability implies global attractivity.
 (b) Determine all special cases and all equilibria for which global attractivity implies local asymptotic stability.
status_search_result: The full characterization across all special cases of the nonnegative planar rational system is an open problem repeatedly highlighted by Camouzis and Ladas. Although partial results exist (e.g., conditions under which local asymptotic stability implies global attractivity for certain monotone or competitive sub-cases, and many individual special cases analyzed in the literature), no complete classification of the equivalence between local asymptotic stability and global attractivity over all special cases and equilibria appears to have been established. Subsequent works tackle particular special cases but do not resolve the global question.

paper_title: Global results on rational systems in the plane, part 1
original_question: For each of the 31 planar rational systems that may be cooperative in some parameter range and nowhere competitive, determine the exact parameter region where the system is cooperative, determine whether the cooperative-system monotonicity hypotheses corresponding to Theorem 3.16 or Theorem 3.17 are satisfied, and determine the global character of all solutions. The 31 systems are (35,40), (35,46), (36,40), (36,46), (45,46); (k,l) with k <= l, k in {34,46}, and l in {34,35,36,40,45,46,47,48,49}; and (k,l) with k <= l, k in {25,40}, and l in {34,35,36,45,46,47,48,49}. The relevant Theorem 3.16 hypothesis is a one-step mixed-direction monotonicity implication for cooperative systems, yielding eventual monotonicity of both component sequences; the relevant Theorem 3.17 hypothesis is the analogous two-step condition yielding eventual monotonicity of the four even and odd component subsequences.
self_contained_problem:
Consider planar systems of rational difference equations of the form
    x_{n+1} = (α₁ + β₁ x_n + γ₁ y_n)/(A₁ + B₁ x_n + C₁ y_n),
    y_{n+1} = (α₂ + β₂ x_n + γ₂ y_n)/(A₂ + B₂ x_n + C₂ y_n),
with nonnegative parameters and nonnegative initial conditions (x₀, y₀) such that the denominators never vanish and the iterates remain nonnegative. Each numerator/denominator pair (k, l) refers to one of the 49 distinct rational expressions obtained by selecting a subset of {1, x, y} for the numerator and a subset of {1, x, y} for the denominator (with arbitrary nonnegative coefficients), enumerated in a fixed standard order in which:
 • k labels the right-hand side of the x-equation,
 • l labels the right-hand side of the y-equation,
 • the convention k ≤ l is taken whenever both equations are interchangeable.

A planar map T(x,y) = (f(x,y), g(x,y)) on a domain in the nonnegative quadrant is called cooperative if ∂f/∂y ≥ 0 and ∂g/∂x ≥ 0 throughout the domain, and competitive if these partial derivatives are ≤ 0. The 31 systems listed below are precisely those (out of the 49×49 possibilities subject to k ≤ l where appropriate) which are cooperative for some open region of parameter space and never competitive on any region of parameter space:

  (35,40), (35,46), (36,40), (36,46), (45,46);
  (k,l) with k ≤ l, k ∈ {34, 46}, l ∈ {34, 35, 36, 40, 45, 46, 47, 48, 49};
  (k,l) with k ≤ l, k ∈ {25, 40}, l ∈ {34, 35, 36, 45, 46, 47, 48, 49}.

For a cooperative planar map T, consider the following two hypotheses governing eventual monotonicity of orbits (x_n, y_n) = T^n(x₀, y₀):

(H1) One-step mixed-direction monotonicity: for every (x,y) in the domain,
    [f(x,y) ≥ x and g(x,y) ≤ y]  or  [f(x,y) ≤ x and g(x,y) ≥ y]
  implies the analogous inequalities at (f(x,y), g(x,y)). Under (H1), both sequences {x_n} and {y_n} are eventually monotonic.

(H2) Two-step analogue of (H1) applied to T², ensuring that the four subsequences {x_{2n}}, {x_{2n+1}}, {y_{2n}}, {y_{2n+1}} are eventually monotonic.

For each of the 31 systems above, solve the following three tasks:
 (a) Determine explicitly the region in parameter space on which the system is cooperative.
 (b) Determine on which subregion of that cooperative region hypothesis (H1) holds, and on which subregion hypothesis (H2) holds.
 (c) Determine the global character of all nonnegative solutions: the set of equilibria and periodic solutions, their local stability, basins of attraction, existence of invariant manifolds, and global asymptotic behavior of every orbit, as a function of the parameters.
status_search_result: No publication was located that resolves, even for all 31 listed systems collectively, the three-part question of cooperative parameter region, verification of the monotonicity hypotheses (H1)/(H2), and full global dynamics. Related follow-up work by Camouzis, Ladas, and collaborators on partial cases of planar rational systems exists, but a comprehensive resolution of this open problem does not appear in the literature, so it is treated as still open.

paper_title: Open Problems in Real-time Scheduling
original_question: For a preemptive uniprocessor real-time system modeled as a finite sporadic task system tau = {tau_1, ..., tau_n}, where each task tau_i has worst-case execution time C_i, relative deadline D_i, and period T_i, generates jobs at least T_i time units apart, and each generated job requires at most C_i execution and has deadline D_i time units after its arrival, determine the computational complexity of deciding fixed-priority schedulability in the implicit-deadline case D_i = T_i for every task. The input includes a specified total priority order on the tasks, and fixed-priority scheduling always executes an incomplete job of the highest-priority task. Is tau schedulable under that specified priority order, meaning that all deadlines are met for every legal sequence of job arrivals?
self_contained_problem:
Consider a preemptive uniprocessor real-time system modeled as a finite sporadic task system τ = {τ₁, …, τₙ}. Each task τᵢ is described by three positive parameters: a worst-case execution time Cᵢ, a relative deadline Dᵢ, and a period Tᵢ. Task τᵢ may generate an infinite sequence of jobs, subject to the constraint that consecutive jobs of τᵢ are released at least Tᵢ time units apart; each released job requires at most Cᵢ units of processor execution and must complete within Dᵢ time units after its release. A scheduling algorithm A is said to schedule τ successfully if, for every legal sequence of job releases that τ may generate, A meets every job's deadline. Fixed-priority (FP) scheduling is the algorithm that, given a total priority order on the tasks, at each instant executes some incomplete job belonging to the highest-priority task that currently has an unfinished released job.

Restrict attention to implicit-deadline task systems, i.e., systems in which Dᵢ = Tᵢ for every i. The decision problem FP-SCHED(implicit) is: given as input an implicit-deadline sporadic task system τ together with a specified total priority ordering on its tasks (with all parameters encoded in binary), decide whether τ is FP-schedulable under the given priority ordering.

Determine the exact computational complexity of FP-SCHED(implicit). In particular, is it decidable in polynomial time, is it NP-hard or coNP-hard, or does it lie at some intermediate level of complexity?
status_search_result: The exact computational complexity of fixed-priority schedulability for implicit-deadline sporadic task systems remains a recognized open problem, but partial results exist. Notably, it has been shown that rate-monotonic schedulability of implicit-deadline tasks becomes NP-hard once the utilization is allowed to exceed the Liu–Layland bound ln 2, while the Liu–Layland test gives a polynomial-time sufficient condition below that bound. A complete classification (e.g., in P vs. NP-complete vs. coNP-complete) for arbitrary priority orderings does not appear to have been established.
